They also explain any significant changes in the carrying amount of that net investment, so a reader can follow how the asset's recorded value is moving over time. <<SECTION:Operating Lease Notes|id=sec-3>> An operating lease is different: the lessor keeps the asset on its books, so <<FOCUS:operating-detail>> what matters most is the income it throws off. <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Operating lease -> lease income|id=text-2>>Here the lessor discloses its lease income, separating out variable lease payments that do not depend on an index or a rate, and gives the usual asset disclosures under the relevant property and equipment standards. So step back and look at <<FOCUS:finance-branch+operating-branch>> the two branches side by side: the same word, disclosure, but the content is steered entirely by whether the risks and rewards left the lessor or stayed with them. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Disclosures = notes that let readers assess lease effects on position, performance & cash flows|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> And remember the purpose tying it all together: these notes exist so that anyone reading the accounts can judge how leases shape the lessor's financial position, performance, and cash flows. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:25>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:25:sublease_chain>> What happens when you rent an apartment from a landlord, and then rent that very same apartment out to someone else? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Sublease|id=sec-1>> Suddenly you are stuck in the middle. You pay <<FOCUS:head-rent-arrow>> rent upward to your landlord, and <<FOCUS:sub-rent-arrow>> someone pays rent up to you. At the top is <<FOCUS:head-lessor>> the head lessor, the original owner you leased from. At the bottom is your new tenant, <<FOCUS:subtenant>> the subtenant. <<UNFOCUS>> You sit in between. When a company rents an asset and then leases it out again, accounting gives that middle role a name: <<FOCUS:intermediate-lessor>> the intermediate lessor. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Rent then sublet then you become the intermediate lessor, sitting between head lessor and subtenant|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So remember this position carefully. The intermediate lessor is the one <<FOCUS:intermediate-lessor+head-lessor+subtenant>> wedged between the head lessor above and the subtenant below. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the question that trips everyone up. When you classify your sublease as finance or operating, what asset do you actually compare it against? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:physical-asset>> Not the building. <<UNFOCUS>> You never owned the building. What you own is <<FOCUS:rou-asset>> the right to use it, granted by the head lease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Classify the sublease against the right-of-use asset, not the physical asset|id=key-2>> So the intermediate lessor classifies the sublease <<FOCUS:classify-link+rou-asset>> by looking at the right-of-use asset, treating that as if it were the underlying asset. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> There is one neat shortcut for the discount rate. If you cannot readily work out the interest rate implicit in the sublease, you simply borrow <<FOCUS:head-rent-arrow>> the rate you already use for the head lease. <<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term head lease then sublease is operating|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> And one special case to lock in: if the head lease was a short-term lease you treated under the short-term exemption, then your sublease is automatically classified as an operating lease. So always picture the chain: head lessor, you in the middle, subtenant, and remember you judge the sublease <<FOCUS:rou-asset>> against your right-of-use asset, never the bricks and mortar.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:26>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:26:saleback_flow>> A company sells its own office building for cash, and the very next morning everyone walks back into the exact same building to work. So did anything really get sold? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Sale and leaseback|id=sec-1>> This move has a name. The company that sells and then rents back <<FOCUS:seller-lessee-box>> is the seller-lessee, and the company that buys and then rents it out <<FOCUS:buyer-lessor-box>> is the buyer-lessor. <<WRITE_TEXT:Asset out, cash in|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Watch what flows. The <<TRACE:asset-arrow>> building goes from the seller to the buyer, and the <<TRACE:cash-arrow>> cash comes straight back the other way. <<PAUSE:short>> But the seller still needs that building, so the buyer immediately <<TRACE:lease-arrow>> leases the right to use it back to them. <<FOCUS:building-icon>> The desks never move. <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the question that decides everything. Was this actually a sale, or was the company just borrowing money with the building as security? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Sale only if it qualifies under Ind AS 115|id=key-1>> To answer that, we do not guess. We test the transfer against Ind AS one hundred fifteen, the standard on revenue from contracts with customers. Only if it passes that test do we call it a sale. <<PAUSE:short>> If it does not pass, then no real sale happened. The cash is simply a loan, and the building stays on the seller's books as if nothing changed. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:26:carrying_split_bar>> <<SECTION:When it is a genuine sale|id=sec-2>> Now suppose it does pass the test. Here is the subtle part. The seller sold the building, but kept the right to use it. So the seller did not give up the whole asset. Think of the building's <<FOCUS:full-carrying-bar>> old book value as one bar. Part of it represents <<FOCUS:retained-portion>> the rights the seller kept, and part represents the <<FOCUS:transferred-portion>> rights handed over to the buyer. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So how much gain does the seller get to book? Only on <<FOCUS:transferred-portion>> the slice they actually gave away, never on <<FOCUS:retained-portion>> the slice they kept using. The right-of-use asset equals the old book value scaled down to just the fraction of rights the seller kept. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{ROU asset} = \text{Previous carrying amount} \times \dfrac{\text{Rights retained}}{\text{Total asset}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:ROU = retained proportion of old carrying amount; gain only on rights transferred|id=key-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> The right-of-use asset is carried at that retained proportion of the old book value, and the seller recognises gain or loss only on the rights transferred to the buyer. <<PAUSE:short>> The gain you may recognise is the total gain scaled down to only the <<FOCUS:transferred-portion+gain-label>> portion of rights you actually transferred to the buyer. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Gain recognised} = \text{Total gain} \times \dfrac{\text{Rights transferred}}{\text{Total asset}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Meanwhile the buyer-lessor has the easy job. They record buying the asset under the normal standards, and account for the lease they granted using the lessor rules you already know. And one last guard. If the price was not fair value or the rent was not at market rates, you adjust, treating any shortfall as a prepayment and any excess as extra financing from the buyer. So the lesson holds together. First ask if it is really a sale under Ind AS one hundred fifteen, and if it is, recognise gain only on what you gave away, because you never truly let go of what you kept using. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:27>>
A lease that was perfectly fine yesterday suddenly has to be re-judged today, not because the contract changed one word, but because the rulebook underneath it did. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:27:sublease_chain>> <<SECTION:The Sandwich Position|id=sec-1>> To see why, picture a company that <<FOCUS:landlord-box>> rents a building from a landlord. That same company then turns around and <<FOCUS:subtenant-box>> rents the building out to someone else, so it sits squarely in the middle of two deals. <<WRITE_TEXT:Intermediate lessor = renter + renter-out|id=text-1>> We call this company <<FOCUS:intermediate-box>> the intermediate lessor, because it rents on one side and rents out on the other. The deal with the landlord <<FOCUS:head-lease-arrow>> is the head lease, and the deal with the new tenant <<FOCUS:sublease-arrow>> is the sublease. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, under the old standard, Ind AS seventeen, leases were sorted into two buckets, operating leases or finance leases, and a great many subleases landed in the operating bucket. So here is the honest question, when you move to the new standard, Ind AS one hundred sixteen, can you just leave those old operating subleases exactly where they were? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Re-test on Transition|id=sec-2>> No. On the date you first apply the new standard, you must take a fresh look at every ongoing sublease that used to be an operating lease and decide all over again. <<PAUSE:short>> And here is the clever part, you do not judge the sublease alone, you judge it against what is left of <<FOCUS:head-lease-arrow+sublease-arrow>> both the head lease and the sublease together. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Why both? Because if you have already handed almost the whole remaining life of the building to your subtenant, you have effectively passed on the risks and rewards of owning that right, and that smells like a finance lease, not an operating one. <<WRITE_KEY:Operating under Ind AS 17 to finance under Ind AS 116 = treat as a NEW finance lease at transition date|id=key-1>> So when a sublease that was operating now qualifies as a finance lease, you do not patch the old one, you <<FOCUS:reassess-marker>> treat it as a brand-new finance lease starting on the transition date. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Same building, new judgement|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Notice what never changed, the building, the landlord, the tenant, the words of the contract, all the same, only the rulebook shifted, and that re-test is the whole story of subleases on transition. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:28>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:28:transition_choice_flow>> Imagine your company has <<FOCUS:contract-pile>> signed three thousand contracts over the past twenty years. <<UNFOCUS>> The accounting rulebook just changed. Do you really have to re-read every single one? <<SECTION:Definition of lease on transition|id=sec-1>> Here is the situation. The old rulebook was called Ind AS seventeen. The new one is Ind AS one hundred sixteen, and it changed, just slightly, what actually counts as a lease. So when a company switches over, it hits <<FOCUS:decision-fork>> a fork in the road. <<WRITE_TEXT:Two choices on transition|id=text-1>> <<TRACE:path-reassess>> Down the first path, the company says yes: apply the brand new definition to <<FOCUS:reassess-box>> every single existing contract, with completely fresh eyes. <<UNFOCUS>> That means digging through hundreds or thousands of old agreements and re-checking each one. It is thorough, but it is an enormous amount of work. So here is the honest question: is there a way to avoid re-reading every old contract you ever signed? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Yes. <<TRACE:path-grandfather>> Down the second path, the standard gives <<FOCUS:grandfather-box>> a friendly shortcut. <<WRITE_KEY:You may choose NOT to reassess contracts not identified as leases under Ind AS 17|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> You can choose not to reassess contracts that were never identified as containing a lease under the old standard. <<PAUSE:short>> In plain terms: if a contract was not a lease under the old rules, you simply trust that and leave it alone. You do not put it through the new definition. <<PAUSE:short>> This shortcut has a name. Accountants call it <<FOCUS:grandfather-box>> a practical expedient — a permitted simplification that saves you from a mountain of work. <<WRITE_TEXT:Practical expedient = permitted shortcut|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> But notice the trade-off. If you take the shortcut, you carry your old conclusions forward, and the new definition only applies to contracts you sign on or after the transition date. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:reassess-box>> Choose the first path and you reassess everything; <<FOCUS:grandfather-box>> choose the second and you grandfather the past, applying fresh eyes only to new contracts. <<WRITE_KEY:Reassess all, OR carry forward old conclusions + new definition for new contracts|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the big idea is simple: the standard lets you trade completeness for effort. Re-check everything, or trust the past and look forward. Both are allowed, and the company picks.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:29>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:29:transition_two_paths>> A company has been renting buildings for years under the old rules. Tomorrow the rulebook changes. What does it do with all the leases it already signed? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It can't just throw out the past, and it can't pretend nothing happened. So the new standard, Ind AS one sixteen, hands the lessee <<FOCUS:decision-node>> a choice between two honest ways to cross over. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Two transition paths|id=sec-1>> The first path is the <<FOCUS:full-retro-branch+full-retro-box>> full retrospective approach. <<UNFOCUS>> Here you pretend Ind AS one sixteen was always in force, and you go back and redo every single period you're showing. Because you're reaching so far back into the past, you even have to lay out <<FOCUS:third-balance-sheet>> an extra third balance sheet, so a reader can see exactly where things stood at the earliest point. <<UNFOCUS>> It is thorough, but it is a mountain of work. <<WRITE_TEXT:Full retro = redo all periods + 3rd balance sheet|id=text-1>> The second path is the <<FOCUS:modified-retro-branch+modified-retro-box>> modified retrospective approach. <<UNFOCUS>> It refuses to restate the comparative periods at all. The past stays exactly as it was printed. Instead of touching the past, it gathers up the entire cumulative impact of switching and drops it as <<FOCUS:equity-adjustment>> one single adjustment to equity, right at the start of the year it first applies the standard. <<UNFOCUS>> We call that the date of initial application. <<PAUSE:short>> So <<FOCUS:decision-node>> here is the fork. <<UNFOCUS>> Same company, same leases, but two very different amounts of work. Which one would you reach for if you only cared about today's numbers? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The modified path, almost every time, because you skip rebuilding history. But now a sharper question hides inside it. If you are not redoing the past, how do you decide what the lease is worth on day one? <<SECTION:Measuring on day one|id=sec-2>> For what used to be an operating lease, you take only the payments still left to make, and you discount them back to today using the lessee's incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application. That discounted figure becomes the lease liability. <<WRITE_KEY:Lease liability = remaining payments, discounted at today's borrowing rate|id=key-1>> And the cumulative effect of all of this lands as a single adjustment to opening equity, not scattered across the old years. That is the whole spirit of the modified approach. <<PAUSE:short>> There is a neat shortcut for the asset side too. You may rebuild the right-of-use asset retrospectively, or simply set it equal to the lease liability, and you can make that call lease by lease. <<WRITE_KEY:Two paths: full retro redoes the past; modified retro adjusts opening equity|id=key-2>> So remember the fork. Full retrospective rewrites history and <<FOCUS:full-retro-box+third-balance-sheet>> needs a third balance sheet. Modified retrospective leaves history untouched and corrects everything with <<FOCUS:modified-retro-box+equity-adjustment>> one clean adjustment to equity on day one. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:30>>
Picture a company with three hundred old rental contracts, and a new rule that says every single one must now be re-calculated from scratch. Sounds like a nightmare, right? Except the rule-makers handed out a set of legal shortcuts so you don't have to. When the new lease standard arrives, all those leases that used to sit quietly off the balance sheet suddenly have to come on, as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. For one lease, that's annoying. For hundreds, it's an enormous amount of work. <<SECTION:Practical Expedients|id=sec-1>> So the standard says, fine, here are some friendly time-savers. We call them practical expedients, and the key idea is this. <<WRITE_KEY:Practical expedients = optional, lease-by-lease shortcuts on transition|id=key-1>> They are optional shortcuts you can apply lease by lease, letting you skip the most painful calculations. <<PAUSE:short>> Let me walk you through the most useful ones, because each shortcut kills a specific headache. The first headache is the discount rate. Normally every lease needs its own discount rate, the interest rate you use to bring future payments back to today's value. <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient A: one rate for similar leases|id=text-1>> The shortcut lets you apply a single rate to a whole bundle of leases that look reasonably alike, say all your photocopiers, instead of pricing each one separately. The next two shortcuts are about leases that are basically not worth the effort. If a lease ends within twelve months of the changeover date, you're allowed to just treat it as a short-term lease and not bring it onto the books at all. <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient C: skip leases ending within 12 months|id=text-2>> Why fully account for something that's about to expire? Here's one that sounds almost like cheating. Instead of doing a fresh impairment review to check if a lease has gone bad, you may simply rely on your earlier onerous-lease assessment. So which is the lazier, faster path here? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient B: reuse old onerous-lease test instead of impairment review|id=text-3>> Reusing the assessment you already did under the provisions standard, just before transition, and then nudging your right-of-use asset by that provision. You skip an entire fresh review. That's the time-saver. Two more quick ones. You can exclude initial direct costs, the little setup fees, from the value of your right-of-use asset. And you can use hindsight, meaning if a contract had an option to extend, you now already know whether it was actually extended, so use that knowledge instead of guessing. Now notice the pattern. <<WRITE_KEY:Each expedient trades precision for less work; you choose lease by lease|id=key-2>> Every single one of these trades a bit of accuracy for a lot less work, and crucially, you decide which to apply, and to which leases. <<PAUSE:short>> That choice matters, because these are optional. A company that wants cleaner numbers might skip a shortcut; one drowning in old contracts will grab every one it can. The shortcuts bend the workload, not the truth, by much. <<PAUSE:short>> So when you face a transition question, don't panic at three hundred leases. Ask, which expedients apply here, and watch the mountain of work shrink. That's the whole point of practical expedients. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:31>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:31:lessor_vs_lessee_impact>> A brand new accounting standard sweeps in, turns the renter's whole world upside down, and the landlord barely lifts a finger. How can the same rulebook leave one side almost untouched? Remember who's who. <<FOCUS:lessor-side>> The lessor is the party that owns an asset and rents it out; <<FOCUS:lessee-side>> the lessee is the one paying to use it. <<SECTION:Lessor on transition|id=sec-1>> For the lessee, Ind AS one sixteen forces a giant change: <<FOCUS:rou-asset>> a brand new right-of-use asset and <<FOCUS:lease-liability>> a lease liability land on the balance sheet. Now <<FOCUS:lessor-side>> look across to the lessor. <<UNFOCUS>> Almost nothing happens. <<WRITE_KEY:Lessor: no adjustment on transition (except 2 cases)|id=key-1>> As a general rule, a lessor <<FOCUS:lessor-tick>> makes no adjustments at all when moving from the old standard to the new one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Why so calm on the lessor's side? Because the old standard already split leases into finance and operating leases for lessors, and the new standard keeps that same split, so there is simply nothing to redo. But I said almost untouched. So where exactly does the lessor's quiet life get interrupted? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> In exactly two situations. <<FOCUS:exception-sublease>> First, subleases, where someone renting an asset turns around and rents it out to yet another party. Second, <<FOCUS:exception-slb>> sale-and-leaseback transactions, where you sell an asset and immediately lease it back. <<WRITE_TEXT:Exceptions: subleases & sale-and-leaseback|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Everywhere else, the lessor does nothing. So the headline to hold onto: on transition, a lessor makes no adjustments at all, except for subleases and sale-and-leaseback transactions. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:31:slb_transition_flow>> Let's zoom into that second exception, the sale-and-leaseback, because that's where students get tangled. <<SECTION:Sale-and-leaseback on transition|id=sec-2>> Picture a deal <<FOCUS:slb-start>> already sitting on the books under the old standard. The first question is how that old deal was classified: was it accounted for as <<FOCUS:branch-finance>> a sale plus a finance lease, or as <<FOCUS:branch-operating>> a sale plus an operating lease? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> If it was a sale plus finance lease, the path is gentle. The seller-lessee carries the leaseback forward exactly like any finance lease already in place, and any gain on the original sale just <<FOCUS:gain-amortise>> keeps amortising over the lease term. <<PAUSE:short>> If instead it was a sale plus operating lease, you treat the leaseback like any other operating lease, but with one tweak: you <<FOCUS:rou-adjust>> adjust the right-of-use asset for any deferred gains or losses tied to off-market terms sitting on the balance sheet just before transition. <<WRITE_STEP:Operating: adjust ROU asset for off-market deferred gains/losses|id=step-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the whole lesson collapses to one calm idea: the lessor mostly does nothing on transition, and only two special deals, subleases and sale-and-leasebacks, ask for any care at all. <<WRITE_KEY:Carry old leaseback forward; keep amortising the gain|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:32>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:32:value_move>> Here is a strange one: you are sitting on an asset on your balance sheet that, the moment you adopt a new accounting standard, simply has to vanish. <<SECTION:Where the asset came from|id=sec-1>> To see why, rewind. Years ago this company bought another whole business — a business combination — and that acquired business had operating leases running. One of those leases was a bargain: the rent locked in was cheaper than anything you could get in the market today. That favourable deal has real worth, so under Ind AS 103 you <<FOCUS:old-lease-asset-box>> recorded it as a separate asset. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Favourable lease = separate asset under Ind AS 103|id=text-1>> So before transition, the picture is simple: a standalone favourable-lease asset, sitting on its own, measured at its carrying amount. <<UNFOCUS>> Now Ind AS 116 arrives. It says every lease gets <<FOCUS:rou-asset-box>> a single right-of-use asset. <<UNFOCUS>> So a question lands: if the lease already created a separate favourable-terms asset, do we now double-count it alongside the new right-of-use asset? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No double-counting allowed. The rule is clean: <<FOCUS:derecognise-cross+old-lease-asset-box>> you derecognise that old favourable or unfavourable lease asset completely. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1 — Derecognise the old Ind AS 103 lease asset or liability|id=step-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> But — and this is the heart of it — the value does not just evaporate. Watch where it goes. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 2 — Adjust the right-of-use asset by the same amount|id=step-2>> That same carrying amount is <<TRACE:value-arrow>> added straight onto the right-of-use asset. The value simply moves home — <<FOCUS:old-lease-asset-box>> out of the separate box, <<FOCUS:rou-asset-box>> into the right-of-use asset. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And it works both ways. If the old lease had been a bad deal — paying more than market — you would have carried an unfavourable lease liability instead. Same move: derecognise it, and reduce the right-of-use asset by that amount. <<WRITE_KEY:Old lease asset/liability is derecognised; its amount adjusts the right-of-use asset at the date of initial application|id=key-1>> So nothing is lost and nothing is invented. The total value on the balance sheet is exactly the same — it has just been <<FOCUS:rou-asset-box>> re-housed inside the right-of-use asset. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is the whole rule. One asset vanishes from its own line, and reappears, to the penny, baked into the right-of-use asset — all on the date you first apply the new standard.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:33>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:33:scope_boundary_map>> You can sign a lease for the land that sits on top of an oilfield and follow the leasing rulebook — but sign a lease for the oil underneath that very same land, and the rulebook hands it back and tells you to look elsewhere. <<SECTION:Scope of Ind AS 116|id=sec-1>> So let's <<TRACE:scope-circle>> draw the boundary. Inside this circle live all the agreements the leasing standard, Ind AS 116, actually governs. <<WRITE_KEY:Ind AS 116 applies to ALL leases except leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, gas and similar non-regenerative resources|id=key-1>> Here is the one rule that does all the work: the standard applies to all leases, with <<FOCUS:carve-out-arrow>> a single carve-out — leases to explore for, or use, minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources. <<PAUSE:short>> Now picture our company, Entity X, holding <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right+surface-land-right+pipeline-right>> three different rights over the same patch of ground. <<UNFOCUS>> The question is honest — which of them actually sit inside that circle? <<PAUSE:long>> Take the first right: the right to explore for, and <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right>> pull oil out of, oilfield Y for twenty-five years. <<UNFOCUS>> Watch where it goes. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Oil extraction right = carved OUT|id=text-1>> The oil is a <<FOCUS:oil-deposit>> non-regenerative resource — once you pump it out, it's gone, it doesn't grow back. That is exactly the carve-out, so this right is <<TRACE:carve-out-arrow>> pushed straight outside the boundary. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Notice what we did NOT exclude: only the resource itself. So what about the second right — <<FOCUS:surface-land-right>> the surface lease, the right just to walk onto and use the land that happens to sit above the oil? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Surface lease = INSIDE scope|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is a lease of land, plain and simple. The land regenerates nothing and gets extracted from nothing — it's just ground you're renting. It <<FOCUS:surface-land-right+scope-circle>> stays firmly inside Ind AS 116. And the third right — <<FOCUS:pipeline-right>> laying water pipelines over the neighbouring land, because Entity X needs water to extract the oil. <<UNFOCUS>> The water is for the oil, but the lease is over the land. <<WRITE_TEXT:Pipeline land lease = INSIDE scope|id=text-3>> Renting the surface of adjacent land is, once again, just a lease of land. It supports the oil business, but it is not a lease of the non-regenerative resource. So it <<FOCUS:pipeline-right+scope-circle>> also sits inside the circle. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Entity X obtains three rights, and we need to decide which fall within the scope of Ind AS 116. <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right>> Right (a) is the rights to explore for oil and use oil from oilfield Y for twenty-five years. <<FOCUS:surface-land-right>> Right (b) is the right to access the land containing the oil, called a surface lease. And <<FOCUS:pipeline-right>> right (c) is the right to lay water pipelines over land adjacent to the oilfield, because water is needed in the extraction process. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Which of rights (a), (b), (c) obtained by Entity X fall within the scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> We start from the scope rule. Ind AS 116 paragraph three excludes leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources. So the test is simple: does the lease give the right to explore for or extract the oil itself? <<WRITE_STEP:Paragraph 3 excludes leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, gas and similar non-regenerative resources.|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now apply it. Right (a) is a right to explore for and use the oil directly, so it falls squarely <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right+carve-out-arrow>> inside the exclusion. <<UNFOCUS>> Right (b), the surface lease, only gives access to the area where the oil lies, but it exists to reach and extract that oil, so it too is tied to the oil itself. That means <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right+surface-land-right>> rights (a) and (b) are not covered by Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_STEP:(a) explore/use oil and (b) surface lease relate to the oil itself, exclusion applies.|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Right (c) is different. <<FOCUS:pipeline-right>> Laying water pipelines is about transporting water used in the extraction process. <<UNFOCUS>> It does not give a right to explore for, or extract, or use the oil. Because it relates to the extraction process rather than the oil itself, it does not fall in the paragraph three exclusion, so <<FOCUS:pipeline-right+scope-circle>> right (c) is covered by Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_STEP:(c) water pipelines support the extraction process, not the oil itself, so the standard applies.|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> And the answer is: rights (a) and (b) are not covered by Ind AS 116, while right (c) is covered by Ind AS 116 because it relates to the extraction process, not to exploring for or extracting the oil itself. <<WRITE_ANSWER:(a) and (b): outside Ind AS 116. (c): within Ind AS 116.|id=ex-ans-1>> You've seen this yourself — think about the toll road you drive on, or the data cables running under your street. The company laying that infrastructure usually doesn't own the land; they pay the landowner for the right to run pipes or cables across it for years. That's the very same situation as Entity X laying its water pipelines. <<WRITE_TEXT:pipeline right-of-way = inside the standard|id=ext-1>> It supports the work, but it isn't a right to explore for or extract oil, so the leasing standard applies to it. Here's something wild about this: the oil you pump out of the ground today took tens of millions of years to form, and on any human timescale it never comes back. That's literally what non-regenerative means. And that permanence is exactly why the standard singles out rights to explore for or extract oil, gas, and minerals. <<WRITE_KEY:non-regenerative resources → excluded from the lease standard|id=ext-key-2>> Because once the resource is consumed it's truly gone, those rights are deliberately pushed outside the leasing standard. <<WRITE_KEY:Carve-out = the resource itself; land leases above/around it stay IN|id=key-2>> See the pattern? Two of three rights are inside, and the only one excluded is the one that <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right>> touches the oil itself. The carve-out is about the <<FOCUS:oil-deposit+ground>> non-regenerative resource, never about the land it lies beneath. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So next time a lease lands on your desk near an oilfield, ask one question: am I leasing the resource, or just the land? Lease the land and you're inside Ind AS 116; lease the oil and you read a different standard entirely. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:34>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:34:scope_decision_flow>> A company gets the exclusive right to run an entire country's air navigation system for ten whole years, and yet, surprisingly, that contract is not a lease. Let me show you why. <<SECTION:Scoping a contract under Ind AS 116|id=sec-1>> Here is <<FOCUS:contract-box>> the contract on the table. <<UNFOCUS>> A private company, Entity X, signs with a Transport Ministry to operate the system that guides airplanes, upgrade it, and charge users at rates it negotiates freely, with no price cap. Your instinct says lease, because Ind AS 116 says <<FOCUS:ind-as-116-gate>> apply this standard to all leases. <<UNFOCUS>> And that word, all, feels airtight. <<PAUSE:short>> But the standard has carve-outs. One of them quietly <<FOCUS:exclusion-branch>> diverts a whole class of contracts out of scope: service concession arrangements that fall under Appendix D of Ind AS 115. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So before we ever call this a lease, we must ask: is it actually one of those service concessions hiding in disguise? <<PAUSE:long>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Service concession needs BOTH tests|id=text-1>> Appendix D gives two conditions, and crucially, you need both of them to be true. The first is about price. <<PAUSE:short>> Test one: <<FOCUS:price-control-test>> does the grantor control or regulate at what price the operator serves users? <<UNFOCUS>> Here the Ministry sets no price cap at all. Entity X negotiates rates directly and freely. <<PAUSE:short>> And that single fact breaks the whole thing. With no price control by the grantor, <<FOCUS:not-concession-result>> the first condition fails, and a service concession needs both conditions. <<PAUSE:short>> The second test, about the grantor <<FOCUS:residual-interest-test>> keeping a significant residual interest in the system at the end, no longer even matters, because one failed test already settles it. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Entity X is a private sector entity, and it enters a contract with the grantor, the Transport Ministry of Country S, to acquire the right to operate the civil air navigation system. Under the contract, the grantor provides the air navigation system, and X is required to upgrade the system. X charges users based on rates negotiated directly with individual users, there is no price-cap mechanism imposed by the grantor, and the contract period is ten years. The question is whether this contract falls within the scope of Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: X (private) operates Country S air navigation system for grantor (Transport Ministry); X sets prices, no price-cap, 10-year term — within scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by checking the test for a service concession arrangement. Such an arrangement requires the grantor to control the services, the recipients, and the price, and to control any significant residual interest in the infrastructure. Here many of those features are present, but the crucial one fails: the grantor does not control prices, because X negotiates rates directly with users and there is no price-cap. <<WRITE_STEP:1. Service concession test: grantor must control services, recipients, price + significant residual interest|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:2. Here grantor does NOT control prices (X negotiates directly, no price-cap) -> service concession test fails|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is: because the grantor does not control prices, <<FOCUS:not-concession-result>> this is not a service concession arrangement, so it falls outside Appendix D of Ind AS 115. Therefore the right to use the air navigation system is <<FOCUS:back-into-116-arrow>> within the scope of Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Grantor doesn't control prices -> not a service concession -> the contract is within the scope of Ind AS 116|id=ex-ans-1>> You've driven this yourself — a private company builds and runs a toll highway, but the government dictates the exact toll they can charge. <<UNFOCUS>> That price cap is the government keeping control of the service, which is exactly the first condition for a service concession arrangement. In our question, Entity X negotiates prices freely with no cap, so that grip is gone — and the whole classification flips back to Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_TEXT:Govt sets toll = price control = condition 1|id=ext-1>> Something wild about this: the air navigation system in our question is guiding thousands of planes through the sky right now, yet the entire accounting answer turns on one small detail — whether the grantor controls the price. Because Entity X sets its own rates with no cap, that single missing condition pulls this giant public system out of service concession accounting and straight into Ind AS 116. One word, the 'and' between two conditions, decides everything. So the exclusion does not catch this contract. It is not a service concession, which means it <<FOCUS:back-into-116-arrow>> falls right back into the scope of Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_KEY:Rule out service concession (both Appendix D tests) before applying Ind AS 116|id=key-1>> So remember the order of thinking: Ind AS 116 covers all leases, except service concessions, and a service concession demands <<FOCUS:price-control-test+residual-interest-test>> both price control by the grantor and a residual interest. <<UNFOCUS>> Fail either one, and the exclusion doesn't apply. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:35>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:35:control_flow_concession>> A company signs a contract, pays for the trains, and runs them every single day for fifteen years — and yet, on its books, there is no lease at all. How can that be? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:The set-up|id=sec-1>> Here is our cast. <<FOCUS:entity-y+rolling-stock>> Entity Y owns the rolling stock — the trains and equipment. <<FOCUS:operator-x+payment-arrow>> Operator X pays Entity Y to use them and runs the actual service. <<UNFOCUS>> But Operator X did not just go into business for itself. X holds a <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> service concession from Grantor G to run a public rail service for fifteen years. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, normally, if you pay to use an identified asset, you ask one simple question to decide if it is a lease: do you control the use of that asset? <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Control = decide how & for what purpose|id=text-1>> And control is not just touching the asset. Control means you decide how it is used and for what purpose — you direct the use. <<PAUSE:short>> So watch the payment. Operator X does pay Entity Y for using the rolling stock — <<TRACE:payment-arrow>> money flows this way. <<UNFOCUS>> Paying looks like a lease. So who actually decides how these trains run — when they run, and what passengers are charged? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Where control really sits|id=sec-2>> It is not Operator X. <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> Grantor G sets the timetable the trains must follow and regulates the price X can charge passengers. <<UNFOCUS>> G directs the use. Look at <<TRACE:control-arrow>> where the control arrow lands. It passes <<FOCUS:operator-x>> straight through Operator X and <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> stops at Grantor G. <<UNFOCUS>> X holds the trains, but X does not direct them. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No right to direct use = not a lease under Ind AS 116|id=key-1>> And that settles it. Because Operator X <<FOCUS:no-lease-stamp>> never gets the right to direct the use, X's contract with Entity Y is not a lease under Ind AS 116. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Operator X enters into a service concession arrangement with Grantor G to operate a rail service for fifteen years, and this arrangement falls within the scope of Appendix D, Service Concession Arrangements, of Ind AS one fifteen. To run the service, X leases the infrastructure, the rolling stock, from Entity Y, the lessor, where the useful life of the rolling stock is twenty-five years, and X has the obligation to pay the lessor. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Is X's lease of rolling stock from Y within the scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>> Now look at who actually controls the use of that rolling stock. During the concession period, <<FOCUS:grantor-g+rolling-stock>> Grantor G controls the services X delivers, G sets the timetable to which the rolling stock must be operated and regulates the price that X charges passengers, and at the end of the concession G has an option to acquire the rolling stock or otherwise direct its use. <<WRITE_STEP:G sets timetable + regulates price + holds end-of-concession option on rolling stock|id=ex-step-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Appendix D of Ind AS one fifteen states that the operator does not have the right to control the use of the infrastructure; it merely has access to operate it on behalf of the grantor. Since X does not control the use of the rolling stock, the contract <<FOCUS:no-lease-stamp>> is not a lease within the scope of Ind AS one sixteen. <<WRITE_STEP:Per Appendix D, X does NOT control use of the infrastructure|id=ex-step-2>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:The contract of X with Y is NOT within the scope of Ind AS 116|id=ex-ans-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> You've seen this yourself with food delivery riders. A rider might use a scooter that the delivery platform owns, driving it every single shift. But the platform sets the routes, fixes the delivery fees, and can pull that scooter back whenever it likes. Sound familiar? That's exactly Operator X with the trains. The rider uses the asset every day, but the platform calls the shots, so there's no control, and without control there's no lease. Here's something wild about this. A huge number of the world's busiest toll roads, airports, and metro lines run on exactly this kind of arrangement. A private operator runs that public infrastructure for twenty, thirty, even forty years, collecting fees the whole time, yet it never sits on their balance sheet as their own property. <<WRITE_KEY:Concession operator runs it, never controls it|id=ext-key-1>> That's the same Appendix D logic from our question. The operator just has access to operate, following the grantor's terms. No control means it isn't theirs, and it isn't a lease. This is why the rolling stock sits inside the service concession rules of Appendix D, not as a leased asset of Operator X. The same trains, but a completely different accounting home. <<WRITE_TEXT:Payment alone never makes a lease|id=text-2>> So the lesson is sharp: paying for an asset is never enough. Lease accounting follows the right to direct the use — and here that right <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> belongs to the Grantor.

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: This chapter follows a single asset from contract to financial statement: first we ask whether a contract even contains a lease, then how the lessee brings it onto the balance sheet and keeps measuring it, how the lessor treats the other side, and finally the special cases — subleases, sale-and-leaseback — and the transition from the old Ind AS 17 world. The spine is the dramatic shift Ind AS 116 made: leases that once hid off the balance sheet now sit right on it.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: For decades, companies rented billions of rupees worth of buildings, planes, and machines without those leases ever appearing as assets or debts on their books. Ind AS 116 ended that vanishing act — let's see how it brings every lease into the light.

coverage_checklist.description: Establish the lessee/lessor vocabulary and the headline change: leases now go on the lessee's balance sheet via a right-of-use asset and lease liability
Walk through the identified-asset / control test that decides whether a contract is a lease, including substitution rights and direction of use
Show the lessee's full lifecycle: initial recognition, subsequent measurement of the right-of-use asset and lease liability, reassessment and modification
Explain the recognition exemptions for short-term and low-value leases as the practical relief valve
Contrast lessor accounting (finance vs operating lease) and show why it largely retains the old Ind AS 17 model
Cover the special transactions: subleases and sale-and-leaseback, and how the intermediate lessee/seller-lessee accounts for them
Explain the transition from Ind AS 17, including the modified retrospective approach and practical expedients
Apply the scope and lease-identification rules to scenario questions to cement the gatekeeper logic

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We began with leases that vanished from the balance sheet — and now you can see exactly how Ind AS 116 dragged them into the light. You can test whether a contract even contains a lease using the identified-asset and control questions; you can take a lessee through the full journey of recognising a right-of-use asset and lease liability, measuring them over time, and reassessing or modifying when facts change; you understand why lessors still split leases into finance and operating types; and you can handle the trickier cases of subleases, sale-and-leaseback, and the transition from old Ind AS 17. The single takeaway: under Ind AS 116, almost every lease a company uses now leaves a visible footprint on its financial statements — no more vanishing act.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:1:balance_sheet_before_after>> Imagine a company paying to use a fifty-story building for fifteen years, and you, reading their balance sheet, would barely know the building existed. <<SECTION:What is a lease?|id=sec-1>> First, let's be clear what a lease even is. It's an arrangement where one party pays to use something — a building, a machine, a vehicle — that belongs to someone else, for a period of time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Lessee = uses asset. Lessor = owns it.|id=text-1>> The party who <<FOCUS:lessee-label>> uses the asset is the lessee, and the party who owns it and rents it out is the lessor. Keep your eye on the lessee — that's where the action is. <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the strange part. Under the old rules, this expensive building the company rented for years would often <<FOCUS:old-balance-sheet+hidden-lease-footnote>> hide away in the footnotes. <<UNFOCUS>> So if a company can pay for fifteen years to use a building, why wouldn't that obligation show up plainly on the balance sheet for everyone to see? <<PAUSE:long>> That is exactly <<FOCUS:transition-arrow>> the gap the new standard, Ind AS one hundred sixteen, was written to close. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Lessee now records a Right-of-use asset AND a Lease liability|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now watch. The standard says the lessee must record <<FOCUS:right-of-use-asset+lease-liability>> two new things: the right to use the asset, and the promise to pay for it. <<PAUSE:short>> On one side, <<FOCUS:right-of-use-asset>> the right-of-use asset — what the company gets to use. On the other side, <<FOCUS:lease-liability>> the lease liability — what the company owes for using it. <<SECTION:Replacing the old standard|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> To make this the rule, Ind AS one hundred sixteen replaces the older standard, Ind AS seventeen, on leases. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Effective from 1 April 2019|id=text-2>> And it took effect for reporting periods beginning on or after the first of April, two thousand nineteen. Notice that almost all of the big changes land on the lessee — the one renting. The lessor's accounting stays largely the same. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Ind AS 116 brings leases onto the balance sheet|id=key-2>> So the whole point is this: the things a company rents no longer hide in the footnotes — Ind AS one hundred sixteen brings them <<FOCUS:new-balance-sheet>> onto the balance sheet, where everyone can see <<FOCUS:right-of-use-asset+lease-liability>> both the asset and the obligation. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:2:scope_funnel>> You sign a contract to rent something for a few years. Does the leasing standard automatically apply? Surprisingly, not always. <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Scope of Ind AS 116|id=sec-1>> When we talk about the scope of an accounting standard, we just mean its boundaries: <<FOCUS:scope-gate>> which contracts the rule covers, and which ones it leaves to somebody else. <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the headline. If a contract <<FOCUS:all-contracts-box>> meets the definition of a lease, then <<FOCUS:in-scope-box>> Ind AS one hundred sixteen generally applies, and its scope is broadly the same as the older standard, Ind AS seventeen. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So back to our question: does the standard always apply to a lease? The honest answer is, almost always, but there is a small list of deliberate exceptions. <<WRITE_KEY:A lease is in scope of Ind AS 116 unless it is one of 5 carve-outs|id=key-1>> These exceptions are carved out on purpose, because another standard already handles them better. There are five of them. <<PAUSE:short>> First, leases to <<FOCUS:exclusion-minerals>> explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas, and similar non-regenerative resources. <<UNFOCUS>> Digging the earth for oil is its own world, so it falls out here. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Exclusions: minerals, biological assets|id=text-1>> Second, leases of <<FOCUS:exclusion-biological>> biological assets held by a lessee, like living plants and animals. <<UNFOCUS>> Those go to the agriculture standard, Ind AS forty one. Third, <<FOCUS:exclusion-service-concession>> service concession arrangements, the kind where a government lets a company run a toll road or an airport. <<UNFOCUS>> Those belong to the revenue standard, Ind AS one hundred fifteen. Fourth, when <<FOCUS:exclusion-ip-lessor>> a lessor grants licences of its intellectual property, that is treated as revenue under Ind AS one hundred fifteen, not as a lease. <<WRITE_TEXT:plus service concessions, IP licences, film/patent rights|id=text-2>> And fifth, <<FOCUS:exclusion-licensing-lessee>> rights a lessee holds under licensing agreements for things like motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents, and copyrights. <<UNFOCUS>> Those sit in the intangible assets standard, Ind AS thirty eight. There is one gentle flexibility. For intangible assets other than that fifth category, a lessee may choose to apply this standard, but is not required to. So remember the shape of it: <<FOCUS:in-scope-box>> every lease falls inside Ind AS one hundred sixteen, except five carve-outs — <<FOCUS:exclusion-minerals>> minerals and oil, <<FOCUS:exclusion-biological>> biological assets, <<FOCUS:exclusion-service-concession>> service concessions, <<FOCUS:exclusion-ip-lessor>> intellectual property licences from a lessor, and <<FOCUS:exclusion-licensing-lessee>> licensing rights held by a lessee. <<PAUSE:short>>

There are five of them. <<POINT:scope-gate>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:exclusion-minerals>> First, leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas, and similar non-regenerative resources. Digging the earth for oil is its own world, so it falls out here. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:exclusion-biological>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Exclusions: minerals, biological assets|id=text-1>>Second, leases of biological assets held by a lessee, like living plants and animals. Those go to the agriculture standard, Ind AS forty one. <<FOCUS:exclusion-service-concession>> Third, service concession arrangements, the kind where a government lets a company run a toll road or an airport. Those belong to the revenue standard, Ind AS one hundred fifteen. <<FOCUS:exclusion-ip-lessor>> Fourth, when a lessor grants licences of its intellectual property, that is treated as revenue under Ind AS one hundred fifteen, not as a lease. <<FOCUS:exclusion-licensing-lessee>> <<WRITE_TEXT:plus service concessions, IP licences, film/patent rights|id=text-2>>And fifth, rights a lessee holds under licensing agreements for things like motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents, and copyrights. Those sit in the intangible assets standard, Ind AS thirty eight. There is one gentle flexibility. For intangible assets other than that fifth category, a lessee may choose to apply this standard, but is not required to. <<POINT:exclusion-licensing-lessee>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:in-scope-box>> So remember the shape of it: every lease falls inside Ind AS one hundred sixteen, except five carve-outs — minerals and oil, biological assets, service concessions, intellectual property licences from a lessor, and licensing rights held by a lessee. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: What if a company could legally choose to keep certain leases completely off its balance sheet — no asset, no liability, nothing at all? <<PAUSE:long>> Normally, the rule is strict: when you lease something, you must record a right-of-use asset and a matching lease liability on your books, and that's a lot of accounting work. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Recognition Exemption|id=sec-1>> So the standard offers a shortcut, called the recognition exemption — for two specific kinds of leases, the lessee, the one renting the asset, can simply skip all that recording. <<WRITE_KEY:Two exemptions: short-term leases and low-value leases|id=key-1>> The two kinds are short-term leases, and leases where the underlying asset is of low value. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term = 12 months or less at start|id=text-1>> Let's nail down the first one. A short-term lease is simply a lease that, at the moment it commences, has a term of twelve months or less. <<PAUSE:short>> So renting a piece of equipment for just six months — that comfortably qualifies as short-term. But here's the catch that trips people up: what happens if that six-month lease also gives you the option to buy the asset at the end? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Purchase option means never short-term|id=key-2>> Then it is never a short-term lease — no matter how short it is. A purchase option signals you really intend to own the asset, so the shortcut is off the table. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Low-value leases|id=sec-2>> The second kind is the low-value lease — think of a laptop or an office phone — something you can use on its own, that isn't tightly bound up with your bigger, more valuable assets. <<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term: by class. Low-value: lease by lease|id=text-2>> Now here's a subtle but important difference in how you apply them. <<PAUSE:short>> The short-term exemption is all-or-nothing for a whole class of assets — choose it for your delivery vans, and it applies to every short-term van lease consistently. The low-value exemption is far more flexible: you decide lease by lease, picking and choosing for each individual low-value asset. <<PAUSE:short>> And whichever exemption you use, you must disclose it — so anyone reading the financial statements knows these leases were deliberately kept off the books.

segments.narration_chapter: You rent a parking spot in a garage where you can park in any free space, and you rent a specific named spot, spot forty-seven, just for you. One of these is a lease and one is not. Which is which? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:4:lease_decision_tree>> <<SECTION:Identifying a lease|id=sec-1>> That puzzle is the single most important question in all of lease accounting, because everything else hangs on the answer. If a contract is a lease, you must follow a whole set of special accounting rules. If it is not, you do not. So this one decision is the gatekeeper for everything that follows. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Lease = right to CONTROL an IDENTIFIED asset for a period, for consideration|id=key-1>> Here is the definition the standard gives us. A contract is, or contains, a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset, for a period of time, in exchange for payment. <<PAUSE:short>> Let us break that into three plain questions. First: <<FOCUS:identified-asset-box>> is there an identified asset? <<WRITE_TEXT:Identified = a specific, named asset|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> An identified asset is a specific one, like spot forty-seven, not just any spot from a pool the supplier can swap around at will. If there is no identified asset, <<FOCUS:no-collector>> we stop right here. <<FOCUS:not-a-lease-outcome>> No lease. <<SECTION:Control|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> But an identified asset alone is not enough. The customer must also control it. And <<FOCUS:control-bracket+control-label>> control has two parts. Second question: does the customer get <<FOCUS:economic-benefits-box>> substantially all the economic benefits from using that asset over the period? Third question: does the customer get to <<FOCUS:direct-use-box>> direct how and for what purpose the asset is used? <<UNFOCUS>> In other words, who calls the shots day to day? When the answer to all three is yes, the customer truly controls the asset, and <<FOCUS:is-a-lease-outcome>> the contract is, or contains, a lease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So back to our puzzle: which parking arrangement is the lease? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:Named spot 47 = lease; any free space = not a lease|id=ans-1>> Spot forty-seven is the lease. It is identified, you get all its benefit, and you decide when to park there. The any-free-space deal <<FOCUS:identified-asset-box>> fails the very first test, because there is no identified asset. <<WRITE_KEY:Assess once at inception; reassess only if terms change|id=key-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> One last thing about timing. You run this test once, at the very inception of the contract. After that, you do not keep second-guessing it. You reassess only if the actual terms and conditions of the contract change. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: If you pay a company to ship your goods, but they get to pick whichever truck is free that day, are you really leasing a truck? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Identified Assets|id=sec-1>> Hold that thought, because it points straight at the very first test any contract must pass before we can call it a lease. <<WRITE_KEY:A lease exists only if there is an identified asset|id=key-1>> Here is the rule: a contract contains a lease only if it relates to an identified asset. <<PAUSE:short>> Think about why that has to be true. A lease is the right to use a specific thing, so if there is no particular thing at the heart of the deal, there is simply nothing to lease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> So back to our trucks: if the shipping company keeps a whole fleet and just sends whichever one is free, you never had a specific truck, so you don't have a lease at all. <<WRITE_TEXT:Two ways to identify: explicit or implicit|id=text-1>> Now, how do we actually know if an asset is identified? There are exactly two routes. The first route is explicit specification. This is the obvious one, where the contract literally names or describes the asset. Picture a rental agreement that says you get the delivery van with a particular registration number, or the office on the third floor. It is spelled out in black and white. <<WRITE_TEXT:Implicit = the only asset available to fulfil the deal|id=text-2>> The second route is implicit specification. Here the contract never names the asset, but only one asset can possibly do the job. <<PAUSE:short>> Imagine a supplier with a single specialised crane at one site. Even if the contract never mentions it by name, that crane is implicitly identified the moment it's made available to you. <<WRITE_KEY:Identified = named explicitly OR the only one available implicitly|id=key-2>> So an asset is identified either explicitly, by being named, or implicitly, by being the only asset available to fulfil the contract. <<PAUSE:short>> Get this first hurdle right, and remember it every time: no identified asset means no lease, and you must check whether it was pinned down explicitly or implicitly. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:6:substitution_decision>> Your contract <<FOCUS:named-asset-box>> names one specific machine, serial number and all, and yet you might still not have a lease. <<UNFOCUS>> How can naming the exact asset not be enough? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Substantive substitution rights|id=sec-1>> Here's the catch. A lease <<FOCUS:outcome-identified>> needs an identified asset, something the customer is genuinely tied to. <<UNFOCUS>> But suppose the supplier can quietly wheel that machine away and roll in any other one whenever it suits them. <<PAUSE:short>> If the supplier holds that swapping power, then you were never really tied to that one machine at all. The asset stops being identified, and without an identified asset, <<FOCUS:outcome-no-lease>> there is simply no lease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> But hold on, does every little swap clause destroy a lease? Surely not, or almost no contract would ever count. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Right must be SUBSTANTIVE, not just on paper|id=text-1>> And it doesn't. The standard says the supplier's right to substitute only counts if it is substantive, which means real in practice, not just words buried in the fine print. Substantive means two things must both be true. So picture <<FOCUS:gate-practical+gate-economic>> two gates the supplier has to pass through before their swap right matters. Gate one, <<FOCUS:gate-practical>> the practical ability. <<UNFOCUS>> Can the supplier actually swap the asset throughout the period of use? If alternative assets aren't readily available, or it would be a huge hassle, the supplier can't really do it. Gate two, <<FOCUS:gate-economic>> the economic benefit. <<UNFOCUS>> Would the supplier actually gain from swapping? The cost of moving the asset must be outweighed by the benefit they'd get. <<WRITE_KEY:Substantive = practical ability AND economic benefit, throughout the period of use|id=key-1>> Only when <<FOCUS:arrow-practical-yes+arrow-economic-yes>> both gates open, practical ability and economic benefit, is the substitution right substantive. Then there's <<FOCUS:outcome-no-lease>> no identified asset, and no lease. <<PAUSE:short>> But if <<FOCUS:arrow-no-branch>> either gate stays shut, say swapping is impractical or there's nothing in it for the supplier, the swap clause is just paper. The <<FOCUS:outcome-identified>> asset stays identified, and a lease can still exist. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Can't tell which asset? Assume no substantive right|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> One more honest point. If you genuinely can't tell whether the supplier could swap the asset, you assume the right is not substantive, so the asset is treated as identified. <<PAUSE:short>> So before you ever ask about payments or terms, you walk the asset <<FOCUS:gate-practical+gate-economic>> through these two gates. <<UNFOCUS>> Named on paper isn't the test. Genuinely yours to use is.

segments.narration_chapter: You rent a delivery van for a year. The fuel it saves you, the cargo it carries, even the cash you'd get if you let a friend borrow it for a weekend — who actually pockets all of that? Hold that question. <<PAUSE:long>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:8:benefits_pie>> <<SECTION:Economic benefits|id=sec-1>> Before accountants can call a contract a lease, they ask one sharp thing: does the customer get <<FOCUS:benefit-pie>> substantially all the economic benefits from using that asset? <<UNFOCUS>> Let's see what's actually on the table. The <<FOCUS:slice-primary>> biggest slice is the primary output — the main job the asset does. <<UNFOCUS>> For our van, that's hauling your goods from place to place. <<WRITE_TEXT:Benefits = primary output + by-products + third-party value|id=text-1>> But benefits are broader than the headline. <<FOCUS:slice-byproducts>> There are by-products — the extra stuff that tags along — and there's <<FOCUS:slice-thirdparty>> value you could get from a third party, like subleasing the van to someone else. That third slice matters: even cash you'd realise by renting it out to an outsider counts as an economic benefit from using the asset. <<PAUSE:short>> So here's the answer to our opening question: if you pocket the hauling, the by-products, AND the sublease cash — <<FOCUS:customer-capture-ring>> you've captured substantially all the benefits, and that's exactly what control of use requires. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Customer must obtain substantially ALL economic benefits over the period of use|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Notice the words: substantially all, and throughout the whole period of use. <<FOCUS:customer-capture-ring>> Grab almost the entire pie, for the entire time — that's the test. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:8:scope_boundary>> <<SECTION:But which benefits count?|id=sec-2>> Now a twist. Suppose the contract says the van may only be driven inside one city. Do we measure all the benefits the van could ever produce, or only some of them? <<PAUSE:long>> We only count <<FOCUS:benefits-inside>> what's inside the fence. The contract's defined scope <<TRACE:scope-fence>> draws a boundary, and benefits within that boundary are the ones we assess. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:benefits-outside>> Anything outside the fence — the trips you could have made if there were no city limit — we simply ignore. <<UNFOCUS>> It's as if it doesn't exist for this test. Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose a contract limits the use of a vehicle to only a particular geographic area. The question is: when we judge whether the customer obtains substantially all the economic benefits, which benefits do we count? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Contract limits vehicle use to one geographic area only. Which economic benefits do we assess?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by scoping our assessment to what the contract actually permits. The question is: which economic benefits does the entity actually assess? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Machine usable only during specific times of day — which economic benefits does the entity assess?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by pinning the scope to what the contract grants. Because use is limited to a specific window, the entity assesses only the economic benefits from using the machinery during that time of the day. <<WRITE_STEP:Assess only economic benefits during the contracted time-of-use window|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the answer is: the assessment is confined to the contracted hours. segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:9:direct_use_decision_tree>> You rent a car for a week. Who decides where it drives, when it stops, and what it carries? If the answer is you, you might be holding a lease without even knowing it. <<SECTION:Right to direct the use|id=sec-1>> We already know a lease needs an identified asset and that you get the economic benefits from it. But there is a second piece, and this is the heart of control: <<FOCUS:root-question>> the right to direct the use. <<UNFOCUS>> Directing the use simply means you call the shots. You decide how the asset is used and for what purpose, like where that truck goes and what it carries. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Control = you decide HOW and WHY the asset is used|id=key-1>> So <<FOCUS:route-one-how-why>> the most direct route is this: if you have the right to decide how and for what purpose the asset is used throughout the period, you control it. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> But here is the puzzle. What if every decision about how and why the asset is used is <<FOCUS:route-two-predetermined>> already locked in before you even sign? <<UNFOCUS>> Can you still be in control? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Yes, you still can, through a second route, and the standard gives two ways it happens. <<WRITE_TEXT:Predetermined use: control via operate OR design|id=text-1>> The first way: you have the <<FOCUS:sub-operate>> right to operate the asset, or to direct others to operate it as you choose, and the supplier cannot change your operating instructions. <<PAUSE:short>> The second way: <<FOCUS:sub-designed>> you designed the asset in a manner that predetermined how and for what purpose it would be used. <<UNFOCUS>> You made the decisions up front, at the drawing board. <<PAUSE:short>> Notice the pattern: either you decide as you go, or the decisions were baked in by you. Both routes <<FOCUS:control-result>> land at the same place. <<WRITE_KEY:Either route -> customer directs use -> lease|id=key-2>>And once you have the right to direct the use on top of the economic benefits, the customer controls the asset, and the contract is a lease. <<UNFOCUS>> So next time you sign a contract for an asset, ask one question: who really decides how and why it gets used? Answer that, and you have answered whether it is a lease.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:10:contract_split>> <<SECTION:One contract, two deals|id=sec-1>> <<FOCUS:contract-box>> You sign one contract to rent a delivery van, but hidden inside that single piece of paper are actually two completely different deals. The first deal is the <<FOCUS:lease-component>> right to use the van itself. The second is <<FOCUS:nonlease-component>> a maintenance service that keeps it running. <<WRITE_TEXT:1 contract = 2 things inside|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the honest question: if the standard cares so much about leases, does it really treat a cleaning crew the same as the van you are driving? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No, it does not. The part that gives you the right to use the asset <<FOCUS:lease-component>> is the lease component, and the service that just helps you run it is <<FOCUS:nonlease-component>> a non-lease component, and the rule is to keep them apart. So the very first move is to <<FOCUS:branch-left+branch-right>> split the contract into its lease component and its non-lease components, and account for each one separately. <<PAUSE:short>> But wait — you only pay <<FOCUS:total-payment>> one combined amount. <<UNFOCUS>> How do you decide how much of that money belongs to the van and how much belongs to the service? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> You look at what each piece would cost on its own — <<FOCUS:lease-price-tag+nonlease-price-tag>> its stand-alone price — and you <<FOCUS:total-payment>> split the total payment in that same proportion. <<WRITE_KEY:Allocate total payment by relative stand-alone prices|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is the heart of it: each lease component is accounted for separately, and the total payment is shared out by the relative stand-alone prices of the parts. <<PAUSE:short>> And if a stand-alone price is not floating around anywhere, you are allowed to estimate it rather than just giving up. Now, all this splitting is fiddly work, so the standard hands the renter a shortcut called <<FOCUS:expedient-banner>> a practical expedient. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Practical expedient = treat whole contract as ONE lease|id=key-2>> If you choose this expedient for a class of asset, you ignore the separation and simply treat the entire contract as <<FOCUS:expedient-text>> one single lease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So remember the fork in the road: either split by stand-alone prices and account separately, or take the expedient and call the whole thing one lease.

segments.narration_chapter: Two companies sign three separate contracts on the same afternoon. On paper, three deals, but in reality it might be just one deal wearing three disguises. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:11:combination_gate>> <<SECTION:Combination of Contracts|id=sec-1>> Here is why this matters. If you treat each contract on its own, the numbers can hide what is really going on. So the standard asks a sharper question: are these truly separate, or secretly one? But you cannot just combine any two contracts you feel like. There is <<FOCUS:gateway-box>> a gate you must pass through first, and the gate has two locks. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Gate lock 1: at or near same time|id=text-1>> Lock one: the contracts must be entered into <<FOCUS:condition-same-time>> at or near the same time. <<WRITE_TEXT:Gate lock 2: same counterparty or related|id=text-2>> Lock two: they must be with <<FOCUS:condition-same-party>> the same counterparty, or with parties closely related to that counterparty. <<WRITE_KEY:Combine ONLY if BOTH gateway conditions hold|id=key-1>> And here is the rule that catches people out: <<FOCUS:condition-same-time+condition-same-party>> both locks must open together. <<UNFOCUS>> Same time alone is not enough. Same party alone is not enough. You need both, or the gate stays shut. <<PAUSE:short>> So suppose both locks open and the gate swings wide. Does that automatically mean we combine the contracts? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Not yet. Past the gate sit <<FOCUS:test-package+test-price-link+test-single-component>> three tests, and you only need ONE of them to fire to force a combination. <<PAUSE:short>> Test one: the contracts were <<FOCUS:test-package>> negotiated as a single package, with one overall commercial objective that makes no sense unless you read them together. Test two: the money you pay in one contract <<FOCUS:test-price-link>> depends on the price or the performance of the other. <<UNFOCUS>> Pull one thread and the other moves. Test three: the rights to use the underlying assets across the contracts actually form <<FOCUS:test-single-component>> one single lease component. <<UNFOCUS>> Different papers, but one real thing being leased. <<WRITE_KEY:Gate open + any ONE test = single contract|id=key-2>> So here is the whole machine. Both gateway conditions open the gate, then any single one of the three tests sends you to one answer: <<FOCUS:combine-result>> treat it all as one combined contract. <<PAUSE:short>> And if the gate never opens, or all three tests fail, you stay here: <<FOCUS:separate-result>> the contracts remain separate, each accounted for on its own.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:12:lease_term_timeline>> You sign a five-year office lease, but you can walk away after three, and you're pretty sure you'll stay two more. So how many years long is your lease, really? <<PAUSE:long>> The answer matters more than it sounds, because almost every number in lease accounting, the asset value, the liability, the yearly charge, depends on this one length. Get the length wrong and everything downstream is wrong. So let's build the timeline. First, when does the clock start? Not the day you sign the paperwork. <<SECTION:When the clock starts|id=sec-1>> It starts on <<FOCUS:commencement-date>> the commencement date, the day the lessor actually hands you the asset to use. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now here's the trap. Suppose your first three months are rent-free, a sweetener to get you to sign. Do those free months count as part of the lease term? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> They absolutely do. <<WRITE_KEY:Term starts at commencement; rent-free and reduced-rent months still count|id=key-1>> A <<FOCUS:rent-free-band>> rent-free or reduced-rent period is still you having the asset, so it is part of the term from day one. <<PAUSE:short>> Next comes the solid core of the term: <<FOCUS:non-cancellable-band>> the non-cancellable period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Non-cancellable = locked in, can't walk away|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> This is the stretch where neither of you can just walk away, you're locked in. <<PAUSE:short>> But leases often have options bolted on. An option to extend, or an option to terminate early. Do we just include every extension option to be safe? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No, and this is the clever part. <<SECTION:The reasonably-certain test|id=sec-2>> You only <<FOCUS:option-band>> include an extension period if you are reasonably certain you'll take it. <<UNFOCUS>> And you only cut off a termination option if you're reasonably certain you won't use it. So in our office example, the three locked-in years are in for certain, and because you're reasonably certain to stay the extra two, <<FOCUS:lease-term-bracket>> those join the term too, giving five. <<PAUSE:short>> Put it together: the lease term is <<FOCUS:non-cancellable-band>> the non-cancellable period, <<FOCUS:option-band>> plus any extension you're reasonably certain to take, plus any termination right you're reasonably certain not to use. <<WRITE_KEY:Term = non-cancellable period + options the lessee is reasonably certain to take|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> One last note: judgement isn't frozen. If the <<FOCUS:non-cancellable-band>> non-cancellable period itself changes, you go back and revise the term, because every downstream number leans on it.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:13:lease_timeline_options>> You sign a five-year lease on a shop, but the contract lets you stay for five more years if you want. So how long is your lease, really? Five years, or ten? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Extension and termination options|id=sec-1>> Here's the honest answer: it depends on a judgment you make right at the start, on what we call <<FOCUS:commencement-date>> the commencement date. <<UNFOCUS>> Look at the timeline. <<FOCUS:guaranteed-period>> This solid bar is the part you are locked into — the years you cannot escape. <<UNFOCUS>> That's the guaranteed period. And <<FOCUS:optional-period>> this dashed bar is the optional bit — the extra years you could take if you choose to extend. <<UNFOCUS>> The big question is whether those dashed years count as part of your lease. <<WRITE_KEY:Lease term set by 'reasonably certain' judgment at commencement|id=key-1>> At the commencement date the entity must ask three things: is the lessee reasonably certain to extend, reasonably certain to buy the asset, and reasonably certain not to terminate early? <<PAUSE:short>> If the answer is yes, you are reasonably certain to extend, then <<TRACE:extend-arrow>> the lease term reaches forward and swallows those optional years. <<PAUSE:short>> But if instead you are reasonably certain to terminate early, <<TRACE:terminate-arrow>> the lease term gets cut short, right here. <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the trap. Reasonably certain is not the same as legally allowed. The contract gives you the option — but the standard asks something deeper. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Test is economic incentive, not the contract wording|id=key-2>> The real test is <<FOCUS:incentive-zone>> economic incentive. <<UNFOCUS>> Is there a strong financial reason that makes exercising the option the obvious choice? <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Consider all facts: fit-out cost, location, below-market rent|id=text-1>> For instance, in any case where you've spent a fortune fitting out the shop, or the rent for the extra years is far below market, walking away would be painful — so you're reasonably certain to stay.
