segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:14:lease_recognition_balance>> You rent a bike from your friend for a whole year. You don't own it, so how could it possibly show up as something you own on your accounts? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here's the trick: you may not own the bike, but you own something real — the right to ride it whenever you like, for a whole year. That right has genuine worth. <<SECTION:Commencement date|id=sec-1>> The moment that matters is the day the lease actually begins, which we call <<FOCUS:commencement-line>> the commencement date. <<UNFOCUS>> On that single day, two entries go into the books. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Day one: recognise a right-of-use asset AND a lease liability|id=key-1>> The first entry is that valuable right we just talked about. We call it <<FOCUS:right-of-use-asset>> the right-of-use asset, and we record it at its cost. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> But there's a flip side. Using that bike for a year isn't free, is it? You've promised to make payments. That promise is an obligation, and an obligation you can't escape is a liability. So the second entry is <<FOCUS:lease-liability>> the lease liability. Look at the board: one event on day one, <<FOCUS:right-of-use-asset>> an asset on this side, <<FOCUS:lease-liability>> a liability on that side. <<PAUSE:short>> Now, <<FOCUS:future-payments>> those future payments stretch out across the whole lease term. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's a fair question: a thousand rupees you pay next year — is that really worth a full thousand rupees to you today? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It isn't. Money in the future is worth less than money right now, because today's money could earn interest. So we shrink each future payment back to what it's worth today — <<FOCUS:discount-arrow>> its present value. <<UNFOCUS>> We measure the lease liability as the present value of all the lease payments that haven't been paid yet at that date. <<TRACE:discount-arrow>> Watch the arrow pull those future payments back into the liability box. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The lease liability is just the sum of every future payment, each one shrunk back to what it's worth today using the interest rate. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Lease liability} = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{P_t}{(1+r)^{t}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:PV = \sum P_t / (1+r)^t|id=eq-1>> In symbols, the liability is each payment P divided by one plus the rate, raised to the power of how many years away it is, all added together. <<WRITE_TEXT:Use implicit rate; else incremental borrowing rate|id=text-1>> The rate r is the interest rate implicit in the lease if you can readily work it out. If you can't, you use the lessee's own incremental borrowing rate instead. <<PAUSE:short>> So on day one, every lease quietly does two things at once: it <<FOCUS:right-of-use-asset>> hands you an asset worth using, and it <<FOCUS:lease-liability>> loads you with a liability worth paying. <<UNFOCUS>> Recognise both, and the books tell the truth.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:15:rou_value_paths>> You sign a five-year lease on a delivery van and put it on your books today. Here's the puzzle: what should that van be worth on your books one year from now? <<PAUSE:long>> The asset can't just sit there frozen at its starting value, because in real life that right to use the van is steadily getting used up. <<SECTION:Subsequent measurement|id=sec-1>> Keeping track of how that value changes over the life of the lease is what we call subsequent measurement. <<PAUSE:short>> And here's the answer to our puzzle: the company actually gets to choose between two different paths for that value, and we draw them both <<FOCUS:start-value-point>> starting from the same point. <<PAUSE:short>> The first path is <<FOCUS:cost-model-path>> the cost model — think of it as the simple, steady road. You begin with the cost and you shave a slice off it each period as depreciation, so the line just glides downward. <<WRITE_TEXT:Cost model = steady decline by depreciation|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Notice this line never jumps around. It only goes down, smoothly, year after year, as the van is used up. The second path is <<FOCUS:revaluation-model-path>> the revaluation model. Watch what's different — it can be reset to the asset's fair value, so instead of only sliding down, it can step back up if the asset is worth more. <<WRITE_TEXT:Revaluation = reset to fair value|id=text-2>> So <<FOCUS:cost-model-path+revaluation-model-path>> one road is steady and predictable, and the other tracks what the asset is really worth in the market. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, a fair question: if the revaluation path can keep your asset closer to its true worth, why wouldn't every company just pick it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because there's a gatekeeper. You're only allowed <<FOCUS:revaluation-date-guide>> onto the revaluation road if the underlying asset belongs to a class for which your company already revalues its own property, plant and equipment under Ind AS sixteen. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Subsequent measurement: cost model OR revaluation model (revaluation only if that asset class is already revalued under Ind AS 16)|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So lock this in: after first recording the right-of-use asset, you measure it using either the cost model or the revaluation model. <<PAUSE:short>> And the revaluation door only opens for an asset class that you're already revaluing under Ind AS sixteen — for everyone else, the steady cost model is the road you travel. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:16:rou_cost_model_waterfall>> You sign a five-year lease on a delivery van. The day after you sign, what is that van worth on your books, and what will it be worth next year? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:The cost model|id=sec-1>> The answer comes from something called the cost model, and it is just a clean recipe for tracking the value of your right to use that van as the years go by. <<PAUSE:short>> You start with <<FOCUS:original-cost-block>> this full block, the original cost of the right-of-use asset, exactly what you measured it at on day one. <<WRITE_TEXT:Depreciation = wearing-down of value over time|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now, the van wears down a little every year, and that wearing-down of value is called depreciation, which we spread across the life of the asset using the rules in Ind AS sixteen. So <<FOCUS:depreciation-cut>> we cut that accumulated depreciation off the top of the block, and the more years pass, the bigger that cut grows. Sometimes something unexpected happens, the asset suddenly loses value beyond ordinary wear, and that is <<FOCUS:impairment-cut>> an impairment loss, which we follow under Ind AS thirty-six. <<WRITE_KEY:Carrying amount = cost less accumulated depreciation less accumulated impairment|id=key-1>> So we subtract any accumulated impairment losses too, and what is left is <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> your net carrying amount, the figure that actually sits on the balance sheet. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Take the original cost, subtract everything the asset has worn down by, then subtract any sudden losses, and the remainder is what the asset is carried at. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Carrying amount} = \text{Cost} - \text{Accumulated depreciation} - \text{Accumulated impairment losses}|id=eq-1|boxed>> But here is a question that trips people up: what if the lease itself changes partway through, say the rent gets revised, so the lease liability you owe is recalculated? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> When the lease liability is remeasured, <<FOCUS:remeasurement-adjustment+carrying-amount-block>> you adjust the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset by the very same amount, up or down, so the two stay linked. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:No adjustment if asset already zero, or change is variable payment (no index/rate)|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> There are just two exceptions: you stop if the asset is already reduced to zero, or if the change relates to a variable payment that does not depend on an index or a rate. So picture the whole journey: <<FOCUS:original-cost-block>> start at cost, <<FOCUS:depreciation-cut>> cut away depreciation, <<FOCUS:impairment-cut>> cut away impairment, then <<FOCUS:remeasurement-adjustment>> nudge for any remeasurement, and you <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> land on the carrying amount. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> That single recipe, cost less depreciation less impairment, adjusted for remeasurement, is the cost model, and it tells you exactly what your leased van is worth on your books, today and every year after. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:remeasurement-adjustment>> When the lease liability is remeasured, you adjust the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset by the very same amount, up or down, so the two stay linked. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:No adjustment if asset already zero, or change is variable payment (no index/rate)|id=text-2>>There are just two exceptions: you stop if the asset is already reduced to zero, or if the change relates to a variable payment that does not depend on an index or a rate. <<POINT:remeasurement-adjustment>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> So picture the whole journey: start at cost, cut away depreciation, cut away impairment, then nudge for any remeasurement, and you land on the carrying amount. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> That single recipe, cost less depreciation less impairment, adjusted for remeasurement, is the cost model, and it tells you exactly what your leased van is worth on your books, today and every year after. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:17:lease_liability_rollforward>> You sign a lease and write down <<FOCUS:opening-balance>> what you owe on day one. <<UNFOCUS>> But by next month that number has already changed. Why won't it sit still? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's the secret: a lease liability behaves almost exactly like a loan. Think about borrowing money from a friend who charges you a little interest. <<SECTION:Amortised cost|id=sec-1>> Every period, two things happen to that balance. First, because you still owe money, <<FOCUS:interest-addition>> interest quietly builds up on top of what you owe. <<PAUSE:short>> Then you make your lease payment, and that payment <<FOCUS:payment-subtraction>> chips the balance back down. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Closing = Opening + Interest - Payment|id=text-1>> So what you're left with at the end of the period is <<FOCUS:opening-balance>> your opening amount, <<FOCUS:interest-addition>> plus the interest, <<FOCUS:payment-subtraction>> minus the payment. That leftover is the <<FOCUS:closing-balance>> new carrying amount. And here's the elegant part: that closing balance simply <<FOCUS:carry-forward-arrow+next-opening>> becomes next period's opening balance, and the whole cycle repeats. <<UNFOCUS>> The closing balance equals the opening balance, plus interest at the effective rate on that opening balance, minus the payment you make. <<WRITE_EQUATION:L_{closing} = L_{opening} + (L_{opening} \times r) - P|id=eq-1|boxed>> Now if the interest keeps getting added every period, you might wonder — does the liability just keep growing forever? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Interest is charged on the shrinking balance, so it gets smaller each period|id=key-1>> No. Because your payment is bigger than the interest, <<FOCUS:closing-balance>> the balance shrinks. And since interest is <<FOCUS:interest-arrow>> charged only on what you still owe, a smaller balance means less interest next time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> This whole method — interest on the outstanding balance, then reduce by payment — is what accountants call the effective interest method. <<WRITE_KEY:Lease liability is carried at amortised cost using the effective interest method|id=key-2>> And carrying the liability this way, period after period, is exactly what we mean when we say it is measured at amortised cost. <<PAUSE:short>> There's one more twist. Sometimes the deal itself changes — payments get revised, or you reassess what you'll actually pay. When that happens, you also remeasure the carrying amount to reflect the new reality. So picture the liability as a living balance: it breathes in interest, breathes out payments, and quietly shrinks toward zero by the end of the lease.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:18:reassessment_fork>> You signed a five-year lease and locked a single number into your books. Two years in, you decide to stay seven years instead. So does that old number just get to stay wrong? <<PAUSE:long>> It can't. That number, <<FOCUS:liability-box>> the lease liability, was only ever your best guess of all the future payments squeezed into one present value. When <<FOCUS:trigger-event>> the facts behind the guess change, the number has to change too. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Reassessment|id=sec-1>> Going back and remeasuring that liability so it matches the new reality is exactly <<FOCUS:liability-box>> what we call reassessment. <<WRITE_TEXT:Reassessment = remeasure liability for new facts|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the clever part. Not every change is the same kind of change, so the rules ask one sharp question before you remeasure anything. The question is this: <<FOCUS:fork-question>> did the very nature of the lease shift, or did only the cash amounts shift? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> If the nature shifted, say you changed the lease term, or you now expect to exercise a purchase option, then you are essentially dealing with a different deal, so you discount the revised payments using <<FOCUS:path-revised-rate>> a revised discount rate. <<UNFOCUS>> What is that revised rate? segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:19:modification_decision_tree>> You rented an office floor two years ago. Today you want a second floor. Is that a brand-new lease, or just a change to the old one? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Lease modifications|id=sec-1>> Here is why it matters. Real contracts don't stay frozen. You add space, you give space back, the rent gets renegotiated. Accountants call any such change <<FOCUS:start-node>> a lease modification. The whole standard hangs on one fork in the road: <<FOCUS:separate-lease-outcome+remeasure-outcome>> do we bolt on a separate lease, or do we surgically adjust the lease we already have? <<UNFOCUS>> Everything else follows from that single decision. So when do we get to treat it as a clean, separate lease? <<FOCUS:gate-adds-asset+gate-fair-price>> There are two gates, and you must pass BOTH. First gate: does the change actually <<FOCUS:gate-adds-asset>> add the right to use a new asset, like that extra floor? Second gate: is the extra payment <<FOCUS:gate-fair-price>> a fair price for that new asset on its own? <<UNFOCUS>> We call that the stand-alone price, roughly what you'd pay if you walked in off the street and rented that floor today. <<WRITE_KEY:Separate lease ONLY IF: adds a new asset AND priced at fair stand-alone price|id=key-1>> Pass both gates, and <<FOCUS:separate-lease-outcome>> it is a separate lease. <<UNFOCUS>> You leave your original lease completely untouched and simply book the new one beside it. <<PAUSE:short>> Now, the question that trips people up: what if you add a floor, but your landlord gives you a sweet discount, well below the stand-alone price? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Then you <<FOCUS:gate-fair-price>> fail the second gate, so it is NOT a separate lease. The discount entangles the old deal with the new, so you must reopen and <<FOCUS:remeasure-outcome>> remeasure the lease you already have. <<WRITE_STEP:Remeasure lease liability using a discount rate at the modification date|id=step-1>> To remeasure, you recompute the lease liability using a fresh discount rate, the rate that fits the conditions on the day of the modification, not the old one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> From here the path splits in two. If the modification <<FOCUS:branch-decrease-scope>> shrinks your scope, say you hand back half a floor, you cut down the right-of-use asset to match and you book the gain or loss for the part you let go. <<WRITE_KEY:Not separate: remeasure liability, adjust right-of-use asset; if scope shrinks, recognise gain or loss|id=key-2>> For <<FOCUS:branch-other>> every other kind of change, no gain or loss, you just make a matching adjustment to the right-of-use asset so the books stay balanced. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the answer to where we started: a separate lease only if it adds an asset at a fair price; otherwise reopen the books, remeasure the liability, and adjust the asset. That one fork decides everything. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:20:statement_drawer_map>> You signed a lease. You now owe money, and you control an asset you don't own. So where exactly do those numbers sit in your three financial statements? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Presentation as sorting|id=sec-1>> Presentation isn't new accounting. It's just deciding which drawer each number belongs in. We have three drawers: <<FOCUS:balance-sheet-box>> the balance sheet, <<FOCUS:pl-box>> the profit and loss, and <<FOCUS:cashflow-box>> the cash flow statement. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Start with the balance sheet. As a lessee you carry two things here: <<FOCUS:rou-asset-slot>> the right-of-use asset, your right to use the item, and <<FOCUS:lease-liability-slot>> the lease liability, what you still owe. <<WRITE_TEXT:ROU asset: own line or tucked into owned-asset line + note|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> The right-of-use asset can sit on its own line, or be folded into the line you'd use if you actually owned that kind of asset. If you fold it in, you must say so in the notes. The lease liability works the same way: a separate line, or buried in another liability line with a note pointing to it. And if the right-of-use asset is really investment property, it lives inside investment property instead. <<SECTION:Profit and loss|id=sec-2>> Now the profit and loss. One lease, but it produces two very different expenses, and here's the rule that trips people up. Why split one lease into two separate expense lines instead of just calling it rent? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:P&L: depreciation of ROU asset shown separately from interest on lease liability|id=key-1>> Because the two pieces are economically different. <<FOCUS:depreciation-slot>> Depreciation spreads the cost of using the asset, while <<FOCUS:interest-slot>> the interest is a finance cost for borrowing. So you present <<FOCUS:depreciation-slot>> the depreciation charge on the right-of-use asset separately from <<FOCUS:interest-slot>> the interest expense on the lease liability. <<PAUSE:short>> And that interest isn't just any expense — it's a component of finance cost, so it must be presented separately within your finance costs. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Cash flows|id=sec-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> Last drawer, the cash flow statement. Every rupee you pay on the lease has to land in one of two bands. <<WRITE_KEY:Cash flows: principal + interest -> financing; short-term, low-value, variable -> operating|id=key-2>>The principal portion and the interest portion of your lease payments <<FOCUS:financing-band>> both go under financing activities. <<PAUSE:short>> But payments that never sat in the liability — short-term leases, low-value asset leases, and variable lease payments — those <<FOCUS:operating-band>> go under operating activities instead. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the whole topic is one habit: balance sheet holds the asset and the liability, profit and loss splits depreciation from interest, and cash flows send principal and interest to financing while the small leftover payments go to operating.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:21:lease_classification_scale>> If you rent a car for a weekend versus paying one off over five years until it's basically yours, should an accountant treat those two deals the same way? <<PAUSE:long>> Of course not — and that gap is the whole idea behind classifying leases. Every lease falls into exactly one of <<FOCUS:tipping-point>> two boxes, and one single question decides which. <<SECTION:Risks and rewards|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Owning something isn't just about holding the title. It comes with <<FOCUS:risks-rewards-bundle>> rewards, like using it and gaining if it holds value, and risks, like repairs and it wearing out. Picture all of that <<FOCUS:risks-rewards-bundle+bundle-label>> as one bundle. <<WRITE_KEY:Finance lease = transfers substantially all risks and rewards of ownership|id=key-1>> Here is the deciding question: does the lease hand <<FOCUS:tipping-point>> substantially all of that bundle over to the person renting the asset? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> If almost the entire bundle <<FOCUS:slide-arrow+lessee-side>> slides across to the lessee, the deal has crossed the line. We call that a <<FOCUS:finance-lease-label>> finance lease. <<PAUSE:short>> But if the owner keeps holding most of those risks and rewards, the bundle <<FOCUS:lessor-side+operating-lease-label>> stays on the lessor's side, and we call it an operating lease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Substance over form|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now, here's the trap. A contract might be titled 'rental agreement' — does that label settle whether it's an operating lease? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Judge by substance, not by the contract's name|id=key-2>> Not at all. We judge by what is really happening in the deal, not by what it's called. Substance beats form, every time. <<PAUSE:short>> So how do we actually tell when the bundle has crossed over? The standard gives us telltale signs. Watch what each one <<FOCUS:beam>> does to our scale. <<WRITE_TEXT:Ownership transfers, or a bargain purchase option|id=text-1>> If ownership transfers by the end, or there's a bargain price to buy it that's almost certain to be taken — the bundle clearly <<FOCUS:risks-rewards-bundle+lessee-side>> moves to the lessee. <<WRITE_TEXT:Most of the asset's life, or PV of payments ≈ fair value|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> If the lease runs for the major part of the asset's life, or the payments add up to nearly its full value, again — almost everything has shifted across. <<PAUSE:short>> And if the asset is so specialised that only the lessee can use it, who really bears its fate? The lessee. The <<FOCUS:finance-lease-label>> bundle has moved, so it's a finance lease. <<UNFOCUS>> So remember: two boxes, one question. If substantially all the risks and rewards move to the renter, it's a finance lease; if not, it's operating — and always judge the substance, never the label. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:22:lessor_books_split>> You own a <<FOCUS:underlying-asset>> delivery van and you rent it out. <<UNFOCUS>> Should that van still sit on your books as something you own, or have you really just turned it into a loan? <<PAUSE:long>> The answer depends entirely on one thing we settled last time: whether the lease is a <<FOCUS:finance-branch+operating-branch>> finance lease or an operating lease. <<SECTION:Finance lease|id=sec-1>> Take <<FOCUS:finance-branch>> the finance lease first. <<UNFOCUS>> Here, in substance, ownership has passed to the renter, even if your name is still on the paperwork. <<PAUSE:short>> So you stop showing the van as your asset. You derecognise it, and in its place you put <<FOCUS:lease-receivable>> a lease receivable. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Finance lease: drop the asset, show a receivable|id=text-1>> That receivable is measured at the net investment in the lease. <<UNFOCUS>> You no longer own equipment; you hold a financial claim, exactly like having lent out money. <<PAUSE:short>> And because it behaves like a loan, the income you earn is finance income, recognised so that you get a constant periodic rate of return on that net investment. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Operating lease|id=sec-2>> Now <<FOCUS:operating-branch>> the operating lease. <<UNFOCUS>> Here ownership has not really moved; you are just letting someone use your van for a while. So you <<FOCUS:asset-stays>> keep the van right there on your balance sheet, and you carry on depreciating it over its useful life, just as you always would. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Operating lease: keep the asset, depreciate it|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> The rent that comes in is recognised as income, normally spread evenly on a straight-line basis across the lease term. There is one more nice touch: any initial direct costs you spend to set up an operating lease get added to the carrying amount of the underlying asset. So why do the same physical van get treated in <<FOCUS:lease-receivable+asset-stays>> two completely opposite ways on your books? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Finance lease = receivable + finance income; Operating lease = keep asset + rental income|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Because accounting follows the substance. If you have effectively sold the van, you show a receivable and earn finance income. If you have merely lent it temporarily, you keep the van, depreciate it, and collect rent. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:23:dealer_lessor_split>> A car company leases you a car instead of selling it outright. So on day one, did they make a sale, or did they make a loan? The strange answer is: both, at the very same moment. <<FOCUS:asset-box>> Here is the asset the company built or bought to sell. <<UNFOCUS>> A normal shop would just sell it and book a profit. But this company is a manufacturer or dealer who also acts as a lessor, so it does something cleverer. <<SECTION:Two events at commencement|id=sec-1>> At the commencement date, the single transaction <<FOCUS:sale-branch+lease-branch>> splits into two branches. <<TRACE:commencement-line>> Watch the line: everything happens right here, on day one. The <<FOCUS:sale-branch>> first branch is a sale. The company hands over the asset's economic value, so it records revenue and a matching cost of sale, and <<FOCUS:selling-profit-marker>> the difference is selling profit, booked instantly. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> But hold on. If they sold it on day one, where does the lease come in? What keeps earning money over the next few years? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Dealer lessor books selling profit at day one AND finance income over the term|id=key-1>> The <<FOCUS:lease-branch>> second branch is the finance lease. The company holds a net investment in the lease, and that investment <<FOCUS:finance-income-stream>> earns finance income period after period, just like a loan. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So one transaction, two streams of profit. <<FOCUS:selling-profit-marker>> A one-off selling profit on day one, plus a <<FOCUS:finance-income-stream>> slow trickle of finance income over the lease term. <<SECTION:Measuring the sale|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now, how much revenue? You cannot just use the asking price. segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:24:disclosure_split>> A company's balance sheet shows it owns a fleet of trucks worth millions, and it's renting them all out, so why is that single number nowhere near enough to understand the business? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:main-statements-box>> The headline statements give you totals, but they don't tell you when the rent is coming in, how the value is changing, or how much profit was baked in on day one. <<SECTION:Why Disclosures Exist|id=sec-1>> That is exactly why <<FOCUS:disclosures-node>> we add disclosures: extra notes that sit alongside the main statements. <<UNFOCUS>> The whole objective is simple to say: these notes, together with the balance sheet, the profit and loss statement, and the cash flow statement, let a reader assess how leases affect the lessor's financial position, performance, and cash flows. <<PAUSE:short>> Now here is the clever part, and it is the one thing to hold onto: what you must disclose <<FOCUS:finance-branch+operating-branch>> depends on the kind of lease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Finance Lease Notes|id=sec-2>> For a finance lease, the lessor has effectively handed over the asset and is owed a stream of payments, so the disclosures circle around <<FOCUS:finance-detail>> the net investment in the lease. <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Finance lease -> net investment in the lease|id=text-1>>Concretely, the lessor discloses any selling profit or loss, the finance income earned on that net investment, and a detailed maturity analysis of the payments still to be received. They also explain any significant changes in the carrying amount of that net investment, so a reader can follow how the asset's recorded value is moving over time. <<SECTION:Operating Lease Notes|id=sec-3>> An operating lease is different: the lessor keeps the asset on its books, so <<FOCUS:operating-detail>> what matters most is the income it throws off. <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Operating lease -> lease income|id=text-2>>Here the lessor discloses its lease income, separating out variable lease payments that do not depend on an index or a rate, and gives the usual asset disclosures under the relevant property and equipment standards. So step back and look at <<FOCUS:finance-branch+operating-branch>> the two branches side by side: the same word, disclosure, but the content is steered entirely by whether the risks and rewards left the lessor or stayed with them. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Disclosures = notes that let readers assess lease effects on position, performance & cash flows|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> And remember the purpose tying it all together: these notes exist so that anyone reading the accounts can judge how leases shape the lessor's financial position, performance, and cash flows. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:25:sublease_chain>> What happens when you rent an apartment from a landlord, and then rent that very same apartment out to someone else? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Sublease|id=sec-1>> Suddenly you are stuck in the middle. You pay <<FOCUS:head-rent-arrow>> rent upward to your landlord, and <<FOCUS:sub-rent-arrow>> someone pays rent up to you. At the top is <<FOCUS:head-lessor>> the head lessor, the original owner you leased from. At the bottom is your new tenant, <<FOCUS:subtenant>> the subtenant. <<UNFOCUS>> You sit in between. When a company rents an asset and then leases it out again, accounting gives that middle role a name: <<FOCUS:intermediate-lessor>> the intermediate lessor. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Rent then sublet then you become the intermediate lessor, sitting between head lessor and subtenant|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So remember this position carefully. The intermediate lessor is the one <<FOCUS:intermediate-lessor+head-lessor+subtenant>> wedged between the head lessor above and the subtenant below. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the question that trips everyone up. When you classify your sublease as finance or operating, what asset do you actually compare it against? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:physical-asset>> Not the building. <<UNFOCUS>> You never owned the building. What you own is <<FOCUS:rou-asset>> the right to use it, granted by the head lease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Classify the sublease against the right-of-use asset, not the physical asset|id=key-2>> So the intermediate lessor classifies the sublease <<FOCUS:classify-link+rou-asset>> by looking at the right-of-use asset, treating that as if it were the underlying asset. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> There is one neat shortcut for the discount rate. If you cannot readily work out the interest rate implicit in the sublease, you simply borrow <<FOCUS:head-rent-arrow>> the rate you already use for the head lease. <<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term head lease then sublease is operating|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> And one special case to lock in: if the head lease was a short-term lease you treated under the short-term exemption, then your sublease is automatically classified as an operating lease. So always picture the chain: head lessor, you in the middle, subtenant, and remember you judge the sublease <<FOCUS:rou-asset>> against your right-of-use asset, never the bricks and mortar.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:26:saleback_flow>> A company sells its own office building for cash, and the very next morning everyone walks back into the exact same building to work. So did anything really get sold? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Sale and leaseback|id=sec-1>> This move has a name. The company that sells and then rents back <<FOCUS:seller-lessee-box>> is the seller-lessee, and the company that buys and then rents it out <<FOCUS:buyer-lessor-box>> is the buyer-lessor. <<WRITE_TEXT:Asset out, cash in|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Watch what flows. The <<TRACE:asset-arrow>> building goes from the seller to the buyer, and the <<TRACE:cash-arrow>> cash comes straight back the other way. <<PAUSE:short>> But the seller still needs that building, so the buyer immediately <<TRACE:lease-arrow>> leases the right to use it back to them. <<FOCUS:building-icon>> The desks never move. <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the question that decides everything. Was this actually a sale, or was the company just borrowing money with the building as security? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Sale only if it qualifies under Ind AS 115|id=key-1>> To answer that, we do not guess. We test the transfer against Ind AS one hundred fifteen, the standard on revenue from contracts with customers. Only if it passes that test do we call it a sale. <<PAUSE:short>> If it does not pass, then no real sale happened. The cash is simply a loan, and the building stays on the seller's books as if nothing changed. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:26:carrying_split_bar>> <<SECTION:When it is a genuine sale|id=sec-2>> Now suppose it does pass the test. Here is the subtle part. The seller sold the building, but kept the right to use it. So the seller did not give up the whole asset. Think of the building's <<FOCUS:full-carrying-bar>> old book value as one bar. Part of it represents <<FOCUS:retained-portion>> the rights the seller kept, and part represents the <<FOCUS:transferred-portion>> rights handed over to the buyer. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So how much gain does the seller get to book? Only on <<FOCUS:transferred-portion>> the slice they actually gave away, never on <<FOCUS:retained-portion>> the slice they kept using. The right-of-use asset equals the old book value scaled down to just the fraction of rights the seller kept. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{ROU asset} = \text{Previous carrying amount} \times \dfrac{\text{Rights retained}}{\text{Total asset}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:ROU = retained proportion of old carrying amount; gain only on rights transferred|id=key-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> The right-of-use asset is carried at that retained proportion of the old book value, and the seller recognises gain or loss only on the rights transferred to the buyer. <<PAUSE:short>> The gain you may recognise is the total gain scaled down to only the <<FOCUS:transferred-portion+gain-label>> portion of rights you actually transferred to the buyer. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Gain recognised} = \text{Total gain} \times \dfrac{\text{Rights transferred}}{\text{Total asset}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<UNFOCUS>> Meanwhile the buyer-lessor has the easy job. They record buying the asset under the normal standards, and account for the lease they granted using the lessor rules you already know. And one last guard. If the price was not fair value or the rent was not at market rates, you adjust, treating any shortfall as a prepayment and any excess as extra financing from the buyer. So the lesson holds together. First ask if it is really a sale under Ind AS one hundred fifteen, and if it is, recognise gain only on what you gave away, because you never truly let go of what you kept using. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: A lease that was perfectly fine yesterday suddenly has to be re-judged today, not because the contract changed one word, but because the rulebook underneath it did. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:27:sublease_chain>> <<SECTION:The Sandwich Position|id=sec-1>> To see why, picture a company that <<FOCUS:landlord-box>> rents a building from a landlord. That same company then turns around and <<FOCUS:subtenant-box>> rents the building out to someone else, so it sits squarely in the middle of two deals. <<WRITE_TEXT:Intermediate lessor = renter + renter-out|id=text-1>> We call this company <<FOCUS:intermediate-box>> the intermediate lessor, because it rents on one side and rents out on the other. The deal with the landlord <<FOCUS:head-lease-arrow>> is the head lease, and the deal with the new tenant <<FOCUS:sublease-arrow>> is the sublease. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, under the old standard, Ind AS seventeen, leases were sorted into two buckets, operating leases or finance leases, and a great many subleases landed in the operating bucket. So here is the honest question, when you move to the new standard, Ind AS one hundred sixteen, can you just leave those old operating subleases exactly where they were? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Re-test on Transition|id=sec-2>> No. On the date you first apply the new standard, you must take a fresh look at every ongoing sublease that used to be an operating lease and decide all over again. <<PAUSE:short>> And here is the clever part, you do not judge the sublease alone, you judge it against what is left of <<FOCUS:head-lease-arrow+sublease-arrow>> both the head lease and the sublease together. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Why both? Because if you have already handed almost the whole remaining life of the building to your subtenant, you have effectively passed on the risks and rewards of owning that right, and that smells like a finance lease, not an operating one. <<WRITE_KEY:Operating under Ind AS 17 to finance under Ind AS 116 = treat as a NEW finance lease at transition date|id=key-1>> So when a sublease that was operating now qualifies as a finance lease, you do not patch the old one, you <<FOCUS:reassess-marker>> treat it as a brand-new finance lease starting on the transition date. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Same building, new judgement|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Notice what never changed, the building, the landlord, the tenant, the words of the contract, all the same, only the rulebook shifted, and that re-test is the whole story of subleases on transition. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:28:transition_choice_flow>> Imagine your company has <<FOCUS:contract-pile>> signed three thousand contracts over the past twenty years. <<UNFOCUS>> The accounting rulebook just changed. Do you really have to re-read every single one? <<SECTION:Definition of lease on transition|id=sec-1>> Here is the situation. The old rulebook was called Ind AS seventeen. The new one is Ind AS one hundred sixteen, and it changed, just slightly, what actually counts as a lease. So when a company switches over, it hits <<FOCUS:decision-fork>> a fork in the road. <<WRITE_TEXT:Two choices on transition|id=text-1>> <<TRACE:path-reassess>> Down the first path, the company says yes: apply the brand new definition to <<FOCUS:reassess-box>> every single existing contract, with completely fresh eyes. <<UNFOCUS>> That means digging through hundreds or thousands of old agreements and re-checking each one. It is thorough, but it is an enormous amount of work. So here is the honest question: is there a way to avoid re-reading every old contract you ever signed? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Yes. <<TRACE:path-grandfather>> Down the second path, the standard gives <<FOCUS:grandfather-box>> a friendly shortcut. <<WRITE_KEY:You may choose NOT to reassess contracts not identified as leases under Ind AS 17|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> You can choose not to reassess contracts that were never identified as containing a lease under the old standard. <<PAUSE:short>> In plain terms: if a contract was not a lease under the old rules, you simply trust that and leave it alone. You do not put it through the new definition. <<PAUSE:short>> This shortcut has a name. Accountants call it <<FOCUS:grandfather-box>> a practical expedient — a permitted simplification that saves you from a mountain of work. <<WRITE_TEXT:Practical expedient = permitted shortcut|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> But notice the trade-off. If you take the shortcut, you carry your old conclusions forward, and the new definition only applies to contracts you sign on or after the transition date. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:reassess-box>> Choose the first path and you reassess everything; <<FOCUS:grandfather-box>> choose the second and you grandfather the past, applying fresh eyes only to new contracts. <<WRITE_KEY:Reassess all, OR carry forward old conclusions + new definition for new contracts|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the big idea is simple: the standard lets you trade completeness for effort. Re-check everything, or trust the past and look forward. Both are allowed, and the company picks.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:29:transition_two_paths>> A company has been renting buildings for years under the old rules. Tomorrow the rulebook changes. What does it do with all the leases it already signed? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It can't just throw out the past, and it can't pretend nothing happened. So the new standard, Ind AS one sixteen, hands the lessee <<FOCUS:decision-node>> a choice between two honest ways to cross over. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Two transition paths|id=sec-1>> The first path is the <<FOCUS:full-retro-branch+full-retro-box>> full retrospective approach. <<UNFOCUS>> Here you pretend Ind AS one sixteen was always in force, and you go back and redo every single period you're showing. Because you're reaching so far back into the past, you even have to lay out <<FOCUS:third-balance-sheet>> an extra third balance sheet, so a reader can see exactly where things stood at the earliest point. <<UNFOCUS>> It is thorough, but it is a mountain of work. <<WRITE_TEXT:Full retro = redo all periods + 3rd balance sheet|id=text-1>> The second path is the <<FOCUS:modified-retro-branch+modified-retro-box>> modified retrospective approach. <<UNFOCUS>> It refuses to restate the comparative periods at all. The past stays exactly as it was printed. Instead of touching the past, it gathers up the entire cumulative impact of switching and drops it as <<FOCUS:equity-adjustment>> one single adjustment to equity, right at the start of the year it first applies the standard. <<UNFOCUS>> We call that the date of initial application. <<PAUSE:short>> So <<FOCUS:decision-node>> here is the fork. <<UNFOCUS>> Same company, same leases, but two very different amounts of work. Which one would you reach for if you only cared about today's numbers? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The modified path, almost every time, because you skip rebuilding history. But now a sharper question hides inside it. If you are not redoing the past, how do you decide what the lease is worth on day one? <<SECTION:Measuring on day one|id=sec-2>> For what used to be an operating lease, you take only the payments still left to make, and you discount them back to today using the lessee's incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application. That discounted figure becomes the lease liability. <<WRITE_KEY:Lease liability = remaining payments, discounted at today's borrowing rate|id=key-1>> And the cumulative effect of all of this lands as a single adjustment to opening equity, not scattered across the old years. That is the whole spirit of the modified approach. <<PAUSE:short>> There is a neat shortcut for the asset side too. You may rebuild the right-of-use asset retrospectively, or simply set it equal to the lease liability, and you can make that call lease by lease. <<WRITE_KEY:Two paths: full retro redoes the past; modified retro adjusts opening equity|id=key-2>> So remember the fork. Full retrospective rewrites history and <<FOCUS:full-retro-box+third-balance-sheet>> needs a third balance sheet. Modified retrospective leaves history untouched and corrects everything with <<FOCUS:modified-retro-box+equity-adjustment>> one clean adjustment to equity on day one. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: Picture a company with three hundred old rental contracts, and a new rule that says every single one must now be re-calculated from scratch. Sounds like a nightmare, right? Except the rule-makers handed out a set of legal shortcuts so you don't have to. When the new lease standard arrives, all those leases that used to sit quietly off the balance sheet suddenly have to come on, as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. For one lease, that's annoying. For hundreds, it's an enormous amount of work. <<SECTION:Practical Expedients|id=sec-1>> So the standard says, fine, here are some friendly time-savers. We call them practical expedients, and the key idea is this. <<WRITE_KEY:Practical expedients = optional, lease-by-lease shortcuts on transition|id=key-1>> They are optional shortcuts you can apply lease by lease, letting you skip the most painful calculations. <<PAUSE:short>> Let me walk you through the most useful ones, because each shortcut kills a specific headache. The first headache is the discount rate. Normally every lease needs its own discount rate, the interest rate you use to bring future payments back to today's value. <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient A: one rate for similar leases|id=text-1>> The shortcut lets you apply a single rate to a whole bundle of leases that look reasonably alike, say all your photocopiers, instead of pricing each one separately. The next two shortcuts are about leases that are basically not worth the effort. If a lease ends within twelve months of the changeover date, you're allowed to just treat it as a short-term lease and not bring it onto the books at all. <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient C: skip leases ending within 12 months|id=text-2>> Why fully account for something that's about to expire? Here's one that sounds almost like cheating. Instead of doing a fresh impairment review to check if a lease has gone bad, you may simply rely on your earlier onerous-lease assessment. So which is the lazier, faster path here? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient B: reuse old onerous-lease test instead of impairment review|id=text-3>> Reusing the assessment you already did under the provisions standard, just before transition, and then nudging your right-of-use asset by that provision. You skip an entire fresh review. That's the time-saver. Two more quick ones. You can exclude initial direct costs, the little setup fees, from the value of your right-of-use asset. And you can use hindsight, meaning if a contract had an option to extend, you now already know whether it was actually extended, so use that knowledge instead of guessing. Now notice the pattern. <<WRITE_KEY:Each expedient trades precision for less work; you choose lease by lease|id=key-2>> Every single one of these trades a bit of accuracy for a lot less work, and crucially, you decide which to apply, and to which leases. <<PAUSE:short>> That choice matters, because these are optional. A company that wants cleaner numbers might skip a shortcut; one drowning in old contracts will grab every one it can. The shortcuts bend the workload, not the truth, by much. <<PAUSE:short>> So when you face a transition question, don't panic at three hundred leases. Ask, which expedients apply here, and watch the mountain of work shrink. That's the whole point of practical expedients. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:31:lessor_vs_lessee_impact>> A brand new accounting standard sweeps in, turns the renter's whole world upside down, and the landlord barely lifts a finger. How can the same rulebook leave one side almost untouched? Remember who's who. <<FOCUS:lessor-side>> The lessor is the party that owns an asset and rents it out; <<FOCUS:lessee-side>> the lessee is the one paying to use it. <<SECTION:Lessor on transition|id=sec-1>> For the lessee, Ind AS one sixteen forces a giant change: <<FOCUS:rou-asset>> a brand new right-of-use asset and <<FOCUS:lease-liability>> a lease liability land on the balance sheet. Now <<FOCUS:lessor-side>> look across to the lessor. <<UNFOCUS>> Almost nothing happens. <<WRITE_KEY:Lessor: no adjustment on transition (except 2 cases)|id=key-1>> As a general rule, a lessor <<FOCUS:lessor-tick>> makes no adjustments at all when moving from the old standard to the new one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Why so calm on the lessor's side? Because the old standard already split leases into finance and operating leases for lessors, and the new standard keeps that same split, so there is simply nothing to redo. But I said almost untouched. So where exactly does the lessor's quiet life get interrupted? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> In exactly two situations. <<FOCUS:exception-sublease>> First, subleases, where someone renting an asset turns around and rents it out to yet another party. Second, <<FOCUS:exception-slb>> sale-and-leaseback transactions, where you sell an asset and immediately lease it back. <<WRITE_TEXT:Exceptions: subleases & sale-and-leaseback|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Everywhere else, the lessor does nothing. So the headline to hold onto: on transition, a lessor makes no adjustments at all, except for subleases and sale-and-leaseback transactions. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:31:slb_transition_flow>> Let's zoom into that second exception, the sale-and-leaseback, because that's where students get tangled. <<SECTION:Sale-and-leaseback on transition|id=sec-2>> Picture a deal <<FOCUS:slb-start>> already sitting on the books under the old standard. The first question is how that old deal was classified: was it accounted for as <<FOCUS:branch-finance>> a sale plus a finance lease, or as <<FOCUS:branch-operating>> a sale plus an operating lease? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> If it was a sale plus finance lease, the path is gentle. The seller-lessee carries the leaseback forward exactly like any finance lease already in place, and any gain on the original sale just <<FOCUS:gain-amortise>> keeps amortising over the lease term. <<PAUSE:short>> If instead it was a sale plus operating lease, you treat the leaseback like any other operating lease, but with one tweak: you <<FOCUS:rou-adjust>> adjust the right-of-use asset for any deferred gains or losses tied to off-market terms sitting on the balance sheet just before transition. <<WRITE_STEP:Operating: adjust ROU asset for off-market deferred gains/losses|id=step-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the whole lesson collapses to one calm idea: the lessor mostly does nothing on transition, and only two special deals, subleases and sale-and-leasebacks, ask for any care at all. <<WRITE_KEY:Carry old leaseback forward; keep amortising the gain|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:32:value_move>> Here is a strange one: you are sitting on an asset on your balance sheet that, the moment you adopt a new accounting standard, simply has to vanish. <<SECTION:Where the asset came from|id=sec-1>> To see why, rewind. Years ago this company bought another whole business — a business combination — and that acquired business had operating leases running. One of those leases was a bargain: the rent locked in was cheaper than anything you could get in the market today. That favourable deal has real worth, so under Ind AS 103 you <<FOCUS:old-lease-asset-box>> recorded it as a separate asset. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Favourable lease = separate asset under Ind AS 103|id=text-1>> So before transition, the picture is simple: a standalone favourable-lease asset, sitting on its own, measured at its carrying amount. <<UNFOCUS>> Now Ind AS 116 arrives. It says every lease gets <<FOCUS:rou-asset-box>> a single right-of-use asset. <<UNFOCUS>> So a question lands: if the lease already created a separate favourable-terms asset, do we now double-count it alongside the new right-of-use asset? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No double-counting allowed. The rule is clean: <<FOCUS:derecognise-cross+old-lease-asset-box>> you derecognise that old favourable or unfavourable lease asset completely. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1 — Derecognise the old Ind AS 103 lease asset or liability|id=step-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> But — and this is the heart of it — the value does not just evaporate. Watch where it goes. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 2 — Adjust the right-of-use asset by the same amount|id=step-2>> That same carrying amount is <<TRACE:value-arrow>> added straight onto the right-of-use asset. The value simply moves home — <<FOCUS:old-lease-asset-box>> out of the separate box, <<FOCUS:rou-asset-box>> into the right-of-use asset. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And it works both ways. If the old lease had been a bad deal — paying more than market — you would have carried an unfavourable lease liability instead. Same move: derecognise it, and reduce the right-of-use asset by that amount. <<WRITE_KEY:Old lease asset/liability is derecognised; its amount adjusts the right-of-use asset at the date of initial application|id=key-1>> So nothing is lost and nothing is invented. The total value on the balance sheet is exactly the same — it has just been <<FOCUS:rou-asset-box>> re-housed inside the right-of-use asset. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is the whole rule. One asset vanishes from its own line, and reappears, to the penny, baked into the right-of-use asset — all on the date you first apply the new standard.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:33:scope_boundary_map>> You can sign a lease for the land that sits on top of an oilfield and follow the leasing rulebook — but sign a lease for the oil underneath that very same land, and the rulebook hands it back and tells you to look elsewhere. <<SECTION:Scope of Ind AS 116|id=sec-1>> So let's <<TRACE:scope-circle>> draw the boundary. Inside this circle live all the agreements the leasing standard, Ind AS 116, actually governs. <<WRITE_KEY:Ind AS 116 applies to ALL leases except leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, gas and similar non-regenerative resources|id=key-1>> Here is the one rule that does all the work: the standard applies to all leases, with <<FOCUS:carve-out-arrow>> a single carve-out — leases to explore for, or use, minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources. <<PAUSE:short>> Now picture our company, Entity X, holding <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right+surface-land-right+pipeline-right>> three different rights over the same patch of ground. <<UNFOCUS>> The question is honest — which of them actually sit inside that circle? <<PAUSE:long>> Take the first right: the right to explore for, and <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right>> pull oil out of, oilfield Y for twenty-five years. <<UNFOCUS>> Watch where it goes. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Oil extraction right = carved OUT|id=text-1>> The oil is a <<FOCUS:oil-deposit>> non-regenerative resource — once you pump it out, it's gone, it doesn't grow back. That is exactly the carve-out, so this right is <<TRACE:carve-out-arrow>> pushed straight outside the boundary. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Notice what we did NOT exclude: only the resource itself. So what about the second right — <<FOCUS:surface-land-right>> the surface lease, the right just to walk onto and use the land that happens to sit above the oil? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Surface lease = INSIDE scope|id=text-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> That is a lease of land, plain and simple. The land regenerates nothing and gets extracted from nothing — it's just ground you're renting. It <<FOCUS:surface-land-right+scope-circle>> stays firmly inside Ind AS 116. And the third right — <<FOCUS:pipeline-right>> laying water pipelines over the neighbouring land, because Entity X needs water to extract the oil. <<UNFOCUS>> The water is for the oil, but the lease is over the land. <<WRITE_TEXT:Pipeline land lease = INSIDE scope|id=text-3>> Renting the surface of adjacent land is, once again, just a lease of land. It supports the oil business, but it is not a lease of the non-regenerative resource. So it <<FOCUS:pipeline-right+scope-circle>> also sits inside the circle. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Entity X obtains three rights, and we need to decide which fall within the scope of Ind AS 116. <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right>> Right (a) is the rights to explore for oil and use oil from oilfield Y for twenty-five years. <<FOCUS:surface-land-right>> Right (b) is the right to access the land containing the oil, called a surface lease. And <<FOCUS:pipeline-right>> right (c) is the right to lay water pipelines over land adjacent to the oilfield, because water is needed in the extraction process. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Which of rights (a), (b), (c) obtained by Entity X fall within the scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> We start from the scope rule. Ind AS 116 paragraph three excludes leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources. So the test is simple: does the lease give the right to explore for or extract the oil itself? <<WRITE_STEP:Paragraph 3 excludes leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, gas and similar non-regenerative resources.|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now apply it. Right (a) is a right to explore for and use the oil directly, so it falls squarely <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right+carve-out-arrow>> inside the exclusion. <<UNFOCUS>> Right (b), the surface lease, only gives access to the area where the oil lies, but it exists to reach and extract that oil, so it too is tied to the oil itself. That means <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right+surface-land-right>> rights (a) and (b) are not covered by Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_STEP:(a) explore/use oil and (b) surface lease relate to the oil itself, exclusion applies.|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Right (c) is different. <<FOCUS:pipeline-right>> Laying water pipelines is about transporting water used in the extraction process. <<UNFOCUS>> It does not give a right to explore for, or extract, or use the oil. Because it relates to the extraction process rather than the oil itself, it does not fall in the paragraph three exclusion, so <<FOCUS:pipeline-right+scope-circle>> right (c) is covered by Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_STEP:(c) water pipelines support the extraction process, not the oil itself, so the standard applies.|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> And the answer is: rights (a) and (b) are not covered by Ind AS 116, while right (c) is covered by Ind AS 116 because it relates to the extraction process, not to exploring for or extracting the oil itself. <<WRITE_ANSWER:(a) and (b): outside Ind AS 116. (c): within Ind AS 116.|id=ex-ans-1>> You've seen this yourself — think about the toll road you drive on, or the data cables running under your street. The company laying that infrastructure usually doesn't own the land; they pay the landowner for the right to run pipes or cables across it for years. That's the very same situation as Entity X laying its water pipelines. <<WRITE_TEXT:pipeline right-of-way = inside the standard|id=ext-1>> It supports the work, but it isn't a right to explore for or extract oil, so the leasing standard applies to it. Here's something wild about this: the oil you pump out of the ground today took tens of millions of years to form, and on any human timescale it never comes back. That's literally what non-regenerative means. And that permanence is exactly why the standard singles out rights to explore for or extract oil, gas, and minerals. <<WRITE_KEY:non-regenerative resources → excluded from the lease standard|id=ext-key-2>> Because once the resource is consumed it's truly gone, those rights are deliberately pushed outside the leasing standard. <<WRITE_KEY:Carve-out = the resource itself; land leases above/around it stay IN|id=key-2>> See the pattern? Two of three rights are inside, and the only one excluded is the one that <<FOCUS:oil-extraction-right>> touches the oil itself. The carve-out is about the <<FOCUS:oil-deposit+ground>> non-regenerative resource, never about the land it lies beneath. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So next time a lease lands on your desk near an oilfield, ask one question: am I leasing the resource, or just the land? Lease the land and you're inside Ind AS 116; lease the oil and you read a different standard entirely. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:34:scope_decision_flow>> A company gets the exclusive right to run an entire country's air navigation system for ten whole years, and yet, surprisingly, that contract is not a lease. Let me show you why. <<SECTION:Scoping a contract under Ind AS 116|id=sec-1>> Here is <<FOCUS:contract-box>> the contract on the table. <<UNFOCUS>> A private company, Entity X, signs with a Transport Ministry to operate the system that guides airplanes, upgrade it, and charge users at rates it negotiates freely, with no price cap. Your instinct says lease, because Ind AS 116 says <<FOCUS:ind-as-116-gate>> apply this standard to all leases. <<UNFOCUS>> And that word, all, feels airtight. <<PAUSE:short>> But the standard has carve-outs. One of them quietly <<FOCUS:exclusion-branch>> diverts a whole class of contracts out of scope: service concession arrangements that fall under Appendix D of Ind AS 115. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So before we ever call this a lease, we must ask: is it actually one of those service concessions hiding in disguise? <<PAUSE:long>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Service concession needs BOTH tests|id=text-1>> Appendix D gives two conditions, and crucially, you need both of them to be true. The first is about price. <<PAUSE:short>> Test one: <<FOCUS:price-control-test>> does the grantor control or regulate at what price the operator serves users? <<UNFOCUS>> Here the Ministry sets no price cap at all. Entity X negotiates rates directly and freely. <<PAUSE:short>> And that single fact breaks the whole thing. With no price control by the grantor, <<FOCUS:not-concession-result>> the first condition fails, and a service concession needs both conditions. <<PAUSE:short>> The second test, about the grantor <<FOCUS:residual-interest-test>> keeping a significant residual interest in the system at the end, no longer even matters, because one failed test already settles it. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Entity X is a private sector entity, and it enters a contract with the grantor, the Transport Ministry of Country S, to acquire the right to operate the civil air navigation system. Under the contract, the grantor provides the air navigation system, and X is required to upgrade the system. X charges users based on rates negotiated directly with individual users, there is no price-cap mechanism imposed by the grantor, and the contract period is ten years. The question is whether this contract falls within the scope of Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: X (private) operates Country S air navigation system for grantor (Transport Ministry); X sets prices, no price-cap, 10-year term — within scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by checking the test for a service concession arrangement. Such an arrangement requires the grantor to control the services, the recipients, and the price, and to control any significant residual interest in the infrastructure. Here many of those features are present, but the crucial one fails: the grantor does not control prices, because X negotiates rates directly with users and there is no price-cap. <<WRITE_STEP:1. Service concession test: grantor must control services, recipients, price + significant residual interest|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:2. Here grantor does NOT control prices (X negotiates directly, no price-cap) -> service concession test fails|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is: because the grantor does not control prices, <<FOCUS:not-concession-result>> this is not a service concession arrangement, so it falls outside Appendix D of Ind AS 115. Therefore the right to use the air navigation system is <<FOCUS:back-into-116-arrow>> within the scope of Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Grantor doesn't control prices -> not a service concession -> the contract is within the scope of Ind AS 116|id=ex-ans-1>> You've driven this yourself — a private company builds and runs a toll highway, but the government dictates the exact toll they can charge. <<UNFOCUS>> That price cap is the government keeping control of the service, which is exactly the first condition for a service concession arrangement. In our question, Entity X negotiates prices freely with no cap, so that grip is gone — and the whole classification flips back to Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_TEXT:Govt sets toll = price control = condition 1|id=ext-1>> Something wild about this: the air navigation system in our question is guiding thousands of planes through the sky right now, yet the entire accounting answer turns on one small detail — whether the grantor controls the price. Because Entity X sets its own rates with no cap, that single missing condition pulls this giant public system out of service concession accounting and straight into Ind AS 116. One word, the 'and' between two conditions, decides everything. So the exclusion does not catch this contract. It is not a service concession, which means it <<FOCUS:back-into-116-arrow>> falls right back into the scope of Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_KEY:Rule out service concession (both Appendix D tests) before applying Ind AS 116|id=key-1>> So remember the order of thinking: Ind AS 116 covers all leases, except service concessions, and a service concession demands <<FOCUS:price-control-test+residual-interest-test>> both price control by the grantor and a residual interest. <<UNFOCUS>> Fail either one, and the exclusion doesn't apply. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:35:control_flow_concession>> A company signs a contract, pays for the trains, and runs them every single day for fifteen years — and yet, on its books, there is no lease at all. How can that be? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:The set-up|id=sec-1>> Here is our cast. <<FOCUS:entity-y+rolling-stock>> Entity Y owns the rolling stock — the trains and equipment. <<FOCUS:operator-x+payment-arrow>> Operator X pays Entity Y to use them and runs the actual service. <<UNFOCUS>> But Operator X did not just go into business for itself. X holds a <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> service concession from Grantor G to run a public rail service for fifteen years. <<UNFOCUS>> Now, normally, if you pay to use an identified asset, you ask one simple question to decide if it is a lease: do you control the use of that asset? <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Control = decide how & for what purpose|id=text-1>> And control is not just touching the asset. Control means you decide how it is used and for what purpose — you direct the use. <<PAUSE:short>> So watch the payment. Operator X does pay Entity Y for using the rolling stock — <<TRACE:payment-arrow>> money flows this way. <<UNFOCUS>> Paying looks like a lease. So who actually decides how these trains run — when they run, and what passengers are charged? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Where control really sits|id=sec-2>> It is not Operator X. <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> Grantor G sets the timetable the trains must follow and regulates the price X can charge passengers. <<UNFOCUS>> G directs the use. Look at <<TRACE:control-arrow>> where the control arrow lands. It passes <<FOCUS:operator-x>> straight through Operator X and <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> stops at Grantor G. <<UNFOCUS>> X holds the trains, but X does not direct them. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No right to direct use = not a lease under Ind AS 116|id=key-1>> And that settles it. Because Operator X <<FOCUS:no-lease-stamp>> never gets the right to direct the use, X's contract with Entity Y is not a lease under Ind AS 116. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. Operator X enters into a service concession arrangement with Grantor G to operate a rail service for fifteen years, and this arrangement falls within the scope of Appendix D, Service Concession Arrangements, of Ind AS one fifteen. To run the service, X leases the infrastructure, the rolling stock, from Entity Y, the lessor, where the useful life of the rolling stock is twenty-five years, and X has the obligation to pay the lessor. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Is X's lease of rolling stock from Y within the scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>> Now look at who actually controls the use of that rolling stock. During the concession period, <<FOCUS:grantor-g+rolling-stock>> Grantor G controls the services X delivers, G sets the timetable to which the rolling stock must be operated and regulates the price that X charges passengers, and at the end of the concession G has an option to acquire the rolling stock or otherwise direct its use. <<WRITE_STEP:G sets timetable + regulates price + holds end-of-concession option on rolling stock|id=ex-step-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Appendix D of Ind AS one fifteen states that the operator does not have the right to control the use of the infrastructure; it merely has access to operate it on behalf of the grantor. Since X does not control the use of the rolling stock, the contract <<FOCUS:no-lease-stamp>> is not a lease within the scope of Ind AS one sixteen. <<WRITE_STEP:Per Appendix D, X does NOT control use of the infrastructure|id=ex-step-2>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:The contract of X with Y is NOT within the scope of Ind AS 116|id=ex-ans-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> You've seen this yourself with food delivery riders. A rider might use a scooter that the delivery platform owns, driving it every single shift. But the platform sets the routes, fixes the delivery fees, and can pull that scooter back whenever it likes. Sound familiar? That's exactly Operator X with the trains. The rider uses the asset every day, but the platform calls the shots, so there's no control, and without control there's no lease. Here's something wild about this. A huge number of the world's busiest toll roads, airports, and metro lines run on exactly this kind of arrangement. A private operator runs that public infrastructure for twenty, thirty, even forty years, collecting fees the whole time, yet it never sits on their balance sheet as their own property. <<WRITE_KEY:Concession operator runs it, never controls it|id=ext-key-1>> That's the same Appendix D logic from our question. The operator just has access to operate, following the grantor's terms. No control means it isn't theirs, and it isn't a lease. This is why the rolling stock sits inside the service concession rules of Appendix D, not as a leased asset of Operator X. The same trains, but a completely different accounting home. <<WRITE_TEXT:Payment alone never makes a lease|id=text-2>> So the lesson is sharp: paying for an asset is never enough. Lease accounting follows the right to direct the use — and here that right <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> belongs to the Grantor.

Grantor G sets the timetable the trains must follow and regulates the price X can charge passengers. G directs the use. <<TRACE:control-arrow>> <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> Look at where the control arrow lands. It passes straight through Operator X and stops at Grantor G. X holds the trains, but X does not direct them. <<POINT:grantor-g>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No right to direct use = not a lease under Ind AS 116|id=key-1>>And that settles it. Because Operator X never gets the right to direct the use, X's contract with Entity Y is not a lease under Ind AS 116. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. Operator X enters into a service concession arrangement with Grantor G to operate a rail service for fifteen years, and this arrangement falls within the scope of Appendix D, Service Concession Arrangements, of Ind AS one fifteen. To run the service, X leases the infrastructure, the rolling stock, from Entity Y, the lessor, where the useful life of the rolling stock is twenty-five years, and X has the obligation to pay the lessor. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Is X's lease of rolling stock from Y within the scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>> Now look at who actually controls the use of that rolling stock. During the concession period, Grantor G controls the services X delivers, G sets the timetable to which the rolling stock must be operated and regulates the price that X charges passengers, and at the end of the concession G has an option to acquire the rolling stock or otherwise direct its use. <<WRITE_STEP:G sets timetable + regulates price + holds end-of-concession option on rolling stock|id=ex-step-1>> Appendix D of Ind AS one fifteen states that the operator does not have the right to control the use of the infrastructure; it merely has access to operate it on behalf of the grantor. Since X does not control the use of the rolling stock, the contract is not a lease within the scope of Ind AS one sixteen. <<WRITE_STEP:Per Appendix D, X does NOT control use of the infrastructure|id=ex-step-2>><<WRITE_ANSWER:The contract of X with Y is NOT within the scope of Ind AS 116|id=ex-ans-1>> You've seen this yourself with food delivery riders. A rider might use a scooter that the delivery platform owns, driving it every single shift. But the platform sets the routes, fixes the delivery fees, and can pull that scooter back whenever it likes. Sound familiar? That's exactly Operator X with the trains. The rider uses the asset every day, but the platform calls the shots, so there's no control, and without control there's no lease. Here's something wild about this. A huge number of the world's busiest toll roads, airports, and metro lines run on exactly this kind of arrangement. A private operator runs that public infrastructure for twenty, thirty, even forty years, collecting fees the whole time, yet it never sits on their balance sheet as their own property. <<WRITE_KEY:Concession operator runs it, never controls it|id=ext-key-1>> That's the same Appendix D logic from our question. The operator just has access to operate, following the grantor's terms. No control means it isn't theirs, and it isn't a lease. <<FOCUS:rolling-stock>> This is why the rolling stock sits inside the service concession rules of Appendix D, not as a leased asset of Operator X. The same trains, but a completely different accounting home. <<FOCUS:control-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Payment alone never makes a lease|id=text-2>>So the lesson is sharp: paying for an asset is never enough. Lease accounting follows the right to direct the use — and here that right belongs to the Grantor.

lesson_plans.title: Ind AS 116 — Leases: Why the Rules Changed

hook.text: Imagine a company paying to use a fifty-story building for fifteen years — and you, reading their balance sheet, would barely know the building existed.

crucial_facts: Ind AS 116 forces lessees to show what they rent — both the right to use the asset and the obligation to pay — right on the balance sheet.
Ind AS 116 replaces the old standard Ind AS 17, and it changes the rules mainly for lessees, the ones who rent.

diagrams.purpose: Show that the same lease that was invisible under the old rules now appears as both an asset and a liability on the lessee's balance sheet under Ind AS 116.

required_elements.description: Left panel: a simple balance sheet under the old Ind AS 17 with the leased building absent, only a small footnote tag hinting at it.
A tiny footnote tag at the bottom of the old balance sheet reading 'lease — see notes', representing the off-balance-sheet treatment.
Right panel: a balance sheet under Ind AS 116 with two new entries clearly visible.
An asset-side entry labelled 'Right-of-use asset' on the new balance sheet.
A liability-side entry labelled 'Lease liability' on the new balance sheet.
A label marking that this balance sheet belongs to the lessee, the renting party.

choreography.narration: Imagine a company paying to use a fifty-story building for fifteen years, and you, reading their balance sheet, would barely know the building existed.

<<SECTION:What is a lease?|id=sec-1>>First, let's be clear what a lease even is. It's an arrangement where one party pays to use something — a building, a machine, a vehicle — that belongs to someone else, for a period of time.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Lessee = uses asset. Lessor = owns it.|id=text-1>>The party who uses the asset is the lessee, and the party who owns it and rents it out is the lessor. Keep your eye on the lessee — that's where the action is.
Here is the strange part. Under the old rules, this expensive building the company rented for years would often hide away in the footnotes.
So if a company can pay for fifteen years to use a building, why wouldn't that obligation show up plainly on the balance sheet for everyone to see?
That is exactly the gap the new standard, Ind AS one hundred sixteen, was written to close.

<<WRITE_KEY:Lessee now records a Right-of-use asset AND a Lease liability|id=key-1>>Now watch. The standard says the lessee must record two new things: the right to use the asset, and the promise to pay for it.
On one side, the right-of-use asset — what the company gets to use. On the other side, the lease liability — what the company owes for using it.
<<SECTION:Replacing the old standard|id=sec-2>>To make this the rule, Ind AS one hundred sixteen replaces the older standard, Ind AS seventeen, on leases.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Effective from 1 April 2019|id=text-2>>And it took effect for reporting periods beginning on or after the first of April, two thousand nineteen.
Notice that almost all of the big changes land on the lessee — the one renting. The lessor's accounting stays largely the same.

<<WRITE_KEY:Ind AS 116 brings leases onto the balance sheet|id=key-2>>So the whole point is this: the things a company rents no longer hide in the footnotes — Ind AS one hundred sixteen brings them onto the balance sheet, where everyone can see both the asset and the obligation.

lesson_plans.title: The Scope of Ind AS 116: Which Leases Are In, Which Are Out

hook.text: You sign a contract to rent something for a few years. Does the leasing standard automatically apply? Surprisingly — not always.

crucial_facts: If a contract meets the definition of a lease, Ind AS one hundred sixteen applies — unless it falls into one of five specific carve-outs handled by other standards.

The five exclusions are: minerals and oil exploration, biological assets, service concession arrangements, intellectual property licences granted by a lessor, and certain licensing rights held by a lessee.

diagrams.purpose: Show that every lease contract enters the standard, but five labelled exclusions get filtered out to other standards — making the boundary of scope concrete and visual.

required_elements.description: A wide box at the top labelled 'Contracts meeting the definition of a lease' — the entry point.
