A funnel or gate in the middle representing the scope test of Ind AS 116.
A box at the bottom labelled 'Ind AS 116 applies' where in-scope leases land.
A side branch labelled 'Minerals, oil, natural gas exploration'.
A side branch labelled 'Biological assets (Ind AS 41)'.
A side branch labelled 'Service concession arrangements (Ind AS 115)'.
A side branch labelled 'IP licences granted by lessor (Ind AS 115)'.
A side branch labelled 'Licensing rights held by lessee, e.g. films, patents (Ind AS 38)'.

choreography.narration: You sign a contract to rent something for a few years. Does the leasing standard automatically apply? Surprisingly, not always.

<<SECTION:Scope of Ind AS 116|id=sec-1>>When we talk about the scope of an accounting standard, we just mean its boundaries: which contracts the rule covers, and which ones it leaves to somebody else.
Here is the headline. If a contract meets the definition of a lease, then Ind AS one hundred sixteen generally applies, and its scope is broadly the same as the older standard, Ind AS seventeen.
So back to our question: does the standard always apply to a lease? The honest answer is, almost always, but there is a small list of deliberate exceptions.

<<WRITE_KEY:A lease is in scope of Ind AS 116 unless it is one of 5 carve-outs|id=key-1>>These exceptions are carved out on purpose, because another standard already handles them better. There are five of them.
First, leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas, and similar non-regenerative resources. Digging the earth for oil is its own world, so it falls out here.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Exclusions: minerals, biological assets|id=text-1>>Second, leases of biological assets held by a lessee, like living plants and animals. Those go to the agriculture standard, Ind AS forty one.
Third, service concession arrangements, the kind where a government lets a company run a toll road or an airport. Those belong to the revenue standard, Ind AS one hundred fifteen.
Fourth, when a lessor grants licences of its intellectual property, that is treated as revenue under Ind AS one hundred fifteen, not as a lease.

<<WRITE_TEXT:plus service concessions, IP licences, film/patent rights|id=text-2>>And fifth, rights a lessee holds under licensing agreements for things like motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents, and copyrights. Those sit in the intangible assets standard, Ind AS thirty eight.
There is one gentle flexibility. For intangible assets other than that fifth category, a lessee may choose to apply this standard, but is not required to.

So remember the shape of it: every lease falls inside Ind AS one hundred sixteen, except five carve-outs — minerals and oil, biological assets, service concessions, intellectual property licences from a lessor, and licensing rights held by a lessee.

lesson_plans.title: The Recognition Exemption: When You Can Skip the Paperwork

hook.text: What if a company could legally choose to keep certain leases completely off its balance sheet — no asset, no liability, nothing?

crucial_facts: A short-term lease is one with a lease term of twelve months or less at commencement, but a lease with a purchase option can never be short-term.
The short-term exemption must be applied to a whole class of assets together, while the low-value exemption is chosen lease by lease.

choreography.narration: What if a company could legally choose to keep certain leases completely off its balance sheet — no asset, no liability, nothing at all?
Normally, the rule is strict: when you lease something, you must record a right-of-use asset and a matching lease liability on your books, and that's a lot of accounting work.

<<SECTION:Recognition Exemption|id=sec-1>>So the standard offers a shortcut, called the recognition exemption — for two specific kinds of leases, the lessee, the one renting the asset, can simply skip all that recording.
<<WRITE_KEY:Two exemptions: short-term leases and low-value leases|id=key-1>>The two kinds are short-term leases, and leases where the underlying asset is of low value.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term = 12 months or less at start|id=text-1>>Let's nail down the first one. A short-term lease is simply a lease that, at the moment it commences, has a term of twelve months or less.
So renting a piece of equipment for just six months — that comfortably qualifies as short-term.
But here's the catch that trips people up: what happens if that six-month lease also gives you the option to buy the asset at the end?

<<WRITE_KEY:Purchase option means never short-term|id=key-2>>Then it is never a short-term lease — no matter how short it is. A purchase option signals you really intend to own the asset, so the shortcut is off the table.

<<SECTION:Low-value leases|id=sec-2>>The second kind is the low-value lease — think of a laptop or an office phone — something you can use on its own, that isn't tightly bound up with your bigger, more valuable assets.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term: by class. Low-value: lease by lease|id=text-2>>Now here's a subtle but important difference in how you apply them.
The short-term exemption is all-or-nothing for a whole class of assets — choose it for your delivery vans, and it applies to every short-term van lease consistently.
The low-value exemption is far more flexible: you decide lease by lease, picking and choosing for each individual low-value asset.
And whichever exemption you use, you must disclose it — so anyone reading the financial statements knows these leases were deliberately kept off the books.

lesson_plans.title: Identifying a Lease: The Gatekeeper Question

hook.text: You rent a parking spot in a garage where you can park in any free space, and you rent a specific named spot, spot forty-seven, just for you. One of these is a lease and one is not. Which is which?

crucial_facts: A contract is, or contains, a lease only if it conveys the right to CONTROL the use of an IDENTIFIED asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration.
You make this lease assessment once, at inception, and you only reassess it if the terms and conditions of the contract actually change.

diagrams.purpose: Show the chain of questions that decides whether control of an identified asset has passed to the customer, so the abstract definition becomes a concrete test.

required_elements.description: Top decision box reading 'Is there an identified asset?' with Yes and No branches.
Second decision box reading 'Does the customer get substantially all the economic benefits from using the asset?'
Third decision box reading 'Does the customer have the right to direct how and for what purpose the asset is used?'
Green terminal box reading 'The contract IS or CONTAINS a lease.'
Grey terminal box reading 'The contract does NOT contain a lease.'
A bracket grouping the economic-benefits box and the direct-use box together, labelled 'CONTROL'.

choreography.narration: You rent a parking spot in a garage where you can park in any free space, and you rent a specific named spot, spot forty-seven, just for you. One of these is a lease and one is not. Which is which?
<<SECTION:Identifying a lease|id=sec-1>>That puzzle is the single most important question in all of lease accounting, because everything else hangs on the answer.
If a contract is a lease, you must follow a whole set of special accounting rules. If it is not, you do not. So this one decision is the gatekeeper for everything that follows.

<<WRITE_KEY:Lease = right to CONTROL an IDENTIFIED asset for a period, for consideration|id=key-1>>Here is the definition the standard gives us. A contract is, or contains, a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset, for a period of time, in exchange for payment.
Let us break that into three plain questions. First: is there an identified asset?
<<WRITE_TEXT:Identified = a specific, named asset|id=text-1>>An identified asset is a specific one, like spot forty-seven, not just any spot from a pool the supplier can swap around at will.
If there is no identified asset, we stop right here. No lease.
<<SECTION:Control|id=sec-2>>But an identified asset alone is not enough. The customer must also control it. And control has two parts.
Second question: does the customer get substantially all the economic benefits from using that asset over the period?
Third question: does the customer get to direct how and for what purpose the asset is used? In other words, who calls the shots day to day?
When the answer to all three is yes, the customer truly controls the asset, and the contract is, or contains, a lease.
So back to our puzzle: which parking arrangement is the lease?

<<WRITE_ANSWER:Named spot 47 = lease; any free space = not a lease|id=ans-1>>Spot forty-seven is the lease. It is identified, you get all its benefit, and you decide when to park there. The any-free-space deal fails the very first test, because there is no identified asset.

<<WRITE_KEY:Assess once at inception; reassess only if terms change|id=key-2>>One last thing about timing. You run this test once, at the very inception of the contract. After that, you do not keep second-guessing it. You reassess only if the actual terms and conditions of the contract change.

lesson_plans.title: Identified Assets: The First Hurdle of a Lease

hook.text: If you pay a company to ship your goods, but they get to pick whichever truck is free that day, are you really leasing a truck?

crucial_facts: A contract contains a lease only if it relates to an identified asset.
An asset can be identified either explicitly, by being named in the contract, or implicitly, by being the only asset made available to fulfil it.

choreography.narration: If you pay a company to ship your goods, but they get to pick whichever truck is free that day, are you really leasing a truck?
<<SECTION:Identified Assets|id=sec-1>>Hold that thought, because it points straight at the very first test any contract must pass before we can call it a lease.
<<WRITE_KEY:A lease exists only if there is an identified asset|id=key-1>>Here is the rule: a contract contains a lease only if it relates to an identified asset.
Think about why that has to be true. A lease is the right to use a specific thing, so if there is no particular thing at the heart of the deal, there is simply nothing to lease.
So back to our trucks: if the shipping company keeps a whole fleet and just sends whichever one is free, you never had a specific truck, so you don't have a lease at all.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Two ways to identify: explicit or implicit|id=text-1>>Now, how do we actually know if an asset is identified? There are exactly two routes.
The first route is explicit specification. This is the obvious one, where the contract literally names or describes the asset.
Picture a rental agreement that says you get the delivery van with a particular registration number, or the office on the third floor. It is spelled out in black and white.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Implicit = the only asset available to fulfil the deal|id=text-2>>The second route is implicit specification. Here the contract never names the asset, but only one asset can possibly do the job.
Imagine a supplier with a single specialised crane at one site. Even if the contract never mentions it by name, that crane is implicitly identified the moment it's made available to you.

<<WRITE_KEY:Identified = named explicitly OR the only one available implicitly|id=key-2>>So an asset is identified either explicitly, by being named, or implicitly, by being the only asset available to fulfil the contract.
Get this first hurdle right, and remember it every time: no identified asset means no lease, and you must check whether it was pinned down explicitly or implicitly.

lesson_plans.title: Substantive Substitution Rights: When a Named Asset Still Isn't "Yours"

hook.text: Your contract names one specific machine, serial number and all — and yet you might still not have a lease. How can naming the exact asset not be enough?

crucial_facts: A supplier's substitution right kills the lease only if it is substantive: the supplier can practically swap the asset throughout the period of use AND profits from doing so.
If you can't realistically identify which asset the customer is using, there is no identified asset, and so there is no lease.

diagrams.purpose: Show the two-gate test that decides whether a supplier's substitution right is substantive and therefore destroys the identified asset.

required_elements.description: A box labelled 'Contract names a specific asset' at the top, representing the starting point.
First decision diamond: 'Can the supplier practically swap it throughout the period of use?'
Second decision diamond below the first: 'Does the supplier benefit economically from swapping?'
Right-hand terminal box: 'Substantive right -> no identified asset -> no lease'.
Bottom terminal box: 'Not substantive -> asset is identified -> lease can exist'.
Arrow labelled YES from the practical gate to the economic gate.
Arrow labelled YES from the economic gate to the no-lease outcome.
Arrows labelled NO from either gate down to the identified-asset outcome.

choreography.narration: Your contract names one specific machine, serial number and all, and yet you might still not have a lease. How can naming the exact asset not be enough?

<<SECTION:Substantive substitution rights|id=sec-1>>Here's the catch. A lease needs an identified asset, something the customer is genuinely tied to. But suppose the supplier can quietly wheel that machine away and roll in any other one whenever it suits them.
If the supplier holds that swapping power, then you were never really tied to that one machine at all. The asset stops being identified, and without an identified asset, there is simply no lease.
But hold on, does every little swap clause destroy a lease? Surely not, or almost no contract would ever count.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Right must be SUBSTANTIVE, not just on paper|id=text-1>>And it doesn't. The standard says the supplier's right to substitute only counts if it is substantive, which means real in practice, not just words buried in the fine print.
Substantive means two things must both be true. So picture two gates the supplier has to pass through before their swap right matters.

Gate one, the practical ability. Can the supplier actually swap the asset throughout the period of use? If alternative assets aren't readily available, or it would be a huge hassle, the supplier can't really do it.
Gate two, the economic benefit. Would the supplier actually gain from swapping? The cost of moving the asset must be outweighed by the benefit they'd get.

<<WRITE_KEY:Substantive = practical ability AND economic benefit, throughout the period of use|id=key-1>>Only when both gates open, practical ability and economic benefit, is the substitution right substantive. Then there's no identified asset, and no lease.
But if either gate stays shut, say swapping is impractical or there's nothing in it for the supplier, the swap clause is just paper. The asset stays identified, and a lease can still exist.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Can't tell which asset? Assume no substantive right|id=text-2>>One more honest point. If you genuinely can't tell whether the supplier could swap the asset, you assume the right is not substantive, so the asset is treated as identified.
So before you ever ask about payments or terms, you walk the asset through these two gates. Named on paper isn't the test. Genuinely yours to use is.

lesson_plans.title: Portions of Assets: When a Piece Counts as a Whole

hook.text: You rent one floor of a building, or one strand of a giant fibre optic cable. One of those is a lease. The other might not be. Why?

crucial_facts: A portion of an asset is an identified asset only if it is physically distinct, like a floor of a building.
A non-physically-distinct portion qualifies only if it is substantially all of the asset's capacity.

diagrams.purpose: Contrast a physically distinct floor of a building against a non-distinct capacity slice of a fibre optic cable, so the student sees why one is an identified asset and the other usually is not.

required_elements.description: A simple multi-storey building drawn as a stack of rectangles, each rectangle a floor with walls and ceiling.
One floor of the building shaded to show it is the portion being used, with clear physical boundaries.
Bold lines around the rented floor marking its walls and ceiling as a physical separation.
A long fibre optic cable drawn as a cylinder carrying many light channels.
An undefined portion of the cable's capacity shaded, with no fixed physical fibre, illustrating it could be any strand at any time.

choreography.narration: You rent one floor of a building, or one strand of a giant fibre optic cable. One of those is a lease. The other might not be. Why?
<<SECTION:Portions of Assets|id=sec-1>>The whole question comes down to a single idea: can you point at the exact piece you are using, and say nobody else can touch this part?
Look at the floor you rent. It has its own walls, its own ceiling, its own boundary. It is physically separate from every other floor.

<<WRITE_KEY:A physically distinct portion, like a floor, is an identified asset|id=key-1>>Because that floor is physically distinct, it counts as an identified asset. And an identified asset is the very thing a lease needs.
Now compare that to the fibre optic cable carrying thousands of light signals at once.
Suppose your contract just says you get some of the cable's capacity. Can you point at one specific fibre and say, this exact strand is mine and nobody else's?
You cannot. Your signal could travel down any strand at any moment. The portion you use is not physically distinct, so it is not an identified asset, and your contract is not a lease.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Not distinct, not identified, not a lease|id=text-1>>So a capacity portion that is not physically distinct fails the test. That is the rule for the fibre optic cable.
But there is one escape hatch. What if your contract gives you almost the entire capacity of that cable, leaving only a sliver for anyone else?

<<WRITE_KEY:Substantially all the capacity also counts as identified|id=key-2>>Then it qualifies after all. If you get substantially all of the capacity, you effectively obtain substantially all of the economic benefits, and the portion becomes an identified asset.
So a physically distinct floor is identified the easy way, by its walls and ceiling.
And a non-distinct capacity slice is identified only the hard way, by being almost the whole thing. Distinct boundary, or nearly all the capacity: those are your two doors into a lease.

lesson_plans.title: Who Gets the Goodies? The Economic-Benefits Test

hook.text: You rent a delivery van for a year. The fuel it saves you, the cargo it carries, even the cash you'd get if you let a friend borrow it for a weekend — who actually pockets all of that? Hold that question.

crucial_facts: To control a leased asset, the customer must obtain SUBSTANTIALLY ALL the economic benefits from using it throughout the period of use.
Economic benefits are judged only within the defined scope of the contract — restrictions on where, when or how you use the asset shrink the pie you measure.

diagrams.purpose: Show that economic benefits are a whole pie made of primary output, by-products, and third-party value like subleasing — and that the customer must capture almost all of it.

required_elements.description: A pie/circle representing the total economic benefits obtainable from using the asset over the period of use.
Largest slice labelled 'Primary output' — the main thing the asset produces.
A slice labelled 'By-products' — extra outputs that come along for the ride.
A slice labelled 'Third-party value (e.g. subleasing)' — cash realisable from a commercial transaction with a third party.
A ring or shaded boundary drawn around almost the entire pie indicating the customer captures substantially all of it.

diagrams.purpose: Show that the scope of the contract (a fence) defines which benefits even count — benefits outside the fence are ignored.

required_elements.description: A rectangular fence/box labelled with the contract's defined scope, for example a permitted geographic area or permitted hours.
Benefits drawn inside the fence, shaded as 'counts'.
Benefits drawn outside the fence, greyed out as 'ignored'.

choreography.narration: You rent a delivery van for a year. The fuel it saves you, the cargo it carries, even the cash you'd get if you let a friend borrow it for a weekend — who actually pockets all of that? Hold that question.

<<SECTION:Economic benefits|id=sec-1>>Before accountants can call a contract a lease, they ask one sharp thing: does the customer get substantially all the economic benefits from using that asset? Let's see what's actually on the table.
The biggest slice is the primary output — the main job the asset does. For our van, that's hauling your goods from place to place.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Benefits = primary output + by-products + third-party value|id=text-1>>But benefits are broader than the headline. There are by-products — the extra stuff that tags along — and there's value you could get from a third party, like subleasing the van to someone else.
That third slice matters: even cash you'd realise by renting it out to an outsider counts as an economic benefit from using the asset.

So here's the answer to our opening question: if you pocket the hauling, the by-products, AND the sublease cash — you've captured substantially all the benefits, and that's exactly what control of use requires.

<<WRITE_KEY:Customer must obtain substantially ALL economic benefits over the period of use|id=key-1>>Notice the words: substantially all, and throughout the whole period of use. Grab almost the entire pie, for the entire time — that's the test.

<<SECTION:But which benefits count?|id=sec-2>>Now a twist. Suppose the contract says the van may only be driven inside one city. Do we measure all the benefits the van could ever produce, or only some of them?
We only count what's inside the fence. The contract's defined scope draws a boundary, and benefits within that boundary are the ones we assess.
Anything outside the fence — the trips you could have made if there were no city limit — we simply ignore. It's as if it doesn't exist for this test.

Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose a contract limits the use of a vehicle to only a particular geographic area. The question is: when we judge whether the customer obtains substantially all the economic benefits, which benefits do we count? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Contract limits vehicle use to one geographic area only. Which economic benefits do we assess?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by scoping our assessment to what the contract actually permits. The entity assesses only the economic benefits from use of the motor vehicle within that territory. So we draw a boundary around the allowed geographic area and look only at the benefits available inside it. <<WRITE_STEP:Assess only economic benefits from use within the permitted territory|id=ex-step-1-1>>

And here's the key move: it does not consider what economic benefits could be obtained had there been no geographical restriction in the contract. We ignore the imagined benefits of unrestricted use entirely. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Count only benefits within the allowed territory; do not consider benefits possible without the geographic restriction|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose a contract specifies that a machine can only be used during specific times of the day. The question is: which economic benefits does the entity actually assess? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Machine usable only during specific times of day — which economic benefits does the entity assess?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by pinning the scope to what the contract grants. Because use is limited to a specific window, the entity assesses only the economic benefits from using the machinery during that time of the day. <<WRITE_STEP:Assess only economic benefits during the contracted time-of-use window|id=ex-step-1-1>>

And the answer is: the assessment is confined to the contracted hours. The entity does not consider what economic benefits could be obtained from using the machine twenty-four hours a day. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Benefits assessed = only during the specified time of day; do NOT consider hypothetical 24-hours-a-day use|id=ex-ans-1>>

You've felt this yourself with a rental car. The contract lets you drive it all weekend, but it also says you can't take it across the border, and you certainly can't sublease it to your neighbor for cash. When accountants ask whether you get substantially all the economic benefits, they only count what you can earn inside those rules. <<WRITE_TEXT:benefits counted only inside contract limits|id=ext-1>>

Something wild about this: when a sawmill leases equipment to cut lumber, the leftover sawdust and wood chips aren't waste, they get sold for particleboard and fuel pellets, and that side stream can be the difference between losing money and making it. That's exactly why economic benefits include by-products, not just the primary output, when we judge whether the customer grabs substantially all the value.

<<WRITE_KEY:Judge benefits only within the contract's defined scope|id=key-2>>So restrictions on where, when, or how you use the asset shrink the pie you're allowed to measure — and you judge benefits only within that defined scope.

Put it together: control of use starts with grabbing substantially all the economic benefits, measured strictly inside the scope the contract draws. Next we tackle the other half of control — who gets to direct how the asset is used.

lesson_plans.title: Right to Direct the Use: Who Calls the Shots?

hook.text: You rent a car for a week. Who decides where it drives, when it stops, and what it carries? If the answer is you, you might be holding a lease without even knowing it.

crucial_facts: A customer has the right to direct the use when they decide HOW and FOR WHAT PURPOSE the asset is used during the period of use.
When the key how-and-why decisions are predetermined, control still passes to the customer if they operate the asset or they designed it.

diagrams.purpose: Show the two routes by which a customer gains the right to direct the use, so the student can see control is a single idea reached by two paths.

required_elements.description: Top box reading 'Does the customer have the right to direct the use?'
Left branch box: 'Customer directs HOW and FOR WHAT PURPOSE throughout the period of use.'
Right branch box: 'How and why are predetermined' leading to two sub-conditions.
Sub-box under route two: 'Customer operates the asset (or directs operation) and lessor cannot change instructions.'
Sub-box under route two: 'Customer designed the asset, predetermining its use.'
Bottom box: 'Customer controls the use -> this is a lease.'

choreography.narration: You rent a car for a week. Who decides where it drives, when it stops, and what it carries? If the answer is you, you might be holding a lease without even knowing it.

<<SECTION:Right to direct the use|id=sec-1>>We already know a lease needs an identified asset and that you get the economic benefits from it. But there is a second piece, and this is the heart of control: the right to direct the use.
Directing the use simply means you call the shots. You decide how the asset is used and for what purpose, like where that truck goes and what it carries.

<<WRITE_KEY:Control = you decide HOW and WHY the asset is used|id=key-1>>So the most direct route is this: if you have the right to decide how and for what purpose the asset is used throughout the period, you control it.
But here is the puzzle. What if every decision about how and why the asset is used is already locked in before you even sign? Can you still be in control?
Yes, you still can, through a second route, and the standard gives two ways it happens.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Predetermined use: control via operate OR design|id=text-1>>The first way: you have the right to operate the asset, or to direct others to operate it as you choose, and the supplier cannot change your operating instructions.
The second way: you designed the asset in a manner that predetermined how and for what purpose it would be used. You made the decisions up front, at the drawing board.
Notice the pattern: either you decide as you go, or the decisions were baked in by you. Both routes land at the same place.

<<WRITE_KEY:Either route -> customer directs use -> lease|id=key-2>>And once you have the right to direct the use on top of the economic benefits, the customer controls the asset, and the contract is a lease.
So next time you sign a contract for an asset, ask one question: who really decides how and why it gets used? Answer that, and you have answered whether it is a lease.

lesson_plans.title: Separating Components of a Lease Contract

hook.text: You sign one contract to rent a delivery van — but hidden inside that single piece of paper are actually two completely different deals.

crucial_facts: You account for each lease component separately from the non-lease components, splitting the total payment by their relative stand-alone prices.
A lessee can use a practical expedient to skip the splitting and treat the whole contract as one single lease.

diagrams.purpose: Show one contract physically splitting into a lease component and a non-lease component, then payment being allocated across the two.

required_elements.description: A single rectangle labelled 'Contract' representing the bundled agreement signed by the lessee.
A box branching from the contract labelled 'Lease component — right to use the van'.
A box branching from the contract labelled 'Non-lease component — maintenance service'.
A figure for the total monthly contract payment sitting on the contract box before it is split.
A stand-alone price tag attached to the lease component.
A stand-alone price tag attached to the non-lease component.
A banner across the whole contract reading 'Practical expedient: treat as ONE lease', appearing only when the shortcut is used.

choreography.narration: <<SECTION:One contract, two deals|id=sec-1>>You sign one contract to rent a delivery van, but hidden inside that single piece of paper are actually two completely different deals.
The first deal is the right to use the van itself. The second is a maintenance service that keeps it running. <<WRITE_TEXT:1 contract = 2 things inside|id=text-1>>
Here is the honest question: if the standard cares so much about leases, does it really treat a cleaning crew the same as the van you are driving?
No, it does not. The part that gives you the right to use the asset is the lease component, and the service that just helps you run it is a non-lease component, and the rule is to keep them apart.
So the very first move is to split the contract into its lease component and its non-lease components, and account for each one separately.
But wait — you only pay one combined amount. How do you decide how much of that money belongs to the van and how much belongs to the service?
You look at what each piece would cost on its own — its stand-alone price — and you split the total payment in that same proportion.

<<WRITE_KEY:Allocate total payment by relative stand-alone prices|id=key-1>>That is the heart of it: each lease component is accounted for separately, and the total payment is shared out by the relative stand-alone prices of the parts.
And if a stand-alone price is not floating around anywhere, you are allowed to estimate it rather than just giving up.
Now, all this splitting is fiddly work, so the standard hands the renter a shortcut called a practical expedient.

<<WRITE_KEY:Practical expedient = treat whole contract as ONE lease|id=key-2>>If you choose this expedient for a class of asset, you ignore the separation and simply treat the entire contract as one single lease.
So remember the fork in the road: either split by stand-alone prices and account separately, or take the expedient and call the whole thing one lease.

lesson_plans.title: Combination of Contracts: When Two Deals Are Really One

hook.text: Two companies sign three separate contracts on the same afternoon. On paper, three deals. In reality? It might be just one deal wearing three disguises.

crucial_facts: You only ever combine contracts when BOTH gateway conditions hold: signed at or near the same time, AND with the same counterparty or its related parties.
Once the gateway is open, meeting even ONE of the three tests forces you to combine the contracts and account for them as a single contract.

diagrams.purpose: Show the two-stage logic: a gateway (two conditions) that must open first, then three tests where any single match triggers combination.

required_elements.description: A box labelled 'Gateway' containing the two conditions: same time, same counterparty.
Condition line: contracts entered at or near the same time.
Condition line: with the same counterparty or its related parties.
Test A: negotiated as a package with one overall commercial objective.
Test B: consideration in one contract depends on price or performance of the other.
Test C: the rights to use the assets form a single lease component.
Outcome box: treat as a single combined contract.
Outcome box: keep contracts separate.

choreography.narration: Two companies sign three separate contracts on the same afternoon. On paper, three deals, but in reality it might be just one deal wearing three disguises.

<<SECTION:Combination of Contracts|id=sec-1>>Here is why this matters. If you treat each contract on its own, the numbers can hide what is really going on. So the standard asks a sharper question: are these truly separate, or secretly one?
But you cannot just combine any two contracts you feel like. There is a gate you must pass through first, and the gate has two locks.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Gate lock 1: at or near same time|id=text-1>>Lock one: the contracts must be entered into at or near the same time.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Gate lock 2: same counterparty or related|id=text-2>>Lock two: they must be with the same counterparty, or with parties closely related to that counterparty.

<<WRITE_KEY:Combine ONLY if BOTH gateway conditions hold|id=key-1>>And here is the rule that catches people out: both locks must open together. Same time alone is not enough. Same party alone is not enough. You need both, or the gate stays shut.
So suppose both locks open and the gate swings wide. Does that automatically mean we combine the contracts?
Not yet. Past the gate sit three tests, and you only need ONE of them to fire to force a combination.
Test one: the contracts were negotiated as a single package, with one overall commercial objective that makes no sense unless you read them together.
Test two: the money you pay in one contract depends on the price or the performance of the other. Pull one thread and the other moves.
Test three: the rights to use the underlying assets across the contracts actually form one single lease component. Different papers, but one real thing being leased.

<<WRITE_KEY:Gate open + any ONE test = single contract|id=key-2>>So here is the whole machine. Both gateway conditions open the gate, then any single one of the three tests sends you to one answer: treat it all as one combined contract.
And if the gate never opens, or all three tests fail, you stay here: the contracts remain separate, each accounted for on its own.

lesson_plans.title: Lease Term: How Long Does the Clock Really Run?

hook.text: You sign a five-year office lease, but you can walk away after three, and you're pretty sure you'll stay for two more after that. So how many years long is your lease, really?

crucial_facts: The lease term starts on the commencement date — the day the asset is made available for use — and it includes rent-free and reduced-rent periods.
The lease term is the non-cancellable period plus any extension or termination option periods the lessee is reasonably certain to take.

diagrams.purpose: Show the lease term as a timeline built from a non-cancellable core plus an option period the lessee is reasonably certain to use, anchored at the commencement date.

required_elements.description: A vertical tick at the left labelled 'Commencement date — asset made available'.
A short shaded band right after commencement labelled 'rent-free / reduced rent — still counts'.
The main solid band representing the non-cancellable period of the lease.
A dashed band after the non-cancellable period labelled 'extension option — included only if reasonably certain'.
A bracket spanning commencement through the end of the included option period labelled 'Lease term'.

choreography.narration: You sign a five-year office lease, but you can walk away after three, and you're pretty sure you'll stay two more. So how many years long is your lease, really?

The answer matters more than it sounds, because almost every number in lease accounting, the asset value, the liability, the yearly charge, depends on this one length. Get the length wrong and everything downstream is wrong.

So let's build the timeline. First, when does the clock start? Not the day you sign the paperwork. <<SECTION:When the clock starts|id=sec-1>>It starts on the commencement date, the day the lessor actually hands you the asset to use.
Now here's the trap. Suppose your first three months are rent-free, a sweetener to get you to sign. Do those free months count as part of the lease term?

They absolutely do. <<WRITE_KEY:Term starts at commencement; rent-free and reduced-rent months still count|id=key-1>>A rent-free or reduced-rent period is still you having the asset, so it is part of the term from day one.

Next comes the solid core of the term: the non-cancellable period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Non-cancellable = locked in, can't walk away|id=text-1>>This is the stretch where neither of you can just walk away, you're locked in.
But leases often have options bolted on. An option to extend, or an option to terminate early. Do we just include every extension option to be safe?

No, and this is the clever part. <<SECTION:The reasonably-certain test|id=sec-2>>You only include an extension period if you are reasonably certain you'll take it. And you only cut off a termination option if you're reasonably certain you won't use it.
So in our office example, the three locked-in years are in for certain, and because you're reasonably certain to stay the extra two, those join the term too, giving five.

Put it together: the lease term is the non-cancellable period, plus any extension you're reasonably certain to take, plus any termination right you're reasonably certain not to use. <<WRITE_KEY:Term = non-cancellable period + options the lessee is reasonably certain to take|id=key-2>>
One last note: judgement isn't frozen. If the non-cancellable period itself changes, you go back and revise the term, because every downstream number leans on it.

lesson_plans.title: Extension and Termination Options: The "Reasonably Certain" Judgment

hook.text: You sign a five-year lease on a shop, but the contract lets you stay for five more years if you want. So tell me — how long is your lease, really? Five years, or ten?

crucial_facts: At the commencement date, the entity assesses whether the lessee is reasonably certain to extend, to purchase, or not to terminate — and that judgment sets the lease term.
The test is economic incentive, not just what the contract says — anything that makes walking away expensive pulls the option into the lease term.

diagrams.purpose: Show one lease timeline with a guaranteed period and an optional period, so the student can see the option visually pulling the lease term longer or shorter.

required_elements.description: A point at the far left of a horizontal timeline labelled 'Commencement date' — where the judgment is made.
A solid horizontal bar covering the non-cancellable years of the lease, the part you are committed to.
A dashed/hatched horizontal bar continuing after the guaranteed period, representing the extension option years.
An arrow showing the lease term reaching forward to include the optional period when extension is reasonably certain.
An arrow showing the lease term cut short at an early termination point when termination is reasonably certain.
A highlighted region over the optional period labelled 'economic incentive?' — where the reasonably-certain judgment lives.

choreography.narration: You sign a five-year lease on a shop, but the contract lets you stay for five more years if you want. So how long is your lease, really? Five years, or ten?
<<SECTION:Extension and termination options|id=sec-1>>Here's the honest answer: it depends on a judgment you make right at the start, on what we call the commencement date.
Look at the timeline. This solid bar is the part you are locked into — the years you cannot escape. That's the guaranteed period.
And this dashed bar is the optional bit — the extra years you could take if you choose to extend. The big question is whether those dashed years count as part of your lease.

<<WRITE_KEY:Lease term set by 'reasonably certain' judgment at commencement|id=key-1>>At the commencement date the entity must ask three things: is the lessee reasonably certain to extend, reasonably certain to buy the asset, and reasonably certain not to terminate early?
If the answer is yes, you are reasonably certain to extend, then the lease term reaches forward and swallows those optional years.
But if instead you are reasonably certain to terminate early, the lease term gets cut short, right here.
Now here is the trap. Reasonably certain is not the same as legally allowed. The contract gives you the option — but the standard asks something deeper.
<<WRITE_KEY:Test is economic incentive, not the contract wording|id=key-2>>The real test is economic incentive. Is there a strong financial reason that makes exercising the option the obvious choice?

<<WRITE_TEXT:Consider all facts: fit-out cost, location, below-market rent|id=text-1>>For instance, in any case where you've spent a fortune fitting out the shop, or the rent for the extra years is far below market, walking away would be painful — so you're reasonably certain to stay.
The entity weighs all relevant facts and circumstances, including expected changes between today and the date the option would be exercised.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Past practice with similar leases also counts|id=text-2>>And don't forget habits — a lessee's past practice with similar leases tells you a lot about how likely an option really is to be used.
So back to our shop: if the economic incentive to stay is strong, your lease is ten years, not five — and that bigger term means a bigger liability and a bigger right-of-use asset.
That single judgment at the start — reasonably certain, based on economic incentive — is what quietly decides how big the whole lease shows up on your books.

lesson_plans.title: Recognition of a Lease: The Day It All Begins

hook.text: You rent a bike from your friend for a whole year. You don't own it — so how could it possibly show up as something you own on your accounts?

crucial_facts: On the commencement date the lessee records two things: a right-of-use asset at cost, and a lease liability at the present value of the lease payments not yet paid.
The lease liability is measured by discounting future lease payments using the interest rate implicit in the lease, or the lessee's incremental borrowing rate if that rate isn't readily determinable.

diagrams.purpose: Show that on day one, a single lease event creates an asset on one side and a liability on the other — the two things the lessee must recognise.

required_elements.description: A vertical line labelled 'Commencement date' marking day one of the lease.
A box on the asset side labelled 'Right-of-use asset', representing the valuable right to use the leased item.
A box on the liability side labelled 'Lease liability', representing the obligation to make future lease payments.
A row of small arrows extending to the right representing future lease payments over the lease term.
An arrow pointing back from the future payments toward the lease-liability box, labelled 'present value', showing the payments are discounted back to today.

choreography.narration: You rent a bike from your friend for a whole year. You don't own it, so how could it possibly show up as something you own on your accounts?
Here's the trick: you may not own the bike, but you own something real — the right to ride it whenever you like, for a whole year. That right has genuine worth.
<<SECTION:Commencement date|id=sec-1>>The moment that matters is the day the lease actually begins, which we call the commencement date. On that single day, two entries go into the books.

<<WRITE_KEY:Day one: recognise a right-of-use asset AND a lease liability|id=key-1>>The first entry is that valuable right we just talked about. We call it the right-of-use asset, and we record it at its cost.
But there's a flip side. Using that bike for a year isn't free, is it? You've promised to make payments. That promise is an obligation, and an obligation you can't escape is a liability.
So the second entry is the lease liability. Look at the board: one event on day one, an asset on this side, a liability on that side.
Now, those future payments stretch out across the whole lease term. Here's a fair question: a thousand rupees you pay next year — is that really worth a full thousand rupees to you today?
It isn't. Money in the future is worth less than money right now, because today's money could earn interest. So we shrink each future payment back to what it's worth today — its present value.
We measure the lease liability as the present value of all the lease payments that haven't been paid yet at that date. Watch the arrow pull those future payments back into the liability box.
<<WRITE_EQUATION:PV = \sum P_t / (1+r)^t|id=eq-1>>In symbols, the liability is each payment P divided by one plus the rate, raised to the power of how many years away it is, all added together.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Use implicit rate; else incremental borrowing rate|id=text-1>>The rate r is the interest rate implicit in the lease if you can readily work it out. If you can't, you use the lessee's own incremental borrowing rate instead.
So on day one, every lease quietly does two things at once: it hands you an asset worth using, and it loads you with a liability worth paying. Recognise both, and the books tell the truth.

equations.explanation_in_words: The lease liability is just the sum of every future payment, each one shrunk back to what it's worth today using the interest rate.

lesson_plans.title: Subsequent Measurement of the Right-of-Use Asset

hook.text: You sign a five-year lease on a delivery van and put it on your books today. Here's the puzzle: what should that van be worth on your books one year from now?

crucial_facts: After initial recognition, the right-of-use asset must be measured using either the cost model or the revaluation model.
The revaluation model is only available if the underlying asset belongs to a class for which the company already revalues its own property, plant and equipment under Ind AS 16.

diagrams.purpose: Show the right-of-use asset's value starting at one point and then following two distinct downstream paths over time — the steady cost-model path versus the revaluation path that can step up or down.

required_elements.description: Horizontal axis labelled as time in years, running across the bottom.
Vertical axis labelled as carrying amount of the right-of-use asset.
A single dot at the top-left where the asset is first recognised, labelled 'initial measurement'.
A smooth steadily-declining line from the start point representing carrying amount falling as depreciation is charged each period.
A line from the start point that depreciates but then steps up at a revaluation date, then continues, showing value being reset to fair value.
Label reading 'Cost model' attached to the steadily declining line.
Label reading 'Revaluation model' attached to the stepping line.

choreography.narration: You sign a five-year lease on a delivery van and put it on your books today. Here's the puzzle: what should that van be worth on your books one year from now?

The asset can't just sit there frozen at its starting value, because in real life that right to use the van is steadily getting used up. <<SECTION:Subsequent measurement|id=sec-1>>Keeping track of how that value changes over the life of the lease is what we call subsequent measurement.
And here's the answer to our puzzle: the company actually gets to choose between two different paths for that value, and we draw them both starting from the same point.
The first path is the cost model — think of it as the simple, steady road. You begin with the cost and you shave a slice off it each period as depreciation, so the line just glides downward.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Cost model = steady decline by depreciation|id=text-1>>Notice this line never jumps around. It only goes down, smoothly, year after year, as the van is used up.
The second path is the revaluation model. Watch what's different — it can be reset to the asset's fair value, so instead of only sliding down, it can step back up if the asset is worth more.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Revaluation = reset to fair value|id=text-2>>So one road is steady and predictable, and the other tracks what the asset is really worth in the market.
Now, a fair question: if the revaluation path can keep your asset closer to its true worth, why wouldn't every company just pick it?

Because there's a gatekeeper. You're only allowed onto the revaluation road if the underlying asset belongs to a class for which your company already revalues its own property, plant and equipment under Ind AS sixteen.

<<WRITE_KEY:Subsequent measurement: cost model OR revaluation model (revaluation only if that asset class is already revalued under Ind AS 16)|id=key-1>>So lock this in: after first recording the right-of-use asset, you measure it using either the cost model or the revaluation model.
And the revaluation door only opens for an asset class that you're already revaluing under Ind AS sixteen — for everyone else, the steady cost model is the road you travel.

lesson_plans.title: The Cost Model: Tracking a Right-of-Use Asset Over Time

hook.text: You sign a five-year lease on a delivery van. The day after you sign, what is that van worth on your books — and what will it be worth next year?

crucial_facts: Under the cost model, the right-of-use asset is carried at original cost minus accumulated depreciation minus accumulated impairment losses.
You also adjust the asset's carrying amount up or down whenever the lease liability is remeasured.

diagrams.purpose: Show the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset as a starting block from which depreciation and impairment are subtracted, plus a remeasurement adjustment, landing on the net carrying amount.

required_elements.description: Tall full-height bar on the left labelled 'Original cost of right-of-use asset', the starting value.
A downward segment subtracted from the cost block, labelled 'less accumulated depreciation (Ind AS 16)'.
A further downward segment subtracted below depreciation, labelled 'less accumulated impairment losses (Ind AS 36)'.
A two-way arrow on the remaining block labelled 'adjust for lease liability remeasurement (up or down)'.
The shorter final bar on the right labelled 'net carrying amount', what shows on the balance sheet.

choreography.narration: You sign a five-year lease on a delivery van. The day after you sign, what is that van worth on your books, and what will it be worth next year?
<<SECTION:The cost model|id=sec-1>>The answer comes from something called the cost model, and it is just a clean recipe for tracking the value of your right to use that van as the years go by.
You start with this full block, the original cost of the right-of-use asset, exactly what you measured it at on day one.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Depreciation = wearing-down of value over time|id=text-1>>Now, the van wears down a little every year, and that wearing-down of value is called depreciation, which we spread across the life of the asset using the rules in Ind AS sixteen.
So we cut that accumulated depreciation off the top of the block, and the more years pass, the bigger that cut grows.
Sometimes something unexpected happens, the asset suddenly loses value beyond ordinary wear, and that is an impairment loss, which we follow under Ind AS thirty-six.

<<WRITE_KEY:Carrying amount = cost less accumulated depreciation less accumulated impairment|id=key-1>>So we subtract any accumulated impairment losses too, and what is left is your net carrying amount, the figure that actually sits on the balance sheet.
But here is a question that trips people up: what if the lease itself changes partway through, say the rent gets revised, so the lease liability you owe is recalculated?
When the lease liability is remeasured, you adjust the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset by the very same amount, up or down, so the two stay linked.

<<WRITE_TEXT:No adjustment if asset already zero, or change is variable payment (no index/rate)|id=text-2>>There are just two exceptions: you stop if the asset is already reduced to zero, or if the change relates to a variable payment that does not depend on an index or a rate.
So picture the whole journey: start at cost, cut away depreciation, cut away impairment, then nudge for any remeasurement, and you land on the carrying amount.

That single recipe, cost less depreciation less impairment, adjusted for remeasurement, is the cost model, and it tells you exactly what your leased van is worth on your books, today and every year after.

equations.explanation_in_words: Take the original cost, subtract everything the asset has worn down by, then subtract any sudden losses, and the remainder is what the asset is carried at.

lesson_plans.title: How a Lease Liability Lives and Shrinks: Amortised Cost

hook.text: You sign a lease and write down what you owe on day one. But that number doesn't sit still — by next month it's already different. Why?

crucial_facts: A lease liability is carried at amortised cost: each period interest is added on, then the payment you make is subtracted off.
Interest is charged on the balance you still owe, so it shrinks every period as the liability shrinks.

diagrams.purpose: Show the period-by-period roll of the lease liability: opening balance, plus interest, minus payment, equals closing balance — and how the closing of one period becomes the opening of the next.

required_elements.description: A vertical bar representing the lease liability at the start of the period (present value of remaining payments).
A small upward block stacked on the opening balance showing interest accrued at the effective rate.
A downward arrow / block showing the lease payment subtracted from the balance.
The resulting shorter bar — the carrying amount at period end, which becomes next period's opening balance.
An arrow linking this period's closing balance to the next period's opening balance.

choreography.narration: You sign a lease and write down what you owe on day one. But by next month that number has already changed. Why won't it sit still?
Here's the secret: a lease liability behaves almost exactly like a loan. Think about borrowing money from a friend who charges you a little interest.
<<SECTION:Amortised cost|id=sec-1>>Every period, two things happen to that balance. First, because you still owe money, interest quietly builds up on top of what you owe.
Then you make your lease payment, and that payment chips the balance back down.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Closing = Opening + Interest - Payment|id=text-1>>So what you're left with at the end of the period is your opening amount, plus the interest, minus the payment. That leftover is the new carrying amount.
And here's the elegant part: that closing balance simply becomes next period's opening balance, and the whole cycle repeats.
Now if the interest keeps getting added every period, you might wonder — does the liability just keep growing forever?

<<WRITE_KEY:Interest is charged on the shrinking balance, so it gets smaller each period|id=key-1>>No. Because your payment is bigger than the interest, the balance shrinks. And since interest is charged only on what you still owe, a smaller balance means less interest next time.
This whole method — interest on the outstanding balance, then reduce by payment — is what accountants call the effective interest method.

<<WRITE_KEY:Lease liability is carried at amortised cost using the effective interest method|id=key-2>>And carrying the liability this way, period after period, is exactly what we mean when we say it is measured at amortised cost.

There's one more twist. Sometimes the deal itself changes — payments get revised, or you reassess what you'll actually pay. When that happens, you also remeasure the carrying amount to reflect the new reality.
So picture the liability as a living balance: it breathes in interest, breathes out payments, and quietly shrinks toward zero by the end of the lease.

equations.explanation_in_words: The closing balance equals the opening balance, plus interest at the effective rate on that opening balance, minus the payment you make.

lesson_plans.title: Reassessment of Lease Liability: When the Story Changes

hook.text: You signed a five-year lease and locked a single number into your books. Two years in, you decide to stay seven years instead. So... does that old number just get to stay wrong?

crucial_facts: When the nature of the lease changes, like the lease term or a purchase option, you must use a revised discount rate; when only the cash amounts change, you keep the original discount rate.
Reassessment means going back and remeasuring the lease liability so it reflects the new reality, not the old assumption.

diagrams.purpose: Show the single decision that splits all reassessment triggers into two paths: revised rate versus unchanged rate.

required_elements.description: A box at the top labelled 'Lease liability already on the books'.
A node below the liability box labelled 'A fact you assumed has changed'.
A diamond decision node asking 'Did the NATURE of the lease change, or only the CASH amounts?'
Left branch leading to a box: 'Change in lease term or purchase option -> remeasure with a REVISED discount rate'.
Right branch leading to a box: 'Change in residual value guarantee or index/rate -> remeasure with the ORIGINAL discount rate'.
Annotation near the left path: 'new rate = implicit rate or incremental borrowing rate at reassessment date'.
Annotation near the right path: 'discount rate unchanged'.

choreography.narration: You signed a five-year lease and locked a single number into your books. Two years in, you decide to stay seven years instead. So does that old number just get to stay wrong?

It can't. That number, the lease liability, was only ever your best guess of all the future payments squeezed into one present value. When the facts behind the guess change, the number has to change too.

<<SECTION:Reassessment|id=sec-1>>Going back and remeasuring that liability so it matches the new reality is exactly what we call reassessment. <<WRITE_TEXT:Reassessment = remeasure liability for new facts|id=text-1>>
Now here is the clever part. Not every change is the same kind of change, so the rules ask one sharp question before you remeasure anything.
The question is this: did the very nature of the lease shift, or did only the cash amounts shift?

If the nature shifted, say you changed the lease term, or you now expect to exercise a purchase option, then you are essentially dealing with a different deal, so you discount the revised payments using a revised discount rate.

What is that revised rate? It is the interest rate implicit in the lease for the rest of the term if you can readily find it, otherwise your incremental borrowing rate on the date you reassess. <<WRITE_TEXT:revised rate: implicit, else IBR at reassess date|id=text-2>>
But if only the cash amounts moved, the deal itself is unchanged. Maybe your residual value guarantee estimate dropped, or an index your rent is tied to ticked up.

In that case you remeasure using the original, unchanged discount rate, because nothing about the riskiness or length of the deal has actually changed. <<WRITE_TEXT:cash-only change: keep original rate|id=text-3>>

So the whole topic collapses into one decision. Nature of the lease changes, you use a revised rate. Only the cash amounts change, you keep the original rate. <<WRITE_KEY:Nature changes -> revised rate. Cash only -> original rate.|id=key-1>>
And both paths share the same engine underneath: discount the new payments back to today and that present value becomes your new lease liability.

That is reassessment in one breath: when life proves your assumptions wrong, you do not leave a stale number sitting there, you remeasure it, choosing the rate by whether the lease itself changed or just the money did.

lesson_plans.title: Lease Modifications: When a Lease Changes Mid-Stream

hook.text: You rented an office floor two years ago. Today you want a second floor. Is that a brand-new lease, or just a change to the old one? Your answer decides which numbers move on the books.

crucial_facts: A modification is a separate lease ONLY when it both adds a new asset AND charges the fair stand-alone price for it.
When it is NOT a separate lease, you remeasure the lease liability with a fresh discount rate, then adjust the right-of-use asset (and book a gain or loss if scope shrinks).

diagrams.purpose: Show the two-condition gate that decides separate-lease vs remeasure, and the two remeasure branches.

required_elements.description: Top box reading 'Lease modification occurs'
Diamond: does it add the right to use a new asset?
Diamond: is the extra payment the fair stand-alone price?
Green box: account for as a SEPARATE lease, leave existing lease untouched
Amber box: remeasure existing lease liability with a new discount rate
Box: scope decreases - reduce right-of-use asset, recognise gain or loss
Box: all other changes - adjust right-of-use asset only

choreography.narration: You rented an office floor two years ago. Today you want a second floor. Is that a brand-new lease, or just a change to the old one?

<<SECTION:Lease modifications|id=sec-1>>Here is why it matters. Real contracts don't stay frozen. You add space, you give space back, the rent gets renegotiated. Accountants call any such change a lease modification.
The whole standard hangs on one fork in the road: do we bolt on a separate lease, or do we surgically adjust the lease we already have? Everything else follows from that single decision.
So when do we get to treat it as a clean, separate lease? There are two gates, and you must pass BOTH. First gate: does the change actually add the right to use a new asset, like that extra floor?
Second gate: is the extra payment a fair price for that new asset on its own? We call that the stand-alone price, roughly what you'd pay if you walked in off the street and rented that floor today.

<<WRITE_KEY:Separate lease ONLY IF: adds a new asset AND priced at fair stand-alone price|id=key-1>>Pass both gates, and it is a separate lease. You leave your original lease completely untouched and simply book the new one beside it.
Now, the question that trips people up: what if you add a floor, but your landlord gives you a sweet discount, well below the stand-alone price?
Then you fail the second gate, so it is NOT a separate lease. The discount entangles the old deal with the new, so you must reopen and remeasure the lease you already have.

<<WRITE_STEP:Remeasure lease liability using a discount rate at the modification date|id=step-1>>To remeasure, you recompute the lease liability using a fresh discount rate, the rate that fits the conditions on the day of the modification, not the old one.

From here the path splits in two. If the modification shrinks your scope, say you hand back half a floor, you cut down the right-of-use asset to match and you book the gain or loss for the part you let go.

<<WRITE_KEY:Not separate: remeasure liability, adjust right-of-use asset; if scope shrinks, recognise gain or loss|id=key-2>>For every other kind of change, no gain or loss, you just make a matching adjustment to the right-of-use asset so the books stay balanced.

So the answer to where we started: a separate lease only if it adds an asset at a fair price; otherwise reopen the books, remeasure the liability, and adjust the asset. That one fork decides everything.

lesson_plans.title: Where Lease Numbers Live: Presentation under Ind AS 116

hook.text: You signed a lease. You now owe money, and you control an asset you don't own. So where exactly do those numbers sit in your three financial statements?

crucial_facts: Interest expense on the lease liability must be shown separately from depreciation of the right-of-use asset in the statement of profit and loss.
In the cash flow statement, the principal AND interest portions of lease payments go under financing activities, while short-term, low-value and variable lease payments go under operating activities.

diagrams.purpose: Show the three financial statements as three labelled containers and place each lease item into its correct slot, so the student sees presentation as a sorting problem.

required_elements.description: A labelled box representing the balance sheet, with two slots inside: an assets side and a liabilities side.
Slot inside the balance sheet assets side holding the right-of-use asset.
Slot inside the balance sheet liabilities side holding the lease liability.
A labelled box representing the statement of profit and loss.
Slot in the profit and loss box for the depreciation charge on the right-of-use asset.
Slot in the profit and loss box for the interest expense, tagged as a finance cost.
A labelled box representing the statement of cash flows, split into a financing activities band and an operating activities band.
Financing activities band holding principal and interest portions of lease payments.
Operating activities band holding short-term, low-value and variable lease payments.

choreography.narration: You signed a lease. You now owe money, and you control an asset you don't own. So where exactly do those numbers sit in your three financial statements?

<<SECTION:Presentation as sorting|id=sec-1>>Presentation isn't new accounting. It's just deciding which drawer each number belongs in. We have three drawers: the balance sheet, the profit and loss, and the cash flow statement.
Start with the balance sheet. As a lessee you carry two things here: the right-of-use asset, your right to use the item, and the lease liability, what you still owe.

<<WRITE_TEXT:ROU asset: own line or tucked into owned-asset line + note|id=text-1>>The right-of-use asset can sit on its own line, or be folded into the line you'd use if you actually owned that kind of asset. If you fold it in, you must say so in the notes.

The lease liability works the same way: a separate line, or buried in another liability line with a note pointing to it. And if the right-of-use asset is really investment property, it lives inside investment property instead.
<<SECTION:Profit and loss|id=sec-2>>Now the profit and loss. One lease, but it produces two very different expenses, and here's the rule that trips people up.
Why split one lease into two separate expense lines instead of just calling it rent?

<<WRITE_KEY:P&L: depreciation of ROU asset shown separately from interest on lease liability|id=key-1>>Because the two pieces are economically different. Depreciation spreads the cost of using the asset, while the interest is a finance cost for borrowing. So you present the depreciation charge on the right-of-use asset separately from the interest expense on the lease liability.
And that interest isn't just any expense — it's a component of finance cost, so it must be presented separately within your finance costs.
<<SECTION:Cash flows|id=sec-3>>Last drawer, the cash flow statement. Every rupee you pay on the lease has to land in one of two bands.

<<WRITE_KEY:Cash flows: principal + interest -> financing; short-term, low-value, variable -> operating|id=key-2>>The principal portion and the interest portion of your lease payments both go under financing activities.
But payments that never sat in the liability — short-term leases, low-value asset leases, and variable lease payments — those go under operating activities instead.

So the whole topic is one habit: balance sheet holds the asset and the liability, profit and loss splits depreciation from interest, and cash flows send principal and interest to financing while the small leftover payments go to operating.

lesson_plans.title: Classification of Leases: Who Really Owns It?

hook.text: If you rent a car for the weekend versus paying it off over five years until it's basically yours — should the accountant treat those two deals the same way?

crucial_facts: A lease is a finance lease if it transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership; otherwise it is an operating lease.
We classify a lease by the substance of the deal, not by what the contract is called.

diagrams.purpose: Show ownership's risks and rewards sliding from lessor to lessee, and the tipping point where a lease becomes a finance lease.

required_elements.description: A box in the centre representing the underlying asset being leased.
Left side labelled 'Lessor' (the owner who rents the asset out).
Right side labelled 'Lessee' (the person renting the asset).
A bundle/stack of tokens labelled 'risks and rewards of ownership' that can sit on the lessor side or move to the lessee side.
A pivot/tipping marker between the two sides indicating the 'substantially all' threshold.
Label that appears on the lessee side reading 'Finance lease' when the bundle crosses over.
Label that appears on the lessor side reading 'Operating lease' when the bundle stays put.

choreography.narration: If you rent a car for a weekend versus paying one off over five years until it's basically yours, should an accountant treat those two deals the same way?
Of course not — and that gap is the whole idea behind classifying leases. Every lease falls into exactly one of two boxes, and one single question decides which.

<<SECTION:Risks and rewards|id=sec-1>>Owning something isn't just about holding the title. It comes with rewards, like using it and gaining if it holds value, and risks, like repairs and it wearing out. Picture all of that as one bundle.

<<WRITE_KEY:Finance lease = transfers substantially all risks and rewards of ownership|id=key-1>>Here is the deciding question: does the lease hand substantially all of that bundle over to the person renting the asset?
If almost the entire bundle slides across to the lessee, the deal has crossed the line. We call that a finance lease.
But if the owner keeps holding most of those risks and rewards, the bundle stays on the lessor's side, and we call it an operating lease.
<<SECTION:Substance over form|id=sec-2>>Now, here's the trap. A contract might be titled 'rental agreement' — does that label settle whether it's an operating lease?
<<WRITE_KEY:Judge by substance, not by the contract's name|id=key-2>>Not at all. We judge by what is really happening in the deal, not by what it's called. Substance beats form, every time.
So how do we actually tell when the bundle has crossed over? The standard gives us telltale signs. Watch what each one does to our scale.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Ownership transfers, or a bargain purchase option|id=text-1>>If ownership transfers by the end, or there's a bargain price to buy it that's almost certain to be taken — the bundle clearly moves to the lessee.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Most of the asset's life, or PV of payments ≈ fair value|id=text-2>>If the lease runs for the major part of the asset's life, or the payments add up to nearly its full value, again — almost everything has shifted across.
And if the asset is so specialised that only the lessee can use it, who really bears its fate? The lessee. The bundle has moved, so it's a finance lease.
So remember: two boxes, one question. If substantially all the risks and rewards move to the renter, it's a finance lease; if not, it's operating — and always judge the substance, never the label.

lesson_plans.title: Finance vs Operating Lease: How the Lessor Keeps the Books

hook.text: You own a delivery van and you rent it out. Should that van still sit on your books as something you own — or have you really just turned it into a loan?

crucial_facts: In a finance lease the lessor derecognises the asset and shows a lease receivable instead; in an operating lease the lessor keeps the asset on its books.
Finance lease earns finance income on a constant rate of return; operating lease earns rental income spread evenly, with depreciation as an expense.

diagrams.purpose: Show the lessor's balance sheet branching into two outcomes depending on lease type, so the student sees the asset either leaving or staying.

required_elements.description: A box labelled 'Underlying asset' representing the van sitting on the lessor's balance sheet at the start.
An arrow leading right labelled 'Finance lease' from the underlying asset.
An arrow leading down labelled 'Operating lease' from the underlying asset.
A box at the end of the finance branch labelled 'Lease receivable = net investment in lease', replacing the asset.
A box at the end of the operating branch labelled 'Asset stays on books + depreciation', keeping the asset.

choreography.narration: You own a delivery van and you rent it out. Should that van still sit on your books as something you own, or have you really just turned it into a loan?
The answer depends entirely on one thing we settled last time: whether the lease is a finance lease or an operating lease.
<<SECTION:Finance lease|id=sec-1>>Take the finance lease first. Here, in substance, ownership has passed to the renter, even if your name is still on the paperwork.
So you stop showing the van as your asset. You derecognise it, and in its place you put a lease receivable.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Finance lease: drop the asset, show a receivable|id=text-1>>That receivable is measured at the net investment in the lease. You no longer own equipment; you hold a financial claim, exactly like having lent out money.
And because it behaves like a loan, the income you earn is finance income, recognised so that you get a constant periodic rate of return on that net investment.
<<SECTION:Operating lease|id=sec-2>>Now the operating lease. Here ownership has not really moved; you are just letting someone use your van for a while.
So you keep the van right there on your balance sheet, and you carry on depreciating it over its useful life, just as you always would.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Operating lease: keep the asset, depreciate it|id=text-2>>The rent that comes in is recognised as income, normally spread evenly on a straight-line basis across the lease term.
There is one more nice touch: any initial direct costs you spend to set up an operating lease get added to the carrying amount of the underlying asset.
So why do the same physical van get treated in two completely opposite ways on your books?

<<WRITE_KEY:Finance lease = receivable + finance income; Operating lease = keep asset + rental income|id=key-1>>Because accounting follows the substance. If you have effectively sold the van, you show a receivable and earn finance income. If you have merely lent it temporarily, you keep the van, depreciate it, and collect rent.

lesson_plans.title: Manufacturer or Dealer as Lessor: Two Events at Once

hook.text: A car company leases you a car instead of selling it. So on day one, did they make a sale, or did they make a loan? The strange answer is: both, at the very same moment.

crucial_facts: A manufacturer or dealer lessor recognises both a sale and a finance lease at commencement, so it books selling profit immediately plus finance income over the lease term.
Revenue is the lower of the asset's fair value and the present value of the lease payments; cost of sale is the asset's cost minus the present value of any unguaranteed residual value.

diagrams.purpose: Show that one lease transaction splits into two simultaneous accounting events at commencement: an instant selling profit and an ongoing finance income stream.

required_elements.description: A box representing the underlying asset the manufacturer built, e.g. a machine or car, sitting with the dealer.
A vertical line marking the lease commencement date, the moment everything happens.
An arrow branching at commencement labelled 'Sale': revenue minus cost of sale equals selling profit, recognised instantly.
An arrow branching at commencement labelled 'Finance lease': a net investment that earns finance income over time.
A marker on the sale branch showing the one-off selling profit booked at day one.
A series of small arrows along the lease branch showing finance income trickling in each period.

choreography.narration: A car company leases you a car instead of selling it outright. So on day one, did they make a sale, or did they make a loan? The strange answer is: both, at the very same moment.

Here is the asset the company built or bought to sell. A normal shop would just sell it and book a profit. But this company is a manufacturer or dealer who also acts as a lessor, so it does something cleverer.
<<SECTION:Two events at commencement|id=sec-1>>At the commencement date, the single transaction splits into two branches. Watch the line: everything happens right here, on day one.
The first branch is a sale. The company hands over the asset's economic value, so it records revenue and a matching cost of sale, and the difference is selling profit, booked instantly.
But hold on. If they sold it on day one, where does the lease come in? What keeps earning money over the next few years?

<<WRITE_KEY:Dealer lessor books selling profit at day one AND finance income over the term|id=key-1>>The second branch is the finance lease. The company holds a net investment in the lease, and that investment earns finance income period after period, just like a loan.
So one transaction, two streams of profit. A one-off selling profit on day one, plus a slow trickle of finance income over the lease term.

<<SECTION:Measuring the sale|id=sec-2>>Now, how much revenue? You cannot just use the asking price. Revenue is the lower of two numbers: the fair value of the asset, or the present value of the lease payments discounted at a market interest rate.

<<WRITE_STEP:Cost of sale = asset cost minus present value of unguaranteed residual|id=step-1>>And the cost of sale is the asset's cost, but minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value, because part of the asset comes back to you and was never really sold.
Subtract that cost of sale from revenue and you get the selling profit, recognised right here at commencement, exactly as you would for any outright sale.

<<SECTION:After commencement|id=sec-3>>After day one, only the lease branch is still alive. Each period you recognise finance income at a constant rate of return on the remaining net investment, then reduce that investment by the payments received.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Sale + finance lease, both at once|id=text-1>>So remember the big idea: a manufacturer or dealer lessor is two businesses in one moment. The maker who books selling profit instantly, and the financier who earns interest over the years.
