equations.explanation_in_words: Revenue is the lower of the asset's fair value and the present value of the lease payments discounted at a market rate of interest.

equations.latex: \text{Cost of Sale} = \text{Asset Cost} - \text{PV of unguaranteed residual value}
equations.explanation_in_words: Cost of sale equals the asset's cost or carrying amount minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value.
Selling profit is simply revenue minus cost of sale, booked at the commencement date.

lesson_plans.title: Lessor Disclosures: Telling the Story Behind the Numbers

hook.text: A company's balance sheet shows it owns a fleet of trucks worth millions, and it's renting them all out. So why is that single number nowhere near enough to understand the business?

crucial_facts: Disclosures are the notes that, alongside the main statements, let a reader assess how leases affect a lessor's financial position, performance, and cash flows.
What a lessor must disclose depends on the lease type: a finance lease focuses on the net investment in the lease, while an operating lease focuses on lease income.

diagrams.purpose: Show that disclosures branch by lease type, with finance-lease notes centred on net investment and operating-lease notes centred on lease income.

required_elements.description: A box labelled 'Main Statements: Balance Sheet, P&L, Cash Flow' showing the headline numbers.
A central node labelled 'Disclosure Notes' branching off from the main statements box.
Branch from disclosures node labelled 'Finance Lease' leading to a box about net investment in the lease.
Branch from disclosures node labelled 'Operating Lease' leading to a box about lease income.
Box listing finance-lease disclosures: selling profit/loss, finance income on net investment, maturity analysis of payments receivable, significant changes in net investment.
Box listing operating-lease disclosures: lease income, variable lease payments not on an index/rate, asset disclosures under other standards.

choreography.narration: A company's balance sheet shows it owns a fleet of trucks worth millions, and it's renting them all out, so why is that single number nowhere near enough to understand the business?
The headline statements give you totals, but they don't tell you when the rent is coming in, how the value is changing, or how much profit was baked in on day one.
<<SECTION:Why Disclosures Exist|id=sec-1>>That is exactly why we add disclosures: extra notes that sit alongside the main statements.

The whole objective is simple to say: these notes, together with the balance sheet, the profit and loss statement, and the cash flow statement, let a reader assess how leases affect the lessor's financial position, performance, and cash flows.
Now here is the clever part, and it is the one thing to hold onto: what you must disclose depends on the kind of lease.

<<SECTION:Finance Lease Notes|id=sec-2>>For a finance lease, the lessor has effectively handed over the asset and is owed a stream of payments, so the disclosures circle around the net investment in the lease.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Finance lease -> net investment in the lease|id=text-1>>Concretely, the lessor discloses any selling profit or loss, the finance income earned on that net investment, and a detailed maturity analysis of the payments still to be received.
They also explain any significant changes in the carrying amount of that net investment, so a reader can follow how the asset's recorded value is moving over time.
<<SECTION:Operating Lease Notes|id=sec-3>>An operating lease is different: the lessor keeps the asset on its books, so what matters most is the income it throws off.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Operating lease -> lease income|id=text-2>>Here the lessor discloses its lease income, separating out variable lease payments that do not depend on an index or a rate, and gives the usual asset disclosures under the relevant property and equipment standards.
So step back and look at the two branches side by side: the same word, disclosure, but the content is steered entirely by whether the risks and rewards left the lessor or stayed with them.

<<WRITE_KEY:Disclosures = notes that let readers assess lease effects on position, performance & cash flows|id=key-1>>And remember the purpose tying it all together: these notes exist so that anyone reading the accounts can judge how leases shape the lessor's financial position, performance, and cash flows.

lesson_plans.title: Sublease: Sitting in the Middle

hook.text: What happens when you rent an apartment, then rent that very same apartment out to someone else? You're suddenly paying rent and collecting it.

crucial_facts: When a company leases an asset and then leases it out again, it becomes an intermediate lessor, sitting between the head lessor and the new tenant.
To classify a sublease as finance or operating, the intermediate lessor looks at the right-of-use asset from the head lease, not the original physical asset.

diagrams.purpose: Show the three-party chain and that the intermediate lessor classifies against the right-of-use asset, not the physical asset.

required_elements.description: Box at the top labelled Head Lessor, the original owner of the physical asset.
Box in the middle labelled Intermediate Lessor, the company that rents then sublets.
Box at the bottom labelled Subtenant, the new party leasing from the intermediate lessor.
Icon of the underlying physical asset such as a building, owned by the head lessor.
Icon of the right-of-use asset held by the intermediate lessor, the thing actually subleased.
Arrow showing rent paid from intermediate lessor up to head lessor.
Arrow showing rent paid from subtenant up to intermediate lessor.

choreography.narration: What happens when you rent an apartment from a landlord, and then rent that very same apartment out to someone else?
<<SECTION:Sublease|id=sec-1>>Suddenly you are stuck in the middle. You pay rent upward to your landlord, and someone pays rent up to you.
At the top is the head lessor, the original owner you leased from. At the bottom is your new tenant, the subtenant. You sit in between.
When a company rents an asset and then leases it out again, accounting gives that middle role a name: the intermediate lessor.

<<WRITE_KEY:Rent then sublet then you become the intermediate lessor, sitting between head lessor and subtenant|id=key-1>>So remember this position carefully. The intermediate lessor is the one wedged between the head lessor above and the subtenant below.
Now here is the question that trips everyone up. When you classify your sublease as finance or operating, what asset do you actually compare it against?
Not the building. You never owned the building. What you own is the right to use it, granted by the head lease.

<<WRITE_KEY:Classify the sublease against the right-of-use asset, not the physical asset|id=key-2>>So the intermediate lessor classifies the sublease by looking at the right-of-use asset, treating that as if it were the underlying asset.
There is one neat shortcut for the discount rate. If you cannot readily work out the interest rate implicit in the sublease, you simply borrow the rate you already use for the head lease.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term head lease then sublease is operating|id=text-1>>And one special case to lock in: if the head lease was a short-term lease you treated under the short-term exemption, then your sublease is automatically classified as an operating lease.
So always picture the chain: head lessor, you in the middle, subtenant, and remember you judge the sublease against your right-of-use asset, never the bricks and mortar.

lesson_plans.title: Sale and Leaseback: Selling What You Keep Using

hook.text: A company sells its own office building for cash, and the very next morning everyone walks back into the exact same building to work. Nothing on the desks moved. So did anything really get sold?

crucial_facts: A sale and leaseback is only treated as a real sale if the transfer qualifies as a sale under Ind AS 115; otherwise it is just financing in disguise.
When it is a genuine sale, the seller-lessee keeps the right-of-use asset at the proportion of the old carrying amount it still uses, and recognises gain only on the rights it actually transferred.

diagrams.purpose: Show the two parties, the asset moving one way and cash moving the other, then the lease bringing the right-of-use back, so the student sees that usage stays put while ownership and cash swap.

required_elements.description: Box on the left labelled Seller-lessee, the company that owns and uses the building.
Box on the right labelled Buyer-lessor, the company that buys the building and leases it out.
Arrow from seller-lessee to buyer-lessor representing the building (the asset) being sold.
Arrow from buyer-lessor back to seller-lessee representing the cash paid.
Arrow from buyer-lessor to seller-lessee representing the right-of-use leased back.
Icon of the building that stays in the same physical place throughout.

diagrams.purpose: Split the old carrying amount of the asset into the portion of rights retained (kept as right-of-use asset) and the portion of rights transferred (on which gain or loss is recognised).

required_elements.description: A full horizontal bar representing the previous carrying amount of the asset.
Left segment of the bar representing the proportion of rights retained, carried forward as the right-of-use asset.
Right segment of the bar representing the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor, on which gain or loss is recognised.
Label on the transferred portion showing that only this slice generates recognised gain or loss.

choreography.narration: A company sells its own office building for cash, and the very next morning everyone walks back into the exact same building to work. So did anything really get sold?
<<SECTION:Sale and leaseback|id=sec-1>>This move has a name. The company that sells and then rents back is the seller-lessee, and the company that buys and then rents it out is the buyer-lessor.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Asset out, cash in|id=text-1>>Watch what flows. The building goes from the seller to the buyer, and the cash comes straight back the other way.
But the seller still needs that building, so the buyer immediately leases the right to use it back to them. The desks never move.
Here is the question that decides everything. Was this actually a sale, or was the company just borrowing money with the building as security?

<<WRITE_KEY:Sale only if it qualifies under Ind AS 115|id=key-1>>To answer that, we do not guess. We test the transfer against Ind AS one hundred fifteen, the standard on revenue from contracts with customers. Only if it passes that test do we call it a sale.
If it does not pass, then no real sale happened. The cash is simply a loan, and the building stays on the seller's books as if nothing changed.

<<SECTION:When it is a genuine sale|id=sec-2>>Now suppose it does pass the test. Here is the subtle part. The seller sold the building, but kept the right to use it. So the seller did not give up the whole asset.
Think of the building's old book value as one bar. Part of it represents the rights the seller kept, and part represents the rights handed over to the buyer.
So how much gain does the seller get to book? Only on the slice they actually gave away, never on the slice they kept using.

<<WRITE_KEY:ROU = retained proportion of old carrying amount; gain only on rights transferred|id=key-2>>The right-of-use asset is carried at that retained proportion of the old book value, and the seller recognises gain or loss only on the rights transferred to the buyer.
Meanwhile the buyer-lessor has the easy job. They record buying the asset under the normal standards, and account for the lease they granted using the lessor rules you already know.
And one last guard. If the price was not fair value or the rent was not at market rates, you adjust, treating any shortfall as a prepayment and any excess as extra financing from the buyer.

So the lesson holds together. First ask if it is really a sale under Ind AS one hundred fifteen, and if it is, recognise gain only on what you gave away, because you never truly let go of what you kept using.

equations.explanation_in_words: The right-of-use asset equals the old book value scaled down to just the fraction of rights the seller kept.
The gain you may recognise is the total gain scaled down to only the portion of rights you actually transferred to the buyer.

lesson_plans.title: Subleases on Transition: A Fresh Look

hook.text: A lease that was perfectly fine yesterday suddenly has to be re-judged today, not because the contract changed, but because the rulebook did.

crucial_facts: On the date you adopt Ind AS 116, you must re-test every ongoing sublease that used to be an operating lease, judging it against the remaining terms of BOTH the head lease and the sublease.
If a sublease that was an operating lease now qualifies as a finance lease, you treat it as a brand-new finance lease starting on the transition date.

diagrams.purpose: Show the intermediate lessor sitting in the middle: renting from the landlord on one side (head lease) and renting out to a subtenant on the other (sublease). The viewer must see WHY two contracts must be judged together.

required_elements.description: A box on the left labelled Landlord, the original owner of the building.
A box in the centre labelled Intermediate Lessor, the company that rents and then rents out.
A box on the right labelled Subtenant, the new tenant who occupies the building.
An arrow from landlord to intermediate lessor labelled Head Lease.
An arrow from intermediate lessor to subtenant labelled Sublease.
A highlight or marker over the sublease arrow indicating the point of reassessment on transition.

choreography.narration: A lease that was perfectly fine yesterday suddenly has to be re-judged today, not because the contract changed one word, but because the rulebook underneath it did.
<<SECTION:The Sandwich Position|id=sec-1>>To see why, picture a company that rents a building from a landlord.
That same company then turns around and rents the building out to someone else, so it sits squarely in the middle of two deals.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Intermediate lessor = renter + renter-out|id=text-1>>We call this company the intermediate lessor, because it rents on one side and rents out on the other.
The deal with the landlord is the head lease, and the deal with the new tenant is the sublease.
Now, under the old standard, Ind AS seventeen, leases were sorted into two buckets, operating leases or finance leases, and a great many subleases landed in the operating bucket.
So here is the honest question, when you move to the new standard, Ind AS one hundred sixteen, can you just leave those old operating subleases exactly where they were?

<<SECTION:Re-test on Transition|id=sec-2>>No. On the date you first apply the new standard, you must take a fresh look at every ongoing sublease that used to be an operating lease and decide all over again.
And here is the clever part, you do not judge the sublease alone, you judge it against what is left of both the head lease and the sublease together.

Why both? Because if you have already handed almost the whole remaining life of the building to your subtenant, you have effectively passed on the risks and rewards of owning that right, and that smells like a finance lease, not an operating one.

<<WRITE_KEY:Operating under Ind AS 17 to finance under Ind AS 116 = treat as a NEW finance lease at transition date|id=key-1>>So when a sublease that was operating now qualifies as a finance lease, you do not patch the old one, you treat it as a brand-new finance lease starting on the transition date.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Same building, new judgement|id=text-2>>Notice what never changed, the building, the landlord, the tenant, the words of the contract, all the same, only the rulebook shifted, and that re-test is the whole story of subleases on transition.

lesson_plans.title: The Lease Definition on Transition: A Shortcut Worth Taking

hook.text: Imagine your company has signed three thousand contracts over the past twenty years. The accounting rulebook just changed. Do you really have to re-read every single one?

crucial_facts: On transition to Ind AS 116, a company may choose NOT to reassess contracts that were not identified as leases under the old standard, Ind AS 17 — this is the practical expedient.
If you skip the reassessment, you carry forward your old lease conclusions; you only apply the new definition to contracts signed on or after the transition date.

diagrams.purpose: Show the fork in the road on transition: reassess everything with the new definition, or grandfather the old conclusions and only apply the new definition going forward.

required_elements.description: A stack of old contracts signed before the transition date, labelled 'Existing contracts'.
A diamond decision node labelled 'Apply new definition to all existing contracts?'
Arrow from the decision node to the 'Yes' outcome: re-check every contract with the new Ind AS 116 definition.
Arrow from the decision node to the 'No' outcome: keep old Ind AS 17 conclusions, apply new definition only to new contracts.
Outcome box for the Yes path: 'Reassess all — heavy work, fresh eyes'.
Outcome box for the No path: 'Carry forward old conclusions — the practical expedient'.

choreography.narration: Imagine your company has signed three thousand contracts over the past twenty years. The accounting rulebook just changed. Do you really have to re-read every single one?

<<SECTION:Definition of lease on transition|id=sec-1>>Here is the situation. The old rulebook was called Ind AS seventeen. The new one is Ind AS one hundred sixteen, and it changed, just slightly, what actually counts as a lease.
So when a company switches over, it hits a fork in the road. <<WRITE_TEXT:Two choices on transition|id=text-1>>
Down the first path, the company says yes: apply the brand new definition to every single existing contract, with completely fresh eyes.
That means digging through hundreds or thousands of old agreements and re-checking each one. It is thorough, but it is an enormous amount of work.
So here is the honest question: is there a way to avoid re-reading every old contract you ever signed?

Yes. Down the second path, the standard gives a friendly shortcut. <<WRITE_KEY:You may choose NOT to reassess contracts not identified as leases under Ind AS 17|id=key-1>>You can choose not to reassess contracts that were never identified as containing a lease under the old standard.
In plain terms: if a contract was not a lease under the old rules, you simply trust that and leave it alone. You do not put it through the new definition.

This shortcut has a name. Accountants call it a practical expedient — a permitted simplification that saves you from a mountain of work. <<WRITE_TEXT:Practical expedient = permitted shortcut|id=text-2>>
But notice the trade-off. If you take the shortcut, you carry your old conclusions forward, and the new definition only applies to contracts you sign on or after the transition date.

Choose the first path and you reassess everything; choose the second and you grandfather the past, applying fresh eyes only to new contracts. <<WRITE_KEY:Reassess all, OR carry forward old conclusions + new definition for new contracts|id=key-2>>
So the big idea is simple: the standard lets you trade completeness for effort. Re-check everything, or trust the past and look forward. Both are allowed, and the company picks.

lesson_plans.title: Switching to Ind AS 116: How a Lessee Crosses Over

hook.text: A company has been renting buildings for years under the old rules. Tomorrow the rulebook changes. What does it do with all the leases it already signed?

crucial_facts: A lessee chooses one of two transition paths: full retrospective, which redoes every past period, or modified retrospective, which leaves the past alone and adjusts opening equity on day one.

Under the modified approach, the lease liability is the remaining payments discounted at today's borrowing rate, and the cumulative effect lands as a single adjustment to equity at the date of initial application.

diagrams.purpose: Show the single decision point splitting into two transition routes and what each one touches on the financial statements.

required_elements.description: A central box labelled 'New standard arrives — choose a path' from which two arrows branch.
Upper branch labelled 'Full retrospective' leading to a box.
Box describing full retrospective: 'Redo every period as if always applied — plus a third balance sheet'.
Lower branch labelled 'Modified retrospective' leading to a box.
Box describing modified retrospective: 'Leave the past alone — adjust opening equity at date of initial application'.
A small icon of an extra balance sheet attached to the full retrospective box, emphasising the extra work.
A small marker on the modified retrospective box showing a single arrow into 'Opening equity'.

choreography.narration: A company has been renting buildings for years under the old rules. Tomorrow the rulebook changes. What does it do with all the leases it already signed?
It can't just throw out the past, and it can't pretend nothing happened. So the new standard, Ind AS one sixteen, hands the lessee a choice between two honest ways to cross over.

<<SECTION:Two transition paths|id=sec-1>>The first path is the full retrospective approach. Here you pretend Ind AS one sixteen was always in force, and you go back and redo every single period you're showing.

Because you're reaching so far back into the past, you even have to lay out an extra third balance sheet, so a reader can see exactly where things stood at the earliest point. It is thorough, but it is a mountain of work.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Full retro = redo all periods + 3rd balance sheet|id=text-1>>The second path is the modified retrospective approach. It refuses to restate the comparative periods at all. The past stays exactly as it was printed.

Instead of touching the past, it gathers up the entire cumulative impact of switching and drops it as one single adjustment to equity, right at the start of the year it first applies the standard. We call that the date of initial application.
So here is the fork. Same company, same leases, but two very different amounts of work. Which one would you reach for if you only cared about today's numbers?

The modified path, almost every time, because you skip rebuilding history. But now a sharper question hides inside it. If you are not redoing the past, how do you decide what the lease is worth on day one?

<<SECTION:Measuring on day one|id=sec-2>>For what used to be an operating lease, you take only the payments still left to make, and you discount them back to today using the lessee's incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application. That discounted figure becomes the lease liability.

<<WRITE_KEY:Lease liability = remaining payments, discounted at today's borrowing rate|id=key-1>>And the cumulative effect of all of this lands as a single adjustment to opening equity, not scattered across the old years. That is the whole spirit of the modified approach.
There is a neat shortcut for the asset side too. You may rebuild the right-of-use asset retrospectively, or simply set it equal to the lease liability, and you can make that call lease by lease.

<<WRITE_KEY:Two paths: full retro redoes the past; modified retro adjusts opening equity|id=key-2>>So remember the fork. Full retrospective rewrites history and needs a third balance sheet. Modified retrospective leaves history untouched and corrects everything with one clean adjustment to equity on day one.

lesson_plans.title: Practical Expedients: The Shortcuts for Old Operating Leases

hook.text: Picture a company with three hundred old rental contracts, and a new rule that says every single one must now be re-calculated from scratch. Sounds like a nightmare, right? Except the rule-makers handed out a set of legal shortcuts so you don't have to.

crucial_facts: Practical expedients are optional, lease-by-lease shortcuts that let a lessee skip the hardest re-calculations when adopting the new lease standard.
Choosing an expedient trades perfect precision for far less work, and you can pick which ones to use for which leases.

choreography.narration: Picture a company with three hundred old rental contracts, and a new rule that says every single one must now be re-calculated from scratch. Sounds like a nightmare, right? Except the rule-makers handed out a set of legal shortcuts so you don't have to.

When the new lease standard arrives, all those leases that used to sit quietly off the balance sheet suddenly have to come on, as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. For one lease, that's annoying. For hundreds, it's an enormous amount of work.

<<SECTION:Practical Expedients|id=sec-1>>So the standard says, fine, here are some friendly time-savers. We call them practical expedients, and the key idea is this. <<WRITE_KEY:Practical expedients = optional, lease-by-lease shortcuts on transition|id=key-1>>They are optional shortcuts you can apply lease by lease, letting you skip the most painful calculations.
Let me walk you through the most useful ones, because each shortcut kills a specific headache. The first headache is the discount rate.

Normally every lease needs its own discount rate, the interest rate you use to bring future payments back to today's value. <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient A: one rate for similar leases|id=text-1>>The shortcut lets you apply a single rate to a whole bundle of leases that look reasonably alike, say all your photocopiers, instead of pricing each one separately.

The next two shortcuts are about leases that are basically not worth the effort. If a lease ends within twelve months of the changeover date, you're allowed to just treat it as a short-term lease and not bring it onto the books at all. <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient C: skip leases ending within 12 months|id=text-2>>Why fully account for something that's about to expire?

Here's one that sounds almost like cheating. Instead of doing a fresh impairment review to check if a lease has gone bad, you may simply rely on your earlier onerous-lease assessment. So which is the lazier, faster path here?

<<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient B: reuse old onerous-lease test instead of impairment review|id=text-3>>Reusing the assessment you already did under the provisions standard, just before transition, and then nudging your right-of-use asset by that provision. You skip an entire fresh review. That's the time-saver.

Two more quick ones. You can exclude initial direct costs, the little setup fees, from the value of your right-of-use asset. And you can use hindsight, meaning if a contract had an option to extend, you now already know whether it was actually extended, so use that knowledge instead of guessing.

Now notice the pattern. <<WRITE_KEY:Each expedient trades precision for less work; you choose lease by lease|id=key-2>>Every single one of these trades a bit of accuracy for a lot less work, and crucially, you decide which to apply, and to which leases.

That choice matters, because these are optional. A company that wants cleaner numbers might skip a shortcut; one drowning in old contracts will grab every one it can. The shortcuts bend the workload, not the truth, by much.
So when you face a transition question, don't panic at three hundred leases. Ask, which expedients apply here, and watch the mountain of work shrink. That's the whole point of practical expedients.

lesson_plans.title: Transition for the Lessor: When Nothing Changes (Almost)

hook.text: A brand new accounting standard sweeps in, turns the renter's whole world upside down, and the landlord barely lifts a finger. How can the same rulebook rewrite one side of the deal and leave the other side untouched?

crucial_facts: On transition to Ind AS one sixteen, a lessor makes no adjustments at all, except for two cases: subleases and sale-and-leaseback transactions.
In a sale-and-leaseback, the seller-lessee carries the old leaseback forward unchanged and keeps amortising any gain over the lease term.

diagrams.purpose: Contrast the two parties so the student sees visually that the standard's weight falls on the lessee, while the lessor side stays quiet except for two flagged exceptions.

required_elements.description: Left panel labelled 'Lessee', showing a big change burst: new right-of-use asset and lease liability appearing on the balance sheet.
Right panel labelled 'Lessor', mostly calm and unchanged, with a green tick meaning 'no adjustment'.
A small flag on the lessor side reading 'Exception 1: Subleases'.
A small flag on the lessor side reading 'Exception 2: Sale-and-leaseback'.

diagrams.purpose: Show the decision split inside a sale-and-leaseback on transition: was it a sale plus finance lease, or a sale plus operating lease under the old standard, and what each path does to the gain and the right-of-use asset.

required_elements.description: Starting node: 'Sale-and-leaseback already on the books under old standard'.
Branch for 'Sale + finance lease': carry leaseback forward as a finance lease, keep amortising the gain over the lease term.
Branch for 'Sale + operating lease': treat leaseback as an operating lease, adjust the right-of-use asset for any off-market deferred gains or losses.
Annotation on the finance branch: 'gain continues to amortise'.
Annotation on the operating branch: 'adjust right-of-use asset for off-market terms'.

choreography.narration: A brand new accounting standard sweeps in, turns the renter's whole world upside down, and the landlord barely lifts a finger. How can the same rulebook leave one side almost untouched?

Remember who's who. The lessor is the party that owns an asset and rents it out; the lessee is the one paying to use it. <<SECTION:Lessor on transition|id=sec-1>>For the lessee, Ind AS one sixteen forces a giant change: a brand new right-of-use asset and a lease liability land on the balance sheet.

Now look across to the lessor. Almost nothing happens. <<WRITE_KEY:Lessor: no adjustment on transition (except 2 cases)|id=key-1>>As a general rule, a lessor makes no adjustments at all when moving from the old standard to the new one.

Why so calm on the lessor's side? Because the old standard already split leases into finance and operating leases for lessors, and the new standard keeps that same split, so there is simply nothing to redo.
But I said almost untouched. So where exactly does the lessor's quiet life get interrupted?

In exactly two situations. First, subleases, where someone renting an asset turns around and rents it out to yet another party. Second, sale-and-leaseback transactions, where you sell an asset and immediately lease it back. <<WRITE_TEXT:Exceptions: subleases & sale-and-leaseback|id=text-1>>Everywhere else, the lessor does nothing.
So the headline to hold onto: on transition, a lessor makes no adjustments at all, except for subleases and sale-and-leaseback transactions.

Let's zoom into that second exception, the sale-and-leaseback, because that's where students get tangled. <<SECTION:Sale-and-leaseback on transition|id=sec-2>>Picture a deal already sitting on the books under the old standard.
The first question is how that old deal was classified: was it accounted for as a sale plus a finance lease, or as a sale plus an operating lease?

If it was a sale plus finance lease, the path is gentle. The seller-lessee carries the leaseback forward exactly like any finance lease already in place, and any gain on the original sale just keeps amortising over the lease term.

If instead it was a sale plus operating lease, you treat the leaseback like any other operating lease, but with one tweak: you adjust the right-of-use asset for any deferred gains or losses tied to off-market terms sitting on the balance sheet just before transition. <<WRITE_STEP:Operating: adjust ROU asset for off-market deferred gains/losses|id=step-1>>

So the whole lesson collapses to one calm idea: the lessor mostly does nothing on transition, and only two special deals, subleases and sale-and-leasebacks, ask for any care at all. <<WRITE_KEY:Carry old leaseback forward; keep amortising the gain|id=key-2>>

lesson_plans.title: The Ghost Asset: Cleaning Up Old Lease Values on Transition

hook.text: Here is a strange one: you are sitting on an asset on your balance sheet that, the moment you adopt a new accounting standard, simply has to vanish. Where does it go?

crucial_facts: On transition to Ind AS 116, you derecognise any favourable or unfavourable lease asset or liability from a past business combination, and fold that amount into the right-of-use asset instead.
The value never disappears from the books — it just moves home, from a separate intangible into the right-of-use asset.

diagrams.purpose: Show the old favourable-lease asset being derecognised and its value flowing into the right-of-use asset, so the student sees the transfer rather than a loss of value.

required_elements.description: A box labelled 'Favourable lease asset (from Ind AS 103)' representing the previously recognised intangible.
A box labelled 'Right-of-use asset' representing the new Ind AS 116 asset.
An arrow flowing from the old lease asset box into the right-of-use asset box, showing the carrying amount being added across.
A cross or strike mark over the old lease asset box indicating it is removed from the balance sheet.

choreography.narration: Here is a strange one: you are sitting on an asset on your balance sheet that, the moment you adopt a new accounting standard, simply has to vanish.

<<SECTION:Where the asset came from|id=sec-1>>To see why, rewind. Years ago this company bought another whole business — a business combination — and that acquired business had operating leases running.

One of those leases was a bargain: the rent locked in was cheaper than anything you could get in the market today. That favourable deal has real worth, so under Ind AS 103 you recorded it as a separate asset.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Favourable lease = separate asset under Ind AS 103|id=text-1>>So before transition, the picture is simple: a standalone favourable-lease asset, sitting on its own, measured at its carrying amount.

Now Ind AS 116 arrives. It says every lease gets a single right-of-use asset. So a question lands: if the lease already created a separate favourable-terms asset, do we now double-count it alongside the new right-of-use asset?
No double-counting allowed. The rule is clean: you derecognise that old favourable or unfavourable lease asset completely.
<<WRITE_STEP:Step 1 — Derecognise the old Ind AS 103 lease asset or liability|id=step-1>>But — and this is the heart of it — the value does not just evaporate. Watch where it goes.

<<WRITE_STEP:Step 2 — Adjust the right-of-use asset by the same amount|id=step-2>>That same carrying amount is added straight onto the right-of-use asset. The value simply moves home — out of the separate box, into the right-of-use asset.

And it works both ways. If the old lease had been a bad deal — paying more than market — you would have carried an unfavourable lease liability instead. Same move: derecognise it, and reduce the right-of-use asset by that amount.

<<WRITE_KEY:Old lease asset/liability is derecognised; its amount adjusts the right-of-use asset at the date of initial application|id=key-1>>So nothing is lost and nothing is invented. The total value on the balance sheet is exactly the same — it has just been re-housed inside the right-of-use asset.
That is the whole rule. One asset vanishes from its own line, and reappears, to the penny, baked into the right-of-use asset — all on the date you first apply the new standard.

lesson_plans.title: Which Leases Live Inside Ind AS 116?

hook.text: You can sign a lease for the land that sits on top of an oilfield and follow the leasing rulebook — but sign a lease for the oil underneath that very same land, and the rulebook tells you to go away.

crucial_facts: Ind AS 116 applies to all leases EXCEPT leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources.
The exclusion is about the non-regenerative resource itself; a lease over the land surface stays inside the scope even when the land happens to sit above oil.

diagrams.purpose: Show a single boundary line that separates rights inside Ind AS 116 from the one right that is carved out, anchored to the same physical oilfield site so the student feels why the oil-itself right is the odd one out.

required_elements.description: A large rounded boundary labelled 'Inside Ind AS 116' enclosing the rights that qualify as leases under the standard.
A card representing the right to explore for and extract oil from oilfield Y, drawn OUTSIDE the boundary, marked as carved out.
A card representing the surface lease — the right to access the land above the oil — drawn INSIDE the boundary.
A card representing the right to lay water pipelines over adjacent land, drawn INSIDE the boundary.
An arrow pushing the oil-extraction-right card out across the boundary, labelled 'non-regenerative resource'.

choreography.narration: You can sign a lease for the land that sits on top of an oilfield and follow the leasing rulebook — but sign a lease for the oil underneath that very same land, and the rulebook hands it back and tells you to look elsewhere.
<<SECTION:Scope of Ind AS 116|id=sec-1>>So let's draw the boundary. Inside this circle live all the agreements the leasing standard, Ind AS 116, actually governs.

<<WRITE_KEY:Ind AS 116 applies to ALL leases except leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, gas and similar non-regenerative resources|id=key-1>>Here is the one rule that does all the work: the standard applies to all leases, with a single carve-out — leases to explore for, or use, minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources.
Now picture our company, Entity X, holding three different rights over the same patch of ground. The question is honest — which of them actually sit inside that circle?
Take the first right: the right to explore for, and pull oil out of, oilfield Y for twenty-five years. Watch where it goes.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Oil extraction right = carved OUT|id=text-1>>The oil is a non-regenerative resource — once you pump it out, it's gone, it doesn't grow back. That is exactly the carve-out, so this right is pushed straight outside the boundary.
Notice what we did NOT exclude: only the resource itself. So what about the second right — the surface lease, the right just to walk onto and use the land that happens to sit above the oil?

<<WRITE_TEXT:Surface lease = INSIDE scope|id=text-2>>That is a lease of land, plain and simple. The land regenerates nothing and gets extracted from nothing — it's just ground you're renting. It stays firmly inside Ind AS 116.
And the third right — laying water pipelines over the neighbouring land, because Entity X needs water to extract the oil. The water is for the oil, but the lease is over the land.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Pipeline land lease = INSIDE scope|id=text-3>>Renting the surface of adjacent land is, once again, just a lease of land. It supports the oil business, but it is not a lease of the non-regenerative resource. So it also sits inside the circle.

Here's an example from the chapter. Entity X obtains three rights, and we need to decide which fall within the scope of Ind AS 116. Right (a) is the rights to explore for oil and use oil from oilfield Y for twenty-five years. Right (b) is the right to access the land containing the oil, called a surface lease. And right (c) is the right to lay water pipelines over land adjacent to the oilfield, because water is needed in the extraction process. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Which of rights (a), (b), (c) obtained by Entity X fall within the scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start from the scope rule. Ind AS 116 paragraph three excludes leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources. So the test is simple: does the lease give the right to explore for or extract the oil itself? <<WRITE_STEP:Paragraph 3 excludes leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, gas and similar non-regenerative resources.|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now apply it. Right (a) is a right to explore for and use the oil directly, so it falls squarely inside the exclusion. Right (b), the surface lease, only gives access to the area where the oil lies, but it exists to reach and extract that oil, so it too is tied to the oil itself. That means rights (a) and (b) are not covered by Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_STEP:(a) explore/use oil and (b) surface lease relate to the oil itself, exclusion applies.|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Right (c) is different. Laying water pipelines is about transporting water used in the extraction process. It does not give a right to explore for, or extract, or use the oil. Because it relates to the extraction process rather than the oil itself, it does not fall in the paragraph three exclusion, so right (c) is covered by Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_STEP:(c) water pipelines support the extraction process, not the oil itself, so the standard applies.|id=ex-step-1-3>>

And the answer is: rights (a) and (b) are not covered by Ind AS 116, while right (c) is covered by Ind AS 116 because it relates to the extraction process, not to exploring for or extracting the oil itself. <<WRITE_ANSWER:(a) and (b): outside Ind AS 116. (c): within Ind AS 116.|id=ex-ans-1>>

You've seen this yourself — think about the toll road you drive on, or the data cables running under your street. The company laying that infrastructure usually doesn't own the land; they pay the landowner for the right to run pipes or cables across it for years. That's the very same situation as Entity X laying its water pipelines. <<WRITE_TEXT:pipeline right-of-way = inside the standard|id=ext-1>> It supports the work, but it isn't a right to explore for or extract oil, so the leasing standard applies to it.

Here's something wild about this: the oil you pump out of the ground today took tens of millions of years to form, and on any human timescale it never comes back. That's literally what non-regenerative means.

And that permanence is exactly why the standard singles out rights to explore for or extract oil, gas, and minerals. <<WRITE_KEY:non-regenerative resources → excluded from the lease standard|id=ext-key-2>> Because once the resource is consumed it's truly gone, those rights are deliberately pushed outside the leasing standard.

<<WRITE_KEY:Carve-out = the resource itself; land leases above/around it stay IN|id=key-2>>See the pattern? Two of three rights are inside, and the only one excluded is the one that touches the oil itself. The carve-out is about the non-regenerative resource, never about the land it lies beneath.

So next time a lease lands on your desk near an oilfield, ask one question: am I leasing the resource, or just the land? Lease the land and you're inside Ind AS 116; lease the oil and you read a different standard entirely.

lesson_plans.title: Is It a Lease? The Air Navigation Trap

hook.text: A company gets the exclusive right to run an entire country's air navigation system for ten years — and yet, surprisingly, that contract is NOT a lease.

crucial_facts: Ind AS 116 explicitly EXCLUDES service concession arrangements that fall within Appendix D of Ind AS 115 — so before calling something a lease, you must rule out a service concession first.

A service concession requires BOTH that the grantor controls the price charged to users AND keeps a significant residual interest in the infrastructure; if either test fails, it is not a service concession.

diagrams.purpose: Show the decision path: does the contract land inside Ind AS 116, or get diverted out by the service concession exclusion, and exactly which test breaks that diversion.

required_elements.description: A box labelled 'Contract: right to operate air navigation system for 10 years'.
A gate/diamond labelled 'Apply Ind AS 116 to all leases'.
An arrow branching off labelled 'EXCEPT service concession arrangements (Appendix D, Ind AS 115)'.
A test box: 'Does grantor control the PRICE charged to users?'
A test box: 'Does grantor keep a significant RESIDUAL interest in the infrastructure?'
A result box: 'Price NOT controlled by grantor -> NOT a service concession'.
An arrow returning the contract into the Ind AS 116 scope after the concession exclusion fails.

choreography.narration: A company gets the exclusive right to run an entire country's air navigation system for ten whole years, and yet, surprisingly, that contract is not a lease. Let me show you why.

<<SECTION:Scoping a contract under Ind AS 116|id=sec-1>>Here is the contract on the table. A private company, Entity X, signs with a Transport Ministry to operate the system that guides airplanes, upgrade it, and charge users at rates it negotiates freely, with no price cap.
Your instinct says lease, because Ind AS 116 says apply this standard to all leases. And that word, all, feels airtight.
But the standard has carve-outs. One of them quietly diverts a whole class of contracts out of scope: service concession arrangements that fall under Appendix D of Ind AS 115.
So before we ever call this a lease, we must ask: is it actually one of those service concessions hiding in disguise?
<<WRITE_TEXT:Service concession needs BOTH tests|id=text-1>>Appendix D gives two conditions, and crucially, you need both of them to be true. The first is about price.
Test one: does the grantor control or regulate at what price the operator serves users? Here the Ministry sets no price cap at all. Entity X negotiates rates directly and freely.
And that single fact breaks the whole thing. With no price control by the grantor, the first condition fails, and a service concession needs both conditions.
The second test, about the grantor keeping a significant residual interest in the system at the end, no longer even matters, because one failed test already settles it.

Here's an example from the chapter. Entity X is a private sector entity, and it enters a contract with the grantor, the Transport Ministry of Country S, to acquire the right to operate the civil air navigation system. Under the contract, the grantor provides the air navigation system, and X is required to upgrade the system. X charges users based on rates negotiated directly with individual users, there is no price-cap mechanism imposed by the grantor, and the contract period is ten years. The question is whether this contract falls within the scope of Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: X (private) operates Country S air navigation system for grantor (Transport Ministry); X sets prices, no price-cap, 10-year term — within scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by checking the test for a service concession arrangement. Such an arrangement requires the grantor to control the services, the recipients, and the price, and to control any significant residual interest in the infrastructure. Here many of those features are present, but the crucial one fails: the grantor does not control prices, because X negotiates rates directly with users and there is no price-cap. <<WRITE_STEP:1. Service concession test: grantor must control services, recipients, price + significant residual interest|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:2. Here grantor does NOT control prices (X negotiates directly, no price-cap) -> service concession test fails|id=ex-step-1-2>>

And the answer is: because the grantor does not control prices, this is not a service concession arrangement, so it falls outside Appendix D of Ind AS 115. Therefore the right to use the air navigation system is within the scope of Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Grantor doesn't control prices -> not a service concession -> the contract is within the scope of Ind AS 116|id=ex-ans-1>>

You've driven this yourself — a private company builds and runs a toll highway, but the government dictates the exact toll they can charge. That price cap is the government keeping control of the service, which is exactly the first condition for a service concession arrangement. In our question, Entity X negotiates prices freely with no cap, so that grip is gone — and the whole classification flips back to Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_TEXT:Govt sets toll = price control = condition 1|id=ext-1>>

Something wild about this: the air navigation system in our question is guiding thousands of planes through the sky right now, yet the entire accounting answer turns on one small detail — whether the grantor controls the price. Because Entity X sets its own rates with no cap, that single missing condition pulls this giant public system out of service concession accounting and straight into Ind AS 116. One word, the 'and' between two conditions, decides everything.
So the exclusion does not catch this contract. It is not a service concession, which means it falls right back into the scope of Ind AS 116.

<<WRITE_KEY:Rule out service concession (both Appendix D tests) before applying Ind AS 116|id=key-1>>So remember the order of thinking: Ind AS 116 covers all leases, except service concessions, and a service concession demands both price control by the grantor and a residual interest. Fail either one, and the exclusion doesn't apply.

lesson_plans.title: When a Lease Isn't a Lease: Control Inside a Concession

hook.text: A company signs a contract, pays for the trains, and runs them every day for fifteen years — and yet, on its books, it owns no lease at all. How?

crucial_facts: A contract is a lease under Ind AS 116 only if you control the use of the asset — and control means deciding HOW and FOR WHAT PURPOSE it is used.
In a service concession, the Grantor sets the timetable and the prices, so the Grantor — not the Operator — directs the use of the rolling stock, and no lease exists for the Operator.

diagrams.purpose: Show that the right to direct the use of the rolling stock flows from Entity Y, past Operator X, to Grantor G — so X is only a conduit, not the controller.

required_elements.description: A box labelled 'Entity Y (lessor)' on the left, owner of the rolling stock.
A box in the middle labelled 'Operator X' who pays Y and physically runs the trains.
A box on the right labelled 'Grantor G' who sets the timetable and regulates passenger prices.
A small train icon representing the rolling stock asset, sitting near Operator X.
An arrow from Operator X back to Entity Y labelled 'pays for use'.
A bold arrow showing the right-to-direct-use passing THROUGH Operator X and landing on Grantor G.
A stamp near Operator X reading 'no right to control = no lease'.

choreography.narration: A company signs a contract, pays for the trains, and runs them every single day for fifteen years — and yet, on its books, there is no lease at all. How can that be?
<<SECTION:The set-up|id=sec-1>>Here is our cast. Entity Y owns the rolling stock — the trains and equipment. Operator X pays Entity Y to use them and runs the actual service.
But Operator X did not just go into business for itself. X holds a service concession from Grantor G to run a public rail service for fifteen years.
Now, normally, if you pay to use an identified asset, you ask one simple question to decide if it is a lease: do you control the use of that asset?
<<WRITE_TEXT:Control = decide how & for what purpose|id=text-1>>And control is not just touching the asset. Control means you decide how it is used and for what purpose — you direct the use.
So watch the payment. Operator X does pay Entity Y for using the rolling stock — money flows this way.
Paying looks like a lease. So who actually decides how these trains run — when they run, and what passengers are charged?
<<SECTION:Where control really sits|id=sec-2>>It is not Operator X. Grantor G sets the timetable the trains must follow and regulates the price X can charge passengers. G directs the use.
Look at where the control arrow lands. It passes straight through Operator X and stops at Grantor G. X holds the trains, but X does not direct them.

<<WRITE_KEY:No right to direct use = not a lease under Ind AS 116|id=key-1>>And that settles it. Because Operator X never gets the right to direct the use, X's contract with Entity Y is not a lease under Ind AS 116.

Here's an example from the chapter. Operator X enters into a service concession arrangement with Grantor G to operate a rail service for fifteen years, and this arrangement falls within the scope of Appendix D, Service Concession Arrangements, of Ind AS one fifteen. To run the service, X leases the infrastructure, the rolling stock, from Entity Y, the lessor, where the useful life of the rolling stock is twenty-five years, and X has the obligation to pay the lessor. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Is X's lease of rolling stock from Y within the scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>>

Now look at who actually controls the use of that rolling stock. During the concession period, Grantor G controls the services X delivers, G sets the timetable to which the rolling stock must be operated and regulates the price that X charges passengers, and at the end of the concession G has an option to acquire the rolling stock or otherwise direct its use. <<WRITE_STEP:G sets timetable + regulates price + holds end-of-concession option on rolling stock|id=ex-step-1>>

Appendix D of Ind AS one fifteen states that the operator does not have the right to control the use of the infrastructure; it merely has access to operate it on behalf of the grantor. Since X does not control the use of the rolling stock, the contract is not a lease within the scope of Ind AS one sixteen. <<WRITE_STEP:Per Appendix D, X does NOT control use of the infrastructure|id=ex-step-2>><<WRITE_ANSWER:The contract of X with Y is NOT within the scope of Ind AS 116|id=ex-ans-1>>

You've seen this yourself with food delivery riders. A rider might use a scooter that the delivery platform owns, driving it every single shift. But the platform sets the routes, fixes the delivery fees, and can pull that scooter back whenever it likes. Sound familiar? That's exactly Operator X with the trains. The rider uses the asset every day, but the platform calls the shots, so there's no control, and without control there's no lease.

Here's something wild about this. A huge number of the world's busiest toll roads, airports, and metro lines run on exactly this kind of arrangement. A private operator runs that public infrastructure for twenty, thirty, even forty years, collecting fees the whole time, yet it never sits on their balance sheet as their own property. <<WRITE_KEY:Concession operator runs it, never controls it|id=ext-key-1>> That's the same Appendix D logic from our question. The operator just has access to operate, following the grantor's terms. No control means it isn't theirs, and it isn't a lease.
This is why the rolling stock sits inside the service concession rules of Appendix D, not as a leased asset of Operator X. The same trains, but a completely different accounting home.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Payment alone never makes a lease|id=text-2>>So the lesson is sharp: paying for an asset is never enough. Lease accounting follows the right to direct the use — and here that right belongs to the Grantor.

segments.raw_narration: What if a company could legally choose to keep certain leases completely off its balance sheet — no asset, no liability, nothing at all?
segments.text_with_markers: What if a company could legally choose to keep certain leases completely off its balance sheet — no asset, no liability, nothing at all? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Normally, the rule is strict: when you lease something, you must record a right-of-use asset and a matching lease liability on your books, and that's a lot of accounting work.
segments.text_with_markers: Normally, the rule is strict: when you lease something, you must record a right-of-use asset and a matching lease liability on your books, and that's a lot of accounting work.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Recognition Exemption|id=sec-1>>So the standard offers a shortcut, called the recognition exemption — for two specific kinds of leases, the lessee, the one renting the asset, can simply skip all that recording.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Two exemptions: short-term leases and low-value leases|id=key-1>>The two kinds are short-term leases, and leases where the underlying asset is of low value.

segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term = 12 months or less at start|id=text-1>>Let's nail down the first one. A short-term lease is simply a lease that, at the moment it commences, has a term of twelve months or less. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Low-value leases|id=sec-2>>The second kind is the low-value lease — think of a laptop or an office phone — something you can use on its own, that isn't tightly bound up with your bigger, more valuable assets.

segments.raw_narration: The short-term exemption is all-or-nothing for a whole class of assets — choose it for your delivery vans, and it applies to every short-term van lease consistently.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Substantive substitution rights|id=sec-1>>Here's the catch. A lease needs an identified asset, something the customer is genuinely tied to. But suppose the supplier can quietly wheel that machine away and roll in any other one whenever it suits them.

segments.raw_narration: If the supplier holds that swapping power, then you were never really tied to that one machine at all. The asset stops being identified, and without an identified asset, there is simply no lease.

segments.raw_narration: But hold on, does every little swap clause destroy a lease? Surely not, or almost no contract would ever count.

segments.raw_narration: Substantive means two things must both be true. So picture two gates the supplier has to pass through before their swap right matters.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:gate-practical>> Substantive means two things must both be true. So picture two gates the supplier has to pass through before their swap right matters.

segments.raw_narration: Gate one, the practical ability. Can the supplier actually swap the asset throughout the period of use? If alternative assets aren't readily available, or it would be a huge hassle, the supplier can't really do it.

segments.raw_narration: Gate two, the economic benefit. Would the supplier actually gain from swapping? The cost of moving the asset must be outweighed by the benefit they'd get.

Then there's no identified asset, and no lease. <<TRACE:arrow-economic-yes>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: But if either gate stays shut, say swapping is impractical or there's nothing in it for the supplier, the swap clause is just paper. The asset stays identified, and a lease can still exist.

segments.raw_narration: You rent one floor of a building, or one strand of a giant fibre optic cable. One of those is a lease. The other might not be. Why?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:building-outline>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:7:portion_comparison>> You rent one floor of a building, or one strand of a giant fibre optic cable. One of those is a lease. The other might not be. Why? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Portions of Assets|id=sec-1>>The whole question comes down to a single idea: can you point at the exact piece you are using, and say nobody else can touch this part?
segments.text_with_markers: <<SECTION:Portions of Assets|id=sec-1>>The whole question comes down to a single idea: can you point at the exact piece you are using, and say nobody else can touch this part? <<POINT:building-outline>>

segments.raw_narration: Look at the floor you rent. It has its own walls, its own ceiling, its own boundary. It is physically separate from every other floor.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:floor-boundary>> Look at the floor you rent. It has its own walls, its own ceiling, its own boundary. It is physically separate from every other floor. <<TRACE:floor-boundary>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:A physically distinct portion, like a floor, is an identified asset|id=key-1>>Because that floor is physically distinct, it counts as an identified asset. And an identified asset is the very thing a lease needs.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:rented-floor>> <<WRITE_KEY:A physically distinct portion, like a floor, is an identified asset|id=key-1>>Because that floor is physically distinct, it counts as an identified asset. And an identified asset is the very thing a lease needs. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Now compare that to the fibre optic cable carrying thousands of light signals at once.
segments.text_with_markers: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:cable-outline>> Now compare that to the fibre optic cable carrying thousands of light signals at once.

segments.raw_narration: Suppose your contract just says you get some of the cable's capacity. Can you point at one specific fibre and say, this exact strand is mine and nobody else's?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:cable-capacity-slice>> Suppose your contract just says you get some of the cable's capacity. Can you point at one specific fibre and say, this exact strand is mine and nobody else's? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: You cannot. Your signal could travel down any strand at any moment. The portion you use is not physically distinct, so it is not an identified asset, and your contract is not a lease.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> You cannot. Your signal could travel down any strand at any moment. The portion you use is not physically distinct, so it is not an identified asset, and your contract is not a lease. <<POINT:cable-capacity-slice>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Not distinct, not identified, not a lease|id=text-1>>So a capacity portion that is not physically distinct fails the test. That is the rule for the fibre optic cable.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:cable-outline>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Not distinct, not identified, not a lease|id=text-1>>So a capacity portion that is not physically distinct fails the test. That is the rule for the fibre optic cable.

segments.raw_narration: But there is one escape hatch. What if your contract gives you almost the entire capacity of that cable, leaving only a sliver for anyone else?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:cable-capacity-slice>> But there is one escape hatch. What if your contract gives you almost the entire capacity of that cable, leaving only a sliver for anyone else? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Substantially all the capacity also counts as identified|id=key-2>>Then it qualifies after all. If you get substantially all of the capacity, you effectively obtain substantially all of the economic benefits, and the portion becomes an identified asset.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:cable-outline>> <<WRITE_KEY:Substantially all the capacity also counts as identified|id=key-2>>Then it qualifies after all. If you get substantially all of the capacity, you effectively obtain substantially all of the economic benefits, and the portion becomes an identified asset. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So a physically distinct floor is identified the easy way, by its walls and ceiling.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:floor-boundary>> So a physically distinct floor is identified the easy way, by its walls and ceiling. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Economic benefits|id=sec-1>>Before accountants can call a contract a lease, they ask one sharp thing: does the customer get substantially all the economic benefits from using that asset? Let's see what's actually on the table.

Let's see what's actually on the table.

segments.raw_narration: The biggest slice is the primary output — the main job the asset does. For our van, that's hauling your goods from place to place.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:slice-primary>> The biggest slice is the primary output — the main job the asset does. For our van, that's hauling your goods from place to place. <<TRACE:slice-primary>>

segments.raw_narration: That third slice matters: even cash you'd realise by renting it out to an outsider counts as an economic benefit from using the asset.

segments.raw_narration: So here's the answer to our opening question: if you pocket the hauling, the by-products, AND the sublease cash — you've captured substantially all the benefits, and that's exactly what control of use requires.

segments.raw_narration: You rent a car for a week. Who decides where it drives, when it stops, and what it carries? If the answer is you, you might be holding a lease without even knowing it.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Right to direct the use|id=sec-1>>We already know a lease needs an identified asset and that you get the economic benefits from it. But there is a second piece, and this is the heart of control: the right to direct the use.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:root-question>> <<SECTION:Right to direct the use|id=sec-1>>We already know a lease needs an identified asset and that you get the economic benefits from it. But there is a second piece, and this is the heart of control: the right to direct the use.

segments.raw_narration: Directing the use simply means you call the shots. You decide how the asset is used and for what purpose, like where that truck goes and what it carries.
segments.text_with_markers: Directing the use simply means you call the shots. You decide how the asset is used and for what purpose, like where that truck goes and what it carries. <<POINT:route-one-how-why>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Control = you decide HOW and WHY the asset is used|id=key-1>>So the most direct route is this: if you have the right to decide how and for what purpose the asset is used throughout the period, you control it.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:route-one-how-why>> <<WRITE_KEY:Control = you decide HOW and WHY the asset is used|id=key-1>>So the most direct route is this: if you have the right to decide how and for what purpose the asset is used throughout the period, you control it. <<TRACE:route-one-how-why>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: But here is the puzzle. What if every decision about how and why the asset is used is already locked in before you even sign? Can you still be in control?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:route-two-predetermined>> But here is the puzzle. What if every decision about how and why the asset is used is already locked in before you even sign? Can you still be in control? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Yes, you still can, through a second route, and the standard gives two ways it happens.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> Yes, you still can, through a second route, and the standard gives two ways it happens. <<TRACE:route-two-predetermined>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Predetermined use: control via operate OR design|id=text-1>>The first way: you have the right to operate the asset, or to direct others to operate it as you choose, and the supplier cannot change your operating instructions.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:sub-operate>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Predetermined use: control via operate OR design|id=text-1>>The first way: you have the right to operate the asset, or to direct others to operate it as you choose, and the supplier cannot change your operating instructions. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: The second way: you designed the asset in a manner that predetermined how and for what purpose it would be used. You made the decisions up front, at the drawing board.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:sub-designed>> The second way: you designed the asset in a manner that predetermined how and for what purpose it would be used. You made the decisions up front, at the drawing board. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Notice the pattern: either you decide as you go, or the decisions were baked in by you. Both routes land at the same place.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:control-result>> Notice the pattern: either you decide as you go, or the decisions were baked in by you. Both routes land at the same place.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Either route -> customer directs use -> lease|id=key-2>>And once you have the right to direct the use on top of the economic benefits, the customer controls the asset, and the contract is a lease.

segments.raw_narration: No, it does not. The part that gives you the right to use the asset is the lease component, and the service that just helps you run it is a non-lease component, and the rule is to keep them apart.

segments.raw_narration: But wait — you only pay one combined amount. How do you decide how much of that money belongs to the van and how much belongs to the service?

segments.raw_narration: You sign a five-year office lease, but you can walk away after three, and you're pretty sure you'll stay two more. So how many years long is your lease, really?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:non-cancellable-band>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:12:lease_term_timeline>> You sign a five-year office lease, but you can walk away after three, and you're pretty sure you'll stay two more. So how many years long is your lease, really? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: The answer matters more than it sounds, because almost every number in lease accounting, the asset value, the liability, the yearly charge, depends on this one length. Get the length wrong and everything downstream is wrong.
segments.text_with_markers: The answer matters more than it sounds, because almost every number in lease accounting, the asset value, the liability, the yearly charge, depends on this one length. Get the length wrong and everything downstream is wrong. <<POINT:lease-term-bracket>>

segments.raw_narration: So let's build the timeline. First, when does the clock start? Not the day you sign the paperwork. <<SECTION:When the clock starts|id=sec-1>>It starts on the commencement date, the day the lessor actually hands you the asset to use.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:commencement-date>> So let's build the timeline. First, when does the clock start? Not the day you sign the paperwork. <<SECTION:When the clock starts|id=sec-1>>It starts on the commencement date, the day the lessor actually hands you the asset to use. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Now here's the trap. Suppose your first three months are rent-free, a sweetener to get you to sign. Do those free months count as part of the lease term?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:rent-free-band>> Now here's the trap. Suppose your first three months are rent-free, a sweetener to get you to sign. Do those free months count as part of the lease term? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: They absolutely do. <<WRITE_KEY:Term starts at commencement; rent-free and reduced-rent months still count|id=key-1>>A rent-free or reduced-rent period is still you having the asset, so it is part of the term from day one.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> They absolutely do. <<WRITE_KEY:Term starts at commencement; rent-free and reduced-rent months still count|id=key-1>>A rent-free or reduced-rent period is still you having the asset, so it is part of the term from day one. <<POINT:rent-free-band>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Next comes the solid core of the term: the non-cancellable period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Non-cancellable = locked in, can't walk away|id=text-1>>This is the stretch where neither of you can just walk away, you're locked in.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:non-cancellable-band>> Next comes the solid core of the term: the non-cancellable period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Non-cancellable = locked in, can't walk away|id=text-1>>This is the stretch where neither of you can just walk away, you're locked in. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: But leases often have options bolted on. An option to extend, or an option to terminate early. Do we just include every extension option to be safe?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:option-band>> But leases often have options bolted on. An option to extend, or an option to terminate early. Do we just include every extension option to be safe? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: No, and this is the clever part. <<SECTION:The reasonably-certain test|id=sec-2>>You only include an extension period if you are reasonably certain you'll take it. And you only cut off a termination option if you're reasonably certain you won't use it.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> No, and this is the clever part. <<SECTION:The reasonably-certain test|id=sec-2>>You only include an extension period if you are reasonably certain you'll take it. And you only cut off a termination option if you're reasonably certain you won't use it. <<POINT:option-band>>

segments.raw_narration: So in our office example, the three locked-in years are in for certain, and because you're reasonably certain to stay the extra two, those join the term too, giving five.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:lease-term-bracket>> So in our office example, the three locked-in years are in for certain, and because you're reasonably certain to stay the extra two, those join the term too, giving five. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Put it together: the lease term is the non-cancellable period, plus any extension you're reasonably certain to take, plus any termination right you're reasonably certain not to use. <<WRITE_KEY:Term = non-cancellable period + options the lessee is reasonably certain to take|id=key-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:lease-term-bracket>> Put it together: the lease term is the non-cancellable period, plus any extension you're reasonably certain to take, plus any termination right you're reasonably certain not to use. <<WRITE_KEY:Term = non-cancellable period + options the lessee is reasonably certain to take|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: One last note: judgement isn't frozen. If the non-cancellable period itself changes, you go back and revise the term, because every downstream number leans on it.
segments.text_with_markers: One last note: judgement isn't frozen. If the non-cancellable period itself changes, you go back and revise the term, because every downstream number leans on it. <<POINT:non-cancellable-band>>

segments.raw_narration: You sign a five-year lease on a shop, but the contract lets you stay for five more years if you want. So how long is your lease, really? Five years, or ten?

So how long is your lease, really? Five years, or ten? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Extension and termination options|id=sec-1>>Here's the honest answer: it depends on a judgment you make right at the start, on what we call the commencement date.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Extension and termination options|id=sec-1>>Here's the honest answer: it depends on a judgment you make right at the start, on what we call the commencement date. <<POINT:commencement-date>>

segments.raw_narration: Look at the timeline. This solid bar is the part you are locked into — the years you cannot escape. That's the guaranteed period.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:guaranteed-period>> Look at the timeline. This solid bar is the part you are locked into — the years you cannot escape. That's the guaranteed period.

segments.raw_narration: And this dashed bar is the optional bit — the extra years you could take if you choose to extend. The big question is whether those dashed years count as part of your lease.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:optional-period>> And this dashed bar is the optional bit — the extra years you could take if you choose to extend. The big question is whether those dashed years count as part of your lease.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Lease term set by 'reasonably certain' judgment at commencement|id=key-1>>At the commencement date the entity must ask three things: is the lessee reasonably certain to extend, reasonably certain to buy the asset, and reasonably certain not to terminate early?

segments.raw_narration: If the answer is yes, you are reasonably certain to extend, then the lease term reaches forward and swallows those optional years.
segments.text_with_markers: If the answer is yes, you are reasonably certain to extend, then the lease term reaches forward and swallows those optional years. <<TRACE:extend-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: But if instead you are reasonably certain to terminate early, the lease term gets cut short, right here.
segments.text_with_markers: But if instead you are reasonably certain to terminate early, the lease term gets cut short, right here. <<TRACE:terminate-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: Now here is the trap. Reasonably certain is not the same as legally allowed. The contract gives you the option — but the standard asks something deeper.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:incentive-zone>> Now here is the trap. Reasonably certain is not the same as legally allowed. The contract gives you the option — but the standard asks something deeper. <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Test is economic incentive, not the contract wording|id=key-2>>The real test is economic incentive. Is there a strong financial reason that makes exercising the option the obvious choice?
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:incentive-zone>> <<WRITE_KEY:Test is economic incentive, not the contract wording|id=key-2>>The real test is economic incentive. Is there a strong financial reason that makes exercising the option the obvious choice? <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Consider all facts: fit-out cost, location, below-market rent|id=text-1>>For instance, in any case where you've spent a fortune fitting out the shop, or the rent for the extra years is far below market, walking away would be painful — so you're reasonably certain to stay.

segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:commencement-date>> The entity weighs all relevant facts and circumstances, including expected changes between today and the date the option would be exercised.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Past practice with similar leases also counts|id=text-2>>And don't forget habits — a lessee's past practice with similar leases tells you a lot about how likely an option really is to be used.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:Past practice with similar leases also counts|id=text-2>>And don't forget habits — a lessee's past practice with similar leases tells you a lot about how likely an option really is to be used. <<POINT:guaranteed-period>>

segments.raw_narration: So back to our shop: if the economic incentive to stay is strong, your lease is ten years, not five — and that bigger term means a bigger liability and a bigger right-of-use asset.
