segments.raw_narration: You sign a five-year lease on a delivery van and put it on your books today. Here's the puzzle: what should that van be worth on your books one year from now?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:start-value-point>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:15:rou_value_paths>> You sign a five-year lease on a delivery van and put it on your books today. Here's the puzzle: what should that van be worth on your books one year from now? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: The asset can't just sit there frozen at its starting value, because in real life that right to use the van is steadily getting used up. <<SECTION:Subsequent measurement|id=sec-1>>Keeping track of how that value changes over the life of the lease is what we call subsequent measurement.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:value-axis>> The asset can't just sit there frozen at its starting value, because in real life that right to use the van is steadily getting used up. <<SECTION:Subsequent measurement|id=sec-1>>Keeping track of how that value changes over the life of the lease is what we call subsequent measurement.

segments.raw_narration: And here's the answer to our puzzle: the company actually gets to choose between two different paths for that value, and we draw them both starting from the same point.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> And here's the answer to our puzzle: the company actually gets to choose between two different paths for that value, and we draw them both starting from the same point. <<POINT:start-value-point>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: The first path is the cost model — think of it as the simple, steady road. You begin with the cost and you shave a slice off it each period as depreciation, so the line just glides downward.
segments.text_with_markers: The first path is the cost model — think of it as the simple, steady road. You begin with the cost and you shave a slice off it each period as depreciation, so the line just glides downward. <<TRACE:cost-model-path>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Cost model = steady decline by depreciation|id=text-1>>Notice this line never jumps around. It only goes down, smoothly, year after year, as the van is used up.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:cost-model-label>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Cost model = steady decline by depreciation|id=text-1>>Notice this line never jumps around. It only goes down, smoothly, year after year, as the van is used up.

segments.raw_narration: The second path is the revaluation model. Watch what's different — it can be reset to the asset's fair value, so instead of only sliding down, it can step back up if the asset is worth more.
segments.text_with_markers: The second path is the revaluation model. Watch what's different — it can be reset to the asset's fair value, so instead of only sliding down, it can step back up if the asset is worth more. <<TRACE:revaluation-model-path>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Revaluation = reset to fair value|id=text-2>>So one road is steady and predictable, and the other tracks what the asset is really worth in the market.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:revaluation-model-label>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Revaluation = reset to fair value|id=text-2>>So one road is steady and predictable, and the other tracks what the asset is really worth in the market.

segments.raw_narration: Now, a fair question: if the revaluation path can keep your asset closer to its true worth, why wouldn't every company just pick it?

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:The cost model|id=sec-1>>The answer comes from something called the cost model, and it is just a clean recipe for tracking the value of your right to use that van as the years go by.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:original-cost-block>> <<SECTION:The cost model|id=sec-1>>The answer comes from something called the cost model, and it is just a clean recipe for tracking the value of your right to use that van as the years go by. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: You start with this full block, the original cost of the right-of-use asset, exactly what you measured it at on day one.
segments.text_with_markers: You start with this full block, the original cost of the right-of-use asset, exactly what you measured it at on day one. <<POINT:original-cost-block>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Depreciation = wearing-down of value over time|id=text-1>>Now, the van wears down a little every year, and that wearing-down of value is called depreciation, which we spread across the life of the asset using the rules in Ind AS sixteen.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:depreciation-cut>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Depreciation = wearing-down of value over time|id=text-1>>Now, the van wears down a little every year, and that wearing-down of value is called depreciation, which we spread across the life of the asset using the rules in Ind AS sixteen. <<TRACE:depreciation-cut>>

segments.raw_narration: So we cut that accumulated depreciation off the top of the block, and the more years pass, the bigger that cut grows.
segments.text_with_markers: So we cut that accumulated depreciation off the top of the block, and the more years pass, the bigger that cut grows. <<POINT:depreciation-cut>>

segments.raw_narration: Sometimes something unexpected happens, the asset suddenly loses value beyond ordinary wear, and that is an impairment loss, which we follow under Ind AS thirty-six.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:impairment-cut>> Sometimes something unexpected happens, the asset suddenly loses value beyond ordinary wear, and that is an impairment loss, which we follow under Ind AS thirty-six. <<TRACE:impairment-cut>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Carrying amount = cost less accumulated depreciation less accumulated impairment|id=key-1>>So we subtract any accumulated impairment losses too, and what is left is your net carrying amount, the figure that actually sits on the balance sheet.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> <<WRITE_KEY:Carrying amount = cost less accumulated depreciation less accumulated impairment|id=key-1>>So we subtract any accumulated impairment losses too, and what is left is your net carrying amount, the figure that actually sits on the balance sheet. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Take the original cost, subtract everything the asset has worn down by, then subtract any sudden losses, and the remainder is what the asset is carried at.
segments.text_with_markers: Take the original cost, subtract everything the asset has worn down by, then subtract any sudden losses, and the remainder is what the asset is carried at. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Carrying amount} = \text{Cost} - \text{Accumulated depreciation} - \text{Accumulated impairment losses}|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: But here is a question that trips people up: what if the lease itself changes partway through, say the rent gets revised, so the lease liability you owe is recalculated?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> But here is a question that trips people up: what if the lease itself changes partway through, say the rent gets revised, so the lease liability you owe is recalculated? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: When the lease liability is remeasured, you adjust the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset by the very same amount, up or down, so the two stay linked.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:remeasurement-adjustment>> When the lease liability is remeasured, you adjust the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset by the very same amount, up or down, so the two stay linked. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:No adjustment if asset already zero, or change is variable payment (no index/rate)|id=text-2>>There are just two exceptions: you stop if the asset is already reduced to zero, or if the change relates to a variable payment that does not depend on an index or a rate.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:No adjustment if asset already zero, or change is variable payment (no index/rate)|id=text-2>>There are just two exceptions: you stop if the asset is already reduced to zero, or if the change relates to a variable payment that does not depend on an index or a rate. <<POINT:remeasurement-adjustment>>

segments.raw_narration: So picture the whole journey: start at cost, cut away depreciation, cut away impairment, then nudge for any remeasurement, and you land on the carrying amount.

segments.raw_narration: You signed a five-year lease and locked a single number into your books. Two years in, you decide to stay seven years instead. So does that old number just get to stay wrong?

Two years in, you decide to stay seven years instead. So does that old number just get to stay wrong? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: It can't. That number, the lease liability, was only ever your best guess of all the future payments squeezed into one present value. When the facts behind the guess change, the number has to change too.
segments.text_with_markers: It can't. That number, the lease liability, was only ever your best guess of all the future payments squeezed into one present value. When the facts behind the guess change, the number has to change too. <<POINT:trigger-event>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Reassessment|id=sec-1>>Going back and remeasuring that liability so it matches the new reality is exactly what we call reassessment. <<WRITE_TEXT:Reassessment = remeasure liability for new facts|id=text-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:trigger-event>> <<SECTION:Reassessment|id=sec-1>>Going back and remeasuring that liability so it matches the new reality is exactly what we call reassessment. <<WRITE_TEXT:Reassessment = remeasure liability for new facts|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Now here is the clever part. Not every change is the same kind of change, so the rules ask one sharp question before you remeasure anything.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:fork-question>> Now here is the clever part. Not every change is the same kind of change, so the rules ask one sharp question before you remeasure anything.

segments.raw_narration: The question is this: did the very nature of the lease shift, or did only the cash amounts shift?
segments.text_with_markers: The question is this: did the very nature of the lease shift, or did only the cash amounts shift? <<POINT:fork-question>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: If the nature shifted, say you changed the lease term, or you now expect to exercise a purchase option, then you are essentially dealing with a different deal, so you discount the revised payments using a revised discount rate.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:path-revised-rate>> If the nature shifted, say you changed the lease term, or you now expect to exercise a purchase option, then you are essentially dealing with a different deal, so you discount the revised payments using a revised discount rate. <<TRACE:path-revised-rate>>

segments.raw_narration: What is that revised rate? It is the interest rate implicit in the lease for the rest of the term if you can readily find it, otherwise your incremental borrowing rate on the date you reassess. <<WRITE_TEXT:revised rate: implicit, else IBR at reassess date|id=text-2>>

segments.raw_narration: But if only the cash amounts moved, the deal itself is unchanged. Maybe your residual value guarantee estimate dropped, or an index your rent is tied to ticked up.

segments.raw_narration: In that case you remeasure using the original, unchanged discount rate, because nothing about the riskiness or length of the deal has actually changed. <<WRITE_TEXT:cash-only change: keep original rate|id=text-3>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:same-rate-label>> In that case you remeasure using the original, unchanged discount rate, because nothing about the riskiness or length of the deal has actually changed. <<WRITE_TEXT:cash-only change: keep original rate|id=text-3>>

segments.raw_narration: And both paths share the same engine underneath: discount the new payments back to today and that present value becomes your new lease liability.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:liability-box>> And both paths share the same engine underneath: discount the new payments back to today and that present value becomes your new lease liability.

segments.raw_narration: That is reassessment in one breath: when life proves your assumptions wrong, you do not leave a stale number sitting there, you remeasure it, choosing the rate by whether the lease itself changed or just the money did.

segments.raw_narration: You rented an office floor two years ago. Today you want a second floor. Is that a brand-new lease, or just a change to the old one?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:start-node>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:19:modification_decision_tree>> You rented an office floor two years ago. Today you want a second floor. Is that a brand-new lease, or just a change to the old one? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Lease modifications|id=sec-1>>Here is why it matters. Real contracts don't stay frozen. You add space, you give space back, the rent gets renegotiated. Accountants call any such change a lease modification.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:start-node>> <<SECTION:Lease modifications|id=sec-1>>Here is why it matters. Real contracts don't stay frozen. You add space, you give space back, the rent gets renegotiated. Accountants call any such change a lease modification.

segments.raw_narration: The whole standard hangs on one fork in the road: do we bolt on a separate lease, or do we surgically adjust the lease we already have? Everything else follows from that single decision.
segments.text_with_markers: The whole standard hangs on one fork in the road: do we bolt on a separate lease, or do we surgically adjust the lease we already have? Everything else follows from that single decision. <<POINT:start-node>>

segments.raw_narration: So when do we get to treat it as a clean, separate lease? There are two gates, and you must pass BOTH. First gate: does the change actually add the right to use a new asset, like that extra floor?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:gate-adds-asset>> So when do we get to treat it as a clean, separate lease? There are two gates, and you must pass BOTH. First gate: does the change actually add the right to use a new asset, like that extra floor?

segments.raw_narration: Second gate: is the extra payment a fair price for that new asset on its own? We call that the stand-alone price, roughly what you'd pay if you walked in off the street and rented that floor today.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:gate-fair-price>> Second gate: is the extra payment a fair price for that new asset on its own? We call that the stand-alone price, roughly what you'd pay if you walked in off the street and rented that floor today.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Separate lease ONLY IF: adds a new asset AND priced at fair stand-alone price|id=key-1>>Pass both gates, and it is a separate lease. You leave your original lease completely untouched and simply book the new one beside it.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:separate-lease-outcome>> <<WRITE_KEY:Separate lease ONLY IF: adds a new asset AND priced at fair stand-alone price|id=key-1>>Pass both gates, and it is a separate lease. You leave your original lease completely untouched and simply book the new one beside it. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Now, the question that trips people up: what if you add a floor, but your landlord gives you a sweet discount, well below the stand-alone price?
segments.text_with_markers: Now, the question that trips people up: what if you add a floor, but your landlord gives you a sweet discount, well below the stand-alone price? <<POINT:gate-fair-price>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Then you fail the second gate, so it is NOT a separate lease. The discount entangles the old deal with the new, so you must reopen and remeasure the lease you already have.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:remeasure-outcome>> Then you fail the second gate, so it is NOT a separate lease. The discount entangles the old deal with the new, so you must reopen and remeasure the lease you already have.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_STEP:Remeasure lease liability using a discount rate at the modification date|id=step-1>>To remeasure, you recompute the lease liability using a fresh discount rate, the rate that fits the conditions on the day of the modification, not the old one.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:remeasure-outcome>> <<WRITE_STEP:Remeasure lease liability using a discount rate at the modification date|id=step-1>>To remeasure, you recompute the lease liability using a fresh discount rate, the rate that fits the conditions on the day of the modification, not the old one. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: From here the path splits in two. If the modification shrinks your scope, say you hand back half a floor, you cut down the right-of-use asset to match and you book the gain or loss for the part you let go.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:branch-decrease-scope>> From here the path splits in two. If the modification shrinks your scope, say you hand back half a floor, you cut down the right-of-use asset to match and you book the gain or loss for the part you let go.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Not separate: remeasure liability, adjust right-of-use asset; if scope shrinks, recognise gain or loss|id=key-2>>For every other kind of change, no gain or loss, you just make a matching adjustment to the right-of-use asset so the books stay balanced.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:branch-other>> <<WRITE_KEY:Not separate: remeasure liability, adjust right-of-use asset; if scope shrinks, recognise gain or loss|id=key-2>>For every other kind of change, no gain or loss, you just make a matching adjustment to the right-of-use asset so the books stay balanced. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So the answer to where we started: a separate lease only if it adds an asset at a fair price; otherwise reopen the books, remeasure the liability, and adjust the asset. That one fork decides everything.
segments.text_with_markers: So the answer to where we started: a separate lease only if it adds an asset at a fair price; otherwise reopen the books, remeasure the liability, and adjust the asset. That one fork decides everything. <<POINT:start-node>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: You signed a lease. You now owe money, and you control an asset you don't own. So where exactly do those numbers sit in your three financial statements?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:balance-sheet-box>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:20:statement_drawer_map>> You signed a lease. You now owe money, and you control an asset you don't own. So where exactly do those numbers sit in your three financial statements? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Presentation as sorting|id=sec-1>>Presentation isn't new accounting. It's just deciding which drawer each number belongs in. We have three drawers: the balance sheet, the profit and loss, and the cash flow statement.
segments.text_with_markers: <<SECTION:Presentation as sorting|id=sec-1>>Presentation isn't new accounting. It's just deciding which drawer each number belongs in. We have three drawers: the balance sheet, the profit and loss, and the cash flow statement. <<POINT:pl-box>> <<POINT:pl-box>>

segments.raw_narration: Start with the balance sheet. As a lessee you carry two things here: the right-of-use asset, your right to use the item, and the lease liability, what you still owe.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rou-asset-slot>> Start with the balance sheet. As a lessee you carry two things here: the right-of-use asset, your right to use the item, and the lease liability, what you still owe. <<TRACE:rou-asset-slot>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:ROU asset: own line or tucked into owned-asset line + note|id=text-1>>The right-of-use asset can sit on its own line, or be folded into the line you'd use if you actually owned that kind of asset. If you fold it in, you must say so in the notes.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:rou-asset-slot>> <<WRITE_TEXT:ROU asset: own line or tucked into owned-asset line + note|id=text-1>>The right-of-use asset can sit on its own line, or be folded into the line you'd use if you actually owned that kind of asset. If you fold it in, you must say so in the notes.

segments.raw_narration: The lease liability works the same way: a separate line, or buried in another liability line with a note pointing to it. And if the right-of-use asset is really investment property, it lives inside investment property instead.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:lease-liability-slot>> The lease liability works the same way: a separate line, or buried in another liability line with a note pointing to it. And if the right-of-use asset is really investment property, it lives inside investment property instead.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Profit and loss|id=sec-2>>Now the profit and loss. One lease, but it produces two very different expenses, and here's the rule that trips people up.
segments.text_with_markers: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:pl-box>> <<SECTION:Profit and loss|id=sec-2>>Now the profit and loss. One lease, but it produces two very different expenses, and here's the rule that trips people up.

segments.raw_narration: Why split one lease into two separate expense lines instead of just calling it rent?
segments.text_with_markers: Why split one lease into two separate expense lines instead of just calling it rent? <<POINT:depreciation-slot>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:P&L: depreciation of ROU asset shown separately from interest on lease liability|id=key-1>>Because the two pieces are economically different. segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:depreciation-slot>> <<WRITE_KEY:P&L: depreciation of ROU asset shown separately from interest on lease liability|id=key-1>>Because the two pieces are economically different. So you present the depreciation charge on the right-of-use asset separately from the interest expense on the lease liability. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: And that interest isn't just any expense — it's a component of finance cost, so it must be presented separately within your finance costs.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:interest-slot>> And that interest isn't just any expense — it's a component of finance cost, so it must be presented separately within your finance costs. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Cash flows|id=sec-3>>Last drawer, the cash flow statement. Every rupee you pay on the lease has to land in one of two bands.

lesson_narrations.full_text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:balance-sheet-box>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:20:statement_drawer_map>> You signed a lease. We have three drawers: the balance sheet, the profit and loss, and the cash flow statement. <<POINT:pl-box>> <<POINT:pl-box>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rou-asset-slot>> Start with the balance sheet. As a lessee you carry two things here: the right-of-use asset, your right to use the item, and the lease liability, what you still owe. <<TRACE:rou-asset-slot>> <<FOCUS:rou-asset-slot>> <<WRITE_TEXT:ROU asset: own line or tucked into owned-asset line + note|id=text-1>>The right-of-use asset can sit on its own line, or be folded into the line you'd use if you actually owned that kind of asset. If you fold it in, you must say so in the notes. <<FOCUS:lease-liability-slot>> The lease liability works the same way: a separate line, or buried in another liability line with a note pointing to it. And if the right-of-use asset is really investment property, it lives inside investment property instead. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:pl-box>> <<SECTION:Profit and loss|id=sec-2>>Now the profit and loss. One lease, but it produces two very different expenses, and here's the rule that trips people up. segments.raw_narration: If you rent a car for a weekend versus paying one off over five years until it's basically yours, should an accountant treat those two deals the same way?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:asset-box>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:21:lease_classification_scale>> If you rent a car for a weekend versus paying one off over five years until it's basically yours, should an accountant treat those two deals the same way? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Of course not — and that gap is the whole idea behind classifying leases. Every lease falls into exactly one of two boxes, and one single question decides which.
segments.text_with_markers: Of course not — and that gap is the whole idea behind classifying leases. Every lease falls into exactly one of two boxes, and one single question decides which. <<POINT:asset-box>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Risks and rewards|id=sec-1>>Owning something isn't just about holding the title. It comes with rewards, like using it and gaining if it holds value, and risks, like repairs and it wearing out. Picture all of that as one bundle.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:risks-rewards-bundle>> <<SECTION:Risks and rewards|id=sec-1>>Owning something isn't just about holding the title. It comes with rewards, like using it and gaining if it holds value, and risks, like repairs and it wearing out. Picture all of that as one bundle. <<POINT:risks-rewards-bundle>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Finance lease = transfers substantially all risks and rewards of ownership|id=key-1>>Here is the deciding question: does the lease hand substantially all of that bundle over to the person renting the asset?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:tipping-point>> <<WRITE_KEY:Finance lease = transfers substantially all risks and rewards of ownership|id=key-1>>Here is the deciding question: does the lease hand substantially all of that bundle over to the person renting the asset? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: If almost the entire bundle slides across to the lessee, the deal has crossed the line. We call that a finance lease.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:finance-lease-label>> If almost the entire bundle slides across to the lessee, the deal has crossed the line. We call that a finance lease. <<POINT:finance-lease-label>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: But if the owner keeps holding most of those risks and rewards, the bundle stays on the lessor's side, and we call it an operating lease.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:operating-lease-label>> But if the owner keeps holding most of those risks and rewards, the bundle stays on the lessor's side, and we call it an operating lease. <<POINT:operating-lease-label>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Substance over form|id=sec-2>>Now, here's the trap. A contract might be titled 'rental agreement' — does that label settle whether it's an operating lease?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:lessor-side>> <<SECTION:Substance over form|id=sec-2>>Now, here's the trap. A contract might be titled 'rental agreement' — does that label settle whether it's an operating lease? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Judge by substance, not by the contract's name|id=key-2>>Not at all. We judge by what is really happening in the deal, not by what it's called. Substance beats form, every time.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:risks-rewards-bundle>> <<WRITE_KEY:Judge by substance, not by the contract's name|id=key-2>>Not at all. We judge by what is really happening in the deal, not by what it's called. Substance beats form, every time. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So how do we actually tell when the bundle has crossed over? The standard gives us telltale signs. Watch what each one does to our scale.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:tipping-point>> So how do we actually tell when the bundle has crossed over? The standard gives us telltale signs. Watch what each one does to our scale.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Ownership transfers, or a bargain purchase option|id=text-1>>If ownership transfers by the end, or there's a bargain price to buy it that's almost certain to be taken — the bundle clearly moves to the lessee.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:Ownership transfers, or a bargain purchase option|id=text-1>>If ownership transfers by the end, or there's a bargain price to buy it that's almost certain to be taken — the bundle clearly moves to the lessee. <<POINT:lessee-side>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Most of the asset's life, or PV of payments ≈ fair value|id=text-2>>If the lease runs for the major part of the asset's life, or the payments add up to nearly its full value, again — almost everything has shifted across.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:Most of the asset's life, or PV of payments ≈ fair value|id=text-2>>If the lease runs for the major part of the asset's life, or the payments add up to nearly its full value, again — almost everything has shifted across. <<POINT:lessee-side>>

segments.raw_narration: And if the asset is so specialised that only the lessee can use it, who really bears its fate? The lessee. The bundle has moved, so it's a finance lease.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:finance-lease-label>> And if the asset is so specialised that only the lessee can use it, who really bears its fate? The lessee. The bundle has moved, so it's a finance lease.

segments.raw_narration: So remember: two boxes, one question. If substantially all the risks and rewards move to the renter, it's a finance lease; if not, it's operating — and always judge the substance, never the label.

segments.raw_narration: You own a delivery van and you rent it out. Should that van still sit on your books as something you own, or have you really just turned it into a loan?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:underlying-asset>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:22:lessor_books_split>> You own a delivery van and you rent it out. Should that van still sit on your books as something you own, or have you really just turned it into a loan? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: The answer depends entirely on one thing we settled last time: whether the lease is a finance lease or an operating lease.
segments.text_with_markers: The answer depends entirely on one thing we settled last time: whether the lease is a finance lease or an operating lease. <<POINT:underlying-asset>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Finance lease|id=sec-1>>Take the finance lease first. Here, in substance, ownership has passed to the renter, even if your name is still on the paperwork.
segments.text_with_markers: <<SECTION:Finance lease|id=sec-1>>Take the finance lease first. Here, in substance, ownership has passed to the renter, even if your name is still on the paperwork. <<TRACE:finance-branch>>

segments.raw_narration: So you stop showing the van as your asset. You derecognise it, and in its place you put a lease receivable.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:lease-receivable>> So you stop showing the van as your asset. You derecognise it, and in its place you put a lease receivable. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Finance lease: drop the asset, show a receivable|id=text-1>>That receivable is measured at the net investment in the lease. You no longer own equipment; you hold a financial claim, exactly like having lent out money.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:Finance lease: drop the asset, show a receivable|id=text-1>>That receivable is measured at the net investment in the lease. You no longer own equipment; you hold a financial claim, exactly like having lent out money. <<POINT:lease-receivable>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: And because it behaves like a loan, the income you earn is finance income, recognised so that you get a constant periodic rate of return on that net investment.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:lease-receivable>> And because it behaves like a loan, the income you earn is finance income, recognised so that you get a constant periodic rate of return on that net investment. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Operating lease|id=sec-2>>Now the operating lease. Here ownership has not really moved; you are just letting someone use your van for a while.
segments.text_with_markers: <<SECTION:Operating lease|id=sec-2>>Now the operating lease. Here ownership has not really moved; you are just letting someone use your van for a while. <<TRACE:operating-branch>>

segments.raw_narration: So you keep the van right there on your balance sheet, and you carry on depreciating it over its useful life, just as you always would.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:asset-stays>> So you keep the van right there on your balance sheet, and you carry on depreciating it over its useful life, just as you always would. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Operating lease: keep the asset, depreciate it|id=text-2>>The rent that comes in is recognised as income, normally spread evenly on a straight-line basis across the lease term.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:Operating lease: keep the asset, depreciate it|id=text-2>>The rent that comes in is recognised as income, normally spread evenly on a straight-line basis across the lease term. <<POINT:asset-stays>>

segments.raw_narration: There is one more nice touch: any initial direct costs you spend to set up an operating lease get added to the carrying amount of the underlying asset.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:asset-stays>> There is one more nice touch: any initial direct costs you spend to set up an operating lease get added to the carrying amount of the underlying asset.

segments.raw_narration: So why do the same physical van get treated in two completely opposite ways on your books?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:underlying-asset>> So why do the same physical van get treated in two completely opposite ways on your books? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Finance lease = receivable + finance income; Operating lease = keep asset + rental income|id=key-1>>Because accounting follows the substance. If you have effectively sold the van, you show a receivable and earn finance income. If you have merely lent it temporarily, you keep the van, depreciate it, and collect rent.

If you have effectively sold the van, you show a receivable and earn finance income. If you have merely lent it temporarily, you keep the van, depreciate it, and collect rent. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: A car company leases you a car instead of selling it outright. So on day one, did they make a sale, or did they make a loan? The strange answer is: both, at the very same moment.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:asset-box>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:23:dealer_lessor_split>> A car company leases you a car instead of selling it outright. So on day one, did they make a sale, or did they make a loan? The strange answer is: both, at the very same moment.

segments.raw_narration: Here is the asset the company built or bought to sell. A normal shop would just sell it and book a profit. But this company is a manufacturer or dealer who also acts as a lessor, so it does something cleverer.
segments.text_with_markers: Here is the asset the company built or bought to sell. A normal shop would just sell it and book a profit. But this company is a manufacturer or dealer who also acts as a lessor, so it does something cleverer. <<POINT:asset-box>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Two events at commencement|id=sec-1>>At the commencement date, the single transaction splits into two branches. Watch the line: everything happens right here, on day one.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:commencement-line>> <<SECTION:Two events at commencement|id=sec-1>>At the commencement date, the single transaction splits into two branches. Watch the line: everything happens right here, on day one. <<TRACE:commencement-line>>

segments.raw_narration: The first branch is a sale. The company hands over the asset's economic value, so it records revenue and a matching cost of sale, and the difference is selling profit, booked instantly.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:sale-branch>> The first branch is a sale. The company hands over the asset's economic value, so it records revenue and a matching cost of sale, and the difference is selling profit, booked instantly. <<TRACE:sale-branch>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: But hold on. If they sold it on day one, where does the lease come in? What keeps earning money over the next few years?
segments.text_with_markers: But hold on. If they sold it on day one, where does the lease come in? What keeps earning money over the next few years? <<POINT:sale-branch>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Dealer lessor books selling profit at day one AND finance income over the term|id=key-1>>The second branch is the finance lease. The company holds a net investment in the lease, and that investment earns finance income period after period, just like a loan.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:lease-branch>> <<WRITE_KEY:Dealer lessor books selling profit at day one AND finance income over the term|id=key-1>>The second branch is the finance lease. The company holds a net investment in the lease, and that investment earns finance income period after period, just like a loan. <<TRACE:lease-branch>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So one transaction, two streams of profit. A one-off selling profit on day one, plus a slow trickle of finance income over the lease term.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:finance-income-stream>> So one transaction, two streams of profit. A one-off selling profit on day one, plus a slow trickle of finance income over the lease term. <<POINT:finance-income-stream>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Measuring the sale|id=sec-2>>Now, how much revenue? You cannot just use the asking price. Revenue is the lower of two numbers: the fair value of the asset, or the present value of the lease payments discounted at a market interest rate.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:selling-profit-marker>> <<SECTION:Measuring the sale|id=sec-2>>Now, how much revenue? You cannot just use the asking price. Revenue is the lower of two numbers: the fair value of the asset, or the present value of the lease payments discounted at a market interest rate. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Revenue is the lower of the asset's fair value and the present value of the lease payments discounted at a market rate of interest.
segments.text_with_markers: Revenue is the lower of the asset's fair value and the present value of the lease payments discounted at a market rate of interest. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Revenue} = \min\left(\text{Fair Value},\ \text{PV of lease payments}\right)|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_STEP:Cost of sale = asset cost minus present value of unguaranteed residual|id=step-1>>And the cost of sale is the asset's cost, but minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value, because part of the asset comes back to you and was never really sold.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_STEP:Cost of sale = asset cost minus present value of unguaranteed residual|id=step-1>>And the cost of sale is the asset's cost, but minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value, because part of the asset comes back to you and was never really sold. <<POINT:sale-branch>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Cost of sale equals the asset's cost or carrying amount minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value.
segments.text_with_markers: Cost of sale equals the asset's cost or carrying amount minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Cost of Sale} = \text{Asset Cost} - \text{PV of unguaranteed residual value}|id=eq-2|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: Subtract that cost of sale from revenue and you get the selling profit, recognised right here at commencement, exactly as you would for any outright sale.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:selling-profit-marker>> Subtract that cost of sale from revenue and you get the selling profit, recognised right here at commencement, exactly as you would for any outright sale.

segments.raw_narration: Selling profit is simply revenue minus cost of sale, booked at the commencement date.
segments.text_with_markers: Selling profit is simply revenue minus cost of sale, booked at the commencement date. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Selling Profit} = \text{Revenue} - \text{Cost of Sale}|id=eq-3|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:After commencement|id=sec-3>>After day one, only the lease branch is still alive. Each period you recognise finance income at a constant rate of return on the remaining net investment, then reduce that investment by the payments received.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:finance-income-stream>> <<SECTION:After commencement|id=sec-3>>After day one, only the lease branch is still alive. Each period you recognise finance income at a constant rate of return on the remaining net investment, then reduce that investment by the payments received. <<POINT:finance-income-stream>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Sale + finance lease, both at once|id=text-1>>So remember the big idea: a manufacturer or dealer lessor is two businesses in one moment. The maker who books selling profit instantly, and the financier who earns interest over the years.

Revenue is the lower of two numbers: the fair value of the asset, or the present value of the lease payments discounted at a market interest rate. <<PAUSE:short>> Revenue is the lower of the asset's fair value and the present value of the lease payments discounted at a market rate of interest. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Revenue} = \min\left(\text{Fair Value},\ \text{PV of lease payments}\right)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_STEP:Cost of sale = asset cost minus present value of unguaranteed residual|id=step-1>>And the cost of sale is the asset's cost, but minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value, because part of the asset comes back to you and was never really sold. <<POINT:sale-branch>> <<PAUSE:short>> Cost of sale equals the asset's cost or carrying amount minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Cost of Sale} = \text{Asset Cost} - \text{PV of unguaranteed residual value}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:selling-profit-marker>> Subtract that cost of sale from revenue and you get the selling profit, recognised right here at commencement, exactly as you would for any outright sale. Selling profit is simply revenue minus cost of sale, booked at the commencement date. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Selling Profit} = \text{Revenue} - \text{Cost of Sale}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:finance-income-stream>> <<SECTION:After commencement|id=sec-3>>After day one, only the lease branch is still alive. Each period you recognise finance income at a constant rate of return on the remaining net investment, then reduce that investment by the payments received. <<POINT:finance-income-stream>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:commencement-line>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Sale + finance lease, both at once|id=text-1>>So remember the big idea: a manufacturer or dealer lessor is two businesses in one moment. segments.raw_narration: The headline statements give you totals, but they don't tell you when the rent is coming in, how the value is changing, or how much profit was baked in on day one.

segments.raw_narration: The whole objective is simple to say: these notes, together with the balance sheet, the profit and loss statement, and the cash flow statement, let a reader assess how leases affect the lessor's financial position, performance, and cash flows.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Finance Lease Notes|id=sec-2>>For a finance lease, the lessor has effectively handed over the asset and is owed a stream of payments, so the disclosures circle around the net investment in the lease.

segments.raw_narration: They also explain any significant changes in the carrying amount of that net investment, so a reader can follow how the asset's recorded value is moving over time.

segments.raw_narration: What happens when you rent an apartment from a landlord, and then rent that very same apartment out to someone else?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:intermediate-lessor>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:25:sublease_chain>> What happens when you rent an apartment from a landlord, and then rent that very same apartment out to someone else? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Sublease|id=sec-1>>Suddenly you are stuck in the middle. You pay rent upward to your landlord, and someone pays rent up to you.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Sublease|id=sec-1>>Suddenly you are stuck in the middle. You pay rent upward to your landlord, and someone pays rent up to you. <<POINT:head-rent-arrow>> <<POINT:head-rent-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: At the top is the head lessor, the original owner you leased from. At the bottom is your new tenant, the subtenant. You sit in between.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:head-lessor>> At the top is the head lessor, the original owner you leased from. At the bottom is your new tenant, the subtenant. You sit in between.

segments.raw_narration: When a company rents an asset and then leases it out again, accounting gives that middle role a name: the intermediate lessor.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:intermediate-lessor>> When a company rents an asset and then leases it out again, accounting gives that middle role a name: the intermediate lessor. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Rent then sublet then you become the intermediate lessor, sitting between head lessor and subtenant|id=key-1>>So remember this position carefully. The intermediate lessor is the one wedged between the head lessor above and the subtenant below.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:subtenant>> <<WRITE_KEY:Rent then sublet then you become the intermediate lessor, sitting between head lessor and subtenant|id=key-1>>So remember this position carefully. The intermediate lessor is the one wedged between the head lessor above and the subtenant below. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Now here is the question that trips everyone up. When you classify your sublease as finance or operating, what asset do you actually compare it against?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:physical-asset>> Now here is the question that trips everyone up. When you classify your sublease as finance or operating, what asset do you actually compare it against? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Not the building. You never owned the building. What you own is the right to use it, granted by the head lease.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rou-asset>> Not the building. You never owned the building. What you own is the right to use it, granted by the head lease. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Classify the sublease against the right-of-use asset, not the physical asset|id=key-2>>So the intermediate lessor classifies the sublease by looking at the right-of-use asset, treating that as if it were the underlying asset.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:rou-asset>> <<WRITE_KEY:Classify the sublease against the right-of-use asset, not the physical asset|id=key-2>>So the intermediate lessor classifies the sublease by looking at the right-of-use asset, treating that as if it were the underlying asset. <<TRACE:rou-asset>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: There is one neat shortcut for the discount rate. If you cannot readily work out the interest rate implicit in the sublease, you simply borrow the rate you already use for the head lease.
segments.text_with_markers: There is one neat shortcut for the discount rate. If you cannot readily work out the interest rate implicit in the sublease, you simply borrow the rate you already use for the head lease. <<POINT:head-rent-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term head lease then sublease is operating|id=text-1>>And one special case to lock in: if the head lease was a short-term lease you treated under the short-term exemption, then your sublease is automatically classified as an operating lease.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:sub-rent-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term head lease then sublease is operating|id=text-1>>And one special case to lock in: if the head lease was a short-term lease you treated under the short-term exemption, then your sublease is automatically classified as an operating lease.

segments.raw_narration: So always picture the chain: head lessor, you in the middle, subtenant, and remember you judge the sublease against your right-of-use asset, never the bricks and mortar.

segments.raw_narration: A company sells its own office building for cash, and the very next morning everyone walks back into the exact same building to work. So did anything really get sold?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:building-icon>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:26:saleback_flow>> A company sells its own office building for cash, and the very next morning everyone walks back into the exact same building to work. So did anything really get sold? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Sale and leaseback|id=sec-1>>This move has a name. The company that sells and then rents back is the seller-lessee, and the company that buys and then rents it out is the buyer-lessor.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:seller-lessee-box>> <<SECTION:Sale and leaseback|id=sec-1>>This move has a name. The company that sells and then rents back is the seller-lessee, and the company that buys and then rents it out is the buyer-lessor. <<POINT:seller-lessee-box>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Asset out, cash in|id=text-1>>Watch what flows. The building goes from the seller to the buyer, and the cash comes straight back the other way.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:Asset out, cash in|id=text-1>>Watch what flows. The building goes from the seller to the buyer, and the cash comes straight back the other way. <<TRACE:cash-arrow>> <<TRACE:cash-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: But the seller still needs that building, so the buyer immediately leases the right to use it back to them. The desks never move.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> But the seller still needs that building, so the buyer immediately leases the right to use it back to them. The desks never move. <<TRACE:lease-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: Here is the question that decides everything. Was this actually a sale, or was the company just borrowing money with the building as security?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:asset-arrow>> Here is the question that decides everything. Was this actually a sale, or was the company just borrowing money with the building as security? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Sale only if it qualifies under Ind AS 115|id=key-1>>To answer that, we do not guess. We test the transfer against Ind AS one hundred fifteen, the standard on revenue from contracts with customers. Only if it passes that test do we call it a sale.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Sale only if it qualifies under Ind AS 115|id=key-1>>To answer that, we do not guess. We test the transfer against Ind AS one hundred fifteen, the standard on revenue from contracts with customers. Only if it passes that test do we call it a sale. <<POINT:asset-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: If it does not pass, then no real sale happened. The cash is simply a loan, and the building stays on the seller's books as if nothing changed.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:building-icon>> If it does not pass, then no real sale happened. The cash is simply a loan, and the building stays on the seller's books as if nothing changed. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:When it is a genuine sale|id=sec-2>>Now suppose it does pass the test. Here is the subtle part. The seller sold the building, but kept the right to use it. So the seller did not give up the whole asset.
segments.text_with_markers: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:full-carrying-bar>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:26:carrying_split_bar>> <<SECTION:When it is a genuine sale|id=sec-2>>Now suppose it does pass the test. Here is the subtle part. The seller sold the building, but kept the right to use it. So the seller did not give up the whole asset.

segments.raw_narration: Think of the building's old book value as one bar. Part of it represents the rights the seller kept, and part represents the rights handed over to the buyer.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:retained-portion>> <<FOCUS:retained-portion>> Think of the building's old book value as one bar. Part of it represents the rights the seller kept, and part represents the rights handed over to the buyer. <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: So how much gain does the seller get to book? Only on the slice they actually gave away, never on the slice they kept using.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:transferred-portion>> So how much gain does the seller get to book? Only on the slice they actually gave away, never on the slice they kept using. <<POINT:transferred-portion>>

segments.raw_narration: The right-of-use asset equals the old book value scaled down to just the fraction of rights the seller kept.
segments.text_with_markers: The right-of-use asset equals the old book value scaled down to just the fraction of rights the seller kept. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{ROU asset} = \text{Previous carrying amount} \times \dfrac{\text{Rights retained}}{\text{Total asset}}|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:ROU = retained proportion of old carrying amount; gain only on rights transferred|id=key-2>>The right-of-use asset is carried at that retained proportion of the old book value, and the seller recognises gain or loss only on the rights transferred to the buyer.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:gain-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:ROU = retained proportion of old carrying amount; gain only on rights transferred|id=key-2>>The right-of-use asset is carried at that retained proportion of the old book value, and the seller recognises gain or loss only on the rights transferred to the buyer. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: The gain you may recognise is the total gain scaled down to only the portion of rights you actually transferred to the buyer.
segments.text_with_markers: The gain you may recognise is the total gain scaled down to only the portion of rights you actually transferred to the buyer. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Gain recognised} = \text{Total gain} \times \dfrac{\text{Rights transferred}}{\text{Total asset}}|id=eq-2|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: Meanwhile the buyer-lessor has the easy job. They record buying the asset under the normal standards, and account for the lease they granted using the lessor rules you already know.
segments.text_with_markers: <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:buyer-lessor-box>> Meanwhile the buyer-lessor has the easy job. They record buying the asset under the normal standards, and account for the lease they granted using the lessor rules you already know.

segments.raw_narration: And one last guard. If the price was not fair value or the rent was not at market rates, you adjust, treating any shortfall as a prepayment and any excess as extra financing from the buyer.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:cash-arrow>> And one last guard. If the price was not fair value or the rent was not at market rates, you adjust, treating any shortfall as a prepayment and any excess as extra financing from the buyer.

segments.raw_narration: So the lesson holds together. First ask if it is really a sale under Ind AS one hundred fifteen, and if it is, recognise gain only on what you gave away, because you never truly let go of what you kept using.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:The Sandwich Position|id=sec-1>>To see why, picture a company that rents a building from a landlord.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:landlord-box>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:27:sublease_chain>> <<SECTION:The Sandwich Position|id=sec-1>>To see why, picture a company that rents a building from a landlord.

segments.raw_narration: That same company then turns around and rents the building out to someone else, so it sits squarely in the middle of two deals.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:intermediate-box>> That same company then turns around and rents the building out to someone else, so it sits squarely in the middle of two deals. <<TRACE:intermediate-box>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Intermediate lessor = renter + renter-out|id=text-1>>We call this company the intermediate lessor, because it rents on one side and rents out on the other.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:Intermediate lessor = renter + renter-out|id=text-1>>We call this company the intermediate lessor, because it rents on one side and rents out on the other. <<TRACE:sublease-arrow>> <<POINT:sublease-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: The deal with the landlord is the head lease, and the deal with the new tenant is the sublease.
segments.text_with_markers: The deal with the landlord is the head lease, and the deal with the new tenant is the sublease. <<POINT:head-lease-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: Now, under the old standard, Ind AS seventeen, leases were sorted into two buckets, operating leases or finance leases, and a great many subleases landed in the operating bucket.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:subtenant-box>> Now, under the old standard, Ind AS seventeen, leases were sorted into two buckets, operating leases or finance leases, and a great many subleases landed in the operating bucket.

segments.raw_narration: So here is the honest question, when you move to the new standard, Ind AS one hundred sixteen, can you just leave those old operating subleases exactly where they were?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:sublease-arrow>> So here is the honest question, when you move to the new standard, Ind AS one hundred sixteen, can you just leave those old operating subleases exactly where they were? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Re-test on Transition|id=sec-2>>No. On the date you first apply the new standard, you must take a fresh look at every ongoing sublease that used to be an operating lease and decide all over again.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:reassess-marker>> <<SECTION:Re-test on Transition|id=sec-2>>No. On the date you first apply the new standard, you must take a fresh look at every ongoing sublease that used to be an operating lease and decide all over again. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: And here is the clever part, you do not judge the sublease alone, you judge it against what is left of both the head lease and the sublease together.
segments.text_with_markers: And here is the clever part, you do not judge the sublease alone, you judge it against what is left of both the head lease and the sublease together. <<POINT:head-lease-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Why both? Because if you have already handed almost the whole remaining life of the building to your subtenant, you have effectively passed on the risks and rewards of owning that right, and that smells like a finance lease, not an operating one.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:intermediate-box>> Why both? Because if you have already handed almost the whole remaining life of the building to your subtenant, you have effectively passed on the risks and rewards of owning that right, and that smells like a finance lease, not an operating one.

segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:sublease-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Operating under Ind AS 17 to finance under Ind AS 116 = treat as a NEW finance lease at transition date|id=key-1>>So when a sublease that was operating now qualifies as a finance lease, you do not patch the old one, you treat it as a brand-new finance lease starting on the transition date. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Down the first path, the company says yes: apply the brand new definition to every single existing contract, with completely fresh eyes.

segments.raw_narration: That means digging through hundreds or thousands of old agreements and re-checking each one. It is thorough, but it is an enormous amount of work.

segments.raw_narration: Yes. segments.raw_narration: In plain terms: if a contract was not a lease under the old rules, you simply trust that and leave it alone. You do not put it through the new definition.

segments.raw_narration: This shortcut has a name. Accountants call it a practical expedient — a permitted simplification that saves you from a mountain of work. <<WRITE_TEXT:Practical expedient = permitted shortcut|id=text-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:grandfather-box>> This shortcut has a name. Accountants call it a practical expedient — a permitted simplification that saves you from a mountain of work. <<WRITE_TEXT:Practical expedient = permitted shortcut|id=text-2>>

segments.raw_narration: But notice the trade-off. If you take the shortcut, you carry your old conclusions forward, and the new definition only applies to contracts you sign on or after the transition date.

segments.raw_narration: A company has been renting buildings for years under the old rules. Tomorrow the rulebook changes. What does it do with all the leases it already signed?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:decision-node>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:29:transition_two_paths>> A company has been renting buildings for years under the old rules. Tomorrow the rulebook changes. What does it do with all the leases it already signed? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: It can't just throw out the past, and it can't pretend nothing happened. So the new standard, Ind AS one sixteen, hands the lessee a choice between two honest ways to cross over.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:decision-node>> It can't just throw out the past, and it can't pretend nothing happened. So the new standard, Ind AS one sixteen, hands the lessee a choice between two honest ways to cross over. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Two transition paths|id=sec-1>>The first path is the full retrospective approach. Here you pretend Ind AS one sixteen was always in force, and you go back and redo every single period you're showing.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:full-retro-branch>> <<SECTION:Two transition paths|id=sec-1>>The first path is the full retrospective approach. Here you pretend Ind AS one sixteen was always in force, and you go back and redo every single period you're showing. <<TRACE:full-retro-branch>>

segments.raw_narration: Because you're reaching so far back into the past, you even have to lay out an extra third balance sheet, so a reader can see exactly where things stood at the earliest point. It is thorough, but it is a mountain of work.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:third-balance-sheet>> Because you're reaching so far back into the past, you even have to lay out an extra third balance sheet, so a reader can see exactly where things stood at the earliest point. It is thorough, but it is a mountain of work. <<POINT:third-balance-sheet>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Full retro = redo all periods + 3rd balance sheet|id=text-1>>The second path is the modified retrospective approach. It refuses to restate the comparative periods at all. The past stays exactly as it was printed.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:modified-retro-branch>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Full retro = redo all periods + 3rd balance sheet|id=text-1>>The second path is the modified retrospective approach. It refuses to restate the comparative periods at all. The past stays exactly as it was printed. <<TRACE:modified-retro-branch>>

segments.raw_narration: Instead of touching the past, it gathers up the entire cumulative impact of switching and drops it as one single adjustment to equity, right at the start of the year it first applies the standard. We call that the date of initial application.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:equity-adjustment>> Instead of touching the past, it gathers up the entire cumulative impact of switching and drops it as one single adjustment to equity, right at the start of the year it first applies the standard. We call that the date of initial application. <<POINT:equity-adjustment>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So here is the fork. Same company, same leases, but two very different amounts of work. Which one would you reach for if you only cared about today's numbers?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:decision-node>> So here is the fork. Same company, same leases, but two very different amounts of work. Which one would you reach for if you only cared about today's numbers? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: The modified path, almost every time, because you skip rebuilding history. But now a sharper question hides inside it. If you are not redoing the past, how do you decide what the lease is worth on day one?

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Measuring on day one|id=sec-2>>For what used to be an operating lease, you take only the payments still left to make, and you discount them back to today using the lessee's incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application. segments.raw_narration: Let me walk you through the most useful ones, because each shortcut kills a specific headache. The first headache is the discount rate.
segments.text_with_markers: Let me walk you through the most useful ones, because each shortcut kills a specific headache. The first headache is the discount rate.

segments.raw_narration: Normally every lease needs its own discount rate, the interest rate you use to bring future payments back to today's value. <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient A: one rate for similar leases|id=text-1>>The shortcut lets you apply a single rate to a whole bundle of leases that look reasonably alike, say all your photocopiers, instead of pricing each one separately.

segments.raw_narration: One of those leases was a bargain: the rent locked in was cheaper than anything you could get in the market today. That favourable deal has real worth, so under Ind AS 103 you recorded it as a separate asset.

segments.raw_narration: Now Ind AS 116 arrives. It says every lease gets a single right-of-use asset. So a question lands: if the lease already created a separate favourable-terms asset, do we now double-count it alongside the new right-of-use asset?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:rou-asset-box>> Now Ind AS 116 arrives. It says every lease gets a single right-of-use asset. So a question lands: if the lease already created a separate favourable-terms asset, do we now double-count it alongside the new right-of-use asset? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: No double-counting allowed. The rule is clean: you derecognise that old favourable or unfavourable lease asset completely.

And right (c) is the right to lay water pipelines over land adjacent to the oilfield, because water is needed in the extraction process. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Which of rights (a), (b), (c) obtained by Entity X fall within the scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>>

So the test is simple: does the lease give the right to explore for or extract the oil itself? <<WRITE_STEP:Paragraph 3 excludes leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, gas and similar non-regenerative resources.|id=ex-step-1-1>>

segments.raw_narration: A company gets the exclusive right to run an entire country's air navigation system for ten whole years, and yet, surprisingly, that contract is not a lease. Let me show you why.

Let me show you why.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Scoping a contract under Ind AS 116|id=sec-1>>Here is the contract on the table. A private company, Entity X, signs with a Transport Ministry to operate the system that guides airplanes, upgrade it, and charge users at rates it negotiates freely, with no price cap.

segments.raw_narration: But the standard has carve-outs. One of them quietly diverts a whole class of contracts out of scope: service concession arrangements that fall under Appendix D of Ind AS 115.

segments.raw_narration: So before we ever call this a lease, we must ask: is it actually one of those service concessions hiding in disguise?

segments.raw_narration: Here's an example from the chapter. Entity X is a private sector entity, and it enters a contract with the grantor, the Transport Ministry of Country S, to acquire the right to operate the civil air navigation system. Under the contract, the grantor provides the air navigation system, and X is required to upgrade the system. X charges users based on rates negotiated directly with individual users, there is no price-cap mechanism imposed by the grantor, and the contract period is ten years. The question is whether this contract falls within the scope of Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: X (private) operates Country S air navigation system for grantor (Transport Ministry); X sets prices, no price-cap, 10-year term — within scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Background 
Ind AS 116 brings significant changes in accounting requirements for lease 
accounting, primarily for lessees. Ind AS 116 replaces the following Indian 
accounting standard and relevant appendix on leases: 
 
Ind AS 17,  Leases 
 
Appendix A - Evaluating the Substance of Transactions Involving the 
Legal Form of a Lease 
 
Appendix B - Operating Leases – Incentives 
 
Appendix C - Determining whether an Arrangement contains a Lease 
The effective date of Ind AS 116 is for annual reporting periods beginning on 
or after 1 April, 2019. For lessees, there is a choice of full retrospective 
application (i.e. restating comparatives as if Ind AS 116 had always been in 
force), or retrospective application without restatement of prior year

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
5 
comparatives. This results in the cumulative impact of adoption being 
recorded as an adjustment to equity at the beginning of the accounting 
period in which the standard is first applied (the date of initial application).
topics.our_understanding:
Let's set the stage for understanding this new accounting standard called Ind AS one hundred sixteen, which deals with leases. A lease, just so we're clear, is an arrangement where one party pays to use something — like a building, a machine, or a vehicle — that belongs to someone else, for a period of time. The party who uses the asset is called the lessee, and the party who owns it and rents it out is called the lessor.

Now here's the big idea. This standard brings significant changes to how leases are accounted for, and most of those changes affect the lessee — the one renting the asset. Why does that matter? Because in the past, many leases didn't show up properly on a company's balance sheet. A company could be paying for years to use an expensive building, but you'd barely see that commitment in their financial statements. This new standard fixes that, making the accounting more honest and more complete.

Ind AS one hundred sixteen replaces the older standard, Ind AS seventeen on leases, along with three appendices that went with it. Those appendices covered things like evaluating the real substance of transactions that just looked like leases, how to handle incentives in operating leases, and how to decide whether an arrangement actually contains a lease at all. So this one new standard sweeps in and takes the place of all of that older guidance.

Now, when does it kick in? The effective date is for annual reporting periods beginning on or after the first of April, two thousand nineteen. Think of that as the starting line.

And here's a thoughtful part. When a company first adopts this standard, it gets a choice about how to apply it. The first option is full retrospective application — that means pretending Ind AS one hundred sixteen had always been in force, and going back to restate the comparative figures from earlier years as if the rules had always applied. The second option is retrospective application without restating those prior year comparatives. In that case, instead of rewriting old numbers, the company records the cumulative impact of adopting the standard as a single adjustment to equity at the beginning of the period when the standard is first applied. That moment is called the date of initial application.

So notice the two paths: either you rewrite history to look consistent, or you leave the old numbers alone and make one clean adjustment to equity at the start. Both are allowed, and a company picks the approach that suits it. This background gives you the why and the when before we dig into the detailed rules.

topics.orig_book_content:
Scope 
The scope of Ind AS 116 is broadly same as Ind AS 17 in that it applies to 
contract meeting the definition of lease except for: 
a) 
Leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-
regenerative resources; 
b) 
Leases of biological assets within the scope of Ind AS 41, Agriculture 
held by a lessee; 
c) 
Service concession arrangements within the scope of Appendix D, 
Service Concession Arrangements of Ind AS 115, Revenue from 
Contracts with Customers; 
d) 
Licences of intellectual property granted by a lessor within the scope 
of Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers; and 
e) 
Rights held by a lessee under licensing agreements within the scope 
of Ind AS 38, Intangible Assets for such items as motion picture films, 
video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents and copyrights. 
Lessee may, but is not required to, apply this Standard to leases of intangible 
assets other than those described in above point (e).
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about scope. When we say the scope of an accounting standard, we just mean the boundaries — which contracts does this rule actually apply to, and which ones does it leave alone? Think of it like the rulebook telling you which games it covers before you start playing.

Indian Accounting Standard one hundred sixteen deals with leases. A lease, in plain terms, is when one party lets another use an asset for a period of time in exchange for payment. This new standard has a scope that is broadly the same as the older standard, Indian Accounting Standard seventeen. So if a contract fits the definition of a lease, this standard generally applies. But — and this is the important part — there are some exceptions. Certain kinds of leases are deliberately carved out and handled by other standards instead.

Let's walk through those exceptions. First, leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas, and similar non-regenerative resources. These are things you dig up or extract, and once they're gone, they don't come back, so they get special treatment elsewhere. Second, leases of biological assets — living things like plants or animals — held by a lessee, because those fall under the agriculture standard. Third, service concession arrangements, which are special public-service contracts covered under the revenue standard. Fourth, licences of intellectual property granted by a lessor, like when a company licenses out its brand or technology — again, that's revenue territory. And fifth, rights held by a lessee under licensing agreements for things like motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents, and copyrights, which are governed by the intangible assets standard.

Now here's a nice little flexibility built into the rule. For leases of intangible assets — other than the ones in that fifth point about films and patents — a lessee may choose to apply this standard, but is not required to. Notice the wording: it's optional. The company can decide. This is what we call a permitted but not mandatory choice.

So why does scope matter so much? Because before you can apply any accounting rule correctly, you have to be sure you're holding the right rulebook. If you treat an oil exploration lease using this standard when it should go under another, your accounts will be wrong. Getting the scope right is the very first checkpoint — it keeps each type of contract under the standard that was designed for it.
