topics.orig_book_content:
Recognition exemption 
In addition to the above scope exclusions, a lessee can elect not to apply Ind 
AS 116’s recognition and requirements to: 
a) 
Short-term leases; and 
b) 
Leases for which the underlying asset is of low value (‘low value 
leases’). 
An underlying asset can be of low value only if: 
(a) 
the lessee can benefit from use of the underlying asset on its own or 
together with other resources that are readily available to the lessee; 
and 
(b) 
the underlying asset is not highly dependent on, or highly interrelated

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
6 
with, other assets. 
Short-term lease: A lease that, at the commencement date, has a lease term 
of 12 months or less. A lease that contains a purchase option is not a short-
term lease. 
The short-term lease exemption must be applied consistently to all 
underlying assets in the same class. The low value lease exemption, in 
contrast, may be applied on a lease-by-lease basis. 
If an entity applies either exemption, it must disclose that fact and certain 
information to make the effect of the exemption known to users of its 
financial statements. (Refer – Disclosure)
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about a helpful shortcut built into this standard. Normally, when a company leases something, it has to record a special asset and a matching liability on its books. That can be a lot of work. So the standard says: for two specific kinds of leases, the lessee — that's the person renting the asset — can choose to skip all that extra recording. They get an exemption.

The first kind is a short-term lease. Think about it simply: a short-term lease is one that, at the moment it starts, has a term of twelve months or less. So if you're renting equipment for just six months, that could qualify. But here's an important catch — if the lease includes an option to buy the asset at the end, it is never treated as a short-term lease, no matter how short it is. The reason is that a purchase option suggests you really intend to keep the asset, so it shouldn't get the easy treatment.

The second kind is a low value lease. This is about renting something that just isn't worth very much — think of things like a laptop, a small piece of office furniture, or a telephone. But the standard sets two tests for whether an asset truly counts as low value. First, the lessee must be able to benefit from using the asset on its own, or together with other resources they already have handy. Second, the asset must not be highly dependent on, or highly tangled up with, other assets. So a car, for example, wouldn't qualify even if it were cheap, because it works as part of a bigger system.

Now notice an important difference in how you apply these two exemptions. The short-term lease exemption must be applied consistently to a whole class of underlying assets — so if you use it for one piece of office equipment, you use it for all of that same type. But the low value lease exemption is more flexible; you can decide lease by lease, one at a time, whether to use it.

Finally, if a company chooses to use either of these exemptions, it can't just quietly do so. It must disclose that fact, and share enough information so that anyone reading the financial statements understands the effect of the choice. Transparency matters, because these shortcuts change what shows up on the books.

A purchase option signals you really intend to own the asset, so the shortcut is off the table. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Low-value leases|id=sec-2>>The second kind is the low-value lease — think of a laptop or an office phone — something you can use on its own, that isn't tightly bound up with your bigger, more valuable assets. <<WRITE_TEXT:Short-term: by class. Low-value: lease by lease|id=text-2>>Now here's a subtle but important difference in how you apply them. <<PAUSE:short>> The short-term exemption is all-or-nothing for a whole class of assets — choose it for your delivery vans, and it applies to every short-term van lease consistently. The low-value exemption is far more flexible: you decide lease by lease, picking and choosing for each individual low-value asset. <<PAUSE:short>> And whichever exemption you use, you must disclose it — so anyone reading the financial statements knows these leases were deliberately kept off the books.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about how you figure out whether a contract is actually a lease, or whether it just contains a lease somewhere inside it. This matters because if a contract is a lease, you have to follow all the special accounting rules for leases. If it isn't, you don't. So this is the gatekeeper question.

Here's the timing first. You make this assessment at the very beginning, what the standard calls the inception of the contract. And once you've decided, you don't keep second-guessing it. You only reassess whether the contract is or contains a lease if the actual terms and conditions of the contract change. So no changes, no re-checking.

Now, what makes a contract a lease? The standard gives a clear definition. A contract is, or contains, a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time, in exchange for consideration. Let's unpack that, because every piece carries weight. You need an identified asset, meaning a specific thing, not just any asset of a type. You need the right to control its use, not just use it occasionally. You need a period of time. And you need consideration, meaning you're paying something for it.

Think of the test as a flowchart of questions you walk through. First, ask, is there an identified asset? If no, there's no lease. If yes, move on. Next, does the customer have the right to obtain substantially all of the economic benefits from using that asset throughout the period of use? In plain words, do you get almost all the value out of it? If yes, keep going.

Then comes the trickiest part, the right to direct how and for what purpose the asset is used throughout the period. You ask, who has that right, the customer, the supplier, or neither? If the supplier directs it, no lease. If the customer directs it, that points to a lease. If neither party directs it because how and for what purpose the asset will be used is already predetermined, then you ask two backup questions. Does the customer have the right to operate the asset throughout the period without the supplier being able to change those operating instructions? Or did the customer design the asset in a way that predetermines how it will be used? If yes to either, the contract contains a lease. If you fail along the way, it does not. That's the whole logic of identifying a lease.

topics.orig_book_content:
Identified assets 
A contract contains a lease only if it relates to an identified asset. An asset 
can be either explicitly specified in a contract or implicitly specified at the 
time it is made available for use by the customer.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what it means for an asset to be 'identified,' because this is the very first hurdle a contract has to clear before we can call it a lease. Think about it this way: a lease is about getting the right to use a specific thing. So the rules say a contract contains a lease only if it relates to an identified asset. If there's no particular asset at the heart of the deal, then there's nothing to lease, and the whole arrangement is something else entirely.

Now, how do we know if an asset is identified? There are two ways. The first is what we call explicit specification. This is the obvious case where the contract literally names or describes the asset. Imagine a rental agreement that says you get to use the delivery truck with a particular registration number, or the office on the third floor of a named building. The asset is written right there in the contract, so there's no question about which thing we're talking about.

The second way is implicit specification. Here the contract might not spell out the exact asset in words, but the asset becomes clear at the moment it is made available for use by the customer. In other words, even if the paperwork doesn't name a specific machine, when the supplier actually hands you one particular machine to use, that machine becomes the identified asset by the way the deal plays out in practice.

Why does this distinction matter so much? Because the whole idea of a lease rests on you controlling the use of a specific asset over time. If the supplier can swap out the asset whenever they like and it makes no difference to you, then you may not really have an identified asset at all, and the arrangement might just be a service rather than a lease. So as you read any contract, your first question should always be: is there a particular asset here, either named in writing or pinned down when it's handed over? If the answer is yes, you've cleared the first gate on the road to identifying a lease. Keep this idea in your back pocket, because it sets up everything that follows about who controls and benefits from the asset.

events.text: A lease exists only if there is an identified asset
Two ways to identify: explicit or implicit
Implicit = the only asset available to fulfil the deal
Identified = named explicitly OR the only one available implicitly

A lease is the right to use a specific thing, so if there is no particular thing at the heart of the deal, there is simply nothing to lease. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> So back to our trucks: if the shipping company keeps a whole fleet and just sends whichever one is free, you never had a specific truck, so you don't have a lease at all. <<WRITE_TEXT:Two ways to identify: explicit or implicit|id=text-1>>Now, how do we actually know if an asset is identified? There are exactly two routes. The first route is explicit specification. This is the obvious one, where the contract literally names or describes the asset. Picture a rental agreement that says you get the delivery van with a particular registration number, or the office on the third floor. It is spelled out in black and white. <<WRITE_TEXT:Implicit = the only asset available to fulfil the deal|id=text-2>>The second route is implicit specification. topics.orig_book_content:
Substantive substitution rights 
Even if an asset is specified, a customer does not have the right to use an 
identified asset if the supplier has the substantive right to substitute the asset 
throughout the period of use. A supplier’s right to substitute an asset is 
substantive if both of the following conditions are met: 
 
The supplier has the practical ability to substitute alternative assets 
throughout the period of use; and 
 
The supplier would benefit economically from the exercise of its right 
to substitute the asset.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what we call substantive substitution rights. This idea sits right at the heart of figuring out whether a lease even exists. Remember, for something to be a lease, the customer needs the right to use an identified asset. Now, here's the twist. Even if a contract names a specific asset, the customer might still not really have the right to use that identified asset. Why? Because the supplier might be able to swap it out for a different one whenever they want. If the supplier holds that power, then the customer isn't truly tied to one particular asset, and so there's no identified asset, and therefore no lease.

But not every substitution right takes away a lease. The standard is careful here. The supplier's right to substitute has to be what we call substantive, meaning real and meaningful, not just words written on paper. Think about it this way. A supplier might say in the contract, oh, I can swap this asset anytime, but in practice they never would and never could. That kind of right doesn't count.

So when is a substitution right actually substantive? Two conditions both have to be true. First, the supplier must have the practical ability to substitute alternative assets throughout the period of use. That means they genuinely can do the swap. There are other assets available, and nothing physically or contractually stops them from making the change while the customer is using the asset. Second, the supplier would benefit economically from exercising that right. In other words, swapping the asset must actually be worth their while. The benefits of substituting need to outweigh the costs of doing it.

Notice that both conditions must be met together. If the supplier can swap but gains nothing from it, the right isn't substantive. And if swapping would help them but they have no practical way to do it, again it's not substantive. Only when both are present does the right truly remove the idea of an identified asset.

Why does this matter so much? Because it decides who carries the asset on their books and how the deal is accounted for. If the supplier can meaningfully control which asset you use, you're really just buying a service, not leasing a specific thing. So whenever you see a contract that names an asset, pause and ask, can the supplier really swap it, and would they actually want to? That simple question protects you from mistaking a service arrangement for a lease.

events.text: Right must be SUBSTANTIVE, not just on paper
Substantive = practical ability AND economic benefit, throughout the period of use
Can't tell which asset? Assume no substantive right

A lease needs an identified asset, something the customer is genuinely tied to. But suppose the supplier can quietly wheel that machine away and roll in any other one whenever it suits them. <<POINT:named-asset-box>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:outcome-no-lease>> If the supplier holds that swapping power, then you were never really tied to that one machine at all. The standard says the supplier's right to substitute only counts if it is substantive, which means real in practice, not just words buried in the fine print. <<FOCUS:gate-practical>> Substantive means two things must both be true. If alternative assets aren't readily available, or it would be a huge hassle, the supplier can't really do it. <<TRACE:arrow-practical-yes>> <<FOCUS:gate-economic>> Gate two, the economic benefit. Would the supplier actually gain from swapping? The cost of moving the asset must be outweighed by the benefit they'd get. <<FOCUS:arrow-economic-yes>> <<WRITE_KEY:Substantive = practical ability AND economic benefit, throughout the period of use|id=key-1>>Only when both gates open, practical ability and economic benefit, is the substitution right substantive. Then there's no identified asset, and no lease. <<TRACE:arrow-economic-yes>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:outcome-identified>> But if either gate stays shut, say swapping is impractical or there's nothing in it for the supplier, the swap clause is just paper. The asset stays identified, and a lease can still exist. <<TRACE:outcome-identified>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Can't tell which asset? Assume no substantive right|id=text-2>>One more honest point. If you genuinely can't tell whether the supplier could swap the asset, you assume the right is not substantive, so the asset is treated as identified. <<POINT:outcome-identified>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:named-asset-box>> So before you ever ask about payments or terms, you walk the asset through these two gates. Named on paper isn't the test. Genuinely yours to use is.

topics.orig_book_content:
Portions of assets 
A capacity portion of an asset is an identified asset if it is physically distinct 
(for example, a floor of a building). A capacity or other portion of an asset 
that is not physically distinct (for example, a capacity portion of a fibre optic 
cable) is not an identified asset, unless it represents substantially all of the 
capacity of the asset and thereby provides the customer with the right to 
obtain substantially all of the economic benefits from use of the asset.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens when a lease doesn't involve a whole asset, but just a piece of one. This matters because many real contracts work this way. Imagine you don't rent an entire building, but only one floor of it. Or imagine you only use part of a long fibre optic cable. The big question is: does that portion count as an identified asset under this standard? Because if it doesn't, the contract isn't a lease.

Here's the key idea. A portion of an asset can be an identified asset, but only if it is physically distinct. Think about a floor of a building. That floor has walls, a ceiling, a clear physical boundary. You can point at it and say, this is the part I'm using, and nobody else can use that same space. Because it is physically separate and distinct, it qualifies as an identified asset.

Now compare that to something that is not physically distinct. Take a fibre optic cable. Suppose a customer is given some capacity within that cable. There's no wall or boundary you can see. The data the customer sends flows through the same physical strands as everyone else's data. You can't point to a specific physical chunk and say, that part is mine. So a capacity portion like this is generally not an identified asset.

But there's an important exception. Even if a portion is not physically distinct, it can still be an identified asset if it represents substantially all of the capacity of the asset. Why? Because if you control almost the entire capacity, then in practice you get substantially all of the economic benefits from using that asset. You're effectively using the whole thing. So the standard says, in that situation, treat it as an identified asset.

Notice the logic here. Physical distinctness is one clear path to being an identified asset. But when something isn't physically distinct, we fall back on a second test, the economic benefits test. If you get almost all the benefits because you control almost all the capacity, that counts too. Both tests are really asking the same underlying question: does the customer have a specific asset that gives them the benefits of using it? Keep this distinction in mind, because deciding whether there's an identified asset is one of the first steps in figuring out whether a contract contains a lease at all.

If you get substantially all of the capacity, you effectively obtain substantially all of the economic benefits, and the portion becomes an identified asset. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:floor-boundary>> So a physically distinct floor is identified the easy way, by its walls and ceiling. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:cable-capacity-slice>> And a non-distinct capacity slice is identified only the hard way, by being almost the whole thing. topics.topic_name: Right to obtain economic benefits from use
topics.orig_book_content:
Right to obtain economic benefits from use 
To determine whether a contract conveys the right to control the use of an 
identified asset, a company assesses whether the customer has the rights to: 
 
obtain substantially all of the economic benefits from use of the 
identified asset throughout the period of use; and 
 
direct the use of the identified asset. 
The economic benefits from using an asset include its primary output, by-
products and other economic benefits from using the asset that could be 
realised from a commercial transaction with a third party (e.g. subleasing the 
asset). 
In assessing whether a customer has a right to obtain substantially all the 
economic benefits from the use of an identified asset, the assessment should

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
9 
be made based on the asset’s use within the defined scope of the contract. 
For example: 
 
If a contract limits the use of a vehicle to only a particular geographic 
area, an entity assesses only the economic benefits from use of the 
motor vehicle within that territory. It does not consider what economic 
benefits could be obtained had there not been any geographical 
restriction in the contract. 
 
If a contract specifies that a machine can only be utilised during 
specific times of the day, an entity assesses only the economic 
benefits from use of the machinery during that time of the day. It does 
not consider what economic benefits could be obtained from using the 
machine for 24 hours a day.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about what it really means to control something you've leased. When a company signs a contract, accountants need to figure out whether that contract gives the customer the right to control the use of a specific asset. There are two big tests for this, and in this section we focus on one of them: does the customer get to obtain substantially all of the economic benefits from using that asset throughout the whole period of use? In a moment we'll talk about the second test, which is about directing the use, but right now we're zooming in on the benefits part.

So what counts as an economic benefit? Think broadly here. It's not just the main thing the asset produces, which we call its primary output. It also includes by-products, the extra stuff that comes along for the ride, and any other benefits you could earn by doing a deal with someone else. A good example of that last one is subleasing, where you rent the asset out to a third party and collect money for it. All of these count when we ask whether the customer is grabbing substantially all the value.

Now here's the really important insight, and it's easy to miss. When we judge whether the customer gets substantially all the benefits, we only look inside the boundaries the contract actually sets. We don't imagine a world without those limits. The contract defines a scope, and we stay inside it.

Let me make that concrete. Suppose a contract says you can only drive a vehicle inside one particular geographic area. When we assess the benefits, we only count the benefits you could earn driving within that territory. We do not ask, what if there were no geographic limit? That imaginary, unrestricted version is irrelevant.

Here's a second case. Imagine a contract that says a machine can only run during certain hours of the day. Again, we only count the benefits earned during those specific hours. We don't picture running the machine twenty-four hours a day and counting those benefits too. The restrictions in the contract become the playing field, and we measure substantially all the benefits only on that field. That's the key takeaway: stay within the defined scope of the contract when you judge who gets the value.

For our van, that's hauling your goods from place to place. <<TRACE:slice-primary>> <<FOCUS:slice-byproducts>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Benefits = primary output + by-products + third-party value|id=text-1>>But benefits are broader than the headline. Grab almost the entire pie, for the entire time — that's the test. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:scope-fence>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:8:scope_boundary>> <<SECTION:But which benefits count?|id=sec-2>>Now a twist. Suppose the contract says the van may only be driven inside one city. Do we measure all the benefits the van could ever produce, or only some of them? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:benefits-inside>> We only count what's inside the fence. The contract's defined scope draws a boundary, and benefits within that boundary are the ones we assess. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:benefits-outside>> Anything outside the fence — the trips you could have made if there were no city limit — we simply ignore. It's as if it doesn't exist for this test. <<POINT:benefits-outside>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose a contract limits the use of a vehicle to only a particular geographic area. The question is: when we judge whether the customer obtains substantially all the economic benefits, which benefits do we count? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Contract limits vehicle use to one geographic area only. Which economic benefits do we assess?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by scoping our assessment to what the contract actually permits. The entity assesses only the economic benefits from use of the motor vehicle within that territory. So we draw a boundary around the allowed geographic area and look only at the benefits available inside it. <<WRITE_STEP:Assess only economic benefits from use within the permitted territory|id=ex-step-1-1>> And here's the key move: it does not consider what economic benefits could be obtained had there been no geographical restriction in the contract. We ignore the imagined benefits of unrestricted use entirely. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Count only benefits within the allowed territory; do not consider benefits possible without the geographic restriction|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose a contract specifies that a machine can only be used during specific times of the day. The question is: which economic benefits does the entity actually assess? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Machine usable only during specific times of day — which economic benefits does the entity assess?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by pinning the scope to what the contract grants. Because use is limited to a specific window, the entity assesses only the economic benefits from using the machinery during that time of the day. <<WRITE_STEP:Assess only economic benefits during the contracted time-of-use window|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the answer is: the assessment is confined to the contracted hours. The entity does not consider what economic benefits could be obtained from using the machine twenty-four hours a day. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Benefits assessed = only during the specified time of day; do NOT consider hypothetical 24-hours-a-day use|id=ex-ans-1>> You've felt this yourself with a rental car. The contract lets you drive it all weekend, but it also says you can't take it across the border, and you certainly can't sublease it to your neighbor for cash. Next we tackle the other half of control — who gets to direct how the asset is used. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Right to direct the use  
A customer has the right to direct the use of an identified asset in either of 
the following situations: 
 
if the customer has the right to direct how and for what purpose the 
asset is used throughout the period of use; or 
 
if the relevant decisions about how and for what purpose the asset is 
used are predetermined and: 
o 
the customer has the right to operate the asset (or to direct 
others to operate the asset in a manner that it determines) 
throughout the period of use, without the lessor having the right 
to change those operating instructions; or 
o 
the customer designed the asset in a way that predetermines 
how and for what purpose the asset will be used throughout the 
period of use.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what it really means to control an asset, because this is the heart of figuring out whether something is a lease. Remember, for a contract to be a lease, the customer needs to control the use of an identified asset. We've already talked about getting the economic benefits from the asset. Now we focus on the second piece: the right to direct the use. Think of it this way: who gets to call the shots about how the asset is used and what it's used for?

The standard gives you two main situations where a customer has this right to direct the use. The first one is the most straightforward. The customer has the right to direct how and for what purpose the asset is used throughout the period of use. In plain words, the customer makes the key decisions, like where a truck goes, what it carries, when it's used, and whether the way it's used changes over time. If you can change those decisions during the period, you're directing the use.

The second situation is a bit more subtle, and it covers cases where those big decisions are already locked in from the start. Maybe how and for what purpose the asset is used is predetermined, so nobody is making fresh decisions during the period. Even then, the customer can still control the asset in one of two ways. The first way is that the customer has the right to operate the asset, or to direct others to operate it in a manner that the customer determines, throughout the period of use, and the supplier cannot change those operating instructions. So even if the purpose is fixed, if you're the one running it and the supplier can't override you, you're in control.

The second way is that the customer designed the asset in a way that predetermines how and for what purpose it will be used throughout the period of use. Here, the customer made the design choices up front that effectively decided everything in advance. By designing it, the customer already directed its use, even before the period began.

Notice the pattern here. Whether decisions are made on the fly or baked in ahead of time, the question is always the same: does the customer, not the supplier, have the real say? That's what makes it a lease rather than just a service.

events.text: Control = you decide HOW and WHY the asset is used
Predetermined use: control via operate OR design

If the answer is you, you might be holding a lease without even knowing it. <<FOCUS:root-question>> <<SECTION:Right to direct the use|id=sec-1>>We already know a lease needs an identified asset and that you get the economic benefits from it. But there is a second piece, and this is the heart of control: the right to direct the use. Directing the use simply means you call the shots. You decide how the asset is used and for what purpose, like where that truck goes and what it carries. <<POINT:route-one-how-why>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:route-one-how-why>> <<WRITE_KEY:Control = you decide HOW and WHY the asset is used|id=key-1>>So the most direct route is this: if you have the right to decide how and for what purpose the asset is used throughout the period, you control it. <<TRACE:route-one-how-why>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:route-two-predetermined>> But here is the puzzle. What if every decision about how and why the asset is used is already locked in before you even sign? Can you still be in control? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Yes, you still can, through a second route, and the standard gives two ways it happens. <<TRACE:route-two-predetermined>> <<FOCUS:sub-operate>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Predetermined use: control via operate OR design|id=text-1>>The first way: you have the right to operate the asset, or to direct others to operate it as you choose, and the supplier cannot change your operating instructions. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:sub-designed>> The second way: you designed the asset in a manner that predetermined how and for what purpose it would be used. You made the decisions up front, at the drawing board. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:control-result>> Notice the pattern: either you decide as you go, or the decisions were baked in by you. Both routes land at the same place. <<FOCUS:control-result>> <<WRITE_KEY:Either route -> customer directs use -> lease|id=key-2>>And once you have the right to direct the use on top of the economic benefits, the customer controls the asset, and the contract is a lease. <<TRACE:control-result>> <<FOCUS:root-question>> So next time you sign a contract for an asset, ask one question: who really decides how and why it gets used? Answer that, and you have answered whether it is a lease.

topics.orig_book_content:
Separating component of contract 
For a contract that contains a lease component, an entity accounts for each 
lease component within the contract separately from non-lease components. 
However, a lessee may apply a practical expedient by class of underlying 
asset, and ignore the requirement to separate non-lease components (such 
as services) from the lease components. Instead it may account for the entire 
contract as a single lease contract.

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
10 
If this practical expedient is not used, a lessee must allocate the total 
contract consideration to the lease and non-lease component on the basis of 
their relative stand-alone prices. If standalone prices are not available, then 
they must be estimated.  
An entity considers the right to use an underlying asset as separate lease 
component if it meets following criteria: 
 
Lessee can benefit from using that underlying asset either on its own 
or together with other resources that are readily available. 
 
Asset is neither highly dependent on nor highly inter related with the 
other assets in contract. 
The charges incurred which are associated with lease that does not transfer 
good or services to lessee do not give rise to a separate component. 
However, they are part of total consideration that an entity allocates to the 
identified component.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about what happens when a single contract bundles together more than one thing. Imagine you sign an agreement that lets you use a piece of equipment, but the same contract also includes a maintenance service to keep that equipment running. Notice that you've actually got two different things tucked inside one piece of paper. One part is the right to use the asset itself, which we call the lease component. The other part is the service, which we call a non-lease component. The general rule under this standard is that you account for each lease component separately from the non-lease components, so they don't get mixed up.

Now, separating things out can be a bit of work, so the standard gives the lessee, the person renting the asset, a shortcut called a practical expedient. If you choose, you can apply this shortcut by class of underlying asset, and simply ignore the requirement to split out the service from the lease. Instead, you treat the entire contract as one single lease. That makes life simpler, but it's a choice, not something forced on you.

If you decide not to use that shortcut, then you have to roll up your sleeves and split the total payment between the lease part and the non-lease part. How do you split it? You use their relative stand-alone prices, meaning what each part would cost on its own if you bought it separately. And if those stand-alone prices aren't sitting there for you to use, you must estimate them as best you can.

There's also a test for whether something even counts as a separate lease component. Two things must both be true. First, the lessee can benefit from using that asset either on its own or together with other resources that are readily available. Second, the asset is not highly dependent on, and not highly interrelated with, the other assets in the contract. If both of those hold, you treat it as its own separate lease component.

Finally, here's a subtle point worth holding onto. Some charges in a contract don't actually deliver any good or service to you, the lessee. Think of administrative charges that don't give you anything extra. Those charges do not create a separate component of their own. But they don't just vanish either. They stay part of the total consideration, the total amount you allocate across the real components you've identified. So you fold them into the overall pie that gets divided up.

events.text: 1 contract = 2 things inside
Allocate total payment by relative stand-alone prices
Practical expedient = treat whole contract as ONE lease

topics.orig_book_content:
Combination of contracts 
An entity shall combine two or more contracts entered into at or near the 
same time with the same counterparty (or related parties of the 
counterparty), and account for the contracts as a single contract if one or 
more of the following criteria are met: 
a) 
contracts are negotiated as a package with an overall commercial 
objective that cannot be understood without considering the 
contracts together; 
b) 
the amount of consideration to be paid in one contract depends on 
the price or performance of the other contract; or 
c) 
the rights to use underlying assets conveyed in the contracts (or 
some rights to use underlying assets conveyed in each of the 
contracts) form a single lease component.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about a situation that happens a lot in business. Sometimes a company doesn't sign just one contract with another party. Instead, they sign two, three, or even more contracts, all around the same time, and all with the same person or company they're dealing with. The question this section answers is simple but important: should we treat each of those contracts on its own, or should we combine them and treat them as if they were really one big contract?

The accounting standard says: in certain cases, you must combine them. Now, this only applies when the contracts are made at or near the same time, and with the same counterparty, or with parties closely related to that counterparty. If those two conditions are true, then you check three tests. If even one of them is met, you combine the contracts and account for them as a single contract.

Here's the first test. The contracts were negotiated together as a package, with one overall commercial goal that you simply cannot make sense of unless you look at all the contracts together. In other words, they were always meant to work as a team, not as separate deals.

The second test is about the money. If the amount you have to pay under one contract depends on the price or the performance of another contract, then those contracts are clearly linked. The price of one only makes sense in light of the other.

The third test is more technical. If the rights to use the underlying assets across the contracts, or even just some of those rights, actually form a single lease component, then they belong together. The assets are so tied to each other that splitting the contracts would give you a misleading picture.

Why does this matter? Because companies might split one economic deal into several contracts, sometimes by accident, sometimes on purpose. If we always looked at each piece separately, the financial statements could hide the true substance of the arrangement. By combining when these signs are present, accounting reflects economic reality rather than just the paperwork. Notice the theme running through all three tests: they each ask whether the contracts are truly independent or whether they're really one deal wearing several costumes. When they're genuinely one deal, we account for them that way.

events.text: Gate lock 1: at or near same time
Gate lock 2: same counterparty or related
Combine ONLY if BOTH gateway conditions hold
Gate open + any ONE test = single contract

Does that automatically mean we combine the contracts? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:test-package>> Not yet. Different papers, but one real thing being leased. <<POINT:test-single-component>> <<FOCUS:combine-result>> <<WRITE_KEY:Gate open + any ONE test = single contract|id=key-2>>So here is the whole machine. Both gateway conditions open the gate, then any single one of the three tests sends you to one answer: treat it all as one combined contract. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:separate-result>> And if the gate never opens, or all three tests fail, you stay here: the contracts remain separate, each accounted for on its own.

topics.orig_book_content:
Lease term 
If a contract is, or contains, a lease, the lease term needs to be determined. 
The lease term begins on the commencement date (i.e. the date on which 
the lessor makes the underlying asset(s) available for use by the lessee) and 
includes any rent-free or reduced rent periods. It comprises:

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
11 
a) 
the non-cancellable period of the lease; 
b) 
periods covered by an option to extend the lease if the lessee is 
reasonably certain to exercise that option; and 
c) 
periods covered by an option to terminate the lease if the lessee is 
reasonably certain not to exercise that option. 
A lease is no longer enforceable when the lessee and the lessor each have 
the right to terminate the lease without permission from the other party with 
no more than an insignificant penalty.  
An entity shall revise the lease term if there is a change in the non-
cancellable period of a lease.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something that sounds simple but really matters in lease accounting: figuring out the lease term. The lease term is basically the length of time the agreement is expected to last, and getting it right affects almost everything else, because so many calculations depend on how long you think the lease will run.

First, when does the clock start? The lease term begins on what we call the commencement date. That's the day the lessor actually makes the asset available for the lessee to use. So it's not the day you signed the paperwork, it's the day you can actually start using the thing. And here's an important detail: even if the first few months are rent-free, or you pay reduced rent at the start, those months still count as part of the lease term. Don't let a free period fool you into thinking the lease is shorter.

Now, what makes up the lease term? Think of it in three pieces. First, there's the non-cancellable period, the part of the lease you're locked into no matter what. Second, you add periods covered by an option to extend the lease, but only if the lessee is reasonably certain they'll choose to extend. Third, you add periods covered by an option to terminate early, but only if the lessee is reasonably certain they will not use that early-exit option. Notice the careful wording there: it always comes down to what the lessee is reasonably certain to do. If they're likely to stay, you include that time; if they're likely to leave, you don't.

There's also the idea of enforceability. A lease stops being enforceable once both the lessee and the lessor can each walk away on their own, without needing the other's permission, and without facing more than a tiny, insignificant penalty. If both sides can freely exit with almost no cost, the lease really doesn't bind anyone anymore.

Finally, the lease term isn't frozen forever. If the non-cancellable period changes, the entity has to revise the lease term to reflect that change. So you keep your eye on it, and you update your thinking when the facts shift. That's the whole idea: start at the commencement date, build the term from those three pieces based on what the lessee is reasonably certain to do, and revise it when circumstances change.

events.text: Term starts at commencement; rent-free and reduced-rent months still count
Non-cancellable = locked in, can't walk away
Term = non-cancellable period + options the lessee is reasonably certain to take

Suppose your first three months are rent-free, a sweetener to get you to sign. Do those free months count as part of the lease term? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> They absolutely do. <<WRITE_KEY:Term starts at commencement; rent-free and reduced-rent months still count|id=key-1>>A rent-free or reduced-rent period is still you having the asset, so it is part of the term from day one. <<POINT:rent-free-band>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:non-cancellable-band>> Next comes the solid core of the term: the non-cancellable period. <<WRITE_TEXT:Non-cancellable = locked in, can't walk away|id=text-1>>This is the stretch where neither of you can just walk away, you're locked in. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:option-band>> But leases often have options bolted on. An option to extend, or an option to terminate early. Do we just include every extension option to be safe? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> No, and this is the clever part. <<SECTION:The reasonably-certain test|id=sec-2>>You only include an extension period if you are reasonably certain you'll take it. And you only cut off a termination option if you're reasonably certain you won't use it. <<POINT:option-band>> <<FOCUS:lease-term-bracket>> So in our office example, the three locked-in years are in for certain, and because you're reasonably certain to stay the extra two, those join the term too, giving five. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:lease-term-bracket>> Put it together: the lease term is the non-cancellable period, plus any extension you're reasonably certain to take, plus any termination right you're reasonably certain not to use. <<WRITE_KEY:Term = non-cancellable period + options the lessee is reasonably certain to take|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> One last note: judgement isn't frozen. If the non-cancellable period itself changes, you go back and revise the term, because every downstream number leans on it. <<POINT:non-cancellable-band>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Extension and termination options 
At commencement date, entity should assess whether lessee is reasonably 
certain: 
 
to exercise an option to extend the lease;  
 
to exercise an option to purchase the underlying asset; or 
 
not to exercise an option to terminate the lease 
In making such assessment entity considers all relevant facts and 
circumstances that creates an economic incentive for the lessee to exercise 
or not to exercise, the option including any expected changes in facts and 
circumstances from the commencement date until exercise date of option. 
The standard also gives examples of factors that may be considered in 
making such an assessment. 
A lessee’s past practice with leases, particularly leases of similar assets, 
should also be considered in determining the likelihood of options being 
exercised.  
Lessee
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something that comes up a lot in real leases: options. When you sign a lease, the contract often gives you choices for later. Maybe you can extend the lease for a few more years. Maybe you can buy the asset outright at the end. Or maybe you can walk away early and terminate the lease before it's done. These choices matter a great deal for accounting, because the length of a lease changes how big your lease liability and your right-of-use asset are.

Here's the key idea. Right at the start of the lease, which we call the commencement date, the entity has to make a judgment. It has to ask itself: is the lessee reasonably certain to extend the lease? Is the lessee reasonably certain to buy the asset? And is the lessee reasonably certain not to terminate early? Notice the phrase 'reasonably certain.' That's a fairly high bar. It's not just 'might happen' — it means the lessee is quite likely to do it.

Now, how do you decide whether someone is reasonably certain? You look at all the relevant facts and circumstances that give the lessee an economic incentive — a money reason — to take the option or to leave it alone. Think about it like this. If the rent during an extension period is much cheaper than what the market charges, the lessee has a strong reason to extend, because it's a good deal. If walking away early triggers a big penalty, the lessee has a reason not to terminate. These incentives push the decision one way or the other.

You also consider how things might change between the start of the lease and the moment the option actually has to be exercised. The world doesn't stand still, so expected changes matter too.

And here's a really practical point: look at the lessee's past behavior. If a business has a long history of always extending leases on similar assets, that history tells you something real about what they'll probably do this time. Past practice is genuine evidence, not just a guess. So putting it all together, judging these options is about reading incentives and history honestly to figure out the true expected length of the lease.

events.text: Lease term set by 'reasonably certain' judgment at commencement
Test is economic incentive, not the contract wording
Consider all facts: fit-out cost, location, below-market rent
Past practice with similar leases also counts

So how long is your lease, really? Five years, or ten? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Extension and termination options|id=sec-1>>Here's the honest answer: it depends on a judgment you make right at the start, on what we call the commencement date. <<POINT:commencement-date>> <<FOCUS:guaranteed-period>> Look at the timeline. This solid bar is the part you are locked into — the years you cannot escape. That's the guaranteed period. <<FOCUS:optional-period>> And this dashed bar is the optional bit — the extra years you could take if you choose to extend. The big question is whether those dashed years count as part of your lease. <<FOCUS:incentive-zone>> <<WRITE_KEY:Lease term set by 'reasonably certain' judgment at commencement|id=key-1>>At the commencement date the entity must ask three things: is the lessee reasonably certain to extend, reasonably certain to buy the asset, and reasonably certain not to terminate early? <<PAUSE:short>> If the answer is yes, you are reasonably certain to extend, then the lease term reaches forward and swallows those optional years. <<TRACE:extend-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> But if instead you are reasonably certain to terminate early, the lease term gets cut short, right here. <<TRACE:terminate-arrow>> <<FOCUS:incentive-zone>> Now here is the trap. Reasonably certain is not the same as legally allowed. The contract gives you the option — but the standard asks something deeper. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:incentive-zone>> <<WRITE_KEY:Test is economic incentive, not the contract wording|id=key-2>>The real test is economic incentive. Is there a strong financial reason that makes exercising the option the obvious choice? <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Consider all facts: fit-out cost, location, below-market rent|id=text-1>>For instance, in any case where you've spent a fortune fitting out the shop, or the rent for the extra years is far below market, walking away would be painful — so you're reasonably certain to stay. <<POINT:optional-period>> <<FOCUS:commencement-date>> The entity weighs all relevant facts and circumstances, including expected changes between today and the date the option would be exercised. <<WRITE_TEXT:Past practice with similar leases also counts|id=text-2>>And don't forget habits — a lessee's past practice with similar leases tells you a lot about how likely an option really is to be used. <<POINT:guaranteed-period>> <<FOCUS:extend-arrow>> So back to our shop: if the economic incentive to stay is strong, your lease is ten years, not five — and that bigger term means a bigger liability and a bigger right-of-use asset. <<TRACE:extend-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:incentive-zone>> That single judgment at the start — reasonably certain, based on economic incentive — is what quietly decides how big the whole lease shows up on your books. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Recognition of lease 
On the commencement of the lease, lessee needs to recognise the right-of-
use asset and measure it at cost. Lessee should also recognise a lease 
liability and measure it at the present value of the lease payments that are 
not paid at that date. The lease payments should be discounted using the

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
12 
interest rate implicit in the lease, if readily determinable or else using the 
lessee’s incremental borrowing rate. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
In-substance fixed lease payments are payments that may, in form, contain 
variability but that, in substance, are unavoidable.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens at the very start of a lease, on the day it actually begins. We call this the commencement date. When a company rents an asset, say a building or a machine, two important things need to be written into their accounting books on that day.

The first thing is something called a right-of-use asset. Now, even though the company doesn't own the asset, it has the right to use it for the length of the lease. That right is valuable, so we treat it like an asset and record it at its cost. Think of it this way: if you pay to use a friend's bike for a year, you don't own the bike, but you do own the right to ride it whenever you want. That right has worth, and the accounting rules say we should put it on the books.

The second thing is the lease liability. A liability is simply something you owe. Because the company has promised to make future lease payments, those promised payments are a kind of debt. So we record a lease liability, and we measure it at the present value of all the lease payments that haven't been paid yet by the commencement date.

Now, why present value and not just the plain total? Because money in the future is worth less than money today. A rupee you'll pay three years from now feels lighter than a rupee you pay right now. So we shrink those future payments down to what they're worth today, and that shrinking process is called discounting.

To discount, we need an interest rate. The standard tells us to use the interest rate implicit in the lease, which is the rate built into the deal itself, if we can easily figure it out. But if that rate is hard to determine, we fall back on the lessee's incremental borrowing rate, meaning the rate the company would have to pay if it borrowed money to buy a similar asset.

There's one more idea here worth noticing. Some lease payments are called in-substance fixed payments. On the surface they might look like they could change or vary, but when you look closer, they're actually unavoidable. In substance, they must be paid. So even though their form looks flexible, we treat them as fixed because the company genuinely cannot escape them. That distinction matters because fixed payments get included in our present value calculation.

events.text: Day one: recognise a right-of-use asset AND a lease liability
Use implicit rate; else incremental borrowing rate

topics.orig_book_content:
Subsequent measurement of right-of-use asset 
Subsequently, the right-of-use asset shall be measured by applying a cost 
model or revaluation model if the underlying asset belongs to the class of 
assets to which the entity applies revaluation model as per Ind AS 16, 
Property, Plant and Equipment.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens to the right-of-use asset after you first record it. When a company signs a lease, it puts a right-of-use asset on its books. That's like saying, I have the right to use this thing, this building or this machine, for the length of the lease. We measured that asset at the start. But assets don't just sit there frozen in time. As months and years go by, we have to keep track of how their value changes. That ongoing tracking is what we call subsequent measurement.

So here's the key idea. After the start, the company gets to choose how it will keep measuring this right-of-use asset, and there are two possible approaches. The first one is the cost model. Think of the cost model as the simple, steady path. You start with the cost of the asset, and over time you reduce it for wear and tear, which we call depreciation, and for any loss in value, which we call impairment. It's a straightforward way of saying, this asset slowly gets used up.

The second approach is the revaluation model. This one means you periodically update the asset's value to reflect what it's actually worth in the market, its fair value. But here's the important condition. You can only use the revaluation model for your right-of-use asset if the underlying asset, the real thing you're leasing, belongs to a class of assets that the company already revalues under another standard, Ind AS 16, which deals with property, plant, and equipment. In other words, you can't just pick revaluation for a lease whenever you feel like it. You only get to do it if you're already treating that same kind of asset that way for the items you own.

Why does this matter? Because it keeps things consistent. Imagine a company that revalues all its buildings that it owns. If it also leases a building of the same kind, it makes sense to treat that leased building's right-of-use asset the same way. Consistency makes financial statements honest and comparable. So the takeaway is simple. After the start, measure the right-of-use asset either at cost, the default choice, or at a revalued amount, but only when that asset class is one you already revalue elsewhere.

events.text: Cost model = steady decline by depreciation
Revaluation = reset to fair value
Subsequent measurement: cost model OR revaluation model (revaluation only if that asset class is already revalued under Ind AS 16)

You begin with the cost and you shave a slice off it each period as depreciation, so the line just glides downward. <<TRACE:cost-model-path>> <<FOCUS:cost-model-label>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Cost model = steady decline by depreciation|id=text-1>>Notice this line never jumps around. It only goes down, smoothly, year after year, as the van is used up. The second path is the revaluation model. Watch what's different — it can be reset to the asset's fair value, so instead of only sliding down, it can step back up if the asset is worth more. <<TRACE:revaluation-model-path>> <<FOCUS:revaluation-model-label>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Revaluation = reset to fair value|id=text-2>>So one road is steady and predictable, and the other tracks what the asset is really worth in the market. Now, a fair question: if the revaluation path can keep your asset closer to its true worth, why wouldn't every company just pick it? <<POINT:revaluation-model-path>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:revaluation-model-label>> Because there's a gatekeeper. You're only allowed onto the revaluation road if the underlying asset belongs to a class for which your company already revalues its own property, plant and equipment under Ind AS sixteen. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:start-value-point>> <<WRITE_KEY:Subsequent measurement: cost model OR revaluation model (revaluation only if that asset class is already revalued under Ind AS 16)|id=key-1>>So lock this in: after first recording the right-of-use asset, you measure it using either the cost model or the revaluation model. <<PAUSE:short>> And the revaluation door only opens for an asset class that you're already revaluing under Ind AS sixteen — for everyone else, the steady cost model is the road you travel. <<TRACE:cost-model-path>> <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Cost model 
Lessee shall measure the right-of-use asset at cost less accumulated 
depreciation as per Ind AS 16 and any accumulated impairment losses as 
per Ind AS 36. 
Lessees adjust the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset for 
remeasurement of the lease liability, unless the carrying amount has already 
been reduced to zero or the change in the lease liability relates to a variable 
lease payment that does not depend on an index or rate.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about the cost model, which is the standard way a lessee keeps track of the value of a right-of-use asset on their books over time. Remember, when you lease something — say a building or a piece of machinery — accounting treats your right to use that thing as an asset. So how much is that asset worth as the years go by? The cost model gives us a clean recipe.

Here's the recipe. You start with the original cost of the right-of-use asset. Then you subtract two things. First, you subtract accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is just the wearing-down of value over time, spread out across the life of the asset, and we follow the rules in Ind AS sixteen for that. Second, you subtract any accumulated impairment losses. Impairment is when something unexpected happens and the asset suddenly becomes worth less than we thought — and for that we follow Ind AS thirty-six. So the carrying amount, which is the value showing on the books, equals cost minus accumulated depreciation minus accumulated impairment losses.

Now there's a second important idea here. The lease liability — the amount you owe — can sometimes change. Maybe the lease terms get reassessed, or interest rates shift. When that lease liability gets remeasured, the lessee also adjusts the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset to match. Think of it as keeping the two sides connected: if what you owe changes, the value of your right to use the asset usually changes too.

But there are two exceptions where you do not make that adjustment. The first exception is when the carrying amount of the asset has already been reduced all the way down to zero. You can't push it below zero, so you stop. The second exception is when the change in the lease liability relates to a variable lease payment that does not depend on an index or a rate. Those particular variable payments get handled differently and don't flow into the asset's carrying amount.

Why does this matter? Because the cost model is the most common, straightforward approach lessees use, and understanding it tells you exactly how a leased asset's value rises and falls on the books — and when changes in what you owe should ripple through to the asset, and when they shouldn't. Keep those two exceptions in mind; they're the kind of detail that trips people up.

events.text: Depreciation = wearing-down of value over time
Carrying amount = cost less accumulated depreciation less accumulated impairment
No adjustment if asset already zero, or change is variable payment (no index/rate)

The day after you sign, what is that van worth on your books, and what will it be worth next year? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:original-cost-block>> <<SECTION:The cost model|id=sec-1>>The answer comes from something called the cost model, and it is just a clean recipe for tracking the value of your right to use that van as the years go by. <<PAUSE:short>> You start with this full block, the original cost of the right-of-use asset, exactly what you measured it at on day one. <<POINT:original-cost-block>> <<FOCUS:depreciation-cut>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Depreciation = wearing-down of value over time|id=text-1>>Now, the van wears down a little every year, and that wearing-down of value is called depreciation, which we spread across the life of the asset using the rules in Ind AS sixteen. <<TRACE:depreciation-cut>> So we cut that accumulated depreciation off the top of the block, and the more years pass, the bigger that cut grows. <<POINT:depreciation-cut>> <<FOCUS:impairment-cut>> Sometimes something unexpected happens, the asset suddenly loses value beyond ordinary wear, and that is an impairment loss, which we follow under Ind AS thirty-six. <<TRACE:impairment-cut>> <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> <<WRITE_KEY:Carrying amount = cost less accumulated depreciation less accumulated impairment|id=key-1>>So we subtract any accumulated impairment losses too, and what is left is your net carrying amount, the figure that actually sits on the balance sheet. <<PAUSE:short>> Take the original cost, subtract everything the asset has worn down by, then subtract any sudden losses, and the remainder is what the asset is carried at. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\text{Carrying amount} = \text{Cost} - \text{Accumulated depreciation} - \text{Accumulated impairment losses}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> But here is a question that trips people up: what if the lease itself changes partway through, say the rent gets revised, so the lease liability you owe is recalculated? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:remeasurement-adjustment>> When the lease liability is remeasured, you adjust the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset by the very same amount, up or down, so the two stay linked. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:No adjustment if asset already zero, or change is variable payment (no index/rate)|id=text-2>>There are just two exceptions: you stop if the asset is already reduced to zero, or if the change relates to a variable payment that does not depend on an index or a rate. <<POINT:remeasurement-adjustment>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> So picture the whole journey: start at cost, cut away depreciation, cut away impairment, then nudge for any remeasurement, and you land on the carrying amount. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:carrying-amount-block>> That single recipe, cost less depreciation less impairment, adjusted for remeasurement, is the cost model, and it tells you exactly what your leased van is worth on your books, today and every year after. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Subsequent measurement of lease liability 
After initial recognition, the lease liability is measured at amortised cost using 
the effective interest method and remeasuring the carrying amount to reflect 
any reassessment or lease modifications or to reflect revised in-substance 
fixed lease payments.  
Cost = Lease Liability + Lease payments made – lease incentives 
received + initial direct costs + estimated dismantling and restoration 
costs. 
Lease Payments = Fixed payments (including in-substance fixed lease 
payments) – lease incentives + variable payments + expected guaranteed 
residual value + exercise price of purchase option (if reasonably certain 
to be exercised) + penalties for termination (if reasonably certain to be 
terminated).

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
13
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens to a lease liability after you first record it on your books. Remember, when a company leases something — say a building or a machine — it promises to make payments over time. On day one, it records a liability, which is basically the present value of all those future payments. But the story doesn't end there. Over the months and years that follow, that liability has to be measured again and again. This is what we call subsequent measurement.

The main idea is that the lease liability is carried at something called amortised cost, using the effective interest method. Now, what does that really mean? Think of it like a loan. Every period, interest builds up on the amount you still owe. So the liability grows a little because of interest, and then it shrinks when you actually make a payment. The effective interest method is just a careful way of spreading that interest evenly across the life of the lease, so each period reflects the true cost of borrowing.

But there's more to it. Sometimes things change. Maybe you reassess your estimates, maybe the lease is modified, or maybe the in-substance fixed payments are revised. When that happens, you have to remeasure the carrying amount of the liability so it reflects the new reality. The liability isn't frozen — it's a living number that adjusts to new information.

The section also reminds us how the cost of a related item is built up. The cost equals the lease liability, plus lease payments already made, minus any lease incentives received, plus initial direct costs, plus estimated dismantling and restoration costs. That last piece matters — if you'll have to take something apart or restore a property at the end, that future obligation counts now.

And what counts as lease payments? It's a careful list. You take the fixed payments, including in-substance fixed ones, subtract lease incentives, add variable payments, add the expected guaranteed residual value, add the exercise price of a purchase option if you're reasonably certain you'll buy, and add penalties for ending the lease early if you're reasonably certain you'll terminate. Notice how each of these only counts when it's reasonably certain. That's the accountant's way of staying honest — you only include amounts you genuinely expect to pay. So the big lesson here is that a lease liability is measured carefully, grows with interest, falls with payments, and gets remeasured whenever circumstances change.

events.text: Closing = Opening + Interest - Payment
Interest is charged on the shrinking balance, so it gets smaller each period
Lease liability is carried at amortised cost using the effective interest method

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:opening-balance>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:17:lease_liability_rollforward>> You sign a lease and write down what you owe on day one. But by next month that number has already changed. Why won't it sit still? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:opening-balance>> Here's the secret: a lease liability behaves almost exactly like a loan. Think about borrowing money from a friend who charges you a little interest. <<SECTION:Amortised cost|id=sec-1>>Every period, two things happen to that balance. First, because you still owe money, interest quietly builds up on top of what you owe. <<POINT:interest-addition>> <<PAUSE:short>> Then you make your lease payment, and that payment chips the balance back down. <<POINT:payment-subtraction>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:closing-balance>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Closing = Opening + Interest - Payment|id=text-1>>So what you're left with at the end of the period is your opening amount, plus the interest, minus the payment. That leftover is the new carrying amount. And here's the elegant part: that closing balance simply becomes next period's opening balance, and the whole cycle repeats. <<TRACE:carry-forward-arrow>> The closing balance equals the opening balance, plus interest at the effective rate on that opening balance, minus the payment you make. <<WRITE_EQUATION:L_{closing} = L_{opening} + (L_{opening} \times r) - P|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:interest-addition>> Now if the interest keeps getting added every period, you might wonder — does the liability just keep growing forever? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:closing-balance>> <<WRITE_KEY:Interest is charged on the shrinking balance, so it gets smaller each period|id=key-1>>No. Because your payment is bigger than the interest, the balance shrinks. And since interest is charged only on what you still owe, a smaller balance means less interest next time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:opening-balance>> This whole method — interest on the outstanding balance, then reduce by payment — is what accountants call the effective interest method. <<FOCUS:closing-balance>> <<WRITE_KEY:Lease liability is carried at amortised cost using the effective interest method|id=key-2>>And carrying the liability this way, period after period, is exactly what we mean when we say it is measured at amortised cost. <<PAUSE:short>> There's one more twist. Sometimes the deal itself changes — payments get revised, or you reassess what you'll actually pay. When that happens, you also remeasure the carrying amount to reflect the new reality. <<POINT:opening-balance>> So picture the liability as a living balance: it breathes in interest, breathes out payments, and quietly shrinks toward zero by the end of the lease. <<TRACE:carry-forward-arrow>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Reassessment of lease liability 
A lessee shall remeasure the lease liability by discounting the revised lease 
payments using a revised discount rate, if either 
 
there is a change in the lease term 
 
there is a change in the assessment of an option to purchase the 
underlying asset 
lessee shall determine the revised discount rate as the interest rate implicit in 
the lease for the remainder of the lease term, if that rate can be readily 
determined, or the lessee’s incremental borrowing rate at the date of 
reassessment, if the interest rate implicit in the lease cannot be readily 
determined. 
A lessee shall remeasure the lease liability by discounting the revised lease 
payments, using unchanged discount rates, if either 
 
there is a change in the amounts expected to be payable under a 
residual value guarantee  
 
there is a change in future lease payments resulting from a change in 
an index or a rate used to determine those payments
topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about what happens after a lease has already started. When you first sign a lease, you make your best estimate of all the future payments and you turn them into a single number on your books called the lease liability. But life changes. Sometimes the facts you assumed at the start turn out to be different later on. When that happens, you can't just leave the old number sitting there — you have to go back and remeasure the lease liability so it reflects the new reality. That process is what we call reassessment.

Now here's the clever part. The rules split these changes into two groups, and they treat each group differently. In the first group, the very nature of the lease has shifted. Maybe you decide you'll keep the asset longer than planned, so the lease term changes. Or maybe you change your mind about whether you'll buy the asset at the end, which is the purchase option. When these big-picture things change, you remeasure the liability by discounting the revised payments using a revised discount rate. Why a new rate? Because the timing and length of the deal have genuinely changed, so the old rate no longer fits. To find this revised rate, you use the interest rate implicit in the lease for the remaining term if you can work it out easily. If you can't, you fall back on the lessee's incremental borrowing rate, which is basically the rate you'd pay to borrow money on the day you reassess.

In the second group, the changes are smaller and more routine. Maybe the amount you expect to owe under a residual value guarantee changes — that's a promise about what the asset will be worth at the end. Or maybe your future payments shift because they're tied to an index or a rate, like inflation, and that index moved. For these, you still remeasure the liability by discounting the revised payments, but you keep the same discount rate you were already using. Notice the logic here: the underlying shape of the lease hasn't changed, only the payment amounts have, so there's no good reason to change the rate. Keeping it simple keeps the accounting honest and consistent.

events.text: Reassessment = remeasure liability for new facts
revised rate: implicit, else IBR at reassess date
cash-only change: keep original rate
