Two years in, you decide to stay seven years instead. So does that old number just get to stay wrong? <<PAUSE:long>> It can't. That number, the lease liability, was only ever your best guess of all the future payments squeezed into one present value. When the facts behind the guess change, the number has to change too. <<POINT:trigger-event>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:trigger-event>> <<SECTION:Reassessment|id=sec-1>>Going back and remeasuring that liability so it matches the new reality is exactly what we call reassessment. <<WRITE_TEXT:Reassessment = remeasure liability for new facts|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:fork-question>> Now here is the clever part. Not every change is the same kind of change, so the rules ask one sharp question before you remeasure anything. The question is this: did the very nature of the lease shift, or did only the cash amounts shift? <<POINT:fork-question>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:path-revised-rate>> If the nature shifted, say you changed the lease term, or you now expect to exercise a purchase option, then you are essentially dealing with a different deal, so you discount the revised payments using a revised discount rate. <<TRACE:path-revised-rate>> <<FOCUS:revised-rate-label>> What is that revised rate? It is the interest rate implicit in the lease for the rest of the term if you can readily find it, otherwise your incremental borrowing rate on the date you reassess. <<WRITE_TEXT:revised rate: implicit, else IBR at reassess date|id=text-2>> <<FOCUS:path-same-rate>> But if only the cash amounts moved, the deal itself is unchanged. Maybe your residual value guarantee estimate dropped, or an index your rent is tied to ticked up. <<TRACE:path-same-rate>> <<FOCUS:same-rate-label>> In that case you remeasure using the original, unchanged discount rate, because nothing about the riskiness or length of the deal has actually changed. <<WRITE_TEXT:cash-only change: keep original rate|id=text-3>> <<FOCUS:fork-question>> So the whole topic collapses into one decision. Nature of the lease changes, you use a revised rate. Only the cash amounts change, you keep the original rate. <<WRITE_KEY:Nature changes -> revised rate. Cash only -> original rate.|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:liability-box>> And both paths share the same engine underneath: discount the new payments back to today and that present value becomes your new lease liability. <<FOCUS:trigger-event>> That is reassessment in one breath: when life proves your assumptions wrong, you do not leave a stale number sitting there, you remeasure it, choosing the rate by whether the lease itself changed or just the money did. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Lease modification 
A lessee accounts for a lease modification as a separate lease if both of the 
following conditions exist:  
 
the modification increases the scope of the lease by adding the right-
to-use one or more underlying assets; and  
 
the consideration for the lease increases by an amount equivalent to 
the stand-alone price for the increase in scope and any appropriate 
adjustments to that stand-alone price to reflect the circumstances of 
the particular contract. 
For a lease modification that is not a separate lease, at the effective date of 
the modification, the lessee accounts for the lease modification by 
remeasuring the lease liability using a discount rate determined at that date 
and: 
 
for lease modifications that decrease the scope of the lease, the 
lessee decreases the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset to 
reflect the partial or full termination of the lease, and recognises a gain 
or loss that reflects the proportionate decrease in scope; and

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
14 
 
for all other lease modifications, the lessee makes a corresponding 
adjustment to the right-of-use asset.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens when a lease changes after it's already started. In the real world, agreements don't always stay frozen. Maybe you rent some office space, and a year later you decide you want an extra floor. Or maybe you decide you actually need less space than before. These changes are called lease modifications, and accountants need rules to handle them properly.

The first big question is this: should we treat the modification as a brand new, separate lease, or should we adjust the lease we already have? The standard says you treat it as a separate lease only when two conditions are both true. First, the change must increase the scope of the lease, meaning you're adding the right to use one or more additional assets. And second, the extra payment you agree to must match the stand-alone price for that increase, adjusted for the specific circumstances of the contract. Think about it this way: if you add a floor and you pay roughly the fair market rent for that floor, that's basically just a fresh deal sitting alongside your old one. So you account for it separately and leave the original lease untouched.

Now, what if it's not a separate lease? Then we have to go back and remeasure the lease liability. Remember, the lease liability is the present value of the payments you still owe, and to find present value we use a discount rate. At the effective date of the modification, you pick a fresh discount rate that fits that date, and you recalculate the liability.

From there, the treatment splits in two directions. If the modification decreases the scope, meaning you're giving back part of what you leased, you reduce the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset to reflect that partial or full termination. And because you're walking away from part of the lease, you record a gain or loss that matches the proportionate decrease in scope. But for every other kind of modification, you simply make a matching adjustment to the right-of-use asset. No gain or loss in that case, just a balancing adjustment so the books stay consistent. Notice the logic here: giving something up triggers a gain or loss, while other changes just shift the asset value to keep things balanced.

Not separate: remeasure liability, adjust right-of-use asset; if scope shrinks, recognise gain or loss

topics.orig_book_content:
Presentation  
The right-of-use assets should be either presented separately from other 
assets in the balance sheet or disclosed in the notes. If not presented 
separately, they should be presented in the appropriate line item of the 
balance sheet as if they were owned and disclose in the notes the line items 
which include such assets. 
The lease liabilities should be presented either separately from other 
liabilities in the balance sheet or disclose in the notes the line items which 
include the lease liabilities. 
Right-of-use assets that meet the definition of investment property are 
presented within investment property. 
In the statement of profit and loss, a lessee shall present interest expense on 
the lease liability separately from the depreciation charge for the right-of-use 
asset. Interest expense on the lease liability is a component of finance cost 
that requires to be presented separately in the statement of profit and loss. 
In the statement of cash flows, a lessee shall classify: 
a) 
cash payments for the principal portion of the lease liability within 
financing activities; 
b) 
cash payments for the interest portion of the lease liability within 
financing activities applying the requirements in Ind AS 7, Statement of 
Cash Flows, for interest paid; and 
c) 
short-term lease payments, payments for leases of low-value assets 
and variable lease payments not included in the measurement of the 
lease liability within operating activities. 
Lessor
topics.our_understanding:
This section is all about presentation, which simply means where you show the lease numbers in your financial statements. Think of it like organizing a wardrobe — everything has its proper drawer, and Ind AS 116 tells you exactly which drawer each item belongs in. Let's walk through the three main financial statements together.

First, the balance sheet. Remember that a lessee, the person renting an asset, records two things: a right-of-use asset, which is their right to use the leased item, and a lease liability, which is what they still owe. For the right-of-use asset, you have a choice. You can show it as its own separate line, or you can tuck it into whatever line item you'd use if you actually owned that kind of asset — but if you do that, you must explain in the notes which line it's hiding inside. There's one special case: if the right-of-use asset fits the definition of investment property, like a rented building you sub-let to earn rent, then it goes inside investment property. The lease liability works the same way — show it separately, or fold it into another line and explain in the notes where it lives.

Second, the statement of profit and loss. Here's a key idea. A lessee splits the cost of a lease into two distinct pieces: depreciation on the right-of-use asset, and interest expense on the lease liability. These two must be shown separately. The interest portion is treated as a finance cost, just like interest on a loan, and it gets its own presentation.

Third, the statement of cash flows. The cash you pay each period also gets split. The principal portion — paying down what you owe — goes under financing activities. The interest portion also goes under financing activities, following the rules in Ind AS 7. But three kinds of payments go under operating activities instead: short-term lease payments, payments for leases of low-value assets, and variable lease payments that weren't built into the lease liability.

Why does all this matter? Because clear, consistent presentation lets anyone reading the accounts compare companies fairly and understand how leasing affects a business. Notice how the lease keeps getting split into a principal part and an interest part — that pattern shows up in profit and loss and in cash flows, and once you see it, the whole section clicks into place.

P&L: depreciation of ROU asset shown separately from interest on lease liability

topics.orig_book_content:
Classification of leases 
A lessor shall classify each of its leases as either an operating lease or a 
finance lease. A lease is classified as a finance lease if it transfers 
substantially all the risks and rewards incidental to ownership of an 
underlying asset. A lease is classified as an operating lease if it does not

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
15 
transfer substantially all the risks and rewards incidental to ownership of an 
underlying asset. 
Whether a lease is a finance lease or an operating lease depends on the 
substance of the transaction rather than the form of the contract. Examples 
of situations that individually or in combination would normally lead to a lease 
being classified as a finance lease are: 
a) 
the lease transfers ownership of the underlying asset to the lessee by 
the end of the lease term; 
b) 
the lessee has the option to purchase the underlying asset at a price 
that is expected to be sufficiently lower than the fair value at the date 
the option becomes exercisable for it to be reasonably certain, at the 
inception date, that the option will be exercised; 
c) 
the lease term is for the major part of the economic life of the 
underlying asset even if title is not transferred; 
d) 
at the inception date, the present value of the lease payments 
amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of the underlying 
asset; and 
e) 
the underlying asset is of such a specialised nature that only the 
lessee can use it without major modifications. 
Indicators of situations that individually or in combination could also lead to a 
lease being classified as a finance lease are: 
a) 
if the lessee can cancel the lease, the lessor’s losses associated with 
the cancellation are borne by the lessee; 
b) 
gains or losses from the fluctuation in the fair value of the residual 
accrue to the lessee (for example, in the form of a rent rebate equaling 
most of the sales proceeds at the end of the lease); and 
c) 
the lessee has the ability to continue the lease for a secondary period 
at a rent that is substantially lower than market rent. 
The above indicators are not always conclusive. If it is clear from other 
features that the lease does not transfer substantially all the risks and 
rewards incidental to ownership of an underlying asset, the lease is classified 
as an operating lease. For example, this may be the case if ownership of the 
underlying asset transfers at the end of the lease for a variable payment 
equal to its then fair value, or if there are variable lease payments, as a

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
16 
result of which the lessor does not transfer substantially all such risks and 
rewards. 
Lease classification is made at the inception date and is reassessed only if 
there is a lease modification. Changes in estimates (for example, changes in 
estimates of the economic life or of the residual value of the underlying 
asset), or changes in circumstances (for example, default by the lessee), do 
not give rise to a new classification of a lease for accounting purposes.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about how a lessor — that's the person or company that owns an asset and rents it out — decides what kind of lease they're dealing with. There are only two boxes a lease can go into: a finance lease or an operating lease. The whole question comes down to one idea: who carries the risks and who gets the rewards of actually owning the asset? If the lease hands over substantially all of those risks and rewards to the person renting it, we call that a finance lease. If it doesn't, it's an operating lease. Simple as that, in principle.

Here's the important thing to keep in mind: we judge by substance, not by form. It doesn't matter what the contract is called or how it's dressed up — what matters is what's really happening in the deal. So the standard gives us some situations that usually point toward a finance lease. For instance, if ownership of the asset passes to the lessee by the end of the lease. Or if the lessee gets a bargain purchase option — a chance to buy the asset for a price so low compared to its fair value that you're pretty sure, right from the start, they'll take it. Or if the lease lasts for the major part of the asset's economic life. Or if the present value of all the lease payments adds up to at least substantially all of the asset's fair value. Or if the asset is so specialised that only that one lessee could use it without big changes.

Then there are softer indicators — clues that, alone or together, could lean toward a finance lease. Like the lessee covering the lessor's losses if they cancel. Or the lessee getting the gains or losses from changes in the leftover value of the asset. Or being able to keep leasing for a second period at a rent far below market.

Now notice — these clues aren't always the final word. If other features make it clear the risks and rewards stayed with the lessor, it's still an operating lease, even if a clue suggested otherwise.

Finally, when do we make this call? At the inception date, the very start. And we only revisit it if there's an actual lease modification. Things like a change in your estimate of the asset's life, or its leftover value, or even the lessee defaulting — none of those make you reclassify. The original judgment stands.

Judge by substance, not by the contract's name
Ownership transfers, or a bargain purchase option
Most of the asset's life, or PV of payments ≈ fair value

Every lease falls into exactly one of two boxes, and one single question decides which. <<POINT:asset-box>> <<FOCUS:risks-rewards-bundle>> <<SECTION:Risks and rewards|id=sec-1>>Owning something isn't just about holding the title. It comes with rewards, like using it and gaining if it holds value, and risks, like repairs and it wearing out. Picture all of that as one bundle. <<POINT:risks-rewards-bundle>> <<FOCUS:tipping-point>> <<WRITE_KEY:Finance lease = transfers substantially all risks and rewards of ownership|id=key-1>>Here is the deciding question: does the lease hand substantially all of that bundle over to the person renting the asset? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:finance-lease-label>> If almost the entire bundle slides across to the lessee, the deal has crossed the line. We judge by what is really happening in the deal, not by what it's called. Substance beats form, every time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:tipping-point>> So how do we actually tell when the bundle has crossed over? The standard gives us telltale signs. Watch what each one does to our scale. <<WRITE_TEXT:Ownership transfers, or a bargain purchase option|id=text-1>>If ownership transfers by the end, or there's a bargain price to buy it that's almost certain to be taken — the bundle clearly moves to the lessee. <<POINT:lessee-side>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Most of the asset's life, or PV of payments ≈ fair value|id=text-2>>If the lease runs for the major part of the asset's life, or the payments add up to nearly its full value, again — almost everything has shifted across. <<POINT:lessee-side>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:finance-lease-label>> And if the asset is so specialised that only the lessee can use it, who really bears its fate? The lessee. The bundle has moved, so it's a finance lease. <<FOCUS:asset-box>> So remember: two boxes, one question. If substantially all the risks and rewards move to the renter, it's a finance lease; if not, it's operating — and always judge the substance, never the label. <<POINT:asset-box>> <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about how a lessor — that's the person who owns an asset and rents it out — handles the two kinds of leases on their books. The first is a finance lease, and the second is an operating lease. The big idea is that these two are treated very differently, and once you see why, the details make sense.

Think about a finance lease first. In a finance lease, ownership has essentially passed to the lessee in substance, even if not in name. So on the lessor's balance sheet, you stop showing the underlying asset — you derecognise it. Instead, you show something called a lease receivable, measured at an amount equal to the net investment in the lease. In other words, the lessor now has a financial claim, like having lent money, rather than owning a piece of equipment. And in the profit and loss statement, the lessor recognises finance income spread over the lease term. The pattern is set so the return is steady — a constant periodic rate of return on the net investment. It behaves like interest earned on a loan.

Now contrast that with an operating lease. Here the lessor keeps the asset on its balance sheet — it continues to present the underlying asset. Any initial direct costs of setting up the lease get added to the carrying amount of that asset. For income, the lessor recognises the lease payments either on a straight-line basis, meaning equal amounts each period, or on another systematic basis if that better reflects how the benefit of the asset is being used up. And because the lessor still owns the asset, it keeps recording depreciation expense over the asset's useful life.

There's also a special case: when the lessor is a manufacturer or dealer. Here, signing a finance lease is also like making a sale. So they recognise revenue at the fair value of the asset, or the present value of the lease payments if that's lower. They record a cost of sale, and they show a selling profit or loss, following the same rules as an outright sale under Ind AS 115.

Finally, notice how the finance lease receivable is first measured. It's the present value of the future lease payments plus any unguaranteed residual value the lessor expects to get back, all discounted using the interest rate implicit in the lease. Those payments include fixed payments less incentives, variable payments tied to an index or rate, residual value guarantees, the price of a purchase option if the lessee will likely exercise it, and termination penalties when the lease term reflects that ending.

topics.orig_book_content:
Manufacturer or dealer as lessor 
At the commencement date, a manufacturer or dealer lessor recognises the 
following: 
 
The fair value of the underlying asset as revenue (or if lower, the 
present value of the lease payments discounted using a market rate of 
interest). 
 
The cost (or carrying amount) of the asset less the present value of 
the unguaranteed residual value, as cost of sale. 
 
The selling profit or loss in accordance with the policy for outright 
sales. A manufacturer or dealer lessor recognises selling profit or loss 
on a finance lease at the commencement date, regardless of whether 
the lessor transfers the underlying asset as described in Ind AS 115. 
After lease commencement, a lessor accounts for a finance lease, as 
follows: 
 
Recognises finance income (in profit or loss) over the lease term in an 
amount that produces a constant periodic rate of return on the 
remaining balance of the net investment in the lease (i.e., using the 
interest rate implicit in the lease). Income is recognised on the 
components of the net investment in the lease, including: 
o

topics.our_understanding:
Let's picture a special kind of lessor — a manufacturer or a dealer. Think of a company that builds machines or sells cars. Instead of selling outright, they sometimes lease their products. Because they are both makers and lessors, two things happen at once when the lease begins: they make a sale, and they start a lease. So the accounting has to capture both.

At the commencement date, the manufacturer or dealer recognises revenue. That revenue equals the fair value of the underlying asset, or, if it's lower, the present value of the lease payments discounted using a market rate of interest. Whichever of those two is lower becomes the revenue. Then they record a cost of sale. The cost of sale equals the cost or carrying amount of the asset, minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value. Notice we subtract that residual piece because that part of the asset isn't really being sold — it's expected to come back.

The difference between revenue and cost of sale is the selling profit or loss, recognised just like any normal outright sale. And here's an important point: this selling profit or loss is recognised at the commencement date, no matter whether the asset is actually transferred the way Ind AS 115 describes.

After the lease begins, the lessor treats it as a finance lease. They recognise finance income over the lease term so that it produces a constant periodic rate of return on the remaining balance of their net investment. This income comes from two sources: interest on the lease receivable, and interest that builds up as the unguaranteed residual asset grows toward its expected end value. As payments come in, the net investment is reduced. Any variable payments, like usage-based or performance-based amounts, are recognised separately when earned. And if the net investment loses value, an impairment is recognised.

The section also touches on lease modifications. A change is treated as a separate lease only if it adds the right to use more assets and the price goes up by an amount that matches the stand-alone price for that extra scope. If it's not separate, and the lease would now look like an operating lease, the lessor treats it as a brand new lease and measures the asset using the net investment just before the change. Otherwise, the rules of Ind AS 109 apply. Finally, for presentation, the lessor shows assets under operating leases on the balance sheet according to the nature of each asset.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about disclosures, and specifically the disclosures a lessor must make. A lessor is the party who owns an asset and lets someone else use it in exchange for payments. Now, why do we even bother with disclosures? Think about it this way. The main financial statements — the balance sheet, the profit and loss statement, and the cash flow statement — give you the headline numbers. But leases can have a real effect on a company's financial position, its performance, and its cash flows. So the goal of disclosures is to add extra notes that, together with those main statements, help anyone reading the accounts understand exactly how leases are shaping the picture.

Now, here's the key idea. The disclosures depend on what kind of lease we're talking about. A finance lease is one where the lessor effectively transfers most of the risks and rewards of owning the asset to the other party. An operating lease is one where the lessor keeps those risks and rewards. Because these two are so different, the things you must disclose are different too.

For a finance lease, the lessor discloses things like selling profit or loss, the finance income earned on what's called the net investment in the lease, and any income from variable lease payments that weren't included in that net investment. They also show significant changes in the carrying amount of that net investment.

For an operating lease, the lessor discloses lease income, including income from variable payments that don't depend on an index or rate, plus other lease income, and where relevant, disclosures following the standards for property, plant and equipment and similar assets.

Notice one especially important requirement: the maturity analysis. The lessor must show the undiscounted lease payments they expect to receive, broken down year by year for at least the first five years, and then a single total for everything beyond that. On top of that, they reconcile those undiscounted payments back to the net investment in the lease. This reconciliation has to point out the unearned finance income and any unguaranteed residual value. Why does this matter? Because it tells readers not just how much money is coming, but when it's coming and how it connects to the figure already sitting in the accounts. That's transparency in action.

topics.orig_book_content:
Sublease  
A lessee may become an intermediate lessor if it subleases an asset leased 
from another lessor (the ‘head lessor’). An intermediate lessor classifies the 
sublease as a finance lease or as an operating lease with reference to the 
right-of-use asset arising from the head lease. That is, the intermediate 
lessor treats the right-of-use asset as the underlying asset in the sublease, 
not the underlying asset that it leases from the head lessor. 
At the commencement date of the sublease, if the intermediate lessor cannot 
readily determine the interest rate implicit in the sublease, then it uses the 
discount rate that it uses for the head lease to account for the sublease, 
adjusted for any initial direct costs associated with the sublease. 
However, if the head lease is a short-term lease for which the company, as a 
lessee, has elected the short-term lease exemption, then as an intermediate 
lessor the company classifies the sublease as an operating lease.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about subleasing. Imagine you rent an apartment from a landlord, and then you turn around and rent that same apartment out to someone else. Now you're stuck in the middle — you're paying rent to your landlord, and someone is paying rent to you. In accounting language, when a company rents an asset and then leases it out to another party, that company becomes what we call an intermediate lessor. There's the head lessor at the top, the original owner you leased from, and then there's the new tenant below you. You sit in between.

Now here's the key insight. When you're deciding whether your sublease is a finance lease or an operating lease, you don't look at the original physical asset — the actual building or machine. Instead, you look at the right-of-use asset, which is the right to use that asset that you got from your head lease. Think about it this way: when you signed your head lease, you didn't buy the building, you bought the right to use it. So when you sublease, what you're really passing along is that right-of-use. That's why the standard tells you to treat the right-of-use asset as the underlying asset in your sublease, not the physical thing itself.

Next, there's the question of what discount rate to use. Leases involve interest rates because future payments need to be valued in today's money. Sometimes you can figure out the interest rate built into the sublease directly. But if you can't readily determine it, then you simply use the same discount rate you used for the head lease, adjusted for any initial direct costs tied to the sublease. It's a sensible fallback — use what you already know.

Finally, there's a special case. Suppose your head lease was a short-term lease, and you used the short-term lease exemption — meaning you chose not to record it on your books as a full lease because it's brief. In that situation, when you sublease it, you must classify the sublease as an operating lease. You can't suddenly call it a finance lease. So the nature of your head lease shapes how you handle the sublease underneath it. Notice how everything flows from that head lease — your classification, your discount rate, and your special treatment all reference back to it.

topics.orig_book_content:
Sale and leaseback transactions 
In a sale-and-leaseback transaction, an entity (seller-lessee) sells an asset to 
another entity (buyer-lessor) who then leases it back to the seller-lessee.  
In order to determine the appropriate accounting treatment under Ind AS 
116, the sale must first be assessed as to whether it qualifies as a sale in 
accordance with the requirements of Ind AS 115, Revenue from Contracts 
with Customers.  
If the transfer of an asset by the seller-lessee satisfies the requirements of 
Ind AS 115 to be accounted for as a sale of the asset: 
a) 
the seller-lessee shall measure the right-of-use asset arising from the 
leaseback transaction at the proportion of the previous carrying 
amount of the asset that relates to the right of use retained by the 
seller-lessee. Accordingly, the seller-lessee shall recognise only the 
amount of any gain or loss that relates to the rights transferred to the 
buyer-lessor. 
b) 
the buyer-lessor shall account for the purchase of the asset applying 
applicable Standards, and for the lease applying the lessor accounting 
requirements in this Standard.

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
22 
Adjustments are required if consideration for the sale is not at fair value 
and/or payments for the lease are not at market rates. These adjustments 
result in recognition of:  
 
Prepayment to reflect below-market terms.  
 
Additional financing provided by the buyer-lessor to the seller-lessee 
to reflect above-market terms. 
If the transfer of an asset by the seller-lessee does not satisfy the 
requirements of Ind AS 115 to be accounted for as a sale of the asset: 
a) 
the seller-lessee shall continue to recognise the transferred asset and 
shall recognise a financial liability equal to the transfer proceeds. It 
shall account for the financial liability applying Ind AS 109. 
b) 
the buyer-lessor shall not recognise the transferred asset and shall 
recognise a financial asset equal to the transfer proceeds. It shall 
account for the financial asset applying Ind AS 109.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about something called a sale and leaseback transaction. Picture a company that owns a building, but it needs cash right now. So it sells that building to another company, and then immediately rents the same building back so it can keep using it. The one who sells and then rents is called the seller-lessee, and the one who buys and then rents it out is called the buyer-lessor. Nothing changes about who's actually using the building day to day, but the ownership has shifted, and cash has changed hands.

Now here's the important question: was this really a sale? That's not always obvious. To decide, we look at the rules in another standard, Ind AS one hundred fifteen, which is about revenue from contracts with customers. That standard tells us whether the transfer truly counts as a sale, mostly by asking whether control of the asset really passed to the buyer.

If it does qualify as a sale, then here's the clever part. The seller is keeping the right to use the asset through the leaseback, so they don't get to record a gain on the whole thing. Instead, the seller measures the right-of-use asset at only the portion of the old carrying amount that relates to the rights they kept. And they only recognize the gain or loss on the rights they actually gave away to the buyer. Meanwhile, the buyer simply records the purchase like buying any asset, and treats the lease using the normal lessor rules.

There's a wrinkle. Sometimes the sale price isn't at fair value, or the rent isn't at market rates. When that happens, we have to make adjustments. If the terms are below market, we treat the difference as a prepayment. If the terms are above market, we treat it as extra financing that the buyer is giving to the seller. This keeps the accounting honest about what's really going on.

Now, what if it does not qualify as a sale? Then we treat it as if no sale happened at all. The seller keeps the asset on its books and records a financial liability equal to the money it received, accounted for under Ind AS one hundred nine. And the buyer does the opposite: it does not record the asset, but instead records a financial asset equal to what it paid. So in that case, the whole thing is really just a loan dressed up as a sale.

topics.orig_book_content:
Sublease on transition 
 
At the date of initial application, an intermediate lessor reassesses 
ongoing subleases that were classified as operating leases under Ind 
AS 17 to determine whether each sublease should be classified as an 
operating lease or a finance lease under Ind AS 116. This assessment 
is made on the basis of the remaining contractual terms and conditions 
of the head lease and sublease. 
 
For subleases classified as operating leases under Ind AS 17 but 
finance leases under Ind AS 116, a lessor accounts for the sublease 
as a new finance lease entered into at the date of initial application. 
Transition date accounting
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens with subleases when a company first moves over to the new leasing standard, Ind AS 116. First, picture the setup. Imagine a company rents a building from a landlord. That company is the lessee on that deal. But then it turns around and rents that same building out to someone else. Now that company sits in the middle, so we call it an intermediate lessor. It is renting on one side and renting out on the other side. The deal it makes with the new tenant is called a sublease.

Here is the key idea. Under the old rules, called Ind AS 17, leases got sorted into two buckets, either operating leases or finance leases, and a lot of subleases ended up in the operating lease bucket. When the company switches to the new standard, it has to take a fresh look at every sublease that is still running and that was previously called an operating lease. It has to ask again, fresh, is this really an operating lease or is it actually a finance lease under the new rules?

Now, why might the answer change? Because under the new standard, the company judges the sublease by looking at the asset it controls, which is its right to use the building, called the right-of-use asset, rather than the building itself. So when it reassesses, it looks at the remaining terms and conditions of both the head lease, that is the deal with the landlord, and the sublease, the deal with the tenant. Based on what is left of those contracts, it decides the proper classification.

Notice the important consequence. If a sublease was an operating lease under the old rules but now counts as a finance lease under the new rules, the company does not pretend it was always a finance lease. Instead, it treats it as a brand new finance lease that begins on the date of initial application, which is simply the date the company starts using the new standard. So it sets up the accounting from that date forward, as if a fresh finance lease just started. This matters because it keeps the transition clean and avoids reaching back into the past to rework old numbers. You only reassess and re-classify based on what remains going forward.

Definition of lease 
On transition to Ind AS 116, companies can choose whether to: 
 
apply the new definition of a lease to all of their contracts; or 
 
not to apply to contracts that were not previously identified as 
containing lease applying Ind AS 17.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens when a company first moves over to the new leasing rules, called Ind AS 116. Before this, companies were using an older rulebook, Ind AS 17. Now, the very idea of what counts as a lease changed a little between the old rules and the new ones. So when a company switches, there's a practical question: do you have to go back and re-check every single contract you've ever signed, using the brand new definition? That could be a huge amount of work, looking through hundreds or thousands of old agreements.

The standard gives companies a friendly choice here, and this is the key insight. A company can decide to apply the new definition of a lease to all of their contracts. That means they look at everything fresh, with the new eyes, and sort out which ones are leases under the new thinking. Or, the company can take a shortcut. They can choose not to re-examine the contracts that were not already identified as containing a lease back when they were following the old rules, Ind AS 17.

Think about why this matters. If a contract was already judged not to be a lease under the old rules, the company can simply trust that earlier judgment and leave it alone, rather than redoing the whole assessment. This saves enormous effort and time during the transition. It's a kind of relief built into the standard so the switch isn't unfairly burdensome.

Notice that this is a choice the company makes, not something forced on them. Some companies might prefer to be thorough and reassess everything for consistency. Others might prefer the practical shortcut. Either approach is allowed. The important thing to understand is that the definition of a lease is the gateway question. Before you apply any of the detailed accounting, you first have to decide whether a contract even is a lease. And on the day a company transitions to the new standard, this rule tells them how much of that gateway question they need to revisit. So the lesson here is simple: changing rulebooks doesn't automatically mean re-judging your entire history, unless the company chooses to do so.

events.text: Two choices on transition
You may choose NOT to reassess contracts not identified as leases under Ind AS 17
Practical expedient = permitted shortcut
Reassess all, OR carry forward old conclusions + new definition for new contracts

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens when a company that rents things — we call them the lessee — switches over to the new leasing rules under Ind AS 116. When a brand new accounting standard arrives, companies need a fair way to move from the old rules to the new ones. This is called transition accounting, and the company gets to choose how to do it.

There are two main paths. The first is the full retrospective approach. Here, you pretend the new standard was always in force. You go back and redo every period you're presenting, as if Ind AS 116 had been there from the very beginning. Because you're reaching so far back, you even have to show an extra, third balance sheet so readers can see where things stood at the earliest point. It's thorough, but it's a lot of work.

The second path is the modified retrospective approach. This one is gentler. You don't go back and restate the earlier comparative periods. Instead, you take the total cumulative effect of applying the new standard and bundle it into one adjustment to equity right at the start of the current period — the moment we call the date of initial application. Whatever choice the lessee makes, they must apply it consistently across all of their leases.

Now, the treatment depends on what kind of lease you had before. For an operating lease, you create a lease liability equal to the remaining lease payments, discounted using the lessee's incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application. For the right-of-use asset, the lessee has two options, and can pick differently for each lease. Option one is to calculate it retrospectively, again using that incremental borrowing rate. Option two is to simply set it equal to the lease liability, adjusted for any prepaid or accrued lease payments already on the books.

For a finance lease, things are much simpler, because these leases already sat on the balance sheet under the old rules. The lease liability just carries over at its carrying amount right before the date of initial application, and the right-of-use asset carries over at the carrying amount of the lease asset just before that same date. So finance leases barely move, while operating leases need real work to bring them onto the books. The big idea here is fairness and consistency — giving companies a practical way to switch without distorting their past numbers.

Two paths: full retro redoes the past; modified retro adjusts opening equity

topics.topic_name: Modified retrospective approach: Practical expedient for operating lease
topics.orig_book_content:
Modified retrospective approach: Practical expedient for 
operating lease 
In applying the modified retrospective approach, several practical expedients 
are available for leases that were previously categorised as operating leases 
under Ind AS 17. On a lease-by-lease basis, a lessee may: 
a) 
Apply a single discount rate to a portfolio of leases with reasonably 
similar characteristics. 
b) 
Rely on its assessment of whether a lease is onerous by applying Ind 
AS 37 immediately before the date of initial application, as an 
alternative to performing an impairment review. If this is chosen, then 
right of use asset should be adjusted by amount of any provisions for 
onerous leases recognized before the date of transition. 
c) 
Not recognise leases whose term ends within 12 months of the date of 
initial application (use short-term lease accounting). 
d) 
Exclude initial direct costs from the measurement of ROU assets at the 
date of initial application. 
e) 
Use hindsight, such as in determining the lease term if the contract 
contains options to extend or terminate the lease.
topics.our_understanding:
When a company first starts using this new leasing standard, it has to go back and deal with leases it already had. Imagine you're a company that has been renting office space, vehicles, and equipment for years. Under the old rules, many of these were called operating leases, and they basically sat off to the side without showing up as big assets or liabilities on your books. Now the new standard wants almost all leases brought onto the balance sheet. That's a lot of work, so the standard offers some shortcuts, which we call practical expedients. Think of these as friendly time-savers that let you avoid doing the hardest, most detailed calculations for every single old lease.

Let me walk you through the shortcuts. First, instead of figuring out a separate discount rate for every lease, you can pick one single rate and apply it to a whole group, or portfolio, of leases that are reasonably similar to each other. That saves a mountain of arithmetic. Second, instead of doing a full impairment review to check whether a lease has become a bad deal, you can lean on the assessment you already made under another standard, Ind AS thirty-seven, about whether the lease was onerous, meaning more costly than it's worth. If you go this route, you simply adjust your right-of-use asset by any provision you'd already set aside for those onerous leases.

Third, if a lease is going to end within twelve months of the day you start applying the new rules, you don't have to bring it onto the balance sheet at all. You can just treat it like a short-term lease, which is much simpler. Fourth, when you measure your right-of-use asset, you're allowed to leave out the initial direct costs, those upfront expenses of setting up the lease. And fifth, you can use hindsight. Since you're looking backward at leases that already exist, you already know how things turned out, so you can use that knowledge, for example when deciding the lease term if the contract had options to extend or end it early.

Notice the key phrase here: these choices are made on a lease-by-lease basis. That means you can pick and choose, using a shortcut for one lease and not another. The whole point is to make the switch to the new standard less painful while keeping the numbers sensible.

events.text: Practical expedients = optional, lease-by-lease shortcuts on transition
Expedient A: one rate for similar leases
Expedient C: skip leases ending within 12 months
Expedient B: reuse old onerous-lease test instead of impairment review
Each expedient trades precision for less work; you choose lease by lease

topics.standalone_narration_text: Picture a company with three hundred old rental contracts, and a new rule that says every single one must now be re-calculated from scratch. Sounds like a nightmare, right? Except the rule-makers handed out a set of legal shortcuts so you don't have to. When the new lease standard arrives, all those leases that used to sit quietly off the balance sheet suddenly have to come on, as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability. For one lease, that's annoying. For hundreds, it's an enormous amount of work. <<SECTION:Practical Expedients|id=sec-1>>So the standard says, fine, here are some friendly time-savers. We call them practical expedients, and the key idea is this. <<WRITE_KEY:Practical expedients = optional, lease-by-lease shortcuts on transition|id=key-1>>They are optional shortcuts you can apply lease by lease, letting you skip the most painful calculations. <<PAUSE:short>> Let me walk you through the most useful ones, because each shortcut kills a specific headache. The first headache is the discount rate. Normally every lease needs its own discount rate, the interest rate you use to bring future payments back to today's value. <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient A: one rate for similar leases|id=text-1>>The shortcut lets you apply a single rate to a whole bundle of leases that look reasonably alike, say all your photocopiers, instead of pricing each one separately. The next two shortcuts are about leases that are basically not worth the effort. If a lease ends within twelve months of the changeover date, you're allowed to just treat it as a short-term lease and not bring it onto the books at all. <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient C: skip leases ending within 12 months|id=text-2>>Why fully account for something that's about to expire? Here's one that sounds almost like cheating. Instead of doing a fresh impairment review to check if a lease has gone bad, you may simply rely on your earlier onerous-lease assessment. So which is the lazier, faster path here? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Expedient B: reuse old onerous-lease test instead of impairment review|id=text-3>>Reusing the assessment you already did under the provisions standard, just before transition, and then nudging your right-of-use asset by that provision. You skip an entire fresh review. That's the time-saver. Two more quick ones. You can exclude initial direct costs, the little setup fees, from the value of your right-of-use asset. And you can use hindsight, meaning if a contract had an option to extend, you now already know whether it was actually extended, so use that knowledge instead of guessing. Now notice the pattern. <<WRITE_KEY:Each expedient trades precision for less work; you choose lease by lease|id=key-2>>Every single one of these trades a bit of accuracy for a lot less work, and crucially, you decide which to apply, and to which leases. <<PAUSE:short>> That choice matters, because these are optional. A company that wants cleaner numbers might skip a shortcut; one drowning in old contracts will grab every one it can. The shortcuts bend the workload, not the truth, by much. <<PAUSE:short>> So when you face a transition question, don't panic at three hundred leases. Ask, which expedients apply here, and watch the mountain of work shrink. That's the whole point of practical expedients. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Transition accounting: In the books of Lessor 
 
Except for subleases and sale-and-leaseback transactions, a lessor does not 
make any adjustments on transition: 
Sales and leaseback transaction: 
For a sale-and-leaseback transaction accounted for as a sale and finance 
lease in accordance with Ind AS 17, the seller-lessee: 
 
accounts for the leaseback in the same way as for any finance lease 
that exists at the date of initial application; and 
 
continues to amortise any gain on the sale over the lease term. 
For a sale-and-leaseback transaction accounted for as a sale and operating 
lease in accordance with Ind AS 17, the seller-lessee: 
 
accounts for the leaseback in the same way as for any other operating 
lease that exists at the date of initial application; and

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
25 
 
adjusts the leaseback right-of-use asset for any deferred gains or 
losses that relate to off-market terms recognised in the statement of 
financial position immediately before the date of initial application.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what happens to a lessor when companies first switch over to the new leasing standard, Ind AS one sixteen. Remember, a lessor is the party that owns an asset and rents it out to someone else. Here's the good news for lessors: in most cases, they don't have to change anything at all when they move from the old standard to the new one. The new rules really shook things up for lessees, the people who rent, but for lessors, life stays pretty much the same. So as a general rule, a lessor makes no adjustments on transition.

But there are two special situations where things get a little more interesting. The first is subleases, where someone who is renting an asset turns around and rents it out to yet another party. The second is sale-and-leaseback transactions. Let me explain that second one, because it sounds tricky but it's actually a clever arrangement. Imagine a company owns a building, sells it to someone, and then immediately rents that same building back so they can keep using it. They get cash from the sale, but they don't have to move out. That's a sale-and-leaseback.

Now, under the old standard, Ind AS seventeen, these deals were classified in one of two ways. If the leaseback was treated as a finance lease, the seller, who is now the lessee, keeps accounting for it as a finance lease that already exists on the day the new rules begin. And importantly, if they made a profit when they sold the asset, they keep spreading that gain out gradually over the length of the lease, rather than recognizing it all at once.

The second way was when the leaseback was treated as an operating lease. In that case, the seller-lessee accounts for it like any other operating lease that exists on the transition date. But there's one extra step: they look at the right-of-use asset, which is the value of their right to use that building, and they adjust it for any deferred gains or losses that came from off-market terms. Off-market just means the rent or price wasn't quite at fair market value, so an adjustment is needed to make things honest and accurate.

The big takeaway here is simple. For lessors, transition is mostly a non-event. The real care is needed only in those special sale-and-leaseback and sublease situations, where the past treatment needs to carry forward in a sensible, consistent way.

events.text: Lessor: no adjustment on transition (except 2 cases)
Exceptions: subleases & sale-and-leaseback
Operating: adjust ROU asset for off-market deferred gains/losses
Carry old leaseback forward; keep amortising the gain

Amount previously recognised in respect of business

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
26 
II. Frequently Asked Questions 
(These FAQs are meant only to illustrate various requirement of Ind AS 116. 
It may be emphasised that where the facts and circumstances are different 
from those described in the relevant FAQ, the response as given herein may 
not hold valid.) 
Scope
topics.our_understanding: Let's unpack what this short but important rule is really saying. Imagine a company buys another whole business. That's what we call a business combination, and there's a separate accounting standard, Ind AS 103, that tells us how to record everything we acquire in that purchase. Now, sometimes when you buy a business, that business already has operating leases running. And here's the interesting part: those leases might be on terms that are better or worse than what the market charges today. Maybe the acquired business locked in a really cheap rent years ago, or maybe it got stuck paying more than it should. Under the old rules, when you bought that business, you had to recognise the value of those favourable or unfavourable lease terms separately. A favourable lease, where you pay less than market, became an asset, because it's a benefit you're getting. An unfavourable lease, where you pay more than market, became a liability, because it's a burden. So you'd see these little asset or liability amounts sitting on the books from the original acquisition. Now Ind AS 116 comes along and changes how leases are treated. When a company first starts applying this new standard, the question is: what do we do with those old favourable or unfavourable lease amounts? The answer is clean and sensible. You take that old asset or liability off the books, which we call derecognising it. But you don't just throw away the value. Instead, you fold it into the new right-of-use asset that Ind AS 116 creates for every lease. So if you had a favourable lease asset, you increase the right-of-use asset by that amount. If you had an unfavourable lease liability, you reduce the right-of-use asset by that amount. The phrase used is to adjust the carrying amount by a corresponding amount, and you do this right at the date you first apply the standard. Why does this matter? Because it avoids double-counting and keeps everything tidy. The favourable or unfavourable nature of the lease is now captured inside the new right-of-use asset, rather than floating around as a separate item. Think of it like merging two folders into one so you don't have the same information stored in two different places. This is a transition rule, meaning it only applies during the changeover from the old way to the new way, but understanding it helps you see how accounting standards carefully connect to each other when one replaces another.

topics.orig_book_content:
Question 1: 
Whether the following rights obtained by Entity X would be within the scope 
of Ind AS 116? 
(a) 
Rights to explore for oil and use oil from an oilfield Y for 25 years  
(b) 
Rights to access the land which contains the oil ( “surface lease”)  
(c) 
Right to lay down water pipelines over the surface of the land adjacent 
to the land which contains oil field. Entity X requires water in the oil 
extraction process). 
Response  
Paragraph 3 of Ind AS 116, Leases states as follows: 
“An entity shall apply this Standard to all leases, including leases of right-of-
use assets in a sublease, except for: 
(a) 
leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-
regenerative resources; 
(b)  
…..” 
Paragraph 3 of Ind AS 16, Property, Plant and Equipment, inter alia, states 
as follows:  
“This Standard does not apply to:  
(a) 
…… 
(c) 
mineral rights and mineral reserves such as oil, natural gas and similar 
non-regenerative resources. 
However, this Standard applies to property, plant and equipment used to 
develop or maintain the assets described in (b)–(d).”

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
27 
The following position emerges on a combined reading of Ind AS 116 and Ind 
AS 16. 
Cases (a) and (b) 
The words “leases to explore for or use minerals, oils…” include only those 
leases that provide the right to explore and/or extract oil (i.e. (a) and (b) 
above). To get access to the actual area where the oil may lie, entities may 
have to enter into another lease for the surface of that area. The lease for the 
surface of the area gives entity the right, for example, drill a well to get 
access to oil that lies within. 
 In view of the above, rights obtained under (a) and (b) above would not get 
covered under Ind AS 116. 
Case (c) 
The assets used in development or maintenance of mineral rights and 
mineral reserves such as oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative 
resources are covered under Ind AS 16 and the rights to explore for or use of 
such assets are covered under Ind AS 116. 
 Thus, the purpose of land adjacent to the oil field ((c) above) is to transport 
water to be used in the extraction process. The lease under (c) relates to the 
process of the  extraction of oil rather than providing right of exploration for, 
or the right of extraction or use of,  the oil. Accordingly, it is not covered by 
the scope exclusion in paragraph 3(a) of Ind AS 116 and the standard 
therefore applies to this lease.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about what kinds of leases the leasing standard, Ind AS 116, actually covers. Imagine you run a company called Entity X, and you've signed up for three different rights. The big question is: which of these rights fall under the leasing standard, and which ones don't? The answer matters because if a right is inside the scope, you account for it one way, and if it's excluded, you have to look somewhere else entirely.

Here's the key rule. The leasing standard says it applies to all leases, but it carves out one important exception: leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas, and similar resources that can't be regenerated. So anything that gives you the right to go looking for oil, or to actually pull the oil out of the ground, is deliberately left out of the leasing standard.

Now look at the first two rights. The first is the right to explore for oil and use oil from an oilfield for twenty-five years. The second is the right to access the land that contains the oil, often called a surface lease. Both of these are really about getting to the oil and extracting it. Sometimes you need a second lease just to reach the spot where the oil sits, so you can drill a well. Because both of these are tied to exploring for or extracting oil, they are excluded. The leasing standard does not apply to them.

The third right is different and trickier. Entity X wants to lay water pipelines over land next to the oilfield, because water is needed in the extraction process. Notice the subtle point here: this lease is not about exploring for oil or extracting oil itself. It's about transporting water that helps the extraction happen. It relates to the process around extraction, not to the right to explore or extract the oil. So it does not fall inside that special exclusion. That means the leasing standard does apply to this third right. The lesson is that you have to read carefully and ask whether the right is truly about the oil itself, or just supports the work around it.

To get access to the actual area where the oil may lie, entities may have to enter into another lease for the surface of that area. In view of the above, rights obtained under (a) and (b) above would not get covered under Ind AS 116. The lease under (c) relates to the process of the extraction of oil rather than providing right of exploration for, or the right of extraction or use of, the oil. topics.orig_book_content:
Question 2 
Entity X, a private sector entity, enters into a contract with the Transport 
Ministry (the grantor) of Country S to acquire the right to operate the civil air 
navigation system in Country S. Under this contract: 
-  
the grantor provides the air navigation system; 
-  
X is required to upgrade the system;   
-  
X will charge users based on rates negotiated directly by it with 
individual users; 
-  
there is no price-cap mechanism imposed by the grantor; and 
-  
the contract is for a period of 10 years. 
Whether the contract would be within the scope of Ind AS 116?

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
28 
Response  
Paragraph 3 of Ind AS 116 inter-alia states as follows: 
“An entity shall apply this Standard to all leases, including leases of right-of-
use assets in a sublease, except for: 
(a)  
…… 
(c) 
service concession arrangements within the scope of Appendix D, 
Service Concession Arrangements, of Ind AS 115, Revenue from 
Contracts with Customers;….” 
Further paragraph 5 of Appendix D to Ind AS 115 states as follows: 
“This Appendix applies to public-to-private service concession arrangements 
if: 
(a) 
the grantor controls or regulates what services the operator must 
provide with the infrastructure, to whom it must provide them, and at 
what price; and 
(b) 
the grantor controls—through ownership, beneficial entitlement or 
otherwise—any significant residual interest in the infrastructure at the 
end of the term of the arrangement.”[Emphasis added] 
If either of the above conditions is not met, the Appendix D to Ind AS 115 
does not apply.  
Paragraph 2 of Appendix D Service Concession Arrangements of Ind AS 
115, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, inter alia states that, “an 
arrangement within the scope of this Appendix typically involves a private 
sector entity (an operator) constructing the infrastructure used to provide the 
public service or upgrading it (for example, by increasing its capacity) and 
operating and maintaining that infrastructure for a specified period of time. 
The operator is paid for its services over the period of the arrangement. The 
arrangement is governed by a contract that sets out performance standards, 
mechanisms for adjusting prices, and arrangements for arbitrating disputes. 
Such an arrangement is often described as a ‘build-operate-transfer’, a 
‘rehabilitate-operate-transfer’ or a ‘public-to-private’ service concession 
arrangement.” 
In the given case, the arrangement has many characteristics of a public-to-
private service concession arrangement - e.g. the grantor is a public sector

Educational Material on Ind AS 116 
29 
body, the operator is a private sector body, the operator is responsible for the 
upgrade and operation of the service concession infrastructure and the 
infrastructure is used pursuant to public policy. However, under the terms of 
the contract the grantor does not control prices. Therefore, the contract is not 
in the scope of Appendix D of Ind AS 115 and the right to use the air 
navigation system would be within the scope of Ind AS 116.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's work through a question about whether a particular contract counts as a lease under Ind AS 116. Here's the situation. A private company, let's call it Entity X, signs a contract with the Transport Ministry of a country. The Ministry is what we call the grantor — the one giving out the right. Entity X gets the right to operate the country's civil air navigation system, which is basically the system that guides airplanes. Now, the grantor provides the system, Entity X has to upgrade it, and X will charge users at rates that it negotiates directly with each user. Importantly, there is no price cap set by the grantor — Entity X is free to set prices. The contract runs for ten years.

The big question is whether this falls inside the scope of Ind AS 116, the standard on leases. Now here's the key idea. Ind AS 116 applies to all leases, but it specifically excludes something called service concession arrangements that fall under another standard, Appendix D of Ind AS 115. So before we can say this is a lease, we have to make sure it's not a service concession arrangement first.

So what makes something a service concession arrangement? Two conditions must both be met. First, the grantor must control or regulate what services the operator provides, to whom, and at what price. Second, the grantor must control any significant leftover value in the infrastructure at the end of the term. Notice the word 'and' — both conditions are required. If even one is missing, Appendix D does not apply.

Now look at our case. Many features do look like a service concession. The grantor is a public body, the operator is private, the operator handles upgrades and operation, and the infrastructure serves public policy. But here's the crucial catch — the grantor does not control prices. Entity X negotiates rates freely with no price cap. That breaks the first condition. Since one condition fails, this is not a service concession arrangement.

And because it's not excluded as a service concession, the right to use the air navigation system falls right back into the scope of Ind AS 116. So the answer is yes — this contract is within the scope of Ind AS 116. The lesson here is to always check the exclusions carefully, because a single missing condition can change the entire classification.

Response: In the given case, the arrangement has many characteristics of a public-to-private service concession arrangement - e.g. the grantor is a public sector body, the operator is a private sector body, the operator is responsible for the upgrade and operation of the service concession infrastructure and the infrastructure is used pursuant to public policy. However, under the terms of the contract the grantor does not control prices. Therefore, the contract is not in the scope of Appendix D of Ind AS 115 and the right to use the air navigation system would be within the scope of Ind AS 116.

extended_examples.hook_text: Think about a toll highway near you — a private company builds and runs it, but the government tells them exactly what toll they're allowed to charge. That price control is the government keeping its grip on the service.

extended_examples.hook_text: The same air navigation system in our question quietly guides thousands of planes overhead at any given moment — and whether one private company controls its pricing is what decides which entire accounting standard applies.

In our question, Entity X negotiates prices freely with no cap, so that grip is gone — and the whole classification flips back to Ind AS 116. <<WRITE_TEXT:Govt sets toll = price control = condition 1|id=ext-1>> Something wild about this: the air navigation system in our question is guiding thousands of planes through the sky right now, yet the entire accounting answer turns on one small detail — whether the grantor controls the price. Because Entity X sets its own rates with no cap, that single missing condition pulls this giant public system out of service concession accounting and straight into Ind AS 116. One word, the 'and' between two conditions, decides everything. <<FOCUS:back-into-116-arrow>> So the exclusion does not catch this contract. It is not a service concession, which means it falls right back into the scope of Ind AS 116. <<TRACE:back-into-116-arrow>> <<FOCUS:ind-as-116-gate>> <<WRITE_KEY:Rule out service concession (both Appendix D tests) before applying Ind AS 116|id=key-1>>So remember the order of thinking: Ind AS 116 covers all leases, except service concessions, and a service concession demands both price control by the grantor and a residual interest. Fail either one, and the exclusion doesn't apply. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.orig_book_content:
Question 3 
Operator X enters into a service concession arrangement, with Grantor G to 
operate a rail service for 15 years. The arrangement is considered to be in 
the scope of Appendix D, Service Concession Arrangements, of Ind AS 115, 
Revenue from Contracts with Customers. X enters into a contract with Entity 
Y (lessor) to lease the infrastructure, i.e. rolling stock to operate the rail 
service.  The useful life of rolling stock is 25 years. X has the obligation to 
pay the lessor. During the concession period, G controls the services that X 
delivers by setting the timetable to which the rolling stock must be operated 
and regulates the price that X charges passengers. At the end of the 
concession, G has an option to acquire the rolling stock or to otherwise direct 
its use. 
Whether the contract of Operator X with Entity Y would be within the scope of 
Ind AS 116?  
Response  
Paragraphs 7 and 11 of Appendix D of Ind AS 115, inter-alia, states as 
follows: 
“7 This Appendix applies to both: 
(a) 
infrastructure that the operator constructs or acquires from a third 
party for  the purpose of the service arrangement; and 
 
(b) 
…..”. 
 
“11 Infrastructure within the scope of this Appendix shall not be 
recognised as property, plant and equipment of the operator because 
the contractual service arrangement does not convey the right to 
control the use of the public service infrastructure to the operator. The 
operator has access to operate the infrastructure to provide the public 
service on behalf of the grantor in accordance with the terms specified 
in the contract.”
topics.our_understanding:
Let's work through a tricky question about when a lease actually counts as a lease under Ind AS 116. Imagine a company, Operator X, that signs a deal with a Grantor, let's call it G, to run a rail service for fifteen years. This kind of deal has a special name — a service concession arrangement — and it falls under a separate set of rules called Appendix D of Ind AS 115, which deals with revenue from customers. So far so good. Now, to actually run the trains, Operator X goes and leases the rolling stock, meaning the trains and equipment, from another company called Entity Y. The trains have a useful life of twenty-five years, and X is the one who has to pay Entity Y for using them. The big question is this: does X's contract with Entity Y count as a lease under Ind AS 116?

Here's where it gets interesting. To have a lease, the customer must control the use of the asset. But think about what's actually happening here. During the fifteen-year concession period, it's the Grantor G — not Operator X — who's calling the shots. G sets the timetable that the trains must follow, and G even regulates the price that X can charge passengers. On top of that, at the end of the period, G has the option to buy the rolling stock or to decide how it gets used. So who really controls these trains? Not X. X is just operating them on behalf of G, following rules that G laid down.

The rules back this up. Appendix D of Ind AS 115 says that infrastructure used in these service concession arrangements should not be recorded as the operator's own property, plant, and equipment. Why? Because the arrangement does not give the operator the right to control the use of that public service infrastructure. The operator merely has access to operate it, on behalf of the grantor, following the agreed terms. So the lesson here is that even though X pays for the trains and uses them daily, X doesn't have the control that a lease requires. Because the service concession arrangement falls within Appendix D of Ind AS 115, this contract sits inside that framework rather than being treated as a standalone lease under Ind AS 116. Control is the key word — without it, you don't have a lease.

At the end of the concession, G has an option to acquire the rolling stock or to otherwise direct its use. Whether the contract of Operator X with Entity Y would be within the scope of Ind AS 116? Q: Is X's lease of rolling stock from Y within the scope of Ind AS 116?

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:operator-x>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:accounting:ind_as_116_leases:35:control_flow_concession>> A company signs a contract, pays for the trains, and runs them every single day for fifteen years — and yet, on its books, there is no lease at all. How can that be? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:entity-y>> <<SECTION:The set-up|id=sec-1>>Here is our cast. Entity Y owns the rolling stock — the trains and equipment. Operator X pays Entity Y to use them and runs the actual service. <<POINT:entity-y>> But Operator X did not just go into business for itself. X holds a service concession from Grantor G to run a public rail service for fifteen years. <<POINT:grantor-g>> <<FOCUS:rolling-stock>> Now, normally, if you pay to use an identified asset, you ask one simple question to decide if it is a lease: do you control the use of that asset? <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Control = decide how & for what purpose|id=text-1>>And control is not just touching the asset. Control means you decide how it is used and for what purpose — you direct the use. <<POINT:rolling-stock>> <<PAUSE:short>> So watch the payment. Operator X does pay Entity Y for using the rolling stock — money flows this way. <<TRACE:payment-arrow>> <<FOCUS:operator-x>> Paying looks like a lease. So who actually decides how these trains run — when they run, and what passengers are charged? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Where control really sits|id=sec-2>>It is not Operator X. Grantor G sets the timetable the trains must follow and regulates the price X can charge passengers. G directs the use. <<TRACE:control-arrow>> <<FOCUS:grantor-g>> Look at where the control arrow lands. It passes straight through Operator X and stops at Grantor G. X holds the trains, but X does not direct them. <<POINT:grantor-g>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No right to direct use = not a lease under Ind AS 116|id=key-1>>And that settles it. Because Operator X never gets the right to direct the use, X's contract with Entity Y is not a lease under Ind AS 116. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. Operator X enters into a service concession arrangement with Grantor G to operate a rail service for fifteen years, and this arrangement falls within the scope of Appendix D, Service Concession Arrangements, of Ind AS one fifteen. To run the service, X leases the infrastructure, the rolling stock, from Entity Y, the lessor, where the useful life of the rolling stock is twenty-five years, and X has the obligation to pay the lessor. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Is X's lease of rolling stock from Y within the scope of Ind AS 116?|id=ex-q-1>> Now look at who actually controls the use of that rolling stock. During the concession period, Grantor G controls the services X delivers, G sets the timetable to which the rolling stock must be operated and regulates the price that X charges passengers, and at the end of the concession G has an option to acquire the rolling stock or otherwise direct its use. <<WRITE_STEP:G sets timetable + regulates price + holds end-of-concession option on rolling stock|id=ex-step-1>> Appendix D of Ind AS one fifteen states that the operator does not have the right to control the use of the infrastructure; it merely has access to operate it on behalf of the grantor. Since X does not control the use of the rolling stock, the contract is not a lease within the scope of Ind AS one sixteen. <<WRITE_STEP:Per Appendix D, X does NOT control use of the infrastructure|id=ex-step-2>><<WRITE_ANSWER:The contract of X with Y is NOT within the scope of Ind AS 116|id=ex-ans-1>> You've seen this yourself with food delivery riders. A rider might use a scooter that the delivery platform owns, driving it every single shift. But the platform sets the routes, fixes the delivery fees, and can pull that scooter back whenever it likes. Sound familiar? That's exactly Operator X with the trains. The rider uses the asset every day, but the platform calls the shots, so there's no control, and without control there's no lease. Here's something wild about this. A huge number of the world's busiest toll roads, airports, and metro lines run on exactly this kind of arrangement. A private operator runs that public infrastructure for twenty, thirty, even forty years, collecting fees the whole time, yet it never sits on their balance sheet as their own property. <<WRITE_KEY:Concession operator runs it, never controls it|id=ext-key-1>> That's the same Appendix D logic from our question. The operator just has access to operate, following the grantor's terms. No control means it isn't theirs, and it isn't a lease. <<FOCUS:rolling-stock>> This is why the rolling stock sits inside the service concession rules of Appendix D, not as a leased asset of Operator X. The same trains, but a completely different accounting home. <<FOCUS:control-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Payment alone never makes a lease|id=text-2>>So the lesson is sharp: paying for an asset is never enough. Lease accounting follows the right to direct the use — and here that right belongs to the Grantor.

questions.q_text: When a company first adopts Ind AS one hundred sixteen, it has two choices for how to apply it. Explain both options and how they differ.
questions.answer: The standard gives a company two transition paths on first adoption. First option — full retrospective application: the company applies the standard as if it had always been in force, going back to restate the comparative figures of earlier years as though the new rules had always applied. This rewrites historical numbers so everything looks consistent. Second option — retrospective application without restating prior year comparatives: instead of rewriting old numbers, the company leaves the prior period comparatives unchanged and records the cumulative impact of adopting the standard as a single adjustment to equity at the beginning of the period when the standard is first applied. That moment is called the date of initial application. So the key difference is that the first path rewrites history to look consistent, while the second leaves the old numbers alone and makes one clean adjustment to opening equity. Both approaches are permitted, and the company chooses whichever suits it.

C. The lessee may choose to apply it but is not required to
D. Only the lessor may apply it

questions.q_text: A farming company, as a lessee, leases dairy cattle for use over several seasons. Should this lease be accounted for under the leases standard? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No, it should not be accounted for under the leases standard. Dairy cattle are living things, which makes them biological assets. The scope exceptions specifically carve out leases of biological assets held by a lessee, because those are governed by the agriculture standard instead. So the correct rulebook here is the agriculture standard, not the leases standard. This is exactly why checking scope first matters — applying the wrong standard would make the accounts incorrect.

questions.q_text: Explain why getting the scope right is described as the very first checkpoint before applying an accounting standard.
questions.answer: Scope defines the boundaries of a standard — which contracts it covers and which it leaves to other standards. It is the first checkpoint because you must confirm you are holding the right rulebook before you can apply any rule correctly. If a contract that belongs under another standard, such as an oil exploration lease, is wrongly treated under the leases standard, the resulting accounts will be wrong.
