Getting scope right ensures each type of contract is accounted for under the standard that was specifically designed for it, which protects the accuracy of the financial statements from the start.

questions.q_text: At the moment a lease begins, what is the maximum lease term for it to qualify as a short-term lease?
options: A. Six months or less
B. Twelve months or less
C. Twenty-four months or less
D. Thirty-six months or less

questions.q_text: A company rents a machine for only four months, but the lease includes an option to buy the machine at the end. Can this be treated as a short-term lease?
options: A. Yes, because the term is well under twelve months
B. Yes, because the machine is being rented temporarily
C. No, because a lease with a purchase option is never a short-term lease
D. No, because four months is too short to qualify

questions.q_text: Which of the following best explains why a cheap car would NOT qualify as a low value lease?
options: A. Because cars are always too expensive to be low value
B. Because the asset is highly dependent on or tangled up with other assets and works as part of a bigger system
C. Because the lessee cannot benefit from using a car at all
D. Because cars always include a purchase option

questions.q_text: How does the way you apply the short-term lease exemption differ from the low value lease exemption?
options: A. The short-term exemption is decided lease by lease, while the low value exemption applies to a whole class of assets
B. The short-term exemption applies to a whole class of underlying assets, while the low value exemption can be decided lease by lease
C. Both must be applied to a whole class of assets
D. Both can be decided lease by lease

questions.q_text: A company decides to use the low value lease exemption for several of its small office items. Explain what the company is required to do beyond simply not recording the asset and liability, and why this requirement exists.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recognise what the exemption does. By using the exemption, the company skips recording the special asset and matching liability that a lease would normally put on its books. Step 2: Identify the obligation. The standard says the company cannot quietly use the exemption — it must disclose that it has chosen to apply the exemption. Step 3: Identify what must be disclosed. It must share enough information so that anyone reading the financial statements can understand the effect of that choice. Step 4: Explain why. Because these shortcuts change what actually shows up on the books, transparency matters — readers need to understand how the financial statements would differ as a result of the company taking the shortcut. So the company must both state that it used the exemption and provide enough detail to convey its impact.

questions.q_text: When are you required to reassess whether a contract is or contains a lease after the initial assessment?
options: A. At the end of every reporting period
B. Only when the terms and conditions of the contract change
C. Whenever the market value of the asset changes
D. Every time a payment is made under the contract

questions.q_text: According to the definition, a contract is or contains a lease if it conveys which of the following?
options: A. The right to own an identified asset permanently
B. The right to use any asset of a particular type for free
C. The right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of time in exchange for consideration
D. The obligation to maintain an asset on behalf of the supplier

questions.q_text: In the flowchart, suppose there is an identified asset and the customer obtains substantially all of the economic benefits, but the supplier has the right to direct how and for what purpose the asset is used. What is the conclusion?
options: A. The contract contains a lease
B. The contract is not a lease
C. You move on to the backup questions
D. You must reassess at the end of the period

questions.q_text: A customer signs a contract for the use of a specific, identified machine for two years. The customer gets substantially all the economic benefits from using it. However, how and for what purpose the machine will be used was predetermined before the contract began, so neither the customer nor the supplier can change that during the period. The customer designed the machine in a way that predetermines how it will be used. Does this contract contain a lease? Walk through the reasoning.
questions.answer: Step 1: Is there an identified asset? Yes — it is a specific, identified machine. So we continue. Step 2: Does the customer obtain substantially all of the economic benefits from using the asset throughout the period of use? Yes, the customer gets almost all the value. So we continue. Step 3: Who has the right to direct how and for what purpose the asset is used? In this case neither party does, because how and for what purpose the asset will be used is predetermined. So we move to the backup questions. Step 4 (backup): Does the customer have the right to operate the asset without the supplier being able to change the operating instructions, OR did the customer design the asset in a way that predetermines how it will be used? Here, the customer designed the asset in a way that predetermines its use, so the answer is yes. Conclusion: Because we passed every stage of the flowchart, the contract contains a lease.

questions.q_text: Why does identifying whether a contract is or contains a lease act as a 'gatekeeper' question?
options: A. Because it determines the market price the customer must pay
B. Because if the contract is a lease, the special lease accounting rules must be applied, and if not, they are not
C. Because it determines who legally owns the asset
D. Because it sets the interest rate used in the contract

questions.q_text: According to this section, what is the very first requirement a contract must meet before it can be called a lease?
options: A. The contract must run for at least one year
B. The contract must relate to an identified asset
C. The supplier must own the asset outright
D. The customer must make fixed monthly payments

questions.q_text: A rental agreement states that the customer may use the delivery truck with a specific registration number. Which type of specification is this an example of?
options: A. Implicit specification
B. Explicit specification
C. Conditional specification
D. Service specification

questions.q_text: Under implicit specification, at what point does the asset typically become identified?
options: A. When the contract is first drafted
B. When the supplier signs the agreement
C. When the asset is made available for use by the customer
D. When the customer makes the first payment

questions.q_text: If a supplier can freely swap out the asset whenever they like and it makes no difference to the customer, what does this suggest about the arrangement?
options: A. It is automatically a lease because an asset is involved
B. There may be no identified asset, so it might be a service rather than a lease
C. It must be an explicitly specified asset
D. It becomes a lease only after the first swap

questions.q_text: Explain why the requirement of an identified asset matters so much for deciding whether a contract is a lease.
questions.answer: The whole idea of a lease rests on the customer controlling the use of a specific asset over time. A lease is about getting the right to use a particular thing. If there is no particular asset at the heart of the deal, then there is nothing to lease, and the arrangement is something else entirely. The identified-asset test is therefore the first gate a contract must clear. If the supplier can swap the asset at will and it makes no difference to the customer, then the customer is not really controlling any specific asset, meaning there may be no identified asset and the arrangement is likely a service rather than a lease. Confirming an identified asset (either named explicitly in writing or pinned down implicitly when handed over) sets up everything that follows about who controls and benefits from the asset.

questions.q_text: For a supplier's substitution right to be considered substantive, which of the following must be true?
options: A. The supplier must have the practical ability to substitute, OR the supplier must benefit economically from substituting
B. The supplier must have the practical ability to substitute, AND the supplier must benefit economically from substituting
C. Only that the contract names a specific asset that can be swapped
D. Only that the customer agrees to allow substitution

questions.q_text: Why does a substantive substitution right prevent a contract from being a lease?
options: A. Because it means the contract is too short in duration to qualify
B. Because the customer is not tied to one particular asset, so there is no identified asset
C. Because the supplier loses all economic benefit from the asset
D. Because the customer gains full ownership of the asset

questions.q_text: A contract states the supplier 'may swap the asset at any time,' but in reality the supplier has no other assets available and would never benefit from swapping. How should this substitution right be treated?
options: A. It is substantive because it is written in the contract
B. It is substantive because the supplier has the legal wording in place
C. It is not substantive because neither practical ability nor economic benefit is present
D. It is not substantive only if the customer objects

questions.q_text: A supplier has many identical machines sitting idle nearby and could easily swap the one the customer is using. However, swapping would cost the supplier money in transport and setup, and they would gain nothing economically from doing it. Does the supplier have a substantive substitution right? Explain.
questions.answer: To be substantive, both conditions must be met. First, does the supplier have the practical ability to substitute? Yes — there are identical machines available nearby and they could easily make the swap. So the first condition is satisfied. Second, would the supplier benefit economically from exercising the right? No — swapping would cost them money in transport and setup, and they gain nothing in return, so the benefits do not outweigh the costs. Because both conditions must be present together and the economic-benefit condition fails, the substitution right is NOT substantive. This means the asset remains an identified asset, and a lease can still exist.

questions.q_text: If a supplier can meaningfully control which asset the customer uses through a substantive substitution right, what does the arrangement most likely represent?
options: A. A lease of a specific identified asset
B. A purchase of the asset by the customer
C. A service arrangement rather than a lease
D. A financing arrangement with the customer as lender

questions.q_text: A company rents one entire floor of an office building, with its own walls and clear boundaries. Does this floor qualify as an identified asset, and why?
options: A. No, because it is only a portion of the building
B. Yes, because it is physically distinct
C. No, because the company does not get substantially all the capacity of the building
D. Yes, but only if it represents substantially all of the building's capacity

questions.q_text: A customer is given a small share of capacity within a fibre optic cable, while other customers use the same cable. Is this capacity portion generally an identified asset?
options: A. Yes, because the customer pays for using the cable
B. Yes, because any portion of an asset is automatically identified
C. No, because it is not physically distinct and is not substantially all the capacity
D. No, because cables can never be identified assets

questions.q_text: Under what circumstance can a portion of an asset that is NOT physically distinct still be an identified asset?
options: A. When the customer signs a long-term contract
B. When the portion represents substantially all of the capacity of the asset
C. When the supplier agrees to it in writing
D. When the portion has a clearly stated price

questions.q_text: Explain why the standard provides a second test based on economic benefits for portions that are not physically distinct, and what underlying question both tests are really answering.
questions.answer: Physical distinctness is one clear path to being an identified asset: if a portion has visible boundaries, like a floor with walls and a ceiling, you can point to exactly the part being used and no one else can use that same space. But some portions, like capacity within a cable, have no physical boundary you can see, so the physical distinctness test fails. The standard provides a second, fall-back test: even without physical distinctness, if the portion represents substantially all of the capacity of the asset, then in practice the customer obtains substantially all of the economic benefits from using that asset, effectively using the whole thing. Both tests are really answering the same underlying question: does the customer have a specific asset that gives them the benefits of using it? The physical test answers it through clear physical separation; the economic test answers it through control of almost all the benefits. This matters because identifying whether there is an identified asset is one of the first steps in deciding whether a contract contains a lease at all.

questions.q_text: A customer is allocated 95 percent of the total capacity of a single fibre optic strand, leaving only a tiny remainder for others. Even though no physical wall separates the data, how should this portion most likely be treated?
options: A. Not an identified asset, because it lacks physical boundaries
B. Not an identified asset, because capacity portions never qualify
C. An identified asset, because it represents substantially all of the capacity
D. An identified asset, because the customer pays the most

questions.q_text: When deciding whether a customer obtains substantially all the economic benefits from using an asset, within what boundaries do we measure those benefits?
options: A. Within the full unrestricted capacity of the asset, ignoring contract limits
B. Within the scope defined by the contract's restrictions
C. Within whatever the supplier later decides to allow
D. Within the legal maximum permitted by regulators

questions.q_text: Which of the following would NOT be considered an economic benefit when assessing this test?
options: A. The primary output the asset produces
B. By-products that come along with using the asset
C. Money earned by subleasing the asset to a third party
D. Benefits that could only be earned if the contract's restrictions did not exist

questions.q_text: A contract lets a customer use a delivery vehicle, but only within one specific city. When assessing whether the customer gets substantially all the economic benefits, should we include the extra benefits the customer could earn by driving the vehicle in other cities outside that limit? Explain.
questions.answer: No. The rule is that we only assess benefits within the scope the contract actually defines. The contract restricts use to one specific city, so that restriction becomes the playing field. We count only the benefits earned by driving within that city. We do not imagine a version of the contract with no geographic limit and count benefits from other cities, because that unrestricted scenario is irrelevant. So the extra benefits from driving elsewhere are excluded from the assessment.

questions.q_text: A contract allows a machine to run only between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. How should the economic benefits be assessed for this test?
options: A. Count benefits as if the machine could run 24 hours a day
B. Count only the benefits earned during the permitted 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. hours
C. Count benefits only if the customer actually uses every permitted hour
D. Ignore the time restriction since it does not affect ownership

questions.q_text: Why does the standard insist that we measure benefits only within the contract's defined scope rather than the asset's full theoretical capacity?
options: A. Because the customer's right to benefits exists only within what the contract grants, so benefits outside that scope were never available to anyone under this contract
B. Because the supplier always retains the primary output
C. Because by-products are too difficult to value otherwise
D. Because regulators require ignoring all contractual restrictions

questions.q_text: When deciding whether a customer has the right to direct the use of an asset, what is the fundamental question we are always trying to answer?
options: A. Whether the asset is physically located on the customer's premises
B. Whether the customer, not the supplier, has the real say over how the asset is used
C. Whether the supplier earns a profit from the arrangement
D. Whether the asset can be replaced by another asset

questions.q_text: A customer rents a delivery truck and can decide each day where it goes, what it carries, and when it is used, and can change those decisions during the rental. Which situation does this represent?
options: A. The decisions are predetermined and the customer operates the asset
B. The customer designed the asset in advance
C. The customer has the right to direct how and for what purpose the asset is used throughout the period
D. This is a service, not a lease

questions.q_text: Suppose how and for what purpose an asset will be used is already locked in from the start. According to the section, in which of the following ways can a customer still have the right to direct the use?
options: A. By paying a higher price than other customers
B. By having the right to operate the asset, with the supplier unable to change the operating instructions
C. By being the only customer the supplier serves
D. By owning a share in the supplier's company

questions.q_text: A customer commissions a specialized piece of equipment and makes all the design choices up front, which effectively determine how and for what purpose the equipment will be used throughout the entire period. No fresh operating decisions are made once the period begins. Does the customer have the right to direct the use of this asset, and why?
questions.answer: Yes, the customer has the right to direct the use. Although the big decisions about how and for what purpose the asset is used are predetermined and no fresh decisions are made during the period of use, the section explains a second way a customer can still control such an asset: by having designed the asset in a way that predetermines how and for what purpose it will be used throughout the period. Because the customer made the design choices up front that effectively decided everything in advance, the customer has already directed the asset's use even before the period began. The key is that the customer, not the supplier, made the decisions that govern the use, which satisfies the right to direct the use.

questions.q_text: Why does the right to direct the use matter when distinguishing a lease from a service?
options: A. Because a service always costs more than a lease
B. Because if the supplier, rather than the customer, retains the real say over use, the arrangement is a service rather than a lease
C. Because leases never involve identified assets
D. Because services never produce economic benefits

questions.q_text: In a contract that gives you the right to use equipment and also includes a maintenance service, how does the standard classify these two parts?
options: A. Both are lease components
B. The right to use the equipment is the lease component and the maintenance is the non-lease component
C. Both are non-lease components
D. The maintenance is the lease component and the equipment use is the non-lease component

questions.q_text: What does the practical expedient available to the lessee allow them to do?
options: A. Ignore the lease entirely and treat everything as a service
B. Estimate stand-alone prices instead of using actual ones
C. Choose, by class of underlying asset, not to separate non-lease components and treat the whole contract as a single lease
D. Force the lessor to split the components on their behalf

questions.q_text: When a lessee does NOT use the practical expedient, on what basis must the total payment be split between the lease and non-lease parts?
options: A. Equally between each component
B. Based on the relative stand-alone prices of each component, estimated if not available
C. Entirely to the lease component
D. Based on whichever the lessee prefers

questions.q_text: A contract bundles together two assets. Asset One can be used by the lessee on its own and does not depend on the other asset. Asset Two only functions when combined with Asset One and is highly interrelated with it. Determine which assets qualify as separate lease components and explain why.
questions.answer:
To be a separate lease component, two conditions must both be true: first, the lessee can benefit from using the asset on its own or together with readily available resources; second, the asset is not highly dependent on, and not highly interrelated with, the other assets in the contract.

For Asset One: it can be used on its own, satisfying the first condition. It does not depend on the other asset, satisfying the second condition. Both conditions hold, so Asset One qualifies as a separate lease component.

For Asset Two: it only functions when combined with Asset One and is highly interrelated with it. This fails the second condition. Therefore Asset Two does not qualify as a separate lease component and is not treated separately.

Conclusion: Only Asset One is a separate lease component.

questions.q_text: A contract includes administrative charges that don't deliver any good or service to the lessee. How are these treated?
options: A. They form their own separate component
B. They are removed entirely from the contract
C. They do not create a separate component but remain part of the total consideration allocated across the real components
D. They are always allocated entirely to the lease component

questions.q_text: Why does the standard say administrative charges that give the lessee nothing extra are not a separate component, yet they still must be included in the total consideration allocated across the identified components?
questions.answer:
A separate component must represent the transfer of a distinct good or service to the lessee. An administrative charge that delivers no good or service fails this test, so it cannot stand as its own component — there's nothing for it to be paid against.

However, the charge is still real money the lessee is obligated to pay under the contract. If it were simply dropped, the total amount allocated would understate the true cost of the arrangement. So instead of disappearing, the charge stays in the overall pool of consideration. That total pool is then divided across the genuine components that were identified, using their relative stand-alone prices. In effect, the admin charge gets spread proportionally over the real components rather than being ignored, ensuring the full economic cost of the contract is properly accounted for.

questions.q_text: Before you even start checking the three tests for combining contracts, what two conditions must be true?
options: A. The contracts must be for the same asset and for the same total value
B. The contracts must be entered into at or near the same time, and with the same counterparty (or related parties)
C. The contracts must be signed in the same financial year and audited together
D. The contracts must each be individually material to the financial statements

questions.q_text: Once the preconditions are satisfied, how many of the three tests must be met before you combine the contracts?
options: A. All three tests must be met
B. At least two of the three tests must be met
C. Just one of the three tests is enough
D. None — meeting the preconditions alone is enough

questions.q_text: Which test is being described when the amount payable under one contract depends on the price or performance of another contract?
options: A. The first test (negotiated as a package with a single commercial objective)
B. The second test (consideration in one depends on the other)
C. The third test (rights to use assets form a single lease component)
D. None of the tests — this would never lead to combination

questions.q_text: What is the main reason the standard requires combining contracts when these signs are present?
options: A. To reduce the number of contracts a company has to disclose
B. To make sure financial statements reflect the true economic substance rather than just the legal paperwork
C. To increase reported revenue by grouping deals together
D. To simplify negotiations between the two parties

questions.q_text: A company signs two leases on the same day with the same landlord. The first lease, for a piece of machinery, has a rent that only makes commercial sense alongside the second lease for a related component. The rent on the machinery lease is also set so that it rises if the second lease performs well. Should these contracts be combined? Walk through the reasoning.
questions.answer: Step 1: Check the preconditions. Both leases were signed on the same day (at or near the same time) and with the same landlord (same counterparty). So the preconditions are satisfied, and we can proceed to the three tests. Step 2: Check the first test — were they negotiated as a package with one overall commercial objective that can't be understood unless you look at both together? Yes: the rent on the machinery lease only makes commercial sense alongside the second lease, indicating a single commercial objective. This test is met. Step 3: Check the second test — does the consideration in one depend on the price or performance of the other? Yes: the machinery rent rises if the second lease performs well, so the price is linked. This test is also met. Step 4: Since only one of the three tests needs to be met and here two are met, the contracts must be combined and accounted for as a single contract. This reflects the economic reality that these are really one deal wearing two costumes.

questions.q_text: On which day does the lease term begin?
options: A. The day the lease contract is signed
B. The day the lessor makes the asset available for the lessee to use
C. The day the first rental payment is made
D. The day the rent-free period ends

questions.q_text: A lease gives the lessee the first three months free of charge before payments begin. How should these three months be treated when determining the lease term?
options: A. They are excluded because no rent is paid
B. They are included as part of the lease term
C. They only count if the lessee extends the lease
D. They count as half the normal period

questions.q_text: When deciding whether to include a period covered by an option to extend the lease, what is the deciding factor?
options: A. Whether the lessor wants the lease to continue
B. Whether the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise the extension option
C. Whether the extension period is longer than the non-cancellable period
D. Whether extra penalties apply for extending

questions.q_text: Under what circumstances does a lease stop being enforceable?
options: A. When the non-cancellable period ends, regardless of penalties
B. When only the lessee can walk away without penalty
C. When both the lessee and the lessor can each walk away without the other's permission and with no more than an insignificant penalty
D. When the rent-free period begins

questions.q_text: A lessee signs a lease with a non-cancellable period of 5 years. There is an option to extend for an additional 3 years, and the lessee is reasonably certain it will exercise this option. There is also an option to terminate after 2 years, but the lessee is reasonably certain it will not use this early-exit option. What is the lease term?
questions.answer: Build the term from the three pieces. First, the non-cancellable period is 5 years. Second, add the extension period only if the lessee is reasonably certain to extend, and here they are, so add 3 years, giving 8 years so far. Third, the termination option after 2 years would only reduce the term if the lessee were reasonably certain to use it, but here they are reasonably certain NOT to terminate early, so we do not subtract anything. The lease term is therefore 5 plus 3, which equals 8 years.

questions.q_text: When an entity assesses whether a lessee will exercise an extension option, what threshold does the standard require?
options: A. That it is merely possible the lessee might extend
B. That the lessee is reasonably certain to extend
C. That it is absolutely guaranteed the lessee will extend
D. That extending is more likely than not by a slim margin

questions.q_text: Suppose the rent during an extension period is much lower than the current market rate for similar assets. How does this affect the assessment of whether the lessee will extend?
options: A. It gives the lessee an economic incentive to extend, making extension more likely
B. It gives the lessee an incentive to terminate early
C. It has no bearing on the lease term judgment
D. It forces the lessee to buy the asset instead

questions.q_text: Why does the standard tell us to consider the lessee's past practice with similar leases when judging options?
options: A. Because past practice is legally binding on future decisions
B. Because a consistent history provides genuine evidence of what the lessee is likely to do
C. Because regulators require a minimum number of past leases to be reviewed
D. Because past practice replaces the need to look at economic incentives

questions.q_text: Explain why the judgment about extension and termination options is so important for lease accounting. What does it actually affect?
questions.answer: The judgment matters because it determines the expected length of the lease. The lease term in turn drives the size of two key figures: the lease liability and the right-of-use asset. If the lessee is reasonably certain to extend, the lease is treated as longer, which makes both the liability and the right-of-use asset larger (more future payments are included). If the lessee is reasonably certain to terminate early, the lease is treated as shorter, making both figures smaller. So the option assessment is not a side detail — it directly changes the amounts the entity records on its balance sheet, which is why the standard requires an honest reading of incentives and history at the commencement date.

questions.q_text: A lessee has a five-year lease with an option to terminate after year three. Terminating early triggers a very large penalty payment. How should the entity factor this penalty into its assessment, and what is the likely conclusion about the lease term?
questions.answer: The large termination penalty is an economic incentive that pushes the lessee away from exercising the termination option, because walking away early would cost a lot of money. When assessing whether the lessee is reasonably certain NOT to terminate early, this penalty is a strong relevant fact. Given the significant cost of leaving, the lessee has a real money reason to stay for the full term. The likely conclusion is that the lessee is reasonably certain not to terminate, so the lease term should be assessed as the full five years rather than three. The entity would therefore include all five years of payments when measuring the lease liability and right-of-use asset.

questions.q_text: On the commencement date of a lease, what two things does the company record in its books?
options: A. A right-of-use asset and a lease liability
B. Rental income and rental expense
C. The full ownership of the asset and a loan payable
D. A right-of-use asset and future profit

questions.q_text: Why does the company measure the lease liability at the present value of future payments rather than at their plain total?
options: A. Because the total is too difficult to calculate
B. Because money to be paid in the future is worth less than money today
C. Because the lease payments increase every year
D. Because the company owns the asset

questions.q_text: Which interest rate should a company use first when discounting its lease payments?
options: A. The lessee's incremental borrowing rate
B. The current market savings rate
C. The interest rate implicit in the lease, if it can be readily determined
D. The central bank's base rate

questions.q_text: What is meant by 'in-substance fixed payments' in a lease?
options: A. Payments that the company can choose to avoid
B. Payments that look like they may vary but are actually unavoidable
C. Payments made only at the end of the lease
D. Payments that are always optional bonuses

questions.q_text: A company rents a machine for three years. It does not own the machine. Explain why the company still records a right-of-use asset, and explain why it also records a lease liability.
questions.answer: First, the right-of-use asset: Even though the company does not own the machine, it has the right to use the machine for the three-year lease term. That right is valuable — it lets the company use the machine whenever it needs to during the lease. Since something valuable should appear on the books, the accounting rules require recording this right as an asset, measured at its cost. Second, the lease liability: The company has promised to make future lease payments over the three years. A promise to pay money in the future is a debt — something the company owes. So the company records a lease liability. This liability is measured at the present value of the lease payments that have not yet been paid by the commencement date, because future payments are worth less today and must be discounted. Together, the right-of-use asset captures what the company gets (the right to use), and the lease liability captures what the company owes (the future payments).

questions.q_text: Under the cost model for subsequent measurement of a right-of-use asset, what two things reduce the asset's value over time?
options: A. Depreciation and impairment
B. Revaluation and fair value gains
C. Interest and dividends
D. Inflation and currency changes

questions.q_text: When is a company allowed to use the revaluation model for its right-of-use asset?
options: A. Whenever the company prefers it
B. Only if the underlying asset belongs to a class the company already revalues under Ind AS 16
C. Only when the lease is longer than five years
D. Only when the asset's market value has fallen

questions.q_text: Which approach is considered the default, simple path for measuring a right-of-use asset after it is first recorded?
options: A. The revaluation model
B. The fair value model
C. The cost model
D. The impairment-only model

questions.q_text: Why does the rule require that revaluation only be used when the same asset class is already revalued elsewhere?
options: A. To make financial statements consistent and comparable
B. To reduce the amount of tax a company pays
C. To avoid recording any depreciation
D. To speed up the leasing process

questions.q_text: A company leases a building. It owns several similar buildings and chooses to revalue all of its owned buildings under Ind AS 16. Can the company measure the right-of-use asset for the leased building using the revaluation model? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: Yes, the company can use the revaluation model for the leased building's right-of-use asset. The rule states that the revaluation model is only permitted when the underlying asset belongs to a class of assets that the company already revalues under Ind AS 16. Here, the leased building is of the same kind as the buildings the company owns, and the company already revalues that class of owned buildings. Because the asset class is one the company treats with revaluation elsewhere, it is consistent and allowed to apply the revaluation model to the leased building's right-of-use asset. This consistency keeps the financial statements honest and comparable across owned and leased assets of the same type.

questions.q_text: Under the cost model, how is the carrying amount of a right-of-use asset calculated?
options: A. Cost plus accumulated depreciation plus accumulated impairment losses
B. Cost minus accumulated depreciation minus accumulated impairment losses
C. Cost minus accumulated depreciation plus remeasured lease liability
D. Fair value minus accumulated impairment losses

questions.q_text: When calculating accumulated depreciation on a right-of-use asset under the cost model, which standard's rules does the lessee follow?
options: A. Ind AS 36
B. Ind AS 16
C. Ind AS 116 only
D. Ind AS 109

questions.q_text: In general, when a lessee remeasures the lease liability, what happens to the right-of-use asset?
options: A. Nothing — the asset is never affected by liability changes
B. The asset is written off entirely
C. The carrying amount of the asset is adjusted to match the change
D. The asset is revalued to fair value

questions.q_text: A lessee remeasures the lease liability and the change would normally reduce the right-of-use asset. However, the asset's carrying amount is already zero. What should the lessee do?
options: A. Push the asset below zero to reflect the full change
B. Stop — the asset cannot go below zero, so no further reduction is made
C. Reverse prior depreciation to absorb the change
D. Adjust accumulated impairment instead

questions.q_text: A company leases a warehouse. Its lease liability is remeasured because of a variable lease payment that does not depend on any index or rate. Should the company adjust the carrying amount of its right-of-use asset for this change? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No, the company should not adjust the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset in this case. Normally, when a lease liability is remeasured, the lessee adjusts the right-of-use asset to keep the two connected. However, there are two exceptions to this rule. The second exception applies here: when the change in the lease liability relates to a variable lease payment that does not depend on an index or a rate. These particular variable payments are handled differently and do not flow into the asset's carrying amount. Therefore, this remeasurement does not ripple through to the asset — it is treated separately rather than adjusting the right-of-use asset's value.

questions.q_text: Why is it important to understand the cost model and its two exceptions when accounting for leased assets?
options: A. Because it is the only method any lessor can ever use
B. Because it shows how a leased asset's value rises and falls on the books and when changes in what you owe should — or should not — ripple through to the asset
C. Because it eliminates the need to record depreciation
D. Because it converts all leases into outright purchases

questions.q_text: After initial recognition, a lease liability is carried at what measurement basis?
options: A. Fair value through profit or loss
B. Amortised cost using the effective interest method
C. Historical cost without adjustment
D. The undiscounted total of future payments

questions.q_text: During a typical lease period, how does the carrying amount of the lease liability change?
options: A. It grows with interest and falls when a payment is made
B. It falls with interest and grows when a payment is made
C. It stays frozen until the lease ends
D. It only changes if the lease is modified

questions.q_text: A purchase option's exercise price is included in lease payments only when which condition is met?
options: A. The option is legally enforceable
B. The lessor approves the purchase
C. The company is reasonably certain it will exercise the option
D. The payment is variable rather than fixed

questions.q_text: When building up the cost of the related leased item, which of the following is subtracted rather than added?
options: A. Initial direct costs
B. Estimated dismantling and restoration costs
C. Lease payments already made
D. Lease incentives received

questions.q_text: Explain why a lease liability is described as a 'living number' and give two situations that would require it to be remeasured.
questions.answer: The lease liability is called a 'living number' because it does not stay fixed after initial recognition — it changes over time and in response to new information. First, in the ordinary course it grows each period as interest accrues under the effective interest method, and it shrinks each time a lease payment is made. Beyond these routine movements, the liability must also be remeasured whenever circumstances change. Two situations that trigger remeasurement are: (1) when the company reassesses its estimates — for example, becoming reasonably certain it will now exercise a purchase option or terminate early; and (2) when the lease is modified or the in-substance fixed payments are revised. In each case the carrying amount is recalculated so it reflects the new reality rather than the original assumptions, which is why the liability is never frozen.

questions.q_text: Several items — guaranteed residual value, purchase option exercise prices, and termination penalties — are only included in lease payments when they are 'reasonably certain.' Why does the standard impose this condition?
questions.answer: The 'reasonably certain' condition exists so that the liability reflects only amounts the company genuinely expects to pay. If accountants included every possible payment — every option that might be exercised or every penalty that might arise — the liability would be overstated and would not represent the company's true obligation. By requiring reasonable certainty, the standard keeps the measurement honest: it captures payments that are expected to actually occur while excluding speculative or unlikely ones. This protects the reliability and faithful representation of the financial statements, ensuring the recorded liability matches the economic reality of what the entity has truly committed to pay.

questions.q_text: Why does a lessee need to reassess its lease liability after the lease has already begun?
options: A. Because the rules require remeasurement every year regardless of circumstances
B. Because the facts assumed at the start may turn out to be different later, so the liability must reflect the new reality
C. Because the asset's market value always rises over time
D. Because the lessor demands an updated figure each reporting period

questions.q_text: A company decides it will keep a leased asset for longer than originally planned, changing the lease term. How should it remeasure the lease liability?
options: A. Discount the revised payments using the same original discount rate
B. Leave the liability unchanged until the lease ends
C. Discount the revised payments using a revised discount rate
D. Simply add the extra payments to the existing liability without discounting

questions.q_text: A lease's future payments rise because they are tied to an inflation index that has moved upward. Which discount rate is used to remeasure the liability?
options: A. A revised rate based on the implicit rate for the remaining term
B. The same discount rate already being used
C. The lessee's incremental borrowing rate on the reassessment date
D. A rate set by the lessor

questions.q_text: When a revised discount rate is needed, what rate does the lessee use first if it can be readily determined?
options: A. The lessee's incremental borrowing rate
B. The interest rate implicit in the lease for the remaining term
C. The original discount rate from the start of the lease
D. The current government bond rate

questions.q_text: For each of the following changes, state whether the lessee keeps the same discount rate or applies a revised discount rate: (1) a change in the lease term, (2) a change in the expected amount owed under a residual value guarantee, (3) a change in whether the purchase option will be exercised, and (4) a change in payments due to a movement in an index.
questions.answer:
Step 1: Recall the two groups. Group one involves changes to the nature of the lease — the lease term and the purchase option — and these require a revised discount rate because the timing and length of the deal have genuinely changed. Group two involves smaller, routine changes — residual value guarantee amounts and index- or rate-linked payment changes — and these keep the same discount rate because only the payment amounts changed, not the underlying shape of the lease.

Step 2: Apply to each item.
(1) Change in lease term — this changes the nature of the lease, so use a REVISED discount rate.
(2) Change in residual value guarantee amount — only the payment amount changes, so keep the SAME discount rate.
(3) Change in the purchase option decision — this changes the nature of the lease, so use a REVISED discount rate.
(4) Change in payments from an index movement — only the payment amount changes, so keep the SAME discount rate.

In all four cases the lessee remeasures the liability by discounting the revised payments; the only difference is whether the rate is revised or held constant.

questions.q_text: What is the underlying logic for keeping the same discount rate when only a residual value guarantee or index-linked payment changes?
options: A. The original rate is always the most accurate available
B. The underlying shape of the lease has not changed — only the payment amounts have — so there is no good reason to change the rate
C. Changing the rate is prohibited once a lease begins
D. The lessee has no way to determine a new rate

questions.q_text: Under the standard, when do you account for a lease modification as a separate lease?
options: A. Whenever the modification changes the lease payments in any way
B. Only when the modification increases the scope AND the extra payment matches the stand-alone price for that increase
C. Only when the modification decreases the scope of the lease
D. Whenever a new discount rate is available at the modification date

questions.q_text: When a lease modification decreases the scope of the lease, how is it accounted for?
options: A. As a separate lease with no change to the original lease
B. By increasing the right-of-use asset with no gain or loss
C. By reducing the right-of-use asset and recording a gain or loss for the proportionate decrease in scope
D. By leaving the lease liability unchanged and only adjusting the asset

questions.q_text: For a modification that is not a separate lease and does NOT decrease the scope, how is the difference handled after remeasuring the liability?
options: A. Recorded as a gain or loss in profit and loss
B. Recorded as a matching adjustment to the right-of-use asset with no gain or loss
C. Spread over the remaining lease term as interest
D. Ignored until the lease ends

questions.q_text: When a lease modification is not treated as a separate lease, which discount rate is used to remeasure the lease liability?
options: A. The original discount rate from the start of the lease
B. A fresh discount rate that fits the effective date of the modification
C. The market average rate over the whole lease term
D. Zero, since the liability is already known

questions.q_text: Explain why a decrease in scope triggers a gain or loss, while other non-separate modifications do not. Use the logic from the section.
questions.answer: A decrease in scope means you are giving back part of what you previously leased — in other words, you are partially or fully terminating the lease. When you walk away from part of a lease, you reduce the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset to reflect that you no longer have rights to that portion. Because part of the asset is being removed from the books, the reduction in the asset will not perfectly match the reduction in the liability, and that difference represents an economic outcome of giving something up. The standard recognizes this as a gain or loss proportionate to the decrease in scope. By contrast, for other modifications you are not giving anything back — you are changing terms or adding scope (when not a separate lease). In those cases the right-of-use asset is simply adjusted by the same amount as the change in the liability, acting as a balancing figure to keep the books consistent. Since nothing is being surrendered, there is no gain or loss — just a shift in the asset's value. The underlying logic is: surrendering rights creates an economic effect to recognize, while merely re-terming or expanding rights just rebalances the asset and liability.

questions.q_text: A company leases a building that it then sub-lets to others to earn rental income. Under Ind AS 116, where should the right-of-use asset for this building be presented on the balance sheet?
options: A. As a separate line item only
B. Inside investment property
C. Inside cash and cash equivalents
D. Inside the lease liability line

questions.q_text: In the statement of profit and loss, how must a lessee present the cost of a lease?
options: A. As a single combined rental expense
B. As depreciation on the right-of-use asset and interest expense on the lease liability, shown separately
C. Entirely as a finance cost
D. Entirely as depreciation

questions.q_text: Under the statement of cash flows, where do short-term lease payments and payments for low-value asset leases belong?
options: A. Financing activities
B. Investing activities
C. Operating activities
D. They are not shown in cash flows

questions.q_text: If a lessee chooses not to show the right-of-use asset as a separate line but instead folds it into the line item used for owned assets of the same kind, what additional obligation does this create?
options: A. They must reclassify it as investment property
B. They must disclose in the notes which line item the right-of-use asset is included in
C. They must show it under financing activities
D. They no longer need to record a lease liability

questions.q_text: A lessee makes a regular lease payment during the year that consists of a principal portion and an interest portion. Explain where each portion is presented in the statement of cash flows, and why this connects to the recurring theme of the section.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recognise that the periodic lease payment is made up of two parts — a principal portion (paying down what is owed) and an interest portion. Step 2: The principal portion is presented under financing activities, because it reduces the outstanding lease liability. Step 3: The interest portion is also presented under financing activities, following the rules in Ind AS 7, since it is treated as a finance cost. Step 4: Note that this is different from short-term lease payments, low-value asset lease payments, and unincluded variable lease payments, which all go under operating activities. Step 5: Connection to the theme — the section repeatedly splits a lease into a principal part and an interest part. This same split appears in the profit and loss statement (depreciation versus interest expense) and here in the cash flow statement, which is why recognising the pattern makes the whole topic clearer.

questions.q_text: What is the single most important idea that decides whether a lease is a finance lease or an operating lease?
options: A. Whether the contract is formally titled a finance lease
B. Whether substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership pass to the lessee
C. Whether the lessor is a bank or a leasing company
D. Whether the lease lasts longer than one year

questions.q_text: A contract is explicitly labelled an 'operating lease', but in reality ownership of the asset passes to the lessee at the end of the term and the lease covers nearly all the asset's economic life. How should it be classified?
options: A. As an operating lease, because that is what the contract is called
B. As a finance lease, because we judge by substance, not by form
C. It cannot be classified until the lease ends
D. As a finance lease only if both parties agree to relabel it

questions.q_text: Two years into a lease, the lessor revises their estimate of the asset's remaining useful life. Does this trigger a reclassification of the lease?
options: A. Yes, any change in estimate forces reclassification
B. Yes, because useful life is a finance lease indicator
C. No, classification is made at inception and only revisited on an actual lease modification
D. No, but only if the lessee agrees

questions.q_text: Which of the following best describes a 'bargain purchase option' that points toward a finance lease?
options: A. An option to buy the asset at its fair market value at the end of the lease
B. An option to renew the lease for a second period at market rent
C. An option to buy the asset for a price so low compared to fair value that the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise it
D. An option that lets the lessor reclaim the asset early

questions.q_text: A lease includes a clue often associated with a finance lease — the lessee can renew for a second period at a rent slightly below market. However, ownership clearly stays with the lessor, the lease covers only a small part of the asset's life, and the present value of payments is well below the asset's fair value. How should the lessor classify this lease, and why?
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall the test. Classification depends on whether substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership pass to the lessee. Step 2: Identify the clue. A below-market renewal option is one of the softer indicators that can lean toward a finance lease. Step 3: Weigh against the other features. Here ownership remains with the lessor, the lease covers only a small part of the asset's economic life, and the present value of payments is well below fair value — all signs the risks and rewards have NOT been transferred. Step 4: Apply the rule that clues aren't the final word. If other features make clear the risks and rewards stayed with the lessor, it remains an operating lease even though a clue suggested otherwise. Conclusion: This is an operating lease. The single soft indicator is outweighed by the substance of the arrangement, which keeps ownership risks and rewards with the lessor.

questions.q_text: After classifying a lease as an operating lease at inception, the lessee defaults on payments. What is the correct treatment of the lease classification?
options: A. It must be reclassified as a finance lease because of the default
B. The original classification stands, since default is not a lease modification
C. It is automatically cancelled and no longer classified
D. It must be reassessed at every reporting date going forward

questions.q_text: Under a finance lease, what happens to the underlying asset on the lessor's balance sheet?
options: A. It remains on the balance sheet and continues to be depreciated
B. It is derecognised and replaced with a lease receivable
C. It is revalued to fair value each year
D. It is moved to inventory until the lease ends

questions.q_text: In an operating lease, why does the lessor continue to record depreciation expense on the asset?
options: A. Because the lessee refuses to take ownership
B. Because the lessor still owns the asset and keeps it on its balance sheet
C. Because depreciation is required to offset the lease receivable
D. Because Ind AS 115 mandates it for all leases

questions.q_text: How does a lessor recognise income from a finance lease over the lease term?
options: A. On a straight-line basis with equal amounts each period
B. As finance income giving a constant periodic rate of return on the net investment
C. All at once when the lease is signed
D. Only when the lessee makes each payment, with no spreading

questions.q_text: Explain how a lessor initially measures the lease receivable in a finance lease. What components are included and how are they discounted?
questions.answer: The lease receivable is measured at an amount equal to the net investment in the lease. To compute this, the lessor takes the future lease payments plus any unguaranteed residual value the lessor expects to recover, and discounts all of these to present value using the interest rate implicit in the lease. The lease payments included in this calculation are: fixed payments less any lease incentives; variable payments that depend on an index or a rate; amounts expected to be paid under residual value guarantees; the exercise price of a purchase option if the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise it; and penalties for terminating the lease where the lease term reflects the lessee ending the lease. Discounting all of these at the implicit rate gives the present value, which is the amount at which the lease receivable is first recognised.

questions.q_text: When a manufacturer or dealer enters into a finance lease, how is it treated differently from a normal finance lease by an ordinary lessor?
options: A. It is treated as an operating lease instead
B. It is treated like a sale, recognising revenue, cost of sale, and a selling profit or loss
C. No finance income is ever recognised
D. The asset stays on the balance sheet and is depreciated

questions.q_text: What is the underlying reason a finance lease is accounted for so differently from an operating lease on the lessor's books?
options: A. Finance leases always involve larger amounts of money
B. In a finance lease, ownership has in substance passed to the lessee, so the lessor effectively holds a financial claim rather than an asset
C. Operating leases are not allowed under Ind AS 115
D. Finance leases never involve depreciation because assets do not wear out

questions.q_text: When a manufacturer-dealer lessor begins a lease, how is the revenue recognised at commencement determined?
options: A. The fair value of the underlying asset, always
B. The lower of the fair value of the asset or the present value of the lease payments discounted at a market rate
C. The higher of the fair value of the asset or the present value of the lease payments
D. The total of all lease payments without discounting

questions.q_text: Why does the cost of sale for a manufacturer-dealer lessor subtract the present value of the unguaranteed residual value?
options: A. Because that portion of the asset is expected to come back and isn't really being sold
B. Because residual values are taxed separately
C. Because it increases the selling profit artificially
D. Because the residual value is always zero

questions.q_text: When is the selling profit or loss on a manufacturer-dealer lease recognised?
options: A. Spread evenly over the lease term
B. Only when the asset physically returns to the lessor
C. At the commencement date, regardless of whether the asset is transferred as Ind AS 115 describes
D. At the end of the lease when net investment is settled

questions.q_text: After the lease begins and is treated as a finance lease, from which two sources does the lessor's finance income arise?
options: A. Variable usage payments and impairment reversals
B. Interest on the lease receivable and interest as the unguaranteed residual asset grows toward its expected value
C. The selling profit and the cost of sale
D. Fair value gains and tax credits

questions.q_text: A machine manufacturer leases a machine. The fair value of the machine is 1,000,000 and the present value of the lease payments at a market rate is 1,050,000. The machine's carrying amount is 700,000, and the present value of the unguaranteed residual value is 40,000. Calculate the revenue, cost of sale, and selling profit recognised at commencement.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Revenue: Revenue is the lower of the fair value of the asset (1,000,000) and the present value of the lease payments (1,050,000). The lower amount is 1,000,000, so revenue = 1,000,000. Step 2 — Cost of sale: Cost of sale equals the carrying amount of the asset minus the present value of the unguaranteed residual value, that is 700,000 minus 40,000 = 660,000. Step 3 — Selling profit: Selling profit equals revenue minus cost of sale, that is 1,000,000 minus 660,000 = 340,000. So the lessor recognises revenue of 1,000,000, cost of sale of 660,000, and a selling profit of 340,000 at the commencement date.

questions.q_text: If a finance lease is modified, the modification is not a separate lease, and after the change the lease would have been classified as an operating lease had the new terms existed at inception, how does the lessor account for it?
options: A. It continues the original finance lease unchanged
B. It treats the modification as a new lease from the effective date, measuring the asset using the net investment just before the change
C. It immediately writes off the entire net investment
D. It applies Ind AS 115 to derecognise the asset

questions.q_text: Why does a lessor provide lease disclosures in addition to the main financial statements?
options: A. Because the main statements are legally invalid without them
B. Because the main statements give headline numbers, and disclosures help readers understand how leases affect financial position, performance, and cash flows
C. Because disclosures replace the need for a balance sheet
D. Because disclosures lower the company's tax liability

questions.q_text: What is the key difference between a finance lease and an operating lease from the lessor's perspective?
options: A. A finance lease transfers most of the risks and rewards of ownership to the other party, while an operating lease keeps them with the lessor
B. A finance lease keeps the risks and rewards with the lessor, while an operating lease transfers them
C. A finance lease is always shorter than an operating lease
D. There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable

questions.q_text: In the maturity analysis, how must a lessor present the undiscounted lease payments they expect to receive?
options: A. As a single combined total for all future years
B. Discounted to present value year by year
C. Broken down year by year for at least the first five years, with a single total for everything beyond that
D. Only for the first year, with everything else lumped together

questions.q_text: Which of the following would a lessor disclose specifically for a finance lease?
options: A. Lease income from variable payments that do not depend on an index or rate
B. Finance income earned on the net investment in the lease
C. Only depreciation of the leased asset
D. The total of all operating lease income

questions.q_text: A lessor presents a maturity analysis of undiscounted lease payments and then reconciles them to the net investment in the lease. Explain what this reconciliation must point out and why it matters to a reader of the accounts.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall what the maturity analysis shows — the undiscounted lease payments the lessor expects to receive, broken down year by year for at least the first five years, with a single total for amounts beyond five years. Step 2: The lessor must then reconcile these undiscounted payments back to the net investment in the lease, which is the figure already sitting in the accounts. Step 3: This reconciliation must specifically point out two things: the unearned finance income and any unguaranteed residual value. These are the items that explain the gap between the raw undiscounted payments and the net investment figure. Step 4: Why it matters — it gives transparency. It tells readers not only how much money is coming in, but when it is coming, and how those future cash flows connect to the value already recorded in the financial statements. This helps users understand the timing and quality of the lessor's future cash inflows rather than just seeing a single carrying amount.

questions.q_text: A company rents a warehouse from its owner and then leases that same warehouse out to another business. What role does this company play in the sublease arrangement?
options: A. Head lessor
B. Intermediate lessor
C. Underlying owner
D. Sublessee tenant

questions.q_text: When classifying a sublease as either a finance lease or an operating lease, what does the intermediate lessor treat as the underlying asset?
options: A. The physical building or machine itself
B. The right-of-use asset arising from the head lease
C. The cash flows from the head lessor
D. The market value of the original asset

questions.q_text: Suppose the intermediate lessor cannot readily determine the interest rate implicit in the sublease. What rate should be used instead?
options: A. The current market borrowing rate
B. A rate of zero, since none can be determined
C. The discount rate used for the head lease, adjusted for initial direct costs of the sublease
D. The sublessee's own borrowing rate

questions.q_text: If the head lease was a short-term lease for which the company applied the short-term lease exemption, how must the resulting sublease be classified?
options: A. As a finance lease
B. As an operating lease
C. The company may choose either classification
D. The sublease cannot be recognized at all

questions.q_text: Explain why a sublease classification looks to the right-of-use asset rather than the physical asset, and describe how the nature of the head lease influences the sublease treatment.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recognize what the intermediate lessor actually holds. When the company signed its head lease, it did not purchase the physical building or machine — it only obtained the right to use that asset for the lease term. So what it controls is the right-of-use asset, not the underlying physical thing. Step 2: Understand what is passed along in the sublease. Because the intermediate lessor only ever held a right of use, the thing it transfers to the sublessee is that same right of use. It cannot pass along more than it has. Step 3: Apply the classification rule. For this reason, the standard instructs the intermediate lessor to treat the right-of-use asset as the underlying asset when deciding whether the sublease is a finance or operating lease — not the physical asset. Step 4: See how the head lease drives everything. The head lease shapes the sublease in several ways: the classification references the right-of-use asset from the head lease; the discount rate, if not readily determinable, defaults to the head lease's rate adjusted for initial direct costs; and if the head lease used the short-term exemption, the sublease must be classified as an operating lease. Conclusion: All key decisions in the sublease flow from the head lease, because the intermediate lessor's position is entirely derived from that original lease.

questions.q_text: In a sale and leaseback transaction, what do we call the party that sells the asset and then rents it back to keep using it?
options: A. Buyer-lessor
B. Seller-lessee
C. Buyer-lessee
D. Seller-lessor

questions.q_text: Which standard do we look to in order to decide whether the transfer of the asset truly qualifies as a sale?
options: A. Ind AS 109, on financial instruments
B. Ind AS 116, on leases
C. Ind AS 115, on revenue from contracts with customers
D. Ind AS 16, on property, plant and equipment

questions.q_text: If the transfer does NOT qualify as a sale, how does the seller-lessee account for the cash it received?
options: A. As a gain on disposal of the asset
B. As a financial liability under Ind AS 109, keeping the asset on its books
C. As a right-of-use asset only
D. As deferred revenue removed from the balance sheet

questions.q_text: When the transaction does qualify as a sale, how much of the gain does the seller-lessee recognize?
options: A. The full gain on the entire asset
B. No gain at all, since they still use the asset
C. Only the gain relating to the rights they transferred to the buyer
D. Only the gain relating to the rights they kept

questions.q_text: A company sells its building and leases it back. The deal is structured so the sale price and the rent are above market rates. Explain how this above-market difference should be treated, and why we make this adjustment.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recognize the issue. When the sale price or the rent in a sale and leaseback is not at fair value or market rates, the headline numbers don't reflect the real economics, so we must adjust them. Step 2: Identify the direction. Here the terms are ABOVE market, meaning the seller received more cash than the asset's fair value would justify. Step 3: Apply the rule. An above-market amount is treated as additional financing that the buyer-lessor is effectively providing to the seller-lessee. In other words, part of the excess cash is really a loan, not sale proceeds. (If instead the terms were below market, the difference would be treated as a prepayment of lease payments.) Step 4: Reason why. This adjustment keeps the accounting honest — it separates the genuine sale and lease economics from any embedded loan, so the gain or loss and the lease are not distorted by off-market pricing.

questions.q_text: If the transaction fails to qualify as a sale, what does the buyer-lessor record?
options: A. The purchased asset plus a lease receivable
B. Nothing at all
C. A financial asset equal to the amount it paid, and no asset
D. The asset at fair value with a gain

questions.q_text: A company rents a building from a landlord and then rents that same building out to another tenant. What do we call this company in the middle?
options: A. Head landlord
B. Intermediate lessor
C. Sub-lessee
D. Operating tenant

questions.q_text: When a company moves to Ind AS 116, which subleases must it take a fresh look at to decide their classification?
options: A. Every sublease that was previously a finance lease
B. Only subleases that have already ended
C. Subleases still running that were previously classified as operating leases
D. All head leases with the landlord

questions.q_text: Under the new standard, what does the intermediate lessor look at when reassessing a sublease's classification?
options: A. The building itself
B. Only the head lease terms
C. The right-of-use asset, using the remaining terms of both the head lease and the sublease
D. The original purchase price of the building

questions.q_text: A sublease was an operating lease under the old rules but now qualifies as a finance lease under Ind AS 116. How does the company treat it on transition?
options: A. As if it had always been a finance lease, reworking past numbers
B. As a new finance lease beginning on the date of initial application
C. It keeps it as an operating lease to avoid changes
D. It cancels the sublease and starts over with the tenant

questions.q_text: Explain why a sublease that was classified as an operating lease under Ind AS 17 might be reclassified as a finance lease under Ind AS 116.
questions.answer: Under the old standard, Ind AS 17, the intermediate lessor judged the sublease by looking at the underlying asset, the building itself, and many subleases fell into the operating lease bucket. Under the new standard, Ind AS 116, the company instead judges the sublease by reference to the right-of-use asset, that is, its own right to use the building, rather than the building itself. Because the asset being assessed is now the remaining right-of-use asset, the sublease often transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of that right-of-use asset to the tenant. When the company reassesses using the remaining terms and conditions of both the head lease and the sublease, the conclusion can shift from operating to finance. If it does shift, the company does not rework the past; it treats it as a brand new finance lease starting on the date of initial application, keeping the transition clean.

questions.q_text: When a company switches from the old leasing rules to the new Ind AS 116, what choice does the standard give them regarding the definition of a lease?
options: A. They must re-examine every contract using the new definition with no exceptions
B. They can either apply the new definition to all contracts, or choose not to reassess contracts not previously identified as leases
C. They must continue using the old Ind AS 17 definition permanently
D. They are forbidden from reassessing any contracts at all

questions.q_text: Why does the standard offer the option to not re-examine contracts that were already judged not to be leases under the old rules?
options: A. Because the new definition is identical to the old one
B. To save enormous effort and time during the transition so the switch isn't unfairly burdensome
C. Because old contracts are legally exempt from new accounting
D. To force companies into a single consistent approach

questions.q_text: Why is the definition of a lease described as the 'gateway question'?
options: A. Because it determines the interest rate used in lease calculations
B. Because you must first decide whether a contract is even a lease before applying any detailed lease accounting
C. Because it is the last step in lease accounting
D. Because it only applies to contracts signed after transition

questions.q_text: Is reassessing all contracts under the new definition something a company is forced to do?
options: A. Yes, every company must reassess all contracts
B. No, it is a choice the company makes, not something forced on them
C. Yes, but only for contracts identified as leases under the old rules
D. No, reassessment is never permitted under the new standard

questions.q_text: A company is transitioning to Ind AS 116. It has 500 old contracts. Under the old Ind AS 17 rules, 50 of these were identified as containing a lease, and 450 were judged not to contain a lease. The company wants to minimise its workload during transition. Explain which contracts it can choose to leave alone and why.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recognise the company's option. Under the transition rules, a company may choose not to re-examine the contracts that were NOT already identified as containing a lease under the old Ind AS 17 rules. Step 2: Identify those contracts. Here, 450 contracts were previously judged not to contain a lease. Step 3: Apply the shortcut. The company can choose to trust that earlier judgment and leave those 450 contracts alone, without redoing the full assessment under the new definition. Step 4: Conclusion. By taking this practical shortcut, the company avoids re-judging the 450 non-lease contracts, saving enormous effort. It only needs to carry forward its existing treatment, while still handling the 50 contracts already identified as leases. This relief is exactly why the standard offers the choice — so transition isn't unfairly burdensome.

questions.q_text: A company decides to apply the new lease definition to ALL of its contracts, including ones previously judged not to be leases. Is this allowed, and what is the tradeoff?
options: A. It is not allowed; the shortcut is mandatory
B. It is allowed; the tradeoff is more effort and time in exchange for thoroughness and consistency
C. It is allowed only if the company has fewer than 100 contracts
D. It is not allowed because the old judgments are legally binding

questions.q_text: Under which transition approach must the lessee present an extra, third balance sheet showing the earliest point?
options: A. The modified retrospective approach
B. The full retrospective approach
C. Both approaches require it
D. Neither approach requires it

questions.q_text: In the modified retrospective approach, how is the cumulative effect of applying the new standard handled?
options: A. It is spread evenly across all comparative periods
B. It is bundled into a single adjustment to equity at the date of initial application
C. It is recorded as profit in the current period
D. It is ignored until the lease ends

questions.q_text: Why do finance leases barely move during transition to the new standard?
options: A. Because they have no lease payments remaining
B. Because they were already on the balance sheet under the old rules and simply carry over their carrying amounts
C. Because they are always restated retrospectively
D. Because they are exempt from the new standard

questions.q_text: A lessee is transitioning to Ind AS 116. It previously had an operating lease with remaining lease payments still to be made. Explain how the lessee should measure the lease liability and what options it has for measuring the right-of-use asset.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the lease type. Since it was an operating lease, it was not previously on the balance sheet, so it must now be brought on. Step 2: Measure the lease liability. The lease liability equals the remaining lease payments, discounted using the lessee's incremental borrowing rate at the date of initial application. Step 3: Measure the right-of-use asset. The lessee has two options and may choose differently for each lease. Option one is to calculate the asset retrospectively using the same incremental borrowing rate. Option two is to set the asset equal to the lease liability, adjusted for any prepaid or accrued lease payments already recorded in the books. Step 4: Apply the chosen method consistently across all leases of that type.

questions.q_text: Why does the standard require a lessee to apply its chosen transition approach consistently across all of its leases?
options: A. To reduce the number of leases on the balance sheet
B. To ensure fairness and avoid distorting past numbers
C. To eliminate the need for an incremental borrowing rate
D. To convert all operating leases into finance leases

questions.q_text: One of the practical expedients lets a company apply a single discount rate instead of calculating one for each lease. To what can this single rate be applied?
options: A. A portfolio of leases that are reasonably similar to each other
B. Every lease the company holds, regardless of type
C. Only leases that end within twelve months
D. Only leases involving vehicles

questions.q_text: Instead of performing a full impairment review of a lease at the transition date, what shortcut does the standard allow?
options: A. Skip checking the lease value entirely
B. Rely on the earlier onerous lease assessment made under Ind AS 37 and adjust the right-of-use asset by any provision already set aside
C. Write the lease off completely
D. Use the discount rate to revalue the lease

questions.q_text: A company is adopting the new leasing standard on 1 April. One of its leases is set to expire on 15 December of that same year. How may the company treat this lease?
options: A. It must bring the full right-of-use asset onto the balance sheet
B. It must calculate a separate discount rate for it
C. It may treat it as a short-term lease and not bring it onto the balance sheet
D. It must perform a full impairment review on it

questions.q_text: The text stresses that these practical expedients are chosen on a lease-by-lease basis. What does this mean in practice?
options: A. The company must apply the same expedient to all its leases for consistency
B. The company can use a shortcut for one lease and choose not to use it for another
C. Each lease must use every available expedient
D. The choice must be made once for the whole portfolio and never changed

questions.q_text: Why is the company permitted to use hindsight, for example when deciding the lease term, under the modified retrospective approach?
options: A. Because the standard requires guessing future outcomes
B. Because the leases being measured already exist, so the company already knows how certain options and events actually turned out
