C. Because hindsight always lowers the lease liability
D. Because hindsight removes the need for a discount rate

questions.q_text: As a general rule, what does a lessor have to do when transitioning from the old standard to Ind AS one sixteen?
options: A. Reclassify all leases as finance leases
B. Make no adjustments on transition
C. Recognize all deferred gains immediately
D. Convert all assets into right-of-use assets

questions.q_text: Which two situations require special attention for a lessor on transition?
options: A. Finance leases and operating leases
B. Short-term leases and low-value leases
C. Subleases and sale-and-leaseback transactions
D. Off-market terms and depreciation adjustments

questions.q_text: What best describes a sale-and-leaseback transaction?
options: A. A company buys an asset and then sells it for profit
B. A company sells an asset and then immediately rents that same asset back to keep using it
C. A company rents an asset and then buys it at the end of the lease
D. A company leases an asset to two parties at once

questions.q_text: Under the old standard, if a sale-and-leaseback was treated as a finance lease and the seller made a profit on the sale, how is that profit handled on transition?
options: A. It is recognized all at once on the transition date
B. It is ignored entirely
C. It continues to be spread out gradually over the length of the lease
D. It is added to the right-of-use asset

questions.q_text: A company previously entered a sale-and-leaseback that was treated as an operating lease under the old standard, and the price was set at off-market terms. Explain how the seller-lessee should handle this on transition to Ind AS one sixteen.
questions.answer: Step one: Recognize that because the leaseback was classified as an operating lease, the seller-lessee accounts for it like any other operating lease that already exists on the transition date. Step two: Since there is an off-market element, an extra step is needed. The seller-lessee looks at the right-of-use asset, which represents the value of their right to use the building. Step three: They adjust that right-of-use asset for any deferred gains or losses arising from the off-market terms. Off-market means the rent or sale price was not at fair market value, so this adjustment corrects for that distortion and makes the accounting honest and accurate. The result is a right-of-use asset that properly reflects the deferred gains or losses carried forward.

questions.q_text: Why does transition to Ind AS one sixteen mostly leave lessor accounting unchanged while significantly affecting lessees?
options: A. Because the new standard primarily reshaped how lessees account for their right to use rented assets, leaving the lessor's accounting model largely as before
B. Because lessors do not own any assets
C. Because lessors never make a profit on leases
D. Because the new standard abolished all operating leases for both parties

questions.q_text: When a company first applies Ind AS 116 and had previously recognised a favourable lease as a separate asset from a business combination, what happens to the right-of-use asset?
options: A. It is increased by the amount of the favourable lease asset
B. It is decreased by the amount of the favourable lease asset
C. It is left unchanged and the favourable lease asset stays separate
D. It is written off entirely to profit or loss

questions.q_text: In the context of this transition rule, what does it mean to 'derecognise' the old favourable or unfavourable lease amount?
options: A. To revalue it to today's market rate
B. To take it off the books as a separate item
C. To transfer it to a reserve account
D. To disclose it only in the notes without removing it

questions.q_text: Why does Ind AS 116 fold the old favourable or unfavourable lease amount into the right-of-use asset rather than leaving it as a separate line item?
options: A. Because the favourable or unfavourable nature is now captured inside the right-of-use asset, avoiding double-counting
B. Because separate lease assets are illegal under Ind AS 103
C. Because the right-of-use asset must always equal the lease liability exactly
D. Because the favourable lease amount must be expensed immediately

questions.q_text: A company acquired a business several years ago, and as part of that acquisition it recognised an unfavourable lease liability of 200, because the acquired business was paying more than the market rate. The company is now first applying Ind AS 116 and recognises a right-of-use asset of 1,000 for that lease. Explain what the company should do with the unfavourable lease liability and what the resulting right-of-use asset value becomes.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the nature of the previously recognised amount. An unfavourable lease means the company pays more than the market rate, so it was recorded as a liability of 200 — a burden. Step 2: Apply the transition rule. On first applying Ind AS 116, the company derecognises this old unfavourable lease liability, taking the 200 off the books as a separate item. Step 3: Adjust the right-of-use asset by a corresponding amount. Because the lease is unfavourable (a burden), the right-of-use asset is reduced by the 200. Step 4: Calculate the new carrying amount. 1,000 minus 200 equals 800. So the right-of-use asset is now carried at 800, and the unfavourable nature of the lease is now captured inside that reduced right-of-use asset rather than as a separate liability.

questions.q_text: When does this rule about adjusting the right-of-use asset for previously recognised favourable or unfavourable lease amounts apply?
options: A. At the end of every reporting period
B. Only at the date the company first applies Ind AS 116
C. Every time a new business combination occurs after adopting Ind AS 116
D. Whenever the lease payments are revised

questions.q_text: Under the leasing standard, which type of right is specifically carved out and excluded from its scope?
options: A. Rights to lease office buildings used by the company
B. Leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources
C. Leases of water pipelines used in extraction
D. All leases lasting more than twenty-five years

questions.q_text: Entity X has a surface lease giving it the right to access the land containing the oil so it can drill a well. Does the leasing standard apply to this right?
options: A. Yes, because accessing land is always a lease
B. Yes, because it lasts more than one year
C. No, because it is tied to exploring for and extracting oil
D. No, because surface leases are never accounted for at all

questions.q_text: Why does the leasing standard apply to Entity X's right to lay water pipelines over land near the oilfield?
options: A. Because all pipeline arrangements are leases by definition
B. Because the right concerns transporting water that supports extraction, not exploring for or extracting the oil itself
C. Because water is a non-regenerative resource
D. Because the lease covers land, and all land leases are included

questions.q_text: Entity X holds three rights: (1) the right to explore for and use oil from an oilfield for twenty-five years; (2) a surface lease to access the land containing the oil to drill a well; (3) the right to lay water pipelines over neighbouring land to transport water used in extraction. For each, state whether the leasing standard applies, and explain why.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Recall the rule: The leasing standard applies to all leases EXCEPT leases to explore for or use minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources. Step 2 — Right 1 (explore for and use oil): This is directly about exploring for and extracting oil, so it falls within the exclusion. The leasing standard does NOT apply. Step 3 — Right 2 (surface lease to access land to drill): Although this is a land access right, its purpose is to reach the oil and drill a well, so it is tied to exploring for and extracting oil. It is also excluded. The leasing standard does NOT apply. Step 4 — Right 3 (water pipelines): This right is about transporting water that supports the extraction process — it is not itself a right to explore for or extract oil. It therefore does not fall within the exclusion. The leasing standard DOES apply. Conclusion: Rights 1 and 2 are excluded; only Right 3 is within the scope of the leasing standard.

questions.q_text: What is the underlying lesson about how to decide whether an oilfield-related right falls within the leasing standard?
options: A. Check whether the right lasts longer than twenty-five years
B. Check whether the right is truly about exploring for or extracting the oil itself, rather than merely supporting the surrounding work
C. Check whether the arrangement involves any payment of money
D. Check whether the right involves land or only equipment

questions.q_text: For an arrangement to qualify as a service concession arrangement under Appendix D of Ind AS 115, how many of the two key conditions must be met?
options: A. Only the first condition about controlling services and price
B. Only the second condition about leftover value
C. Both conditions must be met together
D. At least one of the two conditions

questions.q_text: In the Entity X case, what was the deciding factor that prevented the contract from being a service concession arrangement?
options: A. The contract only ran for ten years
B. The grantor did not control or cap the prices Entity X charged users
C. Entity X was a private company
D. Entity X had to upgrade the infrastructure

questions.q_text: Since the Entity X arrangement was not a service concession arrangement, what was the final conclusion about its accounting treatment?
options: A. It falls outside all standards
B. It falls within the scope of Ind AS 116 on leases
C. It must follow Appendix D of Ind AS 115 anyway
D. It is treated as a service contract only

questions.q_text: Why is it important to check the service concession exclusion before concluding a contract is a lease under Ind AS 116?
options: A. Because Ind AS 116 specifically excludes service concession arrangements covered by Appendix D of Ind AS 115
B. Because all public contracts are automatically leases
C. Because Ind AS 116 only applies to private companies
D. Because service concessions are never accounted for

questions.q_text: Suppose a different entity, Entity Y, signs a contract with a government grantor to operate a public toll road for fifteen years. The grantor sets a strict cap on the tolls Entity Y can charge and controls the road's value at the end of the term. Walk through whether this is a service concession arrangement and how it would be classified.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall the two conditions for a service concession arrangement under Appendix D of Ind AS 115. First, the grantor must control or regulate what services the operator provides, to whom, and at what price. Second, the grantor must control any significant residual value in the infrastructure at the end of the term. Both must be met. Step 2: Check the first condition. Here the grantor sets a strict cap on the tolls Entity Y can charge, so the grantor controls the price. This condition is met. Step 3: Check the second condition. The grantor controls the road's value at the end of the term, so the residual value condition is also met. Step 4: Since both conditions are satisfied, this contract IS a service concession arrangement. Conclusion: Because it qualifies as a service concession arrangement under Appendix D of Ind AS 115, it is excluded from the scope of Ind AS 116. This contrasts with the Entity X case, where the absence of price control caused the first condition to fail and pushed the arrangement back into Ind AS 116.

questions.q_text: According to this section, what is the single most important factor in deciding whether a contract counts as a lease under Ind AS 116?
options: A. Whether the customer pays for using the asset
B. Whether the customer controls the use of the asset
C. Whether the asset has a long useful life
D. Whether the asset is physically delivered to the customer

questions.q_text: In the rail arrangement described, who actually controls the use of the rolling stock during the fifteen-year concession period?
options: A. Operator X, because X uses the trains daily and pays for them
B. Entity Y, because Y owns the trains
C. Grantor G, because G sets the timetable, regulates pricing, and controls end-of-period use
D. The passengers, because they decide when to travel

questions.q_text: Under which framework does Operator X's arrangement ultimately fall, given that it is a service concession arrangement?
options: A. Ind AS 116 as a standalone lease
B. Appendix D of Ind AS 115
C. Ind AS 16 on property, plant and equipment
D. Neither, it falls outside all accounting standards

questions.q_text: Why does Appendix D of Ind AS 115 say the operator should NOT record the service concession infrastructure as its own property, plant, and equipment?
options: A. Because the infrastructure has too short a useful life
B. Because the operator does not have the right to control the use of that infrastructure
C. Because the operator does not pay for the infrastructure
D. Because the infrastructure is owned by the passengers

questions.q_text: Operator X pays Entity Y for the use of the rolling stock and uses the trains every day for fifteen years. Explain why this still does not make the contract a lease under Ind AS 116.
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall the key requirement for a lease under Ind AS 116 — the customer must control the use of the underlying asset. Control is the deciding word. Step 2: Examine what X actually has. X pays Entity Y and physically operates the trains daily, which makes it look like a lease. Step 3: But look at who directs how the trains are used during the concession period. Grantor G sets the timetable the trains must follow, G regulates the price X can charge passengers, and at the end of the period G can buy the rolling stock or decide how it is used. Step 4: Conclude that X is merely operating the trains on behalf of G, following G's rules — X does not control their use. Step 5: Because the overall service concession arrangement falls within Appendix D of Ind AS 115, and because X lacks the control a lease requires, the contract is treated within the Ind AS 115 framework rather than as a standalone lease under Ind AS 116. Paying for and using an asset is not enough; without control there is no lease.
